docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
ThePrototype is a collaborative 3D prototyping app that runs in your browser — sessions are peer-to-peer, and you need no account.

You build scenes from primitives, imported models and packs, wire behavior with a visual node graph, and everything you do is instantly visible to everyone connected to you.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Sessions are peer-to-peer. Your edits, objects, node graphs, voice and chat go straight from your browser to the people you are connected to (WebRTC). Servers do the jobs a browser cannot do alone; on theprototype.app they are ours:

  • Signaling introduces you to each other, and a TURN relay carries a session's encrypted traffic when two networks cannot reach each other directly (Connection).
  • Accounts and cloud saves — optional. Without signing in your scenes stay in your browser; signed in, you can keep cloud saves.
  • Assets — packs, skies and models download from our storage and the jsDelivr CDN (and are kept on your device afterwards).
  • Community pages — published scenes, play links, embeds and the gallery.
  • Anonymous error reports (on by default, one switch turns them off — Privacy) and anonymous aggregate counters, such as page views, with no cookies and nothing that identifies you.

The app is open source: a build pointed at your own signaling server, or fully self-hosted, involves none of our servers.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Open the app in a desktop browser (VR headset browsers work too).
  2. Create something — right-click the empty viewport and pick Add ▸ Mesh ▸ Cube. (If you prefer Shift+A for the Add menu, switch on Shift+A quick add in Settings ▸ Controls ▸ Keyboard & mouse.)
  3. Move it — click the cube to select it, then use the gizmo (1 move, 2 rotate, 3 scale).
  4. Invite a friend — open the Connect panel, copy your peer ID and send it to them. They paste it into their own Connect field and press Connect; you approve the request, and from then on you are editing the same scene together.

Tip

Everything replicates automatically: objects, transforms, materials, the node graph, chat, pings and voice. There is no "sync" button — if you can see it, your peers can too.

Install it as an app. theprototype.app is a web app you can install: your browser's Install app (or Add to Home screen on a phone) puts it on your desktop or home screen, and it opens in its own window without the browser's bars — on a phone that gives the scene the whole height of the screen.

Open source. The app itself is open source under the MIT licence: github.com/theprototype-app/core (also Settings ▸ About ▸ Source Code), with a contributing guide and an llms.txt for coding agents.

docs.title: What's new
docs.text:
1.53 — your tools, connected. Replace a model from a file and keep the object: its place, flows, physics and clips. Edit in Blender downloads the model, and the file you export comes back with Update ""?, wherever you drop it; Chrome and Edge can watch the file and reload on each save. A 100×, Z-up or unapplied export gets a one-click fix. Settings ▸ Tools & connections replaces Settings ▸ AI: one page for chat and mesh providers, voice typing, agents and desktop tools, each with a status and a Test. Skies download the first time you pick one, so the app download is about 6 MB smaller. See Edit in Blender and Tools & connections.

1.52 — sessions in your Explorer. Joining a session shows the host's files as "'s session" in your Explorer, read-only, above your Library: open them, copy them, and Save on host if you can edit. Nothing downloads until you open or copy it, and hosts choose what guests see. Save project now asks about unsaved changes and opens where you left off. On claude.ai, Claude can use physics in your tab, see where you stand, and join a session from a link once you confirm. See A session you joined and Claude connector.

1.51 — characters and motion. Any rigged model is a character, and any clip plays on any humanoid. Clips are small .tpanim files of their own (VRM Animation inside), so they reach your peers once and the model never changes. Free CC0 packs bring 10 characters and 87 motions; VRM avatars arrive with spring bones and expressions. The one-click Locomotion preset makes a character walk, run and jump under the Player controller; trim, split, join, In place and Loop it make clips game-ready. Skeleton… fixes bones and weights, Download… gives you a GLB with every clip for Blender, Unity, Unreal or Godot, and licences that ask for something warn you before you share (Characters and motion).

1.50 — talk to your agent. The AI assistant window lists the AI agents in your session next to your own assistant: pick one and chat, and everyone sees the conversation, the replies as they stream in and every step between them. Claude Code listens after one sentence in its terminal ("listen to my theprototype session"), and what you type there shows "via terminal". Stop cancels what it is doing, the host can mute it, and viewers can ask but it will not change the scene for them. Send it pictures — shrunk and stripped of location data on your device — and agents can bring in GLB models (import_model) and images, sprite sheets and clips (import_file) from their own machine. Every chat is a .tpchat file in Explorer ▸ Scene ▸ chats, saved with the scene and private unless you include it when publishing. In VR the AI panel talks to the same agent (Talk to your agent; recipes: img2threejs, Pixling).

1.48.1 — fixes for AI agents and game logic. Reloading the page while joined takes you straight back into the session, with no new approval. A deleted object's logic stops (undo brings it back), a game round keeps its referee when someone joins, and a shared Set Variable changes once per event in multiplayer. Agents read the scene the way you see it: positions inside a group are local to the group, list_scene shows a shape's sizes and can be narrowed, and a locked object says who has it. Also fixed: every light type survives an autosave restore, Body Wave and Jiggle stack on one object, HUD Text and Bar show wired text, a behaviour's on.load sees the scene a joiner lands in, deleted lights and avatar photos free their memory, and a phone in the background keeps its link for a minute.

1.48 — AI agents in your session. Send Claude (or any MCP agent) your session link and build together: claude mcp add theprototype -- npx -y @theprototype/agent mcp '<link>' and it joins as a peer, builds with the app's own tools — objects, flow nodes, physics — checks its work with screenshots, and lists every step in the AI assistant window for everyone to select or undo (Build with an AI agent). Connect ▸ Request AI makes invite links for agents and people: View or Edit, 10 minutes to a day, one or more uses, revocable, no approval card. Right-click anyone in the Connected panel for the new peer menu — profile, Go to, Hide — and, for the host or an admin, Remove or Remove and block with Allow back.

1.47 — game logic in the headset. Radial ▸ Tools ▸ Logic opens the node graph as a panel in VR: move cards, wire sockets with the laser and set values on a wrist pad, and everyone sees it live — see Logic in the headset. An Android phone can now join a room the headsets calibrated with two taps on the floor and see the scene where they do, and an unfolded phone's Play menu offers the AR table and Join the room.

1.46 — every panel in its own window. Pop out any panel — or a whole dock — into its own browser window and spread the editor over two monitors: the Explorer on one screen, the Node editor and Timeline on another, the 3D view full-size in the app. Drag tabs between windows and docks; a panel lives in one place, and your windows come back on the next visit (Windows on several monitors). The Code tab now makes, renames, moves and deletes files and folders itself — a new script opens from a behaviour template. Also: renaming a shared file reaches everyone, and saving a shared file no longer leaves a copy of its old version in the Library.

1.45 — build in the headset. Everything you need to build a scene now works in VR — see Building in VR. Both grips shrink the world to a 1:50 miniature to work from above (Back to 1:1 on the radial), Tools ▸ Measure snaps points to corners with the laser, Selected ▸ Arrange aligns, spaces and drops a selection, the Sculpt ring gains terrain Paint and the Scatter brushes, and Add ▸ Assets opens an Asset Browser on your wrist with the drag-to-place ghost on your laser. With hand tracking a pinch browses and places. Also: On Impact fires on a hit from any side (new From option; old scenes keep landings only), Rotate / Motor nodes spin up from rest and an auto-starting HUD Timer counts its full time, six nodes show the sockets they read, and the profile button opens with Enter or Space. Someone who joined your room keeps their role after a network or signaling blip — they used to come back View-only (connection drops).

1.44 — quick wins. Play here starts Play where your camera is (Ctrl+Shift+Enter) and Stop puts the camera back. Drop an image on the viewport for a see-through reference image to trace over — hidden in Play, never exported. With the app installed, share files into it from your phone or open a .tpscene from your desktop. Paste a scene link into Notion or WordPress and it plays in place (oEmbed). Movement stays smooth on a lossy connection, and packs and skies are kept on your device. Also: people who drop out leave the Users list on their own, a guest who joins automatically is announced with Remove, rooms and people can be reported, and the AI assistant's objects stay put in Play unless you ask for physics.

1.43.1 — security fix. Code that travels in a scene — Script nodes, Behaviour files, a Character Controller's Player code and Custom (code) HUD elements — now runs in a sandbox with no access to the page, your keys, your sign-in or the network. Built apps ship a Content-Security-Policy (self-hosting), invite links that name another signaling server ask first, and on theprototype.app play links and embeds open from play.theprototype.app. Advisory: GHSA-r74q-9hg7-wrgr.

1.43 — scatter everywhere. Scatter works on any object now, not just terrains — moss on a rock, barnacles on a ship — and moves with it. A set can fill by count or density with a minimum spacing and slope, height or painted-layer masks, mix models by weight with tint and sink, and draw pack items, prefabs (their look) or any object you pick. Edit instances with Rotate, Scale, Relax and a Select tool with a gizmo, and convert both ways — a prefab comes back with its logic. Everyone gets the same layout from a seed + your edits, while far scatter thins to each device's budget.

1.42 — together and anywhere. Open the same code as someone in your session and you type into one text together: two people in one line both keep their typing, everyone's cursor and selection show in their colour, an Editing with you strip names who is where, a late joiner sees the unsaved text, and Ctrl+S saves as before. Explorer text documents open in the Code tab and are shared the same way. Pop out puts the code editor in its own window for a second monitor; Dock back returns it. On an Android phone, AR table puts your scene on a real table through the camera — tap to place, pinch and twist, then Play. Also: checkpoint pictures show the scene without gizmos, and very large scenes skip automatic checkpoints.

1.41 — accessibility. A new Accessibility page in Settings: a UI scale from 90 to 150 % (every panel and the phone layout; the 3D view keeps its full resolution), Motion (Follow system / Reduce / Full) and Show captions. High contrast is a real theme now — text at 7:1, a thick selection outline and bigger handles — and status colours are colour-blind safe in every theme, each with a shape. The whole editor works from the keyboard (a skip link, focus rings, arrow keys in toolbars, F6 between regions, Esc out of everything) and with a screen reader (toasts read aloud, selection says name and kind, the object list is a tree). Every game gets a player Accessibility menu — captions, a colour-blind filter, HUD text size and remappable controls — and VR has a Low / High comfort vignette, Recenter for seated play and One-handed mode: see Making your game accessible.

1.40 — physics and water. A fast, small body can have continuous collision of its own (Properties ▸ Physics ▸ Continuous collision), so a bullet or a thrown ball never passes through a thin wall. On Impact also fires on the static or kinematic object that was hit — a pressure plate, a target, a moving platform — with other = the body that landed. A fluid tank's pour joins the pool it lands in and ripples it, and tanks can run on the graphics card: GPU fluid (Settings ▸ Scene ▸ Performance) measures your device once and uses WebGPU only where it is clearly faster. Also: a View only joiner sees the room's HUD, shader graphs, animation and look at once (Joining), 3D labels and VR panel text work offline, error reports strip server names and IP addresses (Privacy), and the Pool party toys float like foam.

1.39 — logic you can see. The Node Graph Debugger pauses your game when an event reaches a node with a breakpoint (F9), steps event by event (F10), shows the live value on every wire and keeps a watch list — all local to you, while the other players keep playing. The Timeline lays camera shots (with a glide between two cameras), animation clips, sounds and events into a sequence that the Play Sequence node or Autoplay starts — in exported games too — and On Sequence Event wires back into your graph. Measurements are now kept in the scene: in the object list, shared and saved, and Tab edits their points. Scattered rocks and trees can be solid for every player. The app sends anonymous error reports — no account, no IP, no scene content; Settings ▸ Privacy turns them off — and status.theprototype.app says whether the service is up. Also: the budget chip moves and hides in Edit positions, large CC0 materials reach every peer, Settings ▸ About ▸ Third-party licences lists every library the app uses, small models skip the optimizer, Statistics groups with other windows and a floating window drops into a split dock pane.

1.38 — build precisely. Measure snaps to corners, edges and faces, chains segments with a running total and the angle between them, and pins dimension labels only you see; Align, Distribute and Drop to ground line up a selection from the Properties Arrange section or the object menu's Transform ▸, one undo each. The Asset Browser brings free CC0 models, skies and textures from Poly Haven and materials from ambientCG into your Library, sky and material presets — every asset keeps its credit. And a Terrain can be painted with four texture layers and scattered with trees, rocks or any Library model.

1.37 — fast on every device. Big models are optimized as they come in: over 50k triangles or with a texture over 2048 px, an import gets a level-of-detail chain and its textures are resized and GPU-compressed (KTX2/Basis — about an eighth of the texture memory on a Quest), while the original stays in the Library and the toast offers Keep original only. Settings ▸ Import holds the defaults, a file's Properties has its own Import settings and Reimport, and Configure Scene ▸ Level of detail sets one LOD distance for the whole scene. Exports get Optimize for: For Quest / web — a GLTF becomes a compact .glb, a Scene keeps its format with compressed textures and LOD chains. A budget chip beside the toolbar says whether the scene fits a Quest, a phone or a desktop, and Statistics ▸ Budget lists the heaviest objects with what optimizing them would save. HEIC / HEIF photos import as images and textures, and Race keeps its shadows in VR — inside the Quest budget.

1.36 — your 1.35 review. Right-click the Connect bar — or press and hold it on a touch screen — for Move, Pin to top row / Float, Reset position and Reset all, in or out of Edit positions; a moved Connect bar stays where you put it. The buttons beside the logo, hidden by default on a computer, come back from Edit positions: their menu's Show cluster turns them on and their grip moves them like every other cluster. When a sidebar is pinned, unpinned or closed, the logo, the buttons beside it, the corner buttons, the profile and the Connect bar jump to their new place at once instead of sliding, and the profile menu opens under the profile button wherever it is. Hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) while dragging a floating window to place it without docking — over a sidebar or the dock; docking stays the default, and on touch a docked tab's Undock into a floating window takes a window out. Fixed: switching dock tabs no longer flashes a docked Statistics, Objects, Chat or AI assistant window full screen for a frame, and the empty dock's tab strip no longer shows a sliver of a tab bar left of its +. Under the hood: the open security alerts are cleared, Node is pinned, and every release ships an SBOM.

1.35 — your 1.34 review. A floating window now moves by any empty part of it, not only its header, and docks by drag — onto the dock's tab strip, the bottom edge or either sidebar, with the mouse and on an unfolded phone by touch; right-click (or press and hold) its header or a group tab for the window menu: Dock to bottom, Move to the left / right sidebar, Float, Group with…, Bring to front, Reset size, Close. T opens an empty dock that takes a drop, and every + lists every window: one that is already open is ticked, says where it is and comes to the front there — no second copy — and Ctrl- or Shift-click picks several. Sidebars get a + too, stay open when you empty them, and Ctrl+B / Ctrl+Alt+B show and hide the left and right sidebar with their tabs kept open. The dock splits side by side: Split puts two windows in one A / B tab with a draggable divider, and splits are remembered. Every docked window — Statistics, Chat and the AI assistant too — stops at a Full-height sidebar. Edit positions arranges every button cluster — the toolbar, both corner stacks, the buttons beside the logo, the top-right group and the Connect bar: drag one anywhere, it snaps and never overlaps, and Rotate to vertical stands the toolbar on the left edge; Move toolbar works by touch. The Connect bar is Pinned or Float, and a floating one with no room turns compact. In focus mode a Viewport button beside Exit focus shows or hides the 3D preview, and the choice is remembered; Settings no longer closes your sidebars or docked windows. Fixed: a Profiler selection counts exactly the frames you picked, an invite link to a server that cannot be reached puts you back online on your previous server, a big scene no longer stalls a phone while it opens, and repeated lines in Copy diagnostics are counted (×N).

1.34 — your 1.33 review. Right-click any value in Properties or Configure Scene (press and hold on a touch screen) to copy, paste or reset it — one number, a whole vector or just its X, Y or Z, a colour, a choice, or a whole section from its header (also Copy as JSON); Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V over a field skips the menu, a section pastes to every selected object, and every paste is one undo. It is plain text, so 1, 2, 3, Vector3(1, 2, 3), #ff8800 and JSON all paste back. Sidebar tabs get an ×, a right-click menu and sideways scrolling; drag a tab into the 3D view to float it, onto the dock or onto the other side, with every drop highlighted first. Any window — Node editor, Code, Explorer, Statistics… — can live in a sidebar, with no second header, and the header lock sits beside Full height. Toolbar buttons that do not fit fold into a » menu and come back by themselves; a right-click anywhere on the toolbar opens its menu; the … button and the Connect bar can be hidden, and the Connect bar takes its own row only when the top is full. The toolbar keeps clear of full-height sidebars, and with a mouse Edit positions arranges the row beside the logo too. Focus mode on a docked window now fills the whole window while the sidebars step aside, and the 3D view stays with you as a live, resizable picture-in-picture you can orbit, select in and transform with W / E / R. The camera preview resizes too. On a phone Statistics is a dock tab, and the tip in More goes away once you have arranged the bar (Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Reset tips brings it back).

1.33 — your 1.32 review. On a computer each side of the screen has one sidebar, and Configure Scene, Properties, Objects and any window you dock to an edge are its tabs — opening one brings its tab forward instead of a second column. Drag a tab to the other side to dock it there, and the ↕ button runs a sidebar from the top edge to the bottom. A lock in the Properties and Configure Scene headers lets the name and Filter properties scroll away. On a phone you arrange the bottom bar from More: press and hold any item and drag it onto the bar, along it or off it — Play too — up to seven items, with Inspect, Move, Rotate, Scale, Statistics, Tools & View and Focus mode all placeable, and Show switches for the selection toolbar, the dock's tab row and the grab handle; Edit bar… is gone and a 1.32 bar carries over. Every floating window docks by dropping it on the dock's tab row — Objects, Statistics, the Live profiler, Chat and the AI assistant too — and floating windows can overlap the dock. Focus mode (Ctrl+Space) gives the screen to the 3D view or to the docked window under the pointer; Esc brings everything back. Edit positions now reaches the top-right icons and the touch tools, with up to four buttons a corner; Lift corner buttons above docked panels joins the toolbar's menu, and workspace layouts keep the toolbar — the desktop one and the phone bar separately. Configure Scene starts with a Quality preset (Auto / High / Medium / Low, this device), the auto-quality notice is one card instead of a stack, the unsaved-scene notice no longer flickers while a peer edits, and Save options open full screen on a phone.

1.32 — your 1.31 review, fixed. On a phone every sheet has one grab bar: drag it to resize the sheet, swipe it down to close it, and no sheet covers Play. Customize character and Profile settings open again from the profile menu, and in the Explorer you press and hold a file or folder for its actions. Docked windows close from their tab; Undock sits beside Minimize the dock (Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Windows & chrome ▸ Undock button can take every tab out as one window), a floating window with tabs can Dock all tabs, a tab dragged onto a floating window joins it, and the phone's + opens a Windows sheet. Long names stay on one line, and Layouts is a regular dialog (a dock tab on a phone). Automatic quality no longer switches water refraction and the rest off and on, and says what it lowered once, with Keep full quality. A big photo now becomes a texture instead of being refused, and the new Image editor crops, rotates, resizes and adjusts a picture and updates its textures for everyone. Templates ▸ Examples ▸ Aquarium is a reef from the new Aquarium Kit, swimming with four new motion nodes — Follow Path, Wander, Orient to Velocity and Body Wave — with a Fish scales preset. LOD groups no longer stay on their first level in scenes with water.

…and from your review of the 1.32 preview. Right-click (or press and hold) a toolbar button ▸ Edit positions to drag the toolbar and corner buttons into place — − removes, + adds, ✓ applies. On a phone the selection toolbar's Inspect opens and closes the properties, a tap on a selected object deselects it, adding an object no longer opens the properties, and Interact gives your selection back when you leave it and carries things from the point you grabbed. Phone sheets pull down to close from their list, the main menu closes on a press outside it, and a note steps through all the notes. Tabbed windows drag by touch, and on a computer you can drop a window onto the dock's tab bar exactly where you want it; the dock's + lists every window, the Image editor included. Customize character opens a studio around your character, and Surprise me deals a new look on every press. Dialogs cover the whole screen, and questions — Delete flow, Restore previous session? — are dialogs instead of toasts. The connection pill shows a coloured dot, and reconnecting after a tab switch no longer toasts. The node editor has a one-line breadcrumb bar, and the Profiler a Details and Settings sidebar and a resizable split. And from the second look at the preview:

  • On a phone, Properties, Objects, Notes, Configure Scene and Layouts are tabs of the bottom dock beside the Explorer, instead of drawers behind it. Inspect brings Properties to the front, nothing covers Play, and unfolding the phone puts each panel back in its sidebar or window — folding brings the tabs back.
  • Tapping the bottom-bar button of the view on screen minimizes the dock; the main menu closes as Configure Scene opens on a phone (on a computer it stays open).
  • More can come off the phone's bottom bar, and Play can move along it. Play starts as plain Play on a phone; pick VR or AR from its press-and-hold menu and its icon follows.
  • The selection toolbar follows a sheet as you resize it, without lagging behind, and the profile sheet no longer repeats your picture.
  • The phone's Connect chip says Connected, Connecting… or Offline beside the dot when there is room.
  • The peers panel is wider, one row per person; on a phone it is a sheet like the notifications.
  • The main menu's Project section has a compact two-column layout — New from template…, Load | Save ▾, Import | Export… — and ▾ opens one Save options dialog. A phone keeps the list; Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Project actions switches.
  • Settings rows keep a switch, a short list, a colour or a button beside their name again, and stack only what cannot fit.
  • Modules on a phone keep their buttons to the right and expand a long description on a tap. In Browse, install several at once: each card says Installing… until it is done, and a failed one says why with Retry.

1.31 — drag to place. Drag any object from Explorer ▸ Packs or ▸ Library onto the viewport and a ghost shows where it will land and how big it is — width × depth × height in metres beside the pointer, the real model when it is already loaded and light enough, its box otherwise. R or the wheel turns it, Alt drops it at the camera's focus, Esc or dropping back on the Explorer places nothing, and a drop is one undo step that everyone sees. On a phone, press and hold a card to drag it. Settings ▸ Scene ▸ Performance ▸ Placement preview picks how detailed the ghost may be. Packs mark what is downloaded, and a pack item's Delete is now Delete cache — the item stays in the pack.

1.30 — a calm new look, on a desk and in a pocket. Every window, menu, dialog, the main HUD and the phone layout now share one interface: one window header and one tab strip, one menu style with a shorter object menu (rare actions one level down, nothing removed), calmer dialogs, and one accent colour — blue for what you can act on, orange only for Play and live states. The HUD is one glass toolbar, the Connect bar collapses to a chip once you are connected, toasts stack three at a time, and Ctrl+K opens a command palette over every tool, window, menu and setting. While you play a small banner says how to stop (a scene can hide it or use its own words). Customize character is a resizable drawer that puts your view back exactly. On a phone, a decluttered layout keeps the logo, a Connect chip and a bottom bar you can rearrange — Add · Objects · Play · Explorer · More — with windows as bottom sheets that remember their height. Light and custom themes restyle everything. Every shortcut, setting, scrub field and panel works as before.

1.29 — groundwork for cloud saves and kept rooms. Under the hood, the app can now tell the theprototype.app cloud plugin when the scene changes, fingerprint what is in it, and hand over or open a whole project — what cloud saves and rooms that stay open when everyone leaves are built on. They switch on on theprototype.app separately; the open-source app is unchanged. Plugin authors: the new calls are in the module SDK.

1.28 — VR + mesh: sculpt and snap the world from the headset, polyline knife, live symmetry, smart unwrap. In a headset, radial menu ▸ Add ▸ Terrain drops a terrain in front of you and you sculpt it with the trigger — Raise, Lower, Smooth and Flatten, the brush sized and weighted on the thumbstick. Grabbing the world with both grips now turns it in 15° steps and sticks at 1×, 2×, 5× and 10× (World grab snapping, on by default), Scene ▸ Dollhouse shows the scene as a model on a table so you can point into it and stand anywhere, and Add ▸ Architecture ▸ has the desktop's twelve walls, doors, windows and stairs. In Edit Mesh the knife cuts along a polyline — Shift+click for each corner, Enter to finish — and live symmetry mirrors every edit across X, Y or Z as you make it, in one undo step. The new Smart unwrap (xatlas) module adds Unwrap ▸ Smart (xatlas) to the UV editor: automatic seams, packed with no overlaps.

1.27 — world + nodes: sky images, architecture, smarter nodes, particles that trail. A sky image (an HDRI) can now be the scene's sky and its light: objects take its colours, shiny ones reflect it, water mirrors its clouds and the sun sits where the photo's sun is. Pick Clear sky, Meadow, Sunrise, Starlight or Photo studio, or upload your own .hdr / .exr, with Rotation, Image light, Sky blur and Tone mapping, and a quality setting for headsets. Add ▸ Architecture builds walls with doorways and windows, doors and casement windows that open in Interact and Play for everyone, and straight, L, U and spiral stairs, every number editable in the Inspector. Math and Gate take up to eight inputs, the Switcher passes on the value wired into the selected item, and the new Camera Rig node makes a camera object follow or watch something. Particles can be drawn as streaks, trails or a ribbon and inherit the emitter's speed, with new Ribbon trail and Magic wisps presets. Duplicating both ends of a joint copies the joint, and detaching one during a run breaks it with sparks. The Drivable Car steers with its front wheels, Blocks drops a hundred blocks in one draw call, and modules get angle motors, joint limits and their own physics world. Every number field is one undo step per drag or typed edit, Esc cancels typing, and on theprototype.app What's New opens with the cloud's own news.

1.26 — editor productivity: edit many at once, prefabs that update, material presets, a new Settings. With several objects selected, the Inspector edits them all: rows that differ show a dash, setting one sets every object, and one Ctrl+Z puts each back to its own value — lights and the visibility and shadow flags included. The pivot point (Median, Active, Individual, Parent) has a toolbar button, in VR a grip carries the whole selection, and dragging a selection in the object list drops it into a group or under a parent. Placed prefab copies stay linked: editing the prefab offers to update every copy, each keeping its own changes, in one undo step for everyone; copies carry their flow graphs, and the Prefabs tab gets folders and tags. Material presets put Wood, Metal, Plastic, Glass, Stone, Rubber and Neon one click away in the Inspector, and you can save, import and share your own. Settings is redesigned — a grouped menu, sub-pages with a breadcrumb, search that shows where each match lives, a reset per category, About ▸ Danger zone and a Compact density. Also new: workspace layouts (Menu ▸ Layouts), chat with @mentions, emoji shortcodes, an unread badge and history for people who join, threaded replies on notes, Report a problem with a picture you can mark up, an Undo toast after Clear scene, Delete, removing a module and resetting settings, and Z to cycle the render mode. Race plays on a phone with pedals and in VR from the driver's seat, and modules get pointer, camera, play-mode and VR-seat hooks. Characters stand on the floor with planted feet, an idle one gets knocked off (stars, a woozy sway, star eyes), and flying in Play is opt-in per game — a scene can also remove it.

1.25 — your feedback, fixed: panels that keep their keys, water that behaves. Keys follow the panel you are in: WASD no longer fly the camera from the Explorer, the Inspector, a node's graph view, the HUD editor or any tool window, the panel with the keys shows an outline, the object list keeps Delete / F / Ctrl+D, and sliders in nodes never drag the graph. The code workspace gains sidebars — Open editors and a searchable Project tree (Ctrl+B); Outline, Problems, Bound nodes and Find in files (Ctrl+Alt+B, Ctrl+Shift+F) — plus a scrolling tab strip, Ctrl+P quick open, Ctrl+Shift+O go to symbol and a guard before closing unsaved code, and a game's Player has code you can open and save. The node editor opens with the whole graph in view, or where you left it (saved with the scene); Tidy graph (L, Shift+L) lays a graph out in one undo step, and every game's Main graph is tidied. A click now selects what is inside or behind water, Alt+click cycles everything under the cursor, and ping moved to Ctrl+Alt+click; opening a scene while another is loading always gives you the newest one. Things under water rise or sink by their density, every water setting works on every preset, scenes can start their simulation on load with one Reset / Pause for everything, and water gains visible bubble emitters, pour emitters, spilling fluid tanks and a lighter look on phones that still bends the light. New: Fluids — Add ▸ Water ▸ Fluid pours real particle water, Flow path makes rivers, chutes and pipes, the Rotate / Motor and Float Along Flow nodes turn wheels and float boats, and the Water works example runs a closed water loop. Also fixed: an old game scene with two modules no longer opens with its two Code link cards on top of each other, and particle fluid no longer tunnels through thin walls under pressure.

1.24 — characters that walk, a race, and your games' stats. Everyone in a session is now a rigged character — nine CC0 KayKit adventurers and skeletons that walk, run, strafe and jump with their camera and reach for their VR controllers — and Customize Character (profile menu) is a side panel with a live preview on yourself: body, head (the character's own, a stylised one or your photo), hat, outfit colour and your ping; the classic floating head is one click away. Templates ▸ Games has a new game, Race: up to four players, three laps round a valley, with laps, speed and grip on the Race rules node and a road you reshape by moving its points. Edit Mesh gains slide edges, fill holes (F), connect (J) and dissolve vertices, solidify and separate, mitered bevel corners and rounded vertex bevels, and two meshes can be combined with a Boolean union, subtract or intersect from the object menu. Checkpoints (Ctrl+Shift+S) keep named and automatic versions of your scene on this device, with a timeline that restores, compares, notes and pins them, and Settings is a window with a section sidebar. Tools ▸ Recording… films a turntable or a flythrough as a webm, and Publish / Export ▸ Community gallery builds a gallery submission for GitHub. Every game keeps one permanent id, so re-exports and the play link count as one game in Your games & stats; community cards, play links and the pause menu get hearts, and the community browser a Mine filter. In a headset a game's HUD floats in front of you as laid out on the desktop, Tools ▸ AI opens an AI chat panel you can talk to, the assistant gets voice typing, and the VR keyboard and Settings panel gain punctuation and a Search tab. Modules can ask api.hud.vrHud() and give their HUD elements a vrText.

1.23 — readable game logic. Every rebuilt game's rules are now one readable script on its Main graph — Mini Golf, Football, Dungeon Realms, The Alchemist's Escape, Sky Run, Target Toss and Marble Maze — wired to its buttons, HUD, sounds and the kit: tune a number in the node's properties panel, or change the code and press Ctrl+S, and the game plays by your rules on every player's screen, saved with the scene. The scene's graph is the Main graph, and opening an older game adds links to the code that runs it. Every node's properties are in the node editor's side panel (Script inputs, Behaviour params, module nodes), and a double-click opens any node's code — module code read-only, with Make editable copy for nodes bound to it. The code workspace puts scripts, behaviours, script files, module sources and the graph as JSON in tabs; Ctrl+S checks the code and reloads every node that runs it, on every peer, and broken code never applies. Script nodes grow the sockets their code uses and get api.object, raycast, keys and spawn; Math gains pow, sin, cos, abs, round, floor, clamp and negate; and HUD Button, On Game State and HUD Timer now give a value when wired into a number input. The node editor has its own keys — shortcuts follow the panel you clicked, so C opens the chat only from the 3D view — plus groups you open like folders, markdown notes and frames, right-click menus for the canvas, a node and a selection, mute, collapse, align and nudge, undo for every edit, and a ? cheat sheet. Settings ▸ Node types hides the node types you never use, groups save and load as .tpnode files, and the Edit Mesh keys can be rebound. For modules, api.kit.provide lends a game's rules its engine, behaviours get sockets, and api.flow.seedGraph seeds a wired example once.

1.22 — VR + water. Any object can be water: Add ▸ Water makes a tank, a pool or an ocean with waves, refraction, caustics, foam, underwater fog and bubbles, in nine presets from Pool to Lava and Ice, plus Rain and Snow particle presets. Things float — or sink, or drift with a river — and Add ▸ Simulation ▸ Fluid tank is a glass box of liquid you can slosh and pour. The Jiggle node makes anything lag, wobble and sway. Concave scenery collides as it looks with exact mesh colliders, Decompose keeps a moving arch's openings, and collision groups make ghost walls; On Impact / On Enter / On Exit get only with and other. In a headset the radial menu has the desktop's names and icons, every VR setting is in it, every button can be remapped, and seated mode, height, smooth turning and the comfort vignette work everywhere, not only in games. Welcome to ThePrototype VR and a six-step editor tour show newcomers around (Tours), and the Quest browser offers Enter VR by itself. Opening a scene puts the camera on its start view at once — with Hold camera until loaded if you want it kept there — and Modern placeholders are the default. Community joins the profile menu under Support the project (Community), and Templates ▸ Examples has five new scenes: Aquarium, Pool party, Island ocean, Jelly room and Fluid tank toy.

1.21 — quick fixes, publish anywhere. Menu ▸ Publish / Export gathers both ways out: publish to the community with a play link and QR code that open straight into the game, or export a zip of plain HTML that plays on itch.io or any static host, or an iframe snippet — every one with the Made with ThePrototype badge. On a phone, games get touch action buttons you can rearrange and re-skin. A new loading placeholder style fills up as each model downloads, can be moved while it waits, and turns red with Retry and Replace model… when a file fails. Every theme is readable now, Settings has a real search (names, groups and keywords), menus and panels no longer select text when you drag (setting), the logo menu fits and scrolls on short and folding phone screens, the Live profiler moved into the Profiler tab, a phone's automatic quality follows its own refresh rate, hand-set fog keeps its near and far, and Ctrl+D with nothing selected creates nothing.

1.20 — five new games, measure on the device, build games from a kit. Five new games are in the Games tab with no download: The Alchemist's Escape, Marble Maze, Mini Golf, Sky Run and Target Toss. The Profiler records frame time, draw calls and triangles — and, in detail, which objects draw most — against the Quest budget, compares two recordings, and watches a headset live from the desktop; Report this moment keeps the last 30 seconds when something stutters. Games get a game kit (rules, rounds, levels, score, pickups, enemies with health and movers) as Kit: nodes and as code, and game logic can be written as a small behaviour file with a live node view. The Script node gains typed inputs and outputs, Flow Code shows a graph as compact text, and modules now unload completely.

1.19 — doors that open, scenes that load, games that switch. Four new packs (Interiors, Town & Market, Interactive, Arcane Study) and two new example levels; doors, lids and levers work in Interact and Play, and nothing animates by itself any more. Every pack object has levels of detail. Big scenes load with a progress bar and Cancel, opening another scene asks about the game's modules, and Clear scene can clear the game setup too. A frame counter shows FPS and draw calls.

1.18 — menus, levels and smooth frames in a headset. Every game has the same pause menu with per-game Settings and Levels; in VR the left X opens it. The controller laser is easier to see, the radial menu follows the thumbstick, teleport keeps you inside the play area, and some games let your grips move the world. Towers becomes twelve levels with stars, the Stars Room makes stars with a clap, and three new nodes — On Clap, Point Grab and Game Setting — build games out of settings and gestures. A headset starts with lighter quality and simplifies distant models.

1.17 — games that look finished. Edit and Interact (the I key), click-through glass, a Module content section in the object list, and Test play that starts a game from its menu. Every game got a start screen, best scores saved on the device (Store Value), game sounds, music, banners and controller buzz; four kit packs and three walkable levels arrived.

1.16 — Waves, and one world to keep. Waves joins the Games tab, the tab shows every game again, and two people pressing play at once no longer fight over the simulation.

1.15 — where everyone is. Every scene card in the Explorer shows who is in it, with Join ‹name›; scenes can be renamed and their files follow; copy and paste a scene to get a new one. Dungeon Realms and Untangle became games, ?embed=1 hides the editor for embedding, and (1.15.1) public rooms take a code or a knock.

1.14 — heavy models stop being a cliff. A model is weighed before it lands, and one that would hurt asks first, with Reduce on a background worker as a third way out and Restore original model to take it back. See Importing files. Football joins Towers and the Stars Room as a Games-tab template.

1.13 — knock it about. Hit a floating object with your hand and it flies off, with an On Hit node to react to it; the Stars Room and VR Football are built on it. Scene look becomes one section with post-processing node graphs, materials can be shared between duplicates, and proportional editing reaches your peers.

1.12 — hold together. A connection request now ends rather than hanging, a session has a size, the signaling link stops giving up, and a scene too heavy for your machine reduces quality or pauses instead of freezing — with a Statistics panel and a diagnostics bundle you can copy into a bug report.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
Getting started

  • Controls — navigation, selection, the transform gizmo, shortcuts and right-click menus.
  • Tours — the editor tour and the VR welcome, and how to replay them.
  • Settings — the grouped menu, search, sub-pages, resetting a category or everything.
  • Connection — invite links, approving peers, and choosing a signaling server.

Building

  • Explorer — your local asset library: import files, organize folders, drag assets into the scene.
  • Packs — ready-made model and audio collections you can browse and import.
  • Prefabs — save any object as a reusable asset, update every placed copy, sort them into folders and tags.
  • Material Presets — named surface looks, seven built in, saved and shared with your session.
  • Architecture — walls with doorways and windows, doors that open, and stairs, all from numbers you can change.
  • Mesh Editing — vertices, edges and faces: extrude, bevel, polyline knife, loops, and mirroring live or in one go.
  • Snapping — line things up: grid steps, surfaces, and snapping onto real geometry.
  • UV & Textures — unwrap a model, paint on it, and give parts of it their own materials.
  • Scene Look (Post-processing) — grade the finished frame: ambient occlusion, colour, bloom, grain. Saved with the scene and shared with everyone.
  • Animation — keyframe clips with a timeline, curves, markers and onion skin.
  • Physics & Simulation — mass, joints, dropping and throwing objects.
  • Colliders — collider shapes, exact meshes, decomposition, collision groups and sensors.
  • Particle Effects — dust, smoke, fire, sparkles, rain and snow, drawn as sprites, streaks, trails or ribbons.
  • Water — tanks, pools, oceans and lava with waves, refraction, caustics, foam and bubbles.
  • Fluid Tank & Jiggle — particle liquid you can pour, and springy secondary motion.
  • Fluids — particle water poured into the scene, rivers, chutes and pipes, and wheels that turn it.
  • Terrain & Sculpting — add ground and shape it with a brush, on the desktop or in a headset.
  • Saving & Sessions — the .tpscene bundle format, GLTF export, sessions and autosave.

The scene

  • Camera & View — lens presets, render modes, shadows, the grid, the environment and sky images.
  • Notifications & Notes — the notification center, scene notes and pinging.
  • Music & Sound — shared background music, spatial sound and voice chat.

Behavior, AI & more

  • Node System — the Flow editor that drives animation, logic and interactivity, plus a reference page for every node.
  • AI Assistant — build and edit the scene from a prompt.
  • VR Guide — the full room-scale control and radial-menu map.
  • Modules — enable playable content modules or write your own.
  • Community — publish a scene from the app, share its link, play and remix what others made, enter a contest.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
1.41 is an accessibility pass over the editor — for people who need bigger text, more contrast, no mouse, a screen reader or captions. Everything on this page is a choice for this device only: nothing is sent to the other people in your session, and their choices never change your screen.

Most of it lives in Settings ▸ Accessibility (under General, right after Interface). Settings search finds the page by accessibility, a11y, zoom, low vision, contrast, colour blind, motion, captions and similar words.

The games you make have their own Accessibility page for players — see Making your game accessible.

Settings ▸ Accessibility, every row applying to this device.

docs.title: UI scale
docs.text:
Settings ▸ Accessibility ▸ Size ▸ UI scale: 90 %, 100 % (default), 110 %, 120 %, 130 %, 140 %, 150 %.

Every panel, sheet, dock, toolbar, menu, toast and the phone layout grows or shrinks with it.

  • The 3D view is not scaled. It keeps drawing at your screen's full resolution, so a bigger UI does not make the scene blurry or slower.
  • Panels you resized yourself (the side column, the bottom dock, floating windows) follow the scale, so you do not have to resize them again.
  • The scale is applied before the app draws its first frame, so a reload never flashes the old size.
  • On a small phone, 150 % leaves less room for the scene; 120–130 % is often the best balance there.

UI scale at 150 % on a folded phone.

docs.title: High contrast
docs.text:
Settings ▸ Accessibility ▸ Colour ▸ High contrast (the same choice as Interface ▸ Theme ▸ High contrast).

White text on black, a yellow accent, and every surface measured against WCAG: text reaches 7:1 (AAA) on every panel, and buttons, borders and switches reach 3:1. It is built on the same theme tokens as Dark and Light, so every panel, window and the node editor follow it.

The 3D view follows it too, on this device only:

  • the selection outline becomes a thick yellow edge, readable on a dark sky and on a light wall;
  • an object another person is holding gets a pink-red outline;
  • the move / rotate / scale handles are bigger and drawn in brighter axis colours (X red, Y green, Z light blue).

High contrast keeps text at 7:1 and thickens the selection edge and the handles.

If you picked your own selection-outline colour in Settings, High contrast keeps yours. Switching High contrast off here goes back to the theme you had before.

docs.title: Status colours you can tell apart
docs.text:
In every theme, statuses use a colour set that people with red-green (protanopia, deuteranopia) or blue-yellow (tritanopia) colour blindness can tell apart — the scene budget (chip, object list, Statistics), connection and network quality, badges, draw-call counts and the node editor's "can't connect here":

Status Colour (Dark) Shape fine teal ● disc careful amber ▲ triangle over / error crimson ✕ cross not measured / off grey ○ ring

Colour is never the only signal. Every status mark also has its shape, a warning toast shows a triangle and an error toast a crossed circle, and the draw-call count shows ▲ or ✕ before the number (on the desktop counter and in the VR strip).

In the node editor every socket type has a colour and a shape — number disc, vector3 diamond, boolean square, color hexagon, object pentagon, event arrow, effect star, anything else a capsule. The ⚙ panel's Socket types legend shows both, and while you drag a wire a socket that cannot take it becomes a red cross. See Node System.

docs.title: Motion
docs.text:
Settings ▸ Accessibility ▸ Movement ▸ Motion: Follow system (default) / Reduce / Full.

  • Follow system uses your device's own setting (Windows: Animation effects; macOS / iOS: Reduce motion; Android: Remove animations). The row says which one your device asks for now.
  • Reduce makes these instant: sheet swipes, dock and panel slides, pop-up toasts, the camera's fly-to (F, saved views, note jumps) and pulsing indicators — even when your device setting is off.
  • Full keeps every animation, even when your device asks for reduced motion.

Games play normally either way: this covers the editor's own interface and camera moves. For VR comfort see the VR Guide.

docs.title: Keyboard navigation
docs.text:
Everything in the editor can be reached and used from the keyboard.

  • Tab / Shift+Tab move through the controls in reading order — the skip link, the main menu, the touch tools, the Connect bar, the top-right group and your profile, then the toolbar, the corner buttons, the budget chip and any open panel. Every control shows a focus ring in the theme's accent.
  • Toolbars are one stop each. In the bottom toolbar, the corner stacks, the touch tools and the top-right group, ← / → (or ↑ / ↓) move between buttons, Home / End go to the ends and Enter / Space press.
  • Skip to the 3D viewport is the first thing Tab reaches. With the viewport focused the 3D shortcuts work as usual (W A S D, 1 2 3, F, Delete, Tab = Edit Mesh on the selection), and Esc gives the keyboard back — nothing is trapped in the canvas. Tab is Edit Mesh only in the 3D view; on any control it moves focus.
  • F6 / Shift+F6 jump between regions: main menu, Connect, top-right, object list, Properties, windows, docks, toolbar, corner buttons, viewport.
  • Object list: ↑ ↓ select, → / ← expand / collapse (or go to the parent), Home / End, Enter opens Properties, F2 renames, letters jump by name.
  • Menus: the arrow keys walk a menu and its submenus, Enter runs, typing filters, Esc closes and puts focus back where it was. Shift+F10 or the Menu key opens the selection's menu (or the viewport's Add menu when nothing is selected).
  • Dialogs keep Tab inside them; Esc closes them and focus returns to what opened them. The main menu, notifications, the Connect drawer, notes and the peers panel close with Esc too.
  • Number fields in Properties: type a value and Enter commits and keeps your place, so the next Tab goes to the next field.

Settings ▸ Shortcuts lists F6 and "Esc leaves the viewport" under Navigation. F6 cannot be rebound.

docs.title: Screen readers
docs.text:
The editor's interface and your selection work with a screen reader (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack). The 3D scene itself is not narrated.

What is read aloud:

  • Toasts — every notice is spoken politely, after whatever the reader is saying; errors ("Could not …", "… failed", "Something went wrong") interrupt. Toasts you moved into the Connect drawer are still read.
  • Connection requests — "Connection request ABC123", plus the room's label when there is one.
  • Selection — selecting an object says its name and kind ("Crate, box", "Sun, directional light", "Pillars, group"); several objects say "3 objects selected"; clearing says "Nothing selected".

The object list is a tree. Each row is announced with its name, kind and level, whether it is selected or expanded, and its badges ("hidden", "local only", "locked by Ada"). The toolbars are announced as toolbars with a name ("Scene tools", "Notes, notifications and people", "Left corner buttons").

Names. Every icon button, menu row, dialog and floating window has an accessible name; windows are announced by their title ("Explorer, region"), submenu rows say they open a menu, and greyed-out rows say they are unavailable.

Not covered: scene narration, Play-mode announcements, and game HUDs (those are whatever the game's author built).

docs.title: Captions
docs.text:
Settings ▸ Accessibility ▸ Hearing ▸ Show captions shows a caption line for every sound that has one — Timeline audio clips and Sound / Game Sound nodes — everywhere, the editor included (handy while you preview a Timeline sequence). Players also turn captions on in a game's pause menu ▸ Accessibility.

To give a sound a caption: the Caption field of a Timeline audio clip, or the caption field of a Sound or Game Sound node. See Making your game accessible.

docs.title: For contributors: the accessibility check
docs.text: CI runs an axe-core check (npm run e2e -- a11y-axe) over the editor shell, the object list, Properties, Settings, the Asset Browser and the phone shell. It fails on serious or critical violations; moderate and minor findings are listed in the axe-report artifact. New UI uses the kit primitives and theme tokens, which already carry the names, focus ring and contrast this page describes.

docs.title: Animation
docs.text:
Give any object a clip: a named animation made of keyframes. Open a door, run a lift, spin a turntable, blink a light. Clips are stored with the object, replicate to everyone in the session, play on a shared clock, and export with your glTF.

Two different things called animation

This page is about animation you author — keys you place on a timeline. A model you import can also arrive with its own baked clips (a walk cycle from a rigged character); those play from the Animation section of the object's properties, and the Play Animation node drives either kind.

Imported clips do not start by themselves. Placing or loading an animated model leaves it still; previewing a clip from the Animation section in Edit plays it on your screen only, without changing the scene. Only ambient pieces from the packs (a banner, a fan, a torch) move on their own, and only in Interact and Play. Animated pack items carry a small ▶ badge in the Explorer.

docs.title: Opening the timeline
docs.text:
Select an object, then open the ＋ Animation tab — it sits with Flow and the UV editor in the bottom dock, and the dock's Undock button (right end of the tab strip) takes it out as a floating window.

The window has three parts:

Part What it is Clip list (left) Every clip on the selected object. Add creates one; the ✎ renames; drag the divider to resize the list. Timeline (centre) The keys themselves — a dope sheet of channel rows, or a graph of curves. Navigator (above the timeline) The whole clip at a glance, with the visible window as a thumb — drag it to pan.

docs.title: Clips, channels and keys
docs.text:
A clip owns a length, a loop mode (once, loop or ping-pong) and any number of channels. A channel is one animatable property; Add channel lists the ones that apply to the object you picked:

Group Channels Transform pos.x/y/z, rot.x/y/z, scale (uniform) or scale.x/y/z Visibility visible — a stepped channel: it holds its value until the next key instead of fading Look opacity, color.r/g/b, metalness, roughness, Emission Lights light.intensity

A key is a value at a time. Click a channel row at the playhead to add one; drag it to move it; Del removes the selection. Whatever you change — adding a channel, typing a value, retiming, moving a marker — the object re-poses straight away, so you see the result without touching the timeline.

Rotation turns around the object's origin

A door swings on its hinge only if its origin sits on the hinge. Set it from the object's properties (Transform ▸ Origin) before you key the rotation — the animation follows it.

Emission needs a colour

Emission is a strength multiplied by an emission colour, and a default material's is black — so turning the strength up alone would light nothing. The properties panel has one Emission block with both Strength and Colour; leave the colour alone and the object glows in its own.

docs.title: Movements play from where the object is
docs.text:
A position channel is stored as an offset from its first key, not as an absolute place in the world. Move an object after animating it and the clip runs from its new home: a door authored at the origin opens wherever you later put it, and a lift you drag up one floor still travels the same distance from there.

Rotation, scale and the look channels are absolute — only position works this way, because it is the one people move.

This changed in 1.5.0

Clips saved before 1.5.0 are read the same way, so a movement authored in an older version now replays relative to the object's current position instead of snapping back to where it was keyed. For most scenes that is the behaviour you wanted. If a clip depended on returning to a fixed spot, re-key it where it belongs.

docs.title: The transport
docs.text: Control Does ▶ / ⏸ Play or pause on every peer ◀ Play backwards from the playhead — press it again to pause where you are ⏹ Stop and return to where playback started ⏮ / ⏭ Jump to the start / end of the clip A / B Set the loop start / end — playback stays inside that window while you work on one part Speed Playback rate. It changes nothing in the data Fit Frame the whole clip

docs.title: Timing: three separate things
docs.text:
These are deliberately not the same control, because collapsing them means giving a door more room silently makes it slower:

You want Use The clip to be longer or shorter (keys stay where they are) the clip length field The movement itself stretched or squashed Retime — scales every key time It to play faster or slower, changing no data the speed control

Each clip also has its fps — what its key times mean, and the grid the arrow keys step on — and an optional step, which samples the clip on a coarser grid for a deliberately stepped, "on twos" look.

docs.title: The dope sheet and the graph
docs.text:
Switch with the sheet / graph toggle:

  • Dope sheet — one row per channel, keys as diamonds. Best for timing.
  • Graph — the actual curves. Best for how a movement feels.

In the graph, each key carries the easing of the segment that follows it. Drag its tangent handles right on the curve, or type the numbers in the pad. Handles are allowed to overshoot past the value — that overshoot is what makes a bounce read as a bounce.

docs.title: Selecting and editing keys
docs.text:
Action How Select Click a key; Shift+click adds Box / lasso select Drag on an empty part of the plot (the toolbar switches which) Add the key under the playhead Ctrl+Space Drop the selection Esc Move / scale the selection 1 / 2, then Shift+arrows (X = time, Y = value) Grab with the pointer Middle-click — the keys follow the cursor, click or Enter commits, Esc puts them back Copy / paste / duplicate Ctrl+C / V / D Mirror in time M Delete Del

The clipboard is held by channel and relative to the earliest key copied, so a paste works across clips and across objects, creating any channel the target is missing.

docs.title: Navigating
docs.text: Action How Step the playhead by a frame ← / → (Ctrl ×10, Shift ×100) Jump key to key Alt+← / → Zoom Wheel (up = in), or the ± buttons Pan Right- or middle-drag, Shift+wheel, or the navigator thumb

docs.title: On a phone
docs.text: Since 1.30 the Animation window fits a phone (and any window narrower than 640 px): it shows one pane at a time — Channels, Timeline, Key or Clip — from a switch in its header. Drag keys and easing handles with a finger, two fingers pan and pinch-zoom the timeline, and a long press opens the key or plot menu (the right-click menu on a desktop). Tool rows that do not fit scroll sideways.

docs.title: Auto-key
docs.text:
Switch Auto-key on and posing the object records it: drag the gizmo or type a number in the properties panel and a key lands at the playhead, creating the channel if it does not exist yet. Switch it off and the object goes back to being just an object.

Material edits count as posing. Pick a colour, drag Roughness or Metalness, change Emission — the key lands as you make the change, so you can work entirely in the properties panel and watch the channels appear.

If Auto-key is on and the object has no clips at all, the first change you make creates one and tells you it did.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text: Door, Drawer, Elevator, Turntable, Pulse and Blink out drop a finished clip onto the selected object — a starting point you then retime and re-ease. Door and Drawer expect a sensible origin (see the tip above).

docs.title: Markers
docs.text:
Name a moment inside a clip — "footstep", "latch", "dust" — and the Animation Marker node fires as the playhead crosses it, on every peer. Add one at the playhead from the marker row; double-click to rename; ✕ removes it.

Markers ride with the clip, so they save, replicate and undo with it.

docs.title: Onion skin
docs.text: Switch Onion skin on to see faint ghosts of the object at the keys either side of the playhead — the classic way to judge spacing. It is a local view setting: your peers do not see your ghosts. A ghost that would land exactly on the object hides itself, so a clip driving only colour or opacity does not read as a second solid copy.

docs.title: Everyone sees the same thing
docs.text:
Both halves replicate. The data (clips, keys, markers) syncs latest-wins, and the transport (which clip is playing, from when, at what speed, inside which A/B window) rides the session's synced clock, so every peer evaluates the same pose at the same moment. Someone joining late receives all of it.

Every gesture is one undo step — a drag of twelve keys undoes as one, not twelve.

docs.title: Driving clips from the flow graph
docs.text:
Node Does Play Animation Play, stop, restart or toggle a clip — wire On Click to it and a door opens for everyone who sees it clicked Animation Finished Pulses when a once clip reaches its end — hand off to a sound, a counter, or the next door Animation Marker Pulses as a named marker passes Animation State Reads progress, playing, position, duration or remaining as a number

To put several clips, camera shots and sounds into one cutscene, arrange them on the Timeline and start it with Play Sequence.

docs.title: Saving and export
docs.text: Clips are part of the object, so they travel in your .tpscene files and autosaves. Saving a glTF samples every clip into real keyframe tracks, so other tools play them back — with one exception: the look channels (opacity, colour, metalness, roughness, glow, light intensity) are not part of what glTF animation can carry, so they stay in the app.

docs.title: Themes & Appearance
docs.text: How the app's own interface looks is a choice for this device only — your theme is never sent to anyone, and the 3D viewport keeps following the scene's environment (sky, background, grid), whatever the theme.

docs.title: Choosing a theme
docs.text:
Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Appearance ▸ Theme has five built-in themes:

Theme Look Dark the default — dark grey panels, blue accents Light light panels and dark text Green console green-on-black, like an old terminal 8-bit a retro palette High contrast white text on black at 7:1 (AAA), 3:1 borders and switches, a thick selection outline and bigger handles — also a switch in Settings ▸ Accessibility

Dark, Light, Green console, 8-bit and High contrast on the same Settings rows.

Since 1.21 every theme is checked for readable contrast: the Profiler's numbers, the number fields, the Explorer's sidebar, the shader and node editors and the light theme's drawers all keep their text legible (at least 4.5:1 for the Profiler's text).

The theme applies at once and is remembered on this device; a built-in theme is painted before the first frame on the next visit, so it never flashes the default. Icons follow the theme's colours too.

Since 1.30 every theme follows the one-accent rule: blue marks what you can act on or have selected, and orange is kept for Play, recording and live states. The light theme and custom themes now restyle every surface — windows, menus, dialogs, the HUD and the node editor — because every colour comes from the design tokens.

docs.title: Making your own theme
docs.text:
Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Appearance ▸ Custom theme:

  1. Export template downloads the active theme as an editable .theme.json — every colour the interface uses, by name (surfaces, fields, text, muted text, borders, accents, menus, scrollbars…). Since 1.21 a theme also carries state colours — --ink-bad, --ink-warn, --ink-good for error, warning and good text, and --accent-fill / --on-accent for a filled accent chip and the text on it, and a custom theme may set them. Since 1.30 it may also set the redesign's tokens — --bg-app, --surface-1, --surface-2, --surface-inset, --border, --border-strong, --text, --text-2, --text-muted, --text-faint, --accent, --accent-soft, --accent-text, --live, --warn-text, --danger, --badge-bg, --badge-text; any it leaves out are derived from its other colours.
  2. Change the colours in any text editor.
  3. Browse… loads it back. It appears in the Theme list under its own name, and as a chip under Custom theme; the chip's ✕ removes it.

Custom themes are saved in this browser. To use one on another device, copy the .theme.json across and load it there.

docs.title: Other things that are yours to set
docs.text:
• Line colours — the wireframe, the selection outline and the Edit Mesh overlay: Settings ▸ Scene ▸ Wireframe & outline (see Mesh Editing).
  • Density — Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Density: Comfortable (the default) or Compact, tighter rows and controls on a computer screen; see Settings.
  • Render mode — Shaded, Shaded + AO or Wireframe, per device (Z cycles them): see Camera & View.
  • Toolbar — which buttons the bottom bar shows, in what order and where: see The toolbar.

  • FPS and draw calls — a small counter in any mode: Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Viewport ▸ Show FPS + draw calls.

  • Text selection — menus and panels do not select text when you drag across them; Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Allow text selection everywhere turns it back on (see Text selection).

Finding a setting

The search box at the top of Settings matches names, descriptions and keywords — search dark for the theme. Esc clears it. See Settings.

docs.title: Play on a Table (AR)
docs.text: On an Android phone with Chrome, the editor can put the whole scene on a real table in front of you, through the camera — and you can play it there while everyone else in the room keeps playing on their desktop or headset. New in 1.42.

docs.title: Start it
docs.text:
1. Open More ▸ Tools & View ▸ AR table (you can drag it onto the bottom bar), or long-press Play and choose Play on a table (AR) (on an unfolded phone, right-click or long-press Play in the toolbar).
  2. Allow the camera. Point the phone at a table and move it slowly until a white ring sits on the surface.
  3. Tap (or press Place here) to stand the scene there. It is sized to fit the table — the readout at the top shows the scale, for example 1:80.

docs.title: Size, turn, move
docs.text:
• Pinch with two fingers to make it bigger or smaller, twist them to turn it.
  • Move picks a new spot; the size and the turn are kept.

docs.title: Play
docs.text:
Press Play. Taps now press things in the scene — On Click nodes, module buttons, game pieces — and a game's HUD shows on screen. Stop returns taps to looking.

Exit AR (or the phone's Back) returns to the editor exactly as it was.

Where you placed your table is only on your phone: the others see the scene at its normal size, and your edits and theirs travel as always.

docs.title: What it needs
docs.text:
• Chrome on Android with Google Play Services for AR (ARCore). On an iPhone, or in a desktop browser, the item says AR needs Android Chrome and does nothing.
  • In a room where headsets are colocated, Join room (or More ▸ Join room (AR)) puts the phone in that room at full size instead of on a table.
  • A Quest's passthrough (Play ▸ Enter AR passthrough, see the VR Guide) is a different mode and is unchanged.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• While playing on the table, taps click; you cannot drag-carry a physics body across the table yet.
  • At table scale, other players' avatars float above the scene (they are where they stand in the full-size world).
  • A browser that refuses the on-screen overlay still places and clicks, but shows no buttons.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Since 1.27 you can build rooms and houses from parametric pieces: walls with doorways and window openings, doors and windows that open, and four kinds of stairs. Every piece is a set of numbers you can change at any time, and doors swing open for everyone in the session.

A wall with a door and two windows.

docs.title: Adding a piece
docs.text:
Right-click the viewport ▸ Add ▸ Architecture (or type the name into the Add menu's search):

Group Items Walls Wall · Wall with door · Wall with windows · Wall with door and windows Doors Door · Double door Windows Window · Casement window Stairs Stairs (straight) · Stairs (L) · Stairs (U) · Stairs (spiral)

Pieces from the Add menu land on the 1 m grid.

docs.title: In VR
docs.text: Since 1.28 the headset's radial menu has the same twelve pieces under Add ▸ Architecture ▸, with the same names. Each one lands 3 m in front of you. See The first ring.

docs.title: Editing a piece
docs.text:
Select the piece and open its Properties: the Geometry section holds every number. Rows that do not apply are hidden — a wall with no doors has no Door width row.

Properties ▸ Geometry for a wall.

docs.title: Wall
docs.text:
Row What it sets Length · Height · Thickness the size of the wall Doors · Door width · Door height how many doorways and their size Windows · Win width · Win height how many window openings and their size Sill height how far above the floor the window openings start Shift slides the openings along the wall

Openings are spread evenly along the wall, centred on half metres, and a 10 cm pier always stays between them. The wall's origin is its start end, on the floor, so walls of a whole number of metres snap end to end on the grid.

docs.title: Door
docs.text: Row What it sets Width · Height the opening the door fills Frame depth · Frame how deep and how wide the frame is Leaves single or double Hinge left or right (a single door) Opens in or out Swing ° how far it opens Glass panes panes of glass in the leaf (0 for a solid door) Sill a threshold at the bottom Opens on click, or proximity — it opens when someone walks up to it

docs.title: Window
docs.text: Row What it sets Width · Height the size of the window Sill height how far above the floor it sits Frame depth · Frame how deep and how wide the frame is Panes across · Panes up the glazing bars Sill ledge a ledge under the window Opens fixed, or casement (it swings open) Hinge left or right (a casement)

docs.title: Stairs
docs.text: Row What it sets Shape straight, L, U or spiral Width · Steps how wide the stair is and how many steps it has Rise · Run the height and depth of each step Turn left or right (L, U and spiral) Flight gap the space between the two flights of a U stair Column the thickness of a spiral stair's centre column Solid · Tread a solid stair, or open treads of this thickness

docs.title: Fitting a door or window into a wall
docs.text: A door and a window both sit centred on their opening, at floor level. To fit one into a wall, place it on the same grid point as the centre of the wall's opening, with the same size as the opening (and, for a window, the same Sill height). The pieces from the Add menu already match each other.

docs.title: Doors and windows that open
docs.text:
In Interact and Play, click a door to open or close it, or walk up to a door set to open on proximity. Casement windows open the same way. Every peer sees the same swing, and a player who joins later sees the door already open. In Edit a door always shows shut, so it is easy to place.

A door and a casement window open in Interact.

docs.title: Collisions
docs.text:
• Walls and stairs collide with their exact shape: doorways stay open, and a walking player climbs steps up to 0.3 m high.
  • A door's frame blocks around the doorway, and its leaf blocks only while it is shut.
  • A window is a solid slab.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The parts of a door or window are rebuilt from its numbers on every device, so editing the mesh of a door changes only its frame.
  • Very steep stairs (a Rise near 0.3 m) are the most a walking player can climb.

docs.title: Music & Sound
docs.text: Sound in ThePrototype comes in a few flavors: one shared background track for the whole scene, spatial sound effects attached to objects, and live voice chat. All of it is synced so everyone hears the same thing at the same moment.

docs.title: Scene music
docs.text:
Every scene can have one shared background track, synced to the same point in the loop for everyone.

To set it, open 🎛️ Configure Scene ▸ Music:

  1. Import an audio file into your Explorer library (drag an .mp3, .wav or .ogg onto the Explorer).
  2. In the Music section, pick it from the Scene track (shared) dropdown. Choosing a track pushes its bytes to your peers automatically.
  3. Use ▶ Play / ■ Stop to control playback, and Shared volume for everyone's baseline level.

Because it's synced to a shared clock, a peer who joins mid-song hears it from the right point — not restarted.

Your own listening level is separate from the shared volume, under This device:

  • Local volume — trims the music for you only.
  • Mute music on this device — silences it just for you.

Note

The scene track is a single, latest-wins setting — the most recent change wins for everyone — and it's kept separate from the environment preset, so it never leaks into exported presets. If playback doesn't start, browsers block audio until you interact with the page: a "click anywhere to enable audio" hint appears; just click once.

docs.title: Sound effect nodes
docs.text:
For sound tied to a place or object — a fire crackle, a machine hum, a click — use the Sound node in the flow graph. It plays a chosen audio item as spatial 3D sound positioned at the object it's wired to, with controls for:

  • Volume,
  • Radius — how close you must be before it's at full volume,
  • Rolloff — how quickly it fades with distance,
  • Loop — synced to the shared clock so it's in phase for everyone.

Walk (or fly) around and the sound pans and fades with the object's position.

docs.title: Audio packs
docs.text: Audio files can be bundled and shared as Packs, just like models. An audio pack is a .zip containing sound items; import one from the Explorer's Packs section (right-click ▸ Install pack, or ＋ Import pack for a local zip). Its sounds land in your library as ordinary audio items, ready to assign as scene music or wire into Sound nodes. Prefer CC0 loops and one-shots small enough to share with peers.

docs.title: Game volumes
docs.text: Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Sound has two sliders of your own: Game sounds — the built-in effects games play with the Game Sound node (coins, goals, whistles) — and Music, the looping tracks of Game Music. They are per device; nobody else's volume changes.

docs.title: Voice chat
docs.text:
Talk to your peers directly:

  • Toggle your mic on to transmit continuously.
  • While the mic is off, hold V for push-to-talk.
  • Voice is spatial — a peer's voice comes from where their avatar is (toggle spatial voice in Settings).
  • You can mute individual peers.

In VR the mic has three modes — Push-to-talk / Open / Off — set from the radial menu's Settings ▸ Microphone (press it to cycle); the right-hand A button is push-to-talk, and a small mic dot in the corner shows when you're transmitting.

docs.title: Pings
docs.text: Pings play a short synthesized chime at the pinged location — see Notifications & Notes ▸ Pinging for how to ping and pick your chime.

docs.title: Your Character
docs.text:
Since 1.24 everyone in a session appears as a rigged, animated character instead of a floating head. The body stands under the person's viewpoint, walks, runs, strafes, jumps and idles with the way they move, turns to face where they look, and — when they are in VR — reaches for their controllers with its arms. The classic floating head is still there as a choice.

Another person's character stands where their camera is.

docs.title: The characters
docs.text:
Nine characters ship with the app: Knight, Mage, Rogue, Hooded rogue, Barbarian, Skeleton, Skeleton warrior, Skeleton mage and Skeleton rogue, from Kay Lousberg's free CC0 KayKit packs.

The nine characters.

If you never pick one, you get Auto: a character chosen from your id, so everyone sees the same one for you. The same characters are also an Explorer pack, Packs ▸ Adventurers, that you can place in a scene as animated models (see Packs).

docs.title: Customize Character
docs.text:
Profile menu (your picture, top right) ▸ Customize Character — also Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Avatars ▸ Customize character…. A drawer opens (a bottom sheet on a phone) and puts your own character in a plain studio: a neutral backdrop in your theme's colours, a floor disc and a soft key light.

Customize character on a computer. The studio is on the left of the screen, the drawer on the right.

docs.title: The studio
docs.text:
The scene is hidden from your view only while you customise — nothing in it changes, and other people in the session keep seeing the scene (and you) as before.

  • Orbit — drag in the free part of the view to turn the camera around your character like a turntable; the wheel or a pinch zooms.
  • Show in scene — the switch at the top of the panel previews your character in the current scene instead, handy to check how a colour reads against the world. The choice is remembered for next time.
  • Your whole character stays in view whatever the screen does: resize the drawer or the window, rotate a phone, or fold or unfold a foldable — the camera re-frames on every layout change.

docs.title: Choosing a look
docs.text:
