• Presets — Auto (picked from your id), the nine rigged characters (step through them with ‹ ›) and the Classic head. Picking one shows its defaults: its own head, no hat, its own outfit colours.
  • Custom — change any part (head, hat, outfit or head colour) and a Custom entry appears and is selected. Picking a preset again resets to that preset; picking Custom brings your edits back.
  • Surprise me — a new random character on every press: body, head, hat and colours, never the same one twice in a row. A surprise you like is your Custom look; press Apply to keep it.

The name label and your ping colour and sound are your own preferences: presets and Surprise me leave them alone.

Section What you choose Character a preset — Auto, one of the nine, or Classic head — or Surprise me; your own edits are Custom Head the character's own head, a stylised Sphere, Box, Capsule or Cone in your colour, or My photo (your profile picture on a card; needs a profile photo) Hat None, Cap, Top hat or Crown — it sits on whatever head you chose Colours Outfit recolours the character's clothes (skin and face keep theirs; Original puts them back); Head colours a stylised head or the classic avatar Show my name above me your name label Ping the colour and chime of your pings; Preview pings beside your character (only you see and hear it)

Since 1.30 the panel is a drawer on the right (a bottom sheet on a phone): drag its inner edge to make it wider or narrower — the keyboard works too (focus the edge, then the arrow keys; Shift for bigger steps) — and the camera keeps your character in the part of the screen the drawer leaves free. The size is remembered on this device.

Every change shows on your character at once; nothing reaches other people until you press Apply, which saves it and shows it to everyone. Cancel, Esc, ✕ or swiping the sheet away throw the changes away. Either way the camera and the scene come back exactly as they were before you opened it.

docs.title: Showing everyone as classic heads
docs.text: Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Avatars ▸ Show everyone as classic heads draws other people as the floating head instead of their character — on this device only, and lighter on a headset with many people in the room. They still see your character.

docs.title: Knocked-off idle
docs.text:
When someone gives no input for a while, everyone sees their character knocked off: little stars circle its head, the head sways in a slow figure-8, and its eyes turn into spinning stars. Any key, click, mouse move or head move wakes them, and it fades out smoothly.

Knocked off: stars circle the head.

Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Avatars ▸ Knocked-off idle chooses when you count as idle: Off, 10 s, 20 s (the default) or 60 s. It is a setting for this device.

It works on every head — the character's own, the stylised ones, a photo card and the classic floating head — and costs one extra draw call per idle character, none while awake.

docs.title: Feet on the ground
docs.text:
Since 1.26 characters stand on the floor in Play. (Before, a walking player sank about 0.9 m into the ground on everyone else's screen.)

  • A walking player tells the others where their feet are, so the character stands on the same floor — steps and raised floors included — in desktop Play, with a Character Controller node in walk mode, and walking in VR Interact.
  • Each foot stays planted while walking or running: the animation's heel roll no longer pushes a foot through the floor.
  • A player who is flying or editing is still drawn with the body hanging under the head, as before.

docs.title: In VR
docs.text: A VR user's character follows their head, and its arms reach for their controllers; a hand held out of the arm's reach falls back to the floating controller marker. Pointing at an object puts the character's hand on it.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The bodies are stylised (big heads): a character is about 2.2 m tall so its eyes sit where the person's are.
  • In the editor, a character follows the editor camera — flying the camera makes the body float.
  • On a steep slope (20–30°) the feet follow the walker's capsule and can float a couple of centimetres above the slope; there is no foot IK yet.
  • Characters add no network traffic: each screen works the bodies out from the position and hand data already shared.
  • Each character is at most about 6,000 triangles with one material, so eight people stay inside a Quest's budget.

docs.title: Behaviours
docs.text:
Some game logic is easier to write than to wire: a loop over waves, a rule with three exceptions, a timer that calls itself. A behaviour is that logic as one small JavaScript file inside a node — and the app draws it back as nodes, with live values, so you can still see it run.

A behaviour is built on the game kit: it listens to kit events (a round starting, an entity dying, a pickup taken) and acts through the same kit calls the Kit: nodes make.

docs.title: The Behaviour node
docs.text:
Add a Behaviour node from the palette's Logic group, to the Scene flow or to an object's own flow (then the behaviour knows that object as this.object). It has no sockets unless the file declares some (1.23, see For module and game authors). Its card shows the behaviour's name and whether it is running (and with how many handlers), still loading, stopped, or in error — an error names the line.

  • Open view opens the live node view.
  • Code — or a double-click on the node — opens the file in the code workspace; Ctrl+S reloads it, and code that does not parse is not applied.
  • Stop / Run switches the behaviour off and on; its state is kept.
  • Its params are also in the node editor's ⓘ Params tab: changing one there rewrites the number in the code, as one undo step.

Every game rebuilt in 1.23 keeps its rules in one of these — see Game rules on the Main graph.

A new Behaviour node starts with a small working example (a countdown that loses the round when it reaches zero), so the format is there to copy from.

docs.title: The file
docs.text:
export default behaviour({
    name: 'Waves spawner',
    params: {
        waves: { value: 5, min: 1, max: 15, step: 1 },
        interval: { value: 3, min: 0, max: 30, step: 0.5, unit: 's' },
        speed: { value: 1.3, min: 0, max: 6, step: 0.1, unit: 'm/s' }
    },
    state: { wave: 0, alive: 0 },
    on: {
        go() {
            this.startWave(1);
        },
        died({ entity }) {
            if (!entity.is('robot')) return;
            this.state.alive = Math.max(0, this.state.alive - 1);
            if (this.state.alive === 0) this.after(this.params.interval, 'startWave', this.state.wave + 1);
        }
    },
    startWave(n) {
        if (n > this.params.waves) return kit.round.win('All waves cleared');
        this.state.wave = n;
        this.state.alive = n + 1;
        kit.spawner.spawn({
            kind: 'robot',
            template: this.find('Robot')?.uuid ?? '',
            at: this.find('Spawn*')?.pos,
            count: this.state.alive,
            mover: { speed: this.params.speed }
        });
        kit.mover.chase('robot', 'nearestPlayer');
    }
});

When the round's intro ends, wave 1 brings two robots that chase the nearest player; when the last one dies, the next wave comes a few seconds later, one robot bigger; after the last wave the round is won. (Adapted from static/behaviours/waves-spawner.js in the core repo; its neighbour towers-reach.js is Towers' reach rule as a behaviour.)

Part What it is params Numbers you want to tune: a literal (waves: 5) or {value, min, max, step, unit}. Read as this.params.waves. Each one becomes a knob in the node view. state Plain JSON the game keeps — every peer can read it. on Event handlers: start (once per session), load (1.23: once on every peer, read-only; since 1.48.1 a joiner runs it once the host's scene has arrived, and editing the behaviour releases what its last load registered), every kit event (go, won, lost, died, damaged, spawned, emptied, scored, collected, stuck, grabRefused…, or the full 'piece.event' name), and grabRequest — the grab veto, see below. inputs / outputs (1.23, optional) Sockets on the node: event inputs that run the handler of the same name, and outputs that carry a state field or an event fired by this.emit(name). methods Any other function in the file (startWave above), called as this.startWave(…).

Inside the file, this offers:

  • params, state, object and kit (also available as plain kit);
  • after(seconds, 'method', ...args) and cancel(key) — timers on the session clock;
  • rand(), randInt(a, b), pick(list) — random numbers every peer agrees on;
  • now(), find(glob) / findAll(glob) — scene objects by name or tag, as {uuid, name, pos, tags};
  • isAuthority(), me(), log(...);
  • and the helpers dist(a, b), clamp and lerp.

An entity in an event's payload answers is(glob) and hasTag(tag).

docs.title: Who runs it
docs.text:
A behaviour's handlers run on one peer — the kit's authority — and after each one the state is sent to everybody. A player who joins later receives it, and when the authority leaves the next one carries on from it. Timers survive that hand-over too, as long as they name a method (this.after(3, 'startWave', 2)); a timer given a function does not.

The one exception is grabRequest({ piece, distance, refuse }): it is asked on the grabbing player's device, before the grab happens, so it only reads and refuses:

on: {
    grabRequest({ piece, distance, refuse }) {
        if (piece.hasTag('ground')) return;
        if (distance > this.params.reach) refuse('Too far - climb closer');
    }
}

Editing the code swaps the definition and the game keeps running. Deleting or stopping the node takes away what it set up — its kit listeners and the entities it spawned.

docs.title: The determinism lint
docs.text:
Every peer must reach the same result, so a file that would make them disagree — or reach outside the game — does not load. The lint names the line, on every peer. It refuses:

  • Math.random (use this.rand() and friends), Date, Date.now, performance.now;
  • storage, the page (window, document, globalThis), the network;
  • eval / Function, bare timers (use this.after), import.

Loops run under the loop guard: a runaway handler throws and the game goes on.

docs.title: The live node view
docs.text:
Open view draws the behaviour as read-only nodes, derived from the code: ⚡ events → ƒ handlers and methods → ▣ state, with ⊕ kit calls (named exactly like the Kit: nodes), ⏱ timers, ✋ payload actions, and ◆ params.

  • Live values, ten times a second.
  • A glow on whatever just fired — on every peer, not only the one running it.
  • Timer countdowns, and errors with their line.
  • Knobs on the params: dragging one previews the value on your device; releasing it rewrites the number in the code — one edit, one undo step — and everybody's copy reloads with it.

Anything else is changed in the code (the view's Code panel, or the code workspace); ← Graph goes back to the flow.

docs.title: Writing behaviours with the AI assistant
docs.text: The AI assistant can write and change behaviours for you (its create_behaviour and edit_behaviour tools). What it writes goes through the same lint before it is applied, so a suggestion that would make peers disagree is refused rather than loaded.

docs.title: For developers
docs.text: A behaviour can be proved without a browser on the core repo's logic sim (tests/unit/sim/behaviourSim.js): load the source, drive the kit, assert the state. See Behaviours in the core repo's MODULES.md.

docs.title: Example: build a game loop
docs.text:
A complete worked example — a start menu, a walking character, collectibles that count into the HUD, a hold-to-peek map, a pause menu you can click, and a second level to travel to. Everything is authored in the app with the HUD editor and flow nodes — no code, and one optional module for the collectibles.

Allow about twenty minutes. Each step works on its own, so you can stop anywhere and still have something playable, and every piece is visible to the people connected with you as you build it.

What you'll need

A scene with some ground to walk on and a few objects to collect. A gamepad is optional — it works out of the box if you have one. Step 4 uses the Collectibles module: install it once from Menu ▸ Modules ▸ Browse, and have everyone you are playing with install it too — modules do not travel over the connection.

docs.title: 1. A menu on its own camera
docs.text:
A menu belongs to a viewpoint, so give it one.

  1. Add ▸ Camera, and frame your scene from an angle that looks good as a title shot. Rename it Menu cam in the object list.
  2. Open the HUD editor: in the bottom dock's tab strip, press ＋ and choose HUD editor.
  3. In the topbar's document picker, choose Menu cam. This HUD now appears only while you are looking through that camera — attach a HUD to a camera and it travels with the shot.
  4. From the left palette, click Button. Drag it where you want it. In the properties pane on the right, set its label to Start.
  5. On the screen row, set while to menu. That binds the screen to the game state: it shows whenever the game is in its menu, including for someone who joins later and never saw it appear.

The dashed outline

The artboard is a fixed reference size; the dashed rectangle shows the shape of your window on it. Anything outside that outline is outside the frame you are actually looking at.

docs.title: 2. Make Start do something
docs.text:
Select the Start button and open Actions ▸ ＋ Add action in the properties pane. Add three:

Action Group What it does Start the game Game Moves every player's game state to playing Look through a camera Camera Pick your gameplay camera Show a HUD screen HUD Pick your in-game screen (make one with New screen…)

All three hang off a single press, and the Actions pane lists them back to you in plain language. The artboard marks the button as wired, so a button that does nothing is obvious at a glance.

Press Play and click Start: everyone connected moves to the gameplay camera and the menu gives way to your in-game HUD.

docs.title: 3. A character that walks
docs.text:
By default play mode keeps you on the ground at eye height (since 1.26 flying is opt-in). For a character that walks, jumps and falls:

  1. In the node editor, add Character ▸ Character Controller.
  2. Set mode to walk. Adjust jump height and eye height to taste.

Now WASD walks, Space jumps, and gravity is real. If your scene has physics running you get proper collision against walls and slopes; without it you walk along the ground plane. A gamepad drives it too — left stick moves, right stick looks — and you can tune deadzone, sensitivity and invert-Y under Settings ▸ Input.

Scrolling changes your speed, and because a controller node is present a Move Speed node can read or set that same value — so a sprint key is just a key press wired into it.

Since 1.25 the controller card also has code: double-click it to steer speed, jump height, eye height, gravity or walk/fly every frame from this player's keys — see The Player's code.

Note

Delete the Character Controller node and movement is exactly the default again. The controller adds capability without taking the default away.

docs.title: 4. Collectibles that count
docs.text:
This step uses the Collectibles module — install it from Menu ▸ Modules ▸ Browse (and so does everyone playing with you).

  1. Select the objects you want to collect.
  2. Open the Collectibles window: the sidebar's Modules section, or the viewport right-click menu. Leave the fields alone for now and press Make collectible.
  3. On your in-game HUD screen, add a Text element, then Actions ▸ Show a variable and enter gems.

Press Play, walk up to one and click it with the crosshair. It disappears for everyone, the counter goes up on every screen, and clicking the empty space where it was does nothing — it stays collected.

Each object got one Collectible node wired to an Object Selector naming it, in the scene graph, added as one undo step. Open the node editor and you can see it, change it, or wire something else off it — it is an ordinary graph, not a hidden feature.

The node's dials, all optional and all editable either on the card or in the Collectibles window's list:

  • Counts into — the variable, gems by default. Existing names are suggested; type a new one for a second kind of pickup.
  • Scope — shared gives the room one score. player makes it personal: the object vanishes only for whoever picked it up and counts into their number, which is what you want for a race or a co-op scramble. Read a personal number back with the Player Variable node, or show the standings with Leaderboard.
  • Trigger — click (mouse or VR trigger) or touch, which fires when a player walks within Radius metres of it. Touch needs no physics: each player notices the pickup for themselves.
  • Hide — turn it off and you get a counting checkpoint: it still collects and still counts, but it never disappears. That is a lap gate or a pressure plate.
  • Respawn — seconds until it comes back. 0 means gone for good. A re-collect after a respawn counts again.

Two behaviours you get without wiring anything:

  • Collectibles reset when a new round starts and read un-collected while the game sits in its menu, derived from the shared round — so a Restart needs no extra work.
  • When you leave play mode, your collected objects come straight back on your own screen, so the editor never loses an object to a running game — and hiding one from the object list works normally again.

The Collectibles window also lists everything in the scene grouped by variable, with live collected / left of total counts; click a row to select that object in the viewport.

Collectibles (the value node) answers "how many are left". It counts the nodes in the graph rather than the score — a score only goes up, so it would be wrong the first time something respawned. Actions ▸ Show collectibles left wires it to a Text for you.

Two things worth knowing

A scene built with the older seven-node collectible recipe keeps working exactly as it did, and the Collectibles count node counts both shapes together.

A player who joins mid-round sees already-collected objects back on the table: pickups are events, and an event that happened before you connected is not replayed. Everything from the moment they join is in sync. Start the round after everyone is in, or use a Restart to put everybody on the same footing.

docs.title: 5. Hold a key to peek at a map
docs.text:
1. Add a screen called Map with a Minimap element on it.
  2. In the node editor, wire two key presses:
    • Key Press (Tab, edge down) → HUD Screen (show, Map)
    • Key Press (Tab, edge up) → HUD Screen (hide, Map)

Hold Tab in play mode and the map appears; let go and it's gone. The edge setting is what makes this work — down fires when you press, up when you release, and held gives you a value that stays on for as long as the key is down.

docs.title: 6. A pause menu you can actually click
docs.text:
Under pointer lock there is no mouse cursor, so a menu has to ask for one.

  1. Add a screen called Pause with a Resume button, a volume Slider and a difficulty Dropdown.
  2. On the screen row, set input to menu.
  3. Wire Key Press (KeyP, edge down) → HUD Screen (toggle, Pause).

Press P in play mode: the pointer is released, your character stops moving, and you can click and drag the controls. The world keeps running behind you — in a shared session your menu is yours alone. Give Resume the Hide a HUD screen action and the pointer locks again where you left off.

Want the world to stop for everybody? Add the Pause action to a button. That freezes physics, animations and the round timer for the whole session, and Resume continues with no jump.

Keyboard and gamepad

Any menu is navigable without a mouse: arrows or D-pad move the highlight, Enter or A activates, and a highlighted slider or dropdown takes left/right.

You also get the app's own game menu for free (1.18)

In any game, Esc (or the Menu button in the corner) opens the shared game menu: Resume · Restart · Levels · Settings · How to play · Main menu, plus Back to editor on the desktop. In VR it opens with X on the left controller or the Menu button on the game board and the wrist card. Its Settings are per game and per device — music and sound effects on/off with their volumes, controller vibration, Show FPS, VR turning (snap / smooth / off and the snap angle), a comfort vignette and a quality preset (Auto / Low / Medium / High). Your own Pause screen keeps working beside it; a scene that is not a game still leaves play on Esc.

docs.title: 7. Ending, and going round again
docs.text:
Add End the game to a button (or drive it from your own logic) to finish with an outcome, and Back to the menu to return. Because the menu screen is bound to while: menu it comes back by itself — and a Game Start node naming your gameplay camera puts a late arrival on the right view even though they never saw the transition.

That's the loop: menu → play → score → pause → end → menu.

docs.title: Test play
docs.text:
Once a scene has a screen bound to a game state, the editor stops showing it: a game's menu does not sit over your work with live buttons. A small Game · menu chip says the scene is a game instead. Press ▶ Test play on it (or right-click the play button ▸ Test play) to reset the game to its menu, enter Play and get the Start screen in front of you — exactly what a player sees. The HUD editor's eye still previews the screens while you lay them out; the preview is a picture, so it never eats a click.

Leaving Play on your own puts the game back on its menu at once. With other people in the session, the round resets when the last player has been out of Play for ten seconds.

docs.title: Remember a best score
docs.text: The Store Value and Stored Value nodes keep a number on the player's own device — a best score, the level reached. Wire On Game State (over) and your score into a Store Value with mode max and a key of your own (mygame-best), and show it with a Stored Value → HUD Text on the menu. Actions ▸ Save best score on a HUD button builds the chain for you.

docs.title: Games played with the mouse
docs.text: A board game, a puzzle or an instrument wants the real mouse cursor rather than a crosshair. Set the scene's play cursor to free (the physics block's play.cursor: 'free'): Play then takes no pointer lock, the cursor aims, clicks fire On Click and a press-drag carries. Untangle and the Jam Room play this way. The editor grid is hidden in Play either way.

docs.title: 8. A second level
docs.text:
One scene is one level; a game can have many.

  1. Build your first level, then in the Explorer right-click the file grid and choose Save scene… — type the name right there in the grid and press Enter. It lands in a Scenes folder as an ordinary .tpscene file (a tidy default, nothing more: scenes are found by kind wherever they live, and a save lands in whatever library folder you have open). New scene… gives you an empty one to build the next level in.
  2. Where the first level should end — a door, a portal, a Finish button — add a Travel node (Game group) and pick the destination level on its card. Wire any trigger into it, or use Actions ▸ Level complete — travel to a level on a button.
  3. Press it and everyone travels together: each player loads the level themselves, and anyone missing the file pulls it from whoever has it first. The game — state, round, score variables — carries across the hop; the new level's own collectibles start fresh, because their nodes live in the level file. Edits survive the round trip too: leaving an edited scene saves a new version of it automatically — see Projects for version history and the .tp project file.

Two helpers that come with it:

  • All Players (Game group) is the group-travel gate: wire in a condition each player answers for themselves ("I am standing at the portal") and it fires once every player in play mode says yes — spectators in the editor don't count. Feed it into the Travel node and nobody gets left behind.
  • The Debug HUD element (Display group) is a little pill for building: game state, round, elapsed time, your variables, who is playing and fps — plus a line per collectible variable when the Collectibles module is installed. Click it in-game to expand. Take it off the screen when you ship.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Templates ▸ Games ▸ Towers — a finished game made the same way: twelve levels of co-op stacking with a Menu, HUD and Pause screen, Game Start and HUD Button nodes, physics grabbing, limited reach and 1-3 stars a level. Load it and pull it apart; it is authored entirely as scene data, so everything in it is editable.
  • Templates ▸ Games ▸ Stars Room — a smaller one to read: a zero-gravity room where twenty-four stars and two planets are knocked about by hand. It opens on a start screen — Start round (light every star within two minutes; your best round is saved on this device) or Free play — so the HUD carries a Free play screen and a Round screen; in free play the P menu carries Start round: light every star, Restart round and More stars, and two physical pads on the floor (Start and More stars) do the same in VR, where a screen HUD is not there to click. An On Hit per star chimes, lights it and bursts particles in proportion to speed; a second On Hit with who set to me counts that touch on the hitter's own row, which is what the leaderboard reads. It needs no module at all.
  • Templates ▸ Games ▸ Football — the same ideas with the rules in a module instead of loose nodes. Like Waves, Untangle, Dungeon Realms and the Jam Room it needs a module, so its card lists the Football module it requires and loading it offers to install that module for you; see VR Football.
  • Templates ▸ Games ▸ Untangle — a puzzle played with the mouse (a free-cursor game): drag the dots until no edges cross, on a flat board or around a 3D globe. Each mode has 30 levels that unlock as you solve them; your progress is kept on this device with api.storage (the level grid's Reset progress clears it). Every peer sees the same board.
  • Node System — the logic nodes this example leans on: Latch, Delay, Sequence, Counter and the Game group.
  • Physics & Simulation — grabbing, throwing and colliders for the objects you just made collectible.
  • Saving & Sessions — save the whole thing as a .tpscene and share it.
  • Module SDK — when a game outgrows nodes, a module can register its own HUD elements and nodes.

docs.title: Building in VR
docs.text:
Since 1.45 you can build a whole scene with the headset on: measure and line things up, paint terrain and scatter, pull models off your wrist and drop them in, and shrink the world to a miniature to work on it from above. Since the next release you can also edit the game logic — the node graph — without taking the headset off. Everything here works in Edit; the radial menu, grabbing and getting around are on the VR Guide.

Controllers do everything. With hand tracking you can browse and place; tools that need precision ask you to pick up a controller. The comfort settings — vignette, seated, one-handed — apply to every tool on this page.

docs.title: Shrink the world: miniature mode
docs.text:
In Edit, both grips always grab the world, wherever your lasers point and whatever you stand inside.

  • Pull your hands together to shrink the world, apart to grow it, twist to turn it, move them to move it.
  • It sticks, with a tick in your hands, at 1:50 · 1:10 · 1:5 · 1:2 · 1:1 · 2× · 5× · 10×, and a readout between your hands shows the scale (for example 1:10). Turn the steps off with Settings ▸ VR ▸ Controls ▸ World grab snapping.
  • Back to 1:1 appears on the radial's first ring while the world is scaled, turned or moved.
  • The comfort vignette closes in while the world scales or turns around you.
  • Only you see the miniature: it changes your view, not the scene.

To scale or turn an object with two hands, grab it with one hand and move it a little first (about 2 cm), then add the second grip. A grip that has not moved its object yet, joined by the other grip within a quarter of a second, lets the object go back where it was (no undo step) and grabs the world instead.

Grips never take the terrain, locked objects, things bigger than about 2 m, or a room you are standing inside by touch. To move one of those, select it with the trigger first, then grip it (terrain never moves by grip).

Prefer the old way? Settings ▸ VR ▸ Controls ▸ Both grips scale the world: Always (the default) or Only in empty air (two grips on an object scale that object).

docs.title: Measure
docs.text:
A measured chain with its labels.

Radial menu ▸ Tools ▸ Measure — a trigger tool beside Select, Box select and Draw mode.

  • Point the laser of the hand that does not hold the menu. A dashed segment and a marker show where the next point lands.
  • Pull the trigger to put a point down. Points snap like the desktop Measure tool: to a corner, an edge (or its middle) or a face centre within about 3° of the laser, so a slightly shaky hand still measures corner to corner. With grid snapping on, a point on a plain surface or the floor lands on the grid. A harder click tells you a point snapped.
  • Keep pulling to make a chain: each segment shows its length, each corner its angle, and a chain of two or more segments a running Total.
  • Keep it: pull the trigger twice on the same spot, or use the Measure ring the radial opens on while the tool is up — Keep · Undo point · Discard · Snap · Done. A kept chain is a measurement item in the object list, saved with the scene, seen by everyone and undoable, the same as one made on the desktop.
  • Edit one: select it, then Selected ▸ Edit measurement. Point at a point and pull the trigger to pick it up, pull again to put it down; pull anywhere else to add a point at the end. Done on the Measure ring ends editing.
  • The labels face you wherever you stand and stay the same size to your eye at any distance. Labels that would overlap are hidden instead of stacked.

Measuring needs a controller. Switching to Interact, leaving the headset or picking another tool ends it, and a chain of two or more points is kept.

docs.title: Arrange: align, distribute, drop to ground
docs.text:
Select two or more objects, then radial ▸ Selected ▸ Arrange:

Axis (tap to cycle X → Y → Z) · Align min / centre / max · Even centres · Even gaps · Drop to ground · Align to (Selection / Active)

  • Align lines every object's edge or centre up on the chosen axis with the selection's bounds — or, with Align to: Active, with the last object you picked, which stays put.
  • Even centres and Even gaps need three or more objects; the two outermost stay where they are.
  • Drop to ground rests each object on the surface below it (or the floor), lowest first.

The results are the same as the desktop's Arrange, each press is one undo step for the whole set, and everyone in the session sees the objects move.

docs.title: Brushes on the controller
docs.text:
The terrain sculpt brush now has two more tool sets on its Sculpt ring:

  • Paint ▸ — terrain layers 1 – 4, the same layers as the desktop's terrain paint.
  • Scatter ▸ — Paint, Erase, Rotate, Scale, Relax, and Source ▸ to choose what you scatter (the current source, the ones already in use, or a primitive). See Scatter.

Pull the trigger to paint. The pointing hand's thumbstick sets the brush: left / right the radius, up / down the strength (or the density while you scatter-paint). A ring on the surface shows the brush, a short buzz starts each stroke, and the label on your hand reads, for example, Paint 3 · 3.0 m · 50% or Sphere · 3.0 m · 0.50/m². Brushes work in a miniature too: the ring and the stroke follow your laser at the world's scale.

docs.title: The Asset Browser on your wrist
docs.text:
The Asset Browser panel.

Radial menu ▸ Add ▸ Assets opens a panel on the wrist of your menu hand, facing you. Point at it with the other hand.

  • Packs — the packs in your Explorer. Press a pack to open it, ‹ Packs to go back.
  • Free CC0 — free models from Poly Haven. A card with ↓ downloads first (the card shows the progress) into your Library, folder Poly Haven, with its credit; ✓ means it is already in your Library.
  • My library — your models and prefabs.
  • Search — press the search box: the VR keyboard opens and the cards filter as you type. Page with ‹ ›, or push the stick up and down while you point at the panel.

docs.title: Placing
docs.text:
The same drag-to-place ghost as the desktop: the item's size before it loads, its real look when it is ready, resting on whatever you point at — amber when it overlaps something, red when there is nowhere to put it.

  • Trigger-drag a card out of the panel and let go where it should land: it is placed there, once.
  • Click a card and it rides your laser: each trigger places one more, the stick sideways turns it 15° a flick, and the grip stops. The panel's bottom line says what the trigger does right now.
  • Each placement is one undo step, and everyone sees it.
  • In a miniature the object still lands at full size, at the spot under your laser.

Placing: "Duck.

Pin it: grip the panel and let go in the air — it stays there, bigger. Grip it again and let go near your wrist to put it back (or press Pin / To wrist). In one-handed mode it opens pinned in front of you.

Add ▸ Prefabs uses the same ghost: real size, the stick turns it, it rests on surfaces and snaps.

docs.title: Logic in the headset
docs.text:
The Logic panel on the Spinner object's flow.

Radial menu ▸ Tools ▸ Logic opens the scene's node graph as a panel in front of you. With one object selected, Selected ▸ Edit logic opens that object's own flow instead (tabs at the top switch between the two). It is the same graph as the desktop node editor: every change is one undo step, and everyone in the session sees it land live.

Do this With Move a card trigger-drag the card Wire two sockets trigger-drag from a socket and let go on another. The wire is green while the types fit and red when they don't; a wire into a value input that already has one replaces it Move or remove a wire trigger-drag from an input that already has a wire: drop it on another socket to move it, or on the empty graph to remove it Pan trigger-drag the empty graph Zoom push the stick up or down while your laser is on the panel (it zooms where you point) Move the panel grip it and let go where it should stay

The buttons along the top: + Node opens a palette with the desktop's groups — pick a node and it lands in the middle of the view; ↶ / ↷ undo and redo; Fit frames every card; − / + zoom; ✕ closes the panel.

The wrist pad for a Number node.

Click a card (trigger, no drag) to select it: its values open on a wrist pad on your other hand.

  • − / + step a number; press the value itself to type it on the VR keyboard.
  • ‹ › cycle a choice or a colour; toggles flip on a press.
  • Rename, Unwire (removes its wires) and Delete act on the selected card.
  • A node with more values than fit has pages: push the stick up or down while you point at the pad.

In one-handed mode the pad sits beside the panel instead of on your wrist. A viewer sees the panel read-only, and it says so.

Limits

  • Groups are read-only in VR: you can move a collapsed group's card, but not wire into it or delete it. Edit groups on the desktop.
  • Custom (code) nodes, Object Flow nodes and Sound nodes need desktop pickers, so the palette leaves them out — add them on the desktop, then wire and tune them here.

docs.title: Hands
docs.text:
Without controllers, a pinch is the trigger: pinch a card to pick it, pinch-drag it out of the panel and let go to drop it, or pinch a card and pinch again to place it. Tools that need precision — the sculpt, paint and scatter brushes, measuring, moving vertices or faces — show Pick up a controller next to your hand instead.

Limits

  • Hands cannot turn the ghost (there is no stick); pick up a controller for that.
  • The Free CC0 tab lists Poly Haven models. Skies, textures and materials stay in the desktop Asset Browser.
  • A pinned panel's place is not remembered for the next session.

docs.title: Camera & View
docs.text: Everything about how the scene looks on your screen — the camera lens, render mode, shadows, the grid and the environment — lives in one place: Configure Scene.

docs.title: Opening Configure Scene
docs.text:
Click 🎛️ Configure Scene in the sidebar menu. It opens as a tab of the sidebar on the right (drag its tab to the left to keep it there) with these sections:

  • Quality — the quality preset and the automatic-quality, shadow and model switches (your device only; see The Quality preset).
  • Environment — lighting preset, exposure, sky image, saved presets (shared).
  • Music — the shared background track and your local volume (see Music & Sound).
  • View — render mode, the scene-look overrides and light helpers (your device only).
  • Camera — lens presets, field of view and clip planes (your device only).
  • Background and Fog (shared).

A dot appears next to the menu item while the panel is open; click it again to close.

Shared vs. this device

The Environment, Background and Fog settings replicate to everyone. The View and Camera sections — render mode, lens and clip planes — are local to your device, so you can zoom, wireframe or dim shadows without changing what your peers see.

docs.title: Render mode (View)
docs.text:
Three per-device render modes under Viewport — this device:

Mode Look Shaded Plain lit shading. Shaded + AO Adds ambient occlusion — soft contact shadows in creases and corners (the default on a desktop; phones and tablets start in plain Shaded). Wireframe Shows every edge.

Shaded, Shaded + AO and Wireframe. AO darkens creases and the ground where objects touch it.

Try it

Z in the 3D view cycles them: Shaded → Shaded + AO → Wireframe (Shaded + AO is skipped when the scene's own look already sets ambient occlusion). Rebind it in Settings ▸ Shortcuts.

Ambient occlusion and wireframe are desktop-only and never shown to peers. AO detail follows your shadow-quality setting (below), so lowering shadow quality also lightens the AO cost.

These are SHADING modes — they are not how you see the scene's own look. A scene look renders for everyone in every mode except Wireframe, and you switch it off for yourself under Overrides — this device. If the scene sets its own ambient occlusion, Shaded + AO switches off and says so: the scene's setting is used instead of yours.

Configure Scene ▸ View: how the scene is drawn on your screen.

  1. The render mode switch.
  2. Show light helpers.

Try it

The Show light helpers toggle here draws icons for lights so you can see where they are — in the editor only; see Helpers hide in Play.

docs.title: Camera objects
docs.text:
Besides your own view, a scene can hold cameras of its own — the shot a game starts from, a cutscene angle, a security monitor. Add one from right-click ▸ Add ▸ Camera ▸ Perspective (or Orthographic). It appears as a small camera marker you move and turn like any object; selecting it opens Properties ▸ Camera:

A camera's properties, with its preview window at the lower left.

Row What it does Kind Perspective or Orthographic FOV (perspective) field of view, 10–140° Size (orthographic) how much of the scene fits, 0.5–50 Near / Far the clip planes Framing 16:9 · 4:3 · 1:1 · 2.39:1 · free (follows the viewport) Letterbox guide while previewing bars that show the framing while you look through it Preview look through the camera. A banner says Previewing ‹camera›; its Control button lets you fly the camera with WASD and the mouse (its new pose is kept, as one undo step) Set from view move the camera to where your view is (and take its FOV) Align view fly your view to look through this camera (it stays your camera) Capture render one frame through this camera and download it as a PNG at the framing aspect Preview window while selected the picture-in-picture window (below), on by default Show camera frustums — this device draw every camera's viewing pyramid

The camera itself — including its Letterbox guide and Preview window while selected switches — is shared with everyone; previewing and the frustum lines are yours alone. The object's right-click menu has Preview camera and Set from current view too.

Picture-in-picture. While a camera is selected, a small window shows what it sees, live. ⤢ looks through it full screen, ✕ hides the window (the Preview window while selected row brings it back), and right-drag moves it. Since 1.34 it resizes too: drag the grip in its top-left corner (the picture keeps the camera's framing), or double-click the grip for the default size. The size is remembered.

A game uses cameras through the Set Active Camera node, the Game Start node's camera, Set Look for each camera's own look, and since 1.27 the Camera Rig node, which makes a camera follow or watch an object.

docs.title: Camera lens
docs.text:
The default camera is a 40° field of view — a natural, product-viz look with real depth and little wide-angle distortion. You can change it in the Camera section:

Lens presets (labelled by their full-frame focal-length equivalent):

Preset Feel Wide (24 mm) Roomy, exaggerated depth. Classic (35 mm) Reportage, slightly wide. Natural (50 mm) Close to how the eye sees. Portrait (85 mm) Compressed, telephoto.

Below the presets, the Camera FOV slider gives fine control (15°–120°).

Note

Your FOV is broadcast, but a peer only sees through it while they're spectating your view — during normal editing everyone keeps their own camera.

docs.title: Clip planes
docs.text:
In the Camera section, the near/far clip planes control the depth range the camera renders (per-device):

  • Near clip (0.01–2) — surfaces closer than this are cut away. Lower it if very close objects vanish.
  • Far clip (from 10) — the far limit. It grows automatically to fit the scene, and the orbit zoom-out limit is paired to it so you can never dolly past the far plane and blank the scene.

docs.title: Shadow quality
docs.text: Shadow quality is a per-machine performance knob in the Settings dialog: Off · Low · Medium · High (default High). It caps every light's shadow-map size on your computer — Off disables shadows entirely. Per-light shadow settings still replicate; this only changes what your machine renders.

docs.title: The grid
docs.text: The floor grid can be toggled from the viewport right-click menu ▸ View ▸ Show/Hide grid, or the Show grid checkbox in Settings. Its fade distance scales with how far you've zoomed out, so it stays visible when you pull the camera way back. The grid hides itself in wireframe mode.

docs.title: Environment presets
docs.text:
The Environment section sets the scene's lighting and sky. Pick a preset chip:

Preset Look Studio Neutral grey studio (the default). Daylight Bright sky, strong sun, soft fog. Sunset Warm, low sun. Night Dim and cool. Classic The pre-lighting look with the rig off — bring your own lights.

Studio, Daylight, Sunset and Night on the same three objects.

Try it

Since 1.27 five more chips — Clear sky, Meadow, Sunrise, Starlight and Photo studio — use a real sky photo; see Sky images.

An Exposure slider tunes overall brightness. The lit presets add a sun that casts shadows, with a shadow-catcher disc under the scene so shadows land even on the infinite grid.

Environment is a shared, latest-wins setting — the most recent change wins for everyone. You can also save, export and import custom presets (stored locally), and adopt presets other peers have shared.

Below Environment, Background sets the clear color and Fog adds distance fog (color + near/far), both shared. A fog you set by hand keeps exactly the near and far you typed; a preset's fog still grows with a big scene.

docs.title: Sky images (HDRI)
docs.text:
Since 1.27 a sky image — an HDRI, a 360° photo that keeps the real brightness of the sun and the sky — can be the scene's sky and its light. Every object picks up the image's colours and brightness, shiny objects reflect it, and water mirrors the real clouds. The scene's sun is placed where the photo's sun is, so shadows agree with the sky.

The Meadow sky image lighting a mirror sphere and a box.

It lives in Configure Scene ▸ Environment ▸ Sky image (HDRI), under the preset chips and the Exposure slider. Click a card to switch to that sky; like every Environment setting, everyone in the session sees it.

Since 1.53 a sky downloads the first time you pick it and stays on this device. Offline or with the download blocked, the preset's flat colours show until the sky can load. Exported games still carry their sky.

Sky What it looks like Clear sky open blue sky with clouds, haze on the horizon Meadow a sunny meadow with trees Sunrise a low warm sun and long shadows Starlight dusk under the stars Photo studio softbox lighting over a plain grey backdrop — light only; reflections show the studio

The five skies are also preset chips, and in VR they are in the radial menu's Scene ▸ Environment. All five are CC0 images from Poly Haven.

Configure Scene ▸ Environment, with its Sky image section.

Row What it does Upload HDRI… use your own equirectangular .hdr or .exr file (up to 25 MB; 1k–2k is plenty). It is added to the Explorer, your peers download it from you automatically, and it is saved inside .tpscene files and exports Rotation turns the sky; the sun and its shadows turn with it Image light how strongly the image lights objects (the sky itself is unchanged) Show as sky off keeps the image's light and reflections but shows the colour sky instead Sky blur softens the background — handy behind a product shot Tone mapping ACES Filmic (the default), AgX or Neutral: how the bright image is fitted to the screen None (the first card) back to the colour sky and the light rig

Exposure, above the cards, brightens or darkens the whole picture, and while a sky image shows it works on the desktop whatever else is on. Editing any of these turns the preset into Custom, like any other sky edit; Save preset keeps it.

A short tour points at the cards the first time you see them (Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Tours ▸ Reset all shows it again).

docs.title: Sky image quality
docs.text:
How sharp the sky and its reflections are is a setting for this device only — Settings ▸ Scene ▸ Performance ▸ Sky image quality:

Choice What it does Auto (the default) Low in a headset, in VR, or once the scene is too heavy for effects; Full otherwise Full (1k) prepares the image at 1024 px Low (headset) prepares it at 512 px — a quarter of the memory

The scene and your peers are unaffected.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Only equirectangular images (twice as wide as they are tall); cube-map files are not supported. An .exr must be RGB or RGBA.
  • Files over 25 MB are refused — your peers could not receive them.
  • Someone on an app older than 1.27 in the same session sees the preset's flat colours instead of the image.
  • A scene look with its own Tone mapping effect keeps its own curve.

docs.title: Lights
docs.text:
A directional or spot light shines where it points. Turn it with the rotate gizmo — or type into the rotation rows — and the beam and its shadow follow, the way a light behaves in any 3D tool. Older scenes that aimed a spot at a saved point load aimed the same way.

Aim at, in the Properties panel's Light section, points the light once at a spot: type a world X / Y / Z, or press Pick in viewport and click a surface (Esc cancels). It writes the rotation, so the gizmo and the rows agree afterwards.

A directional light has a direction, not a distance. Its helper line reaches as far as Settings ▸ Scene ▸ Light helper length says — display only.

Light helpers show where each light is and where it shines; they are editor-only.

  1. A point light's helper.
  2. A spot light's helper, with the cone it shines into.

docs.title: A light with an origin
docs.text: Lights have an origin like any other object. Give a sun one — type it in the Transform section's Origin block, or press World 0 — and Rotate swings the light around that point instead of turning it in place: a sun on an orbit, in one gesture. Move still moves the light and carries its origin along.

docs.title: Helpers hide in Play
docs.text:
Light helpers, camera frustums and camera markers are editor furniture. They disappear when Play starts, and camera previews and captures never show them, so a screenshot is the game and nothing else.

Show helpers in Play (debug) — on the viewport menu under View, and in Settings ▸ Controls — brings them back while you debug a scene, with an amber DEBUG · HELPERS chip in the corner so a capture cannot be mistaken for the real thing. It is your setting alone.

docs.title: Characters and motion
docs.text: Any rigged model is a character, any clip plays on any humanoid, and the clips are small files of their own. Characters and motions come as free CC0 packs, and a character downloads with its clips for Blender, Unity, Unreal or Godot.

docs.title: Rigged characters
docs.text:
• Any model with a skeleton — a .vrm, a rigged .glb / .fbx (Mixamo, Meshy, UniRig, KayKit, Quaternius, VRoid) — is a character. It reaches every peer as its original file, so its rig is exact everywhere.
  • Inspector ▸ Character shows the rig family and how much of the VRM 1.0 humanoid it maps ("Mixamo · 52 of 55 humanoid bones"), the clips applied to it, its licence, and three ways in: Apply clip…, Skeleton…, Download…. The same three are under the object's right-click menu ▸ Character.

docs.title: Humanoid map + Apply clip…
docs.text:
• Every character's bones are named onto VRM 1.0's humanoid bone set, detected automatically: by bone names (Mixamo, KayKit, Meshy, VRoid/UniRig J_Bip_*, Unreal pelvis/thigh_l, Rigify/Quaternius DEF-*), by the hierarchy (which spine bone is the chest is read from the path between hips and head), and — for numbered bones such as UniRig's bone_0… — by the rig's shape. A VRM brings its own map.
  • Apply clip… plays a clip on any mapped humanoid: pick the clip (one another model in the scene plays, or the built-in avatar motions, a .tpanim clip file in your Explorer, listed under Clip files, or any clip of the Motion pack), tick the characters, Apply. The clip is fitted to each character's own skeleton — rest pose and facing corrected, the hips' travel scaled to its size — on every peer for itself: the model's file never changes, and a late joiner computes the same clip. Also from the Animation window's Imported clips header: Apply to….
  • Remove an applied clip with ✕ in Inspector ▸ Character. Undo works.
  • Fix the map in Skeleton… ▸ Humanoid map: each VRM bone shows the rig bone it uses (detected or your pick, or not mapped); Reset fixes goes back to the detected map. Fixes travel to peers; the file is untouched.

docs.title: VRM characters
docs.text:
• .vrm files (VRM 0.x and 1.0, also a VRM renamed .glb) import with spring bones (hair, cloth swing as the character moves), expressions (Inspector ▸ Character ▸ Expression + weight, or the Set Expression flow node: expression name + weight when a pulse arrives) and their licence meta (title, authors, commercial use, redistribution, modification, credit, licence link) in the Inspector.
  • The VRM runtime is loaded only when a scene has a VRM. VRM 0.x models are turned to face +Z like everything else.
  • Limits: MToon materials render as standard materials; VRM characters as player avatars is a follow-up (they need LODs: the avatar budget is 10k triangles, 1 material).

docs.title: Skeleton… (rig fix-ups)
docs.text:
• Tabs Humanoid map, Bones, Weights. Loaded only when opened (a player of an exported game never downloads it). The viewport shows the skeleton and the picked bone while it is open.
  • Bones: pick a bone in the tree, then Rename, set its Rest position and Move, Add child, Delete (its children move up to its parent, its weights go to the parent), Mirror left → right / right → left (bones paired by name: Left/Right, .l/.r, _l/_r, L_/R_).
  • Weights: Automatic weights (bone heat: every vertex starts on its nearest bone and the heat diffuses over the surface — never across a gap between two legs — computed in a worker), Smooth, Normalize (≤ 4 bones per vertex), a weight brush for the picked bone (radius, strength, erase; paint on the model) and a test pose slider that bends the picked bone here only.
  • Each edit rewrites the model's file and sends it to peers once when it ends (a brush stroke is one edit); one Undo puts the old file back everywhere. Rig fix-ups edit GLB / VRM files — an FBX character must be downloaded as GLB and re-imported first. Full rigging stays a Blender job.

docs.title: Download…
docs.text:
• Object ▸ Download… (or Inspector ▸ Character ▸ Download…): tick the clips and pick a layout — One GLB (default: the model with the clips embedded — what Blender, Unity, Unreal and Godot expect), Model + clips (a zip: the model and one .tpanim per clip), Model only. Applied clips are baked onto the character's own skeleton. The model's bytes are its own: a GLB/VRM keeps everything it had (a VRM stays a .vrm).
  • One clip downloads as .tpanim, .glb (skeleton + clip), .vrma (VRM Animation, humanoids only) or .bvh (for Blender, MotionBuilder, Cascadeur: every joint at the same place as in the app).
  • FBX / USD are listed but off: they need an AI box with the convert capability (roadmap 58).
  • Several selected objects download as one zip (with a CREDITS.txt).

docs.title: Provenance + licence warnings
docs.text:
• Every imported, generated, rigged, retargeted or converted asset records where it came from: {tool, model, version, licence, prompt?, date} (on the object, in the scene file, and in a downloaded GLB's extras). Inspector ▸ Character shows the licence and the last step.
  • Licences that ask something — credit (CC-BY), non-commercial, no modification, or a VRM that says "no redistribution" — show a warning at the top of Publish, Export, Community gallery and Download. It never blocks: you decide. Exports write a CREDITS.txt for everything that carries a licence.

docs.title: Packs (CC0 only)
docs.text:
• Characters (characters-kit): 8 VRM avatars from 100Avatars by Polygonal Mind (CC0) and Quaternius' two mannequins (CC0). Every one is a full humanoid, so every motion plays on it.
  • Motion (motion-kit): 87 humanoid clips from Quaternius' Universal Animation Library 1 + 2 (free Standard tiers, CC0): locomotion, jumps, sitting, swimming, combat, interactions… each a .tpanim (VRM Animation inside). Asset Browser ▸ Motion lists them: Add to Explorer, then drag one onto a character. Apply clip… lists them too, and the Locomotion preset fills whatever a humanoid lacks from this pack.
  • Asset Browser ▸ Avatars: VRM avatars from the Open Source Avatars registry. CC0 collections are listed by default; tick Include CC-BY for the ones that ask for credit. Add to scene places the avatar as a VRM character, and a CC-BY one keeps its credit, so Export and Publish remind you of it.
  • The packs CI lints the licence of every file: each one needs a CC0 record, and a VRM must say CC0 in its own meta.

docs.title: Animation clips are their own files (.tpanim)
docs.text:
A clip is a small file in the Explorer (kind Animation clips, the standing-figure icon). The model it plays on never changes: assigning a clip adds a reference to the model, the clip's bytes travel to your peers once, and every peer applies it to its own copy of the model.

  • Import: drop a .tpanim, .vrma, .bvh, an animation-only .glb (nodes + animations, no meshes) or an animation-only .fbx (Mixamo "Without Skin") into the Explorer. Each animation in the file becomes one .tpanim clip (<file> - <animation>.tpanim when there are several). A model file (it has meshes) imports as a model, as before.
  • Play on a character: drag a clip from the Explorer onto a rigged model in the scene. It is assigned and starts playing on every peer. One undo step removes it again.
  • Rigged models with no clips of their own (a character exported without animations) now import as animated models, so clips can be assigned to them.
  • Clips assigned to a model are saved with the scene; a .tpscene bundles the clip files the scene uses (and only those). A late joiner receives the clip once.

docs.title: Which clips fit which model
docs.text:
• Humanoid clips are stored on the standard VRM 1.0 humanoid bone set, so one clip plays on any character whose bones are mapped (VRM characters map themselves; other rigs are mapped by name — Mixamo names out of the box, more rigs with the humanoid map from Characters).
  • Other clips (a creature, a machine, a door) play on models with the same skeleton — the same bone names. A clip made for another skeleton says so when you drop it.

docs.title: The .tpanim format (spec, format 1)
docs.text:
A .tpanim file is a binary glTF 2.0 file (GLB). Rename it to .glb and any glTF tool opens it.

  • Humanoid clips are valid VRM Animation (VRMC_vrm_animation 1.0): rename one to .vrma and it plays in VRM tools (three-vrm, UniVRM, VRoid-compatible viewers). They are written in VRM's normalized space: one node per humanoid bone, named after the bone (hips, spine, leftUpperArm, …), every rest rotation identity, offsets in metres in the character's frame. The rotations stored are the normalized local rotations; only hips carries a translation track. The node offsets keep the source character's rest pose (an A-pose arm points down), which a rest-pose correction uses when the clip is applied to a T-pose character.
  • Other clips are a plain GLB holding the source skeleton's nodes in their rest pose (no meshes, no skin) and one animation targeting those nodes by name.
  • Both carry extras.theprototype on the glTF root:
{
  "format": 1,
  "kind": "clip",
  "skeleton": { "sig": "sk1-42-1a2b3c4d", "humanoid": false },
  "fps": 30,
  "frames": 24,
  "loop": true,
  "rootMotion": "moving",
  "provenance": { "tool": "import", "source": "walk.fbx", "date": "2026-10-23" }
}
field meaning format 1 kind always "clip" skeleton.sig the skeleton signature: a hash of the bone names + parents (sk1-<bones>-<hash>); humanoid clips use vrm1-… over the humanoid bones they carry skeleton.humanoid true = a VRMA humanoid clip fps the rate the keys were made at (the Animation window's frame grid) frames length in frames (duration = frames / fps) loop the clip is meant to loop rootMotion "moving" (the root travels) or "inplace" (forward travel stripped, height kept) provenance where it came from: {tool, model?, version?, licence?, prompt?, date, source?}

A file without these extras (a .vrma from another tool, an animation .glb) is read with defaults (fps from the key spacing, loop off, moving) and gains them when it is imported.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One animation per .tpanim file. Morph-target (blend-shape) and material tracks are not part of a clip file.
  • Humanoid clips carry rotations for every bone plus the hips' position (the VRMA rule); a clip that moves other bones' positions keeps only their rotations as a humanoid clip.

docs.title: Game-ready clips (Animation window ▸ clip tools)
docs.text:
The clip tools in the Animation window.

Select a character and open the Animation window. Under its clips, the clip tools show for the clip that is playing:

  • fps · frames · length of the clip, whether it is humanoid, and the loop seam: "seamless loop" when the last frame meets the first, or "loop seam 4.2°" when the loop jumps.
  • In place / Moving: In place keeps the clip's height but removes its forward travel, so the character controller (or a Blend by Speed node) moves the character; Moving lets the clip carry it.
  • loop (off = play once and hold the last frame), speed (this clip's own speed on this character), Rename, Remove (the file stays in the Explorer).
  • Loop it makes a new clip whose last frames blend into its first, so it loops without a jump.

These settings belong to the character (another character using the same clip file keeps its own). Loop it, Trim, Split and Join make new clip files; the original stays in the Explorer.

docs.title: Split and join (cut a long take into Walk, Turn, Stop)
docs.text:
• Move the playhead to preview a moment (only on your screen), set the in and out markers (or Mark in / Mark out at the playhead), then Trim keeps the part between them, or Split at playhead makes two clips.
  • Join clips…: tick two or more clips in order, choose a crossfade, and Join makes one clip that plays them one after another, blending at each seam. The character keeps travelling across the seams.
  • Extract clips (for a model that brought its own clips): turns them into .tpanim files in the Explorer, so they also play on other characters. use the files instead switches the model's own clips off and plays the files under the same names (the model file is not changed; undo brings the embedded clips back).

docs.title: Flow nodes
docs.text:
• Play Animation gains Crossfade (s): changing clip blends from the one already playing.
  • Blend by Speed (Animation group): blends a character's idle, walk and run clips by a speed — the character's own speed when nothing is wired — so it never snaps between poses. Empty clip fields pick the character's clips by name (Idle / Walk / Run). Walk and run play faster or slower to match the speed.

docs.title: Animation states (a locomotion state machine)
docs.text:
The Animation states window for a Knight.

Animation window ▸ Animation states… opens the states window for the selected character.

  • Locomotion preset: one click builds Move (idle / walk / run blended by speed), Jump and Fall from the character's clips (a humanoid gets the ones it lacks from the Motion pack, so a fresh VRM works at once), driven by how the character moves — possess it (Player), drive it from logic, or let an NPC wander, and it walks, runs, jumps and lands with crossfades. No wiring.
  • States are a clip (loop or once) or a Blend by speed; transitions go from a state (or Any state) to another when all their conditions hold (speed > 2, grounded true, jump trigger), with a fade time; a once-state can wait for its clip (exit time).
  • Parameters: numbers, yes/no values and triggers. With from its motion on, speed, vy (vertical speed) and grounded come from how the object moves. The live values and the current state show in the window; Fire fires a trigger on every peer.
  • Nodes: Set Animation Parameter (set a value on a pulse, hold a wired value, or fire a trigger such as jump) and On Animation State (a pulse when the character enters a state).
  • The graph is part of the character: it is saved, replicated and exported with it, and every peer runs it itself, so a character looks the same for everyone without extra traffic.

docs.title: Animate imported parts
docs.text: A model's named parts (child nodes — a rotor, a door, a lid; what an img2threejs model brings) can be animated: drop a clip on the model, or let the assistant do it with animate_parts ("make the rotor spin": one clip on the named part, saved as a .tpanim, one undo step). Attach to Socket (node): on a pulse, an object follows one of a model's named nodes (a sword in a hand, a lamp on a rotor arm) — or lets go, staying where it was.

docs.title: animate_parts (assistant / agent tool)
docs.text:
{ "object": "<uuid or name>", "clip": "Spin", "loop": true, "mode": "relative",
  "tracks": [ { "part": "rotor", "keys": [ { "t": 0, "rot": [0, 0, 0] }, { "t": 1, "rot": [0, 360, 0] } ] } ] }

keys[].pos metres [x, y, z], rot Euler degrees [x, y, z] (or a quaternion), scale a factor; mode: "relative" (default) = offsets from each part's rest pose, "absolute" = local values. A turn longer than 90° between two keys is split so a full turn spins. play: false assigns without playing.

docs.title: Re-rigged in another tool?
docs.text: Replace model… swaps the file and keeps your clips, embedded and .tpanim, when their bones still exist.

docs.title: Limits (motion)
docs.text:
• Blend by Speed and the states graph blend at most the clips they name; their phases are per device (a walk's step can be a fraction of a cycle apart between two screens).
  • Possess (the Player) has no jump of its own: a jump comes from vertical motion (a physics hop, logic) or the jump trigger (Set Animation Parameter, the window's Fire).
  • A part clip binds by node name: renaming a part in the model breaks the clip for that part.
  • A clip whose share weight in a blend falls under 1 % is skipped (the rest renormalize), so a settled Move state costs one clip, not three.

docs.title: What it costs (Quest profile)
docs.text:
Animation tick per frame, measured on the CPU throttled ×4 (the Quest budget), 1280×720, KayKit knights:

Knights One clip, median (p95) Locomotion states, median (p95) Scene 1 0.1 (0.7) ms 0.5 (1.1) ms 2 draw calls · 4.8 k tris 4 0.3 (1.1) ms 0.8 (1.6) ms 5 draw calls · 18.9 k tris 8 0.7 (1.2) ms 1.3 (3.0) ms 9 draw calls · 37.7 k tris

A 72 Hz frame is 13.9 ms. Measured on a busy build machine (load ≈ 18 on 16 cores), so the p95 column is pessimistic; a real-headset row is owed.

docs.title: Third-party notices
docs.text:
• Characters pack: 100Avatars by Polygonal Mind (CC0 1.0), mannequins by Quaternius (CC0 1.0).
  • Motion pack: Universal Animation Library 1 + 2, Standard tiers, by Quaternius (CC0 1.0).
  • Runtime: three-vrm by pixiv (MIT), loaded only for scenes with a VRM.
  • Avatars tab: the Open Source Avatars registry; each collection has its own licence, shown on its avatars.

docs.title: Checkpoints
docs.text:
A checkpoint is a copy of the scene as it is right now — objects, node graphs, HUD, sky, physics, the camera — kept on this device, with a name, an optional note, a picture and a time. Autosave only remembers the last state; checkpoints let you go back to any earlier one.

The Checkpoints timeline comparing two checkpoints with the swipe slider.

docs.title: Saving a checkpoint
docs.text: Menu (the logo button) ▸ Save checkpoint…, or press Ctrl+Shift+S. Type a name and, if you like, a note ("before lighting", "try the red version next"), then press Save checkpoint.

docs.title: The timeline
docs.text:
Menu ▸ Checkpoints lists every checkpoint, newest first, grouped by day. In it you can:

Action How Restore replaces the open scene with the checkpoint. The scene you leave is kept in the timeline as "Before restoring …", so a restore can itself be undone. With people connected, they are asked to accept first (the same as opening a saved session) Rename double-click the name Note click the note line to edit it (Ctrl+Enter saves) Pin a pinned checkpoint is never removed to make room Delete removes the checkpoint Compare press Compare, then tick two checkpoints: their pictures sit on top of each other with a swipe slider, plus what changed (object count, size, time apart, "same content"). Tick just one to compare it with the scene as it is now

Two filters narrow the list: show only This scene's checkpoints, or hide the Automatic ones.

docs.title: Automatic checkpoints
docs.text:
While you work, autosave also adds an automatic checkpoint every few minutes — only when the scene actually changed since the last one, and never while a scene is loading or a simulation is running.

In the Checkpoints window the Automatic switch shows or hides the automatic checkpoints in the timeline.

A checkpoint's picture (and a saved scene's) shows the scene only — no gizmo, grid, light or camera helpers or selection outline, whatever was selected when it was cut.

docs.title: Very large scenes
docs.text:
A very large scene — over the budget meter's Desktop line for triangles (4 M) or texture memory (512 MB) — skips automatic checkpoints, because each one copies the whole scene. The first time it happens a notice says so, with a Settings button. Named checkpoints (Ctrl+Shift+S) always work.

The notice when a large scene skips its automatic checkpoint.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Settings ▸ Scene ▸ Checkpoints:

Setting Default What it does Keep automatic checkpoints on autosave adds rows to the timeline Automatic checkpoint every 10 min 5 / 10 / 30 / 60 min — the shortest gap between two Checkpoint storage 250 MB 100 MB / 250 MB / 500 MB / 1 GB that this device may use Auto checkpoints on large scenes off automatic checkpoints for very large scenes too (1.42)

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Checkpoints stay on this device (this browser). They are not shared with other people and are not part of a project file — use Save and scene versions (Saving & Sessions) for that.
  • When a new checkpoint would not fit, the oldest unpinned ones are removed — automatic ones before named ones. If even that is not enough (everything else is pinned), the save is refused and a message says so. At most 60 checkpoints are kept.
  • A scene larger than the storage limit cannot be checkpointed.

docs.title: Code workspace
docs.text:
The code workspace is one place for every piece of code in a scene: a Script node's code, a behaviour, a .js script file from your Library, a module's own source (read-only), and the flow graph itself as JSON. Each source is a tab, and your edits stay in the tab until you save.

The code workspace docked beside the Explorer and the Node editor.

docs.title: Where it is
docs.text:
It opens by itself when you ask for code:

  • Edit code on a Script node, Code on a Behaviour node, or a double-click on any node that has code (see Open code) — since 1.25 that includes a game's Player;
  • a double-click on a .js file in the Explorer, or right-click it ▸ Open in code editor;
  • the dock's ＋ menu ▸ Code, or the optional {} toolbar button (add it with Customize the toolbar);
  • Graph JSON in the workspace's header opens the graph the Node editor is showing.

It docks as a tab at the bottom, beside the Node editor and the Explorer, or floats as a window (the dock's Undock button to float, the window's Dock to put it back). Everything on this page works in both. In a narrow window or on a phone the sidebars open over the editor, one at a time (toggle buttons in the header); on a phone they start hidden, and one you open stays open next time.

When the workspace has the keyboard, it keeps it: WASD never fly the camera from here (see Keys follow the panel you are in). In the undocked window the tabs sit in the title bar and can be clicked; the title bar around them still drags the window.

docs.title: Editing and saving
docs.text:
Type, then press Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on a Mac) or Save. A ● on a tab means it has unsaved edits; Revert throws them away.

Saving checks the code first. If it does not parse, nothing is applied: the tab shows a red !, the banner names the line (click it to jump there), and every node the code feeds shows an amber edit not applied badge while it keeps running the last good version.

A save refused.

When the code is good, everything that runs it reloads — on every player's screen.

Unsaved changes are guarded. Closing a tab with unsaved edits asks first. Closing the whole workspace with unsaved files asks Save all / Don't save / Cancel — a file whose code has an error is not saved, and the dialog says so. Leaving the page with unsaved code shows the browser's warning.

Undo and redo (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y) step through saved code edits, on every peer; an open tab follows them.

docs.title: Editing together
docs.text:
Since 1.42, when two or more people in a session open the same code — a Script node, a Behaviour node, a script file, or a text document — they type into one shared text. Everyone sees the others' typing as it happens, and two people typing in the same line both keep what they typed: nothing is overwritten.

Editing together.

  • The other person's caret and selection show in their colour (hover the caret for their name). The strip under the toolbar, Editing with you, lists everyone in the file and the line they are on; a screen reader reads it as "Ana is on line 4, 12 characters selected".
  • Ctrl+S saves exactly as before: the node (or file) gets the text as it is now, for everyone. A tab shows ● while anybody's edits are unsaved; once somebody saves, every person's tab is clean.
  • Ctrl+Z undoes only your own typing, never someone else's.
  • Revert on a shared tab throws away the unsaved edits of everyone in that file.
  • Someone who joins later and opens the file sees the current text, including edits nobody has saved yet.
  • A viewer (a cloud room's read-only role) sees the text move but cannot type.

The shared text lives only while somebody has the file open; what lands in the scene or the file is always what someone saved. It travels over the same direct peer-to-peer connection as everything else — no server.

docs.title: Text documents
docs.text: Text files in the Explorer (.txt, .md …) open in the Code tab too: select one and press Edit in its preview, double-click it, or right-click ▸ Edit in the Code tab — and they are shared the same way.

docs.title: Pop out to its own window
docs.text:
Pop out (↗) in the workspace header opens the whole code workspace in its own browser window — drag it to a second monitor and keep the 3D view full-size in the app. Desktop browsers only (hidden on phones, touch screens and in VR).

The code workspace in its own window.

  • Everything stays live both ways: typing, Ctrl+S applying the script to the scene, the error banner and Problems, the sidebars, quick open, menus — and editing together.
  • While the window is open the app's own Code panel steps aside; opening code anywhere in the app (Edit code on a node, a .js file in the Explorer) brings that window to the front.
  • Dock back in the window's header — or simply closing the window — puts the editor back in the app, docked or floating as it was. Closing or reloading the app tab closes the code window too.
  • The window follows the app's theme, High contrast and UI scale, and remembers its size and place for next time.
  • If the browser blocks pop-ups, a notice says so with Try again (or allow pop-ups for the site).
  • Since 1.46 every other panel can pop out the same way, and the code window takes more tabs — see Windows on several monitors.

docs.title: Sidebars
docs.text: The code workspace.

docs.title: Left: Open editors and Project
docs.text:
Ctrl+B shows or hides the left sidebar. (Outside the code workspace the same keys, and Ctrl+Alt+B, show and hide the app's own sidebars.)

  • Open editors lists every open tab, in the same order as the tab strip. Drag a row to reorder (the strip follows); ✕ closes it (unsaved files ask first).
  • Project lists every script in the scene as a tree, with a search box:
    • Graphs — per graph (Main first, then each object's), its Script nodes, Behaviour nodes and the Player's code, plus graph.json (the whole graph as editable JSON).
    • Files — the text files in your Library (.js .md .json .txt .cfg) and their folders, with how many nodes run each script. You can make and manage them right here — see Files and folders.
    • Module sources — the module and kit files the game uses, read-only (see Module code).
  • The search also matches folder names (minigolf rules).
  • Drag the line between the two sections to share the height; double-click it to reset. Drag the sidebar's edge to resize it — the width is remembered.

docs.title: Files and folders
docs.text:
Since 1.46 the Files group of the Project tree is a real file tree: what you make here are ordinary Explorer files, so they follow the Explorer's sharing rules and everyone in the session sees them.

The Project tree's menu on a script.

  • New file (the page-with-plus button in the Project header, or the right-click menu) offers Script (a behaviour with the lifecycle functions ready to fill in), Note (.md) and JSON. A new script opens in a tab straight away.
  • New folder makes a folder inside the one you right-clicked (or at the top).
  • Rename (F2): type a bare name and the extension is kept (boss stays boss.js). Text file names are unique across the library, because shared typing keys on the name.
  • Move: drag a file or folder onto another folder, use Move to ▸, or Ctrl+X then Ctrl+V on the destination.
  • Delete (Del) moves it to Deleted, where Restore brings it back.
  • Undo: Ctrl+Z while the tree has focus (or Undo on the toast) undoes the last file operation — one step each. It never touches the scene's own undo history.
  • The menu also opens with Shift+F10 or the Menu key, and works in the pop-out window too.
  • Viewers can browse and read; making, renaming, moving and deleting say why they are not available.

docs.title: Right: Outline, Problems, Bound nodes, Find
docs.text:
Ctrl+Alt+B shows or hides the right sidebar. It has four tool tabs:

  • Outline — the active file's params, state, handlers, methods and functions, a script's inputs and returned outputs, a graph's nodes. Click one to jump to its line.
  • Problems — syntax errors and lint advice (for example, Math.random breaks peer sync) for every open file as you type, plus anything a node reported while running. The tab shows a count; click a problem to jump to it.
  • Bound nodes — which graph nodes run this file. Click one to select it in the Node editor (entering its group if it is inside one).
  • Find in files (Ctrl+Shift+F) — searches every script in the project, open files' unsaved text first. Toggles: match case, whole word, regular expression, include module sources. Click a result to open it at its line.

docs.title: Tabs, quick open and the keyboard
docs.text:
• With many tabs the tab strip scrolls: the mouse wheel scrolls it sideways and a thin scrollbar shows. The active tab is always scrolled into view. Drag a tab to reorder it.
  • Ctrl+P — quick open: open any script in the project by typing part of its name (letters in order: plwa finds Player: walk). ↑/↓ and Enter.
  • Ctrl+Shift+O — go to symbol: jump to a function, handler, param or state key of the current file.
  • The tab strip, Open editors, the Project tree and the tool tabs are each one Tab stop. ←/→ (strip, tools) and ↑/↓ (lists) move, ←/→ in the tree close and open folders, Enter opens, Delete closes a tab.

docs.title: The Player's code
docs.text:
Since 1.25 the Player card in a game's graph (a Character Controller, such as Player: walk in Mini Golf, Escape Room, Sky Run and Towers) opens its code like any other code node: double-click it, or right-click ▸ Open code. The code runs every frame on each player's own machine and decides how that player moves:

// settings = the card's values { mode, speed, jumpHeight, eyeHeight, gravity }
// input    = this player's keys { x, z, jump, sprint (Shift), crouch (Ctrl) }
// time     = seconds since Play started
if (input.sprint) return { speed: settings.speed * 1.8 };   // hold Shift to run
return {};                                                  // anything left out keeps the card's value
  • Ctrl+S saves it — checked first (broken code never applies), sent to everyone, one undo step.
  • A wrong key or type in what you return shows on the node's red error badge.
  • Engine source (toolbar) shows the built-in walker code it steers, read-only.
  • With no code saved, the Player behaves exactly as before.

Player: walk open in the code workspace.

docs.title: Code and files
docs.text:
• Save as file turns a node's inline code into a script file in your Explorer and binds the node to it.
  • Use file… binds a node to a script file you already have.
