That includes the numbers inside node editor cards, shader nodes and the animation window — dragging one of those scrubs the value without dragging the card. Scrubbing an animation key or a shader parameter is one undo step, not one per pixel.

Since 1.25 that holds for every slider and number field inside a node — every node type, and the knobs in a behaviour's Open view: a drag changes the value, never the node and never the whole graph, and the behaviour view no longer flickers the cursor.

In a behaviour's Open view, a param's knob drags its value, not the graph.

Fields that hold a distance or an angle also accept a typed unit (12cm, 4in, 90deg) — see Units.

docs.title: Number fields and undo
docs.text:
Since 1.27 every number field you can drag — the Inspector's Position / Rotation / Scale and its other values, shader-node vectors, and the Animation window's length, speed, fps, step and key fields — works the same way with undo:

  • One drag is one undo step. However far you scrub, one Ctrl+Z puts the value back where the drag started. (Before, a shader vector took two, and the Animation window's length, fps and step took one per pixel moved.)
  • One typed edit is one undo step. Click a field, type a value (it applies as you type) and press Enter: that is one step, even if you paused between keys.
  • Esc cancels typing. It puts back the value the field had before you started, as it already did for arrow-key steps, and leaves nothing on the undo stack.
  • Undo shows at once. After Ctrl+Z the Position / Rotation / Scale rows show the restored numbers straight away — before, they kept the old number until you clicked something, and dragging from it made the object jump.
  • The Animation window's playback Speed is undoable now too.
  • Selecting a shader node is not an edit. Clicking a node in the Shader editor selects it on your screen only: it adds no undo step and is not sent to the other people in the session.

docs.title: Copy, paste and reset values
docs.text:
Since 1.34 every value in the Properties panel and in Configure Scene can be copied, pasted and reset — one number, a whole vector (Position / Rotation / Scale), a colour, a choice, an on/off switch, or a whole section (all of Transform, all of Material…). What you copy is plain text, so you can paste it into a notepad or a code editor, edit it there, and paste it back.

Where:

  • Right-click a value (desktop) or press and hold it (phone or tablet): Copy, Paste, Reset to default.
  • Right-click a vector's name (Position): Copy vector, Paste vector, Reset, and Paste X / Y / Z only. Right-click one of its X / Y / Z boxes for that single number.
  • Right-click a section header (TRANSFORM): Copy section, Copy as JSON (indented, for a code editor), Paste section, Reset section. With several objects selected: Paste to all selected (N).
  • Keyboard (as in Blender): point at a field or a section header and press Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V (⌘C / ⌘V on a Mac). While you are typing in a box, Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy text as usual.

A vector row's right-click menu: copy, paste, reset, or paste one axis.

A section header's right-click menu.

What the clipboard holds:

Copied Text one value 1.25 a vector position: 1.25, 0, -3 a colour #ff8800 a choice Median point (the label you see) a section {"transform":{"position":[1.25,0,-3],"rotation":[0,90,0],"scale":[1,1,1]}}

Numbers are in the units the panel shows (Settings ▸ Units) — metres, centimetres… — and rotations in degrees.

What you can paste: a number; 1, 2, 3; 1 2 3; Vector3(1, 2, 3); new THREE.Vector3(1, 2, 3); [1, 2, 3]; (1, 2, 3); position: 1, 2, 3; {"x": 1, "y": 2, "z": 3}; { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }; the JSON blocks above; several name: value lines (a section); a unit suffix (12cm, 0, 4in, 90deg); colours as #f80, #ff8800, 0xff8800, rgb(255, 128, 0) or [1, 0.5, 0]; true / off.

  • A vector pastes into any vector: copy a Position and paste it as a Scale.
  • A section paste applies only the keys that section has.
  • If the clipboard holds the wrong kind of thing, the paste is refused with a short reason (Expected x, y, z — the clipboard holds one number) and nothing changes.
  • Every paste is one undo step — one value, a vector, a section or a paste to all selected; one Ctrl+Z puts it back.

Reset to default is greyed out where a row has no known default. The first Paste from a menu may ask the browser for clipboard permission; Ctrl+V over a field never asks. Text boxes (names, banner text) keep the browser's own text menu.

docs.title: Text selection
docs.text: Dragging across a menu, a toolbar or a panel does not paint a text selection, and a drag that starts in the 3D view or the node editor never selects text. Text fields, code, chat, logs and help text stay selectable as usual. Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Allow text selection everywhere turns selection back on in all the interface (this device only).

docs.title: The menu on a phone
docs.text: The logo menu fits a short screen — a landscape phone, or a docked Connect bar — and scrolls with a finger, with no visible scrollbar. On a folding phone it stays right through folding and unfolding with the page open.

docs.title: Floating windows
docs.text:
The toolboxes, the Explorer, the flow and animation windows and the panels all behave the same way: drag the header (or, since 1.35, any empty part of the window) to move, drag the bottom-right corner to resize. A window can never be sized past the edge of the screen — the resize corner always stays reachable — and double-clicking the corner resets it to its default size while leaving it where you parked it. Size and position are remembered per window.

A window also keeps its header: it cannot be dragged so far down that the header hides under the Controls pill, the bottom band on a touch or narrow screen, the dock, or a browser overlay — there is always something left to grab. A tall toolbox parked near the bottom scrolls its body instead of losing its head.

A right-click while you drag a window — by its title bar, a resize corner or a tab — no longer pops up the browser's menu; a normal right-click elsewhere behaves as before. Tabs that sit in a window's title bar, like the undocked Code window's, can be clicked, while the title bar around them still drags the window.

Move a window by any empty part of it (since 1.35): press and drag anywhere on a floating window that is not a control — the filter row's padding, the empty space under a list, the space around a table — and the window moves, with a mouse or a finger. A plain click or tap still does what it always did: buttons press, filters toggle, rows select. Lists that scroll, text fields, sliders, graphs and 3D views keep their own drag. A window that is a tab of a group moves by its tab strip, as before.

Dock it by dragging. Drag a floating window (by its header or its body) onto the dock's tab strip to make it a dock tab at that spot, onto the bottom edge to add it at the end, or to the left or right edge (or over an open sidebar) to make it a sidebar tab. A highlight shows where it will land before you let go. This works on a touch screen too — on an unfolded phone or a tablet the same targets are there.

docs.title: Moving a floating window
docs.text:
A floating window dragged by its header over a sidebar, the dock's tab strip, the bottom edge or another window's header docks there by default — the target lights up and says what will happen (Add as tab, Move to dock, a marker between dock tabs, a highlighted header). Under the target a second line reads Hold Ctrl to place without docking (Cmd on a Mac).

Hold Ctrl (Cmd) while you drag to place the window floating exactly where you drop it, even on top of a sidebar or the dock: every dock target stands down, and a small label beside the pointer reads Placing without docking — release Ctrl to dock. You can press or release the key at any moment during the drag; the target follows the key at once. It works for a single window, a window group dragged by its tab strip, and a tab torn out of a group.

A floating window dragged over a sidebar: drop to add it as a tab, or hold Ctrl.

The same drag with Ctrl held: the window will land over the sidebar, not in it.

On a touch screen there is no key to hold: drop the window anywhere it is not over a target, or press and hold a docked window's tab and pick Undock into a floating window to take it out as a floating one.

docs.title: The window menu
docs.text:
Right-click a floating window's header — or press and hold it on a touch screen — for:

Entry What it does Dock to bottom the window becomes a tab of the bottom dock Move to left sidebar / Move to right sidebar the window becomes a tab of that sidebar Float (undock) on a tab of a window group: takes that window out of the group Group with… lists the other open windows that can share tabs (the toolbox cannot; Statistics can since 1.39) Bring to front puts it above the other floating windows Reset size back to its default size, where it is Close closes it

The same menu opens on a tab of a floating window with tabs. The header itself is unchanged.

A floating window's header menu.

For the bottom dock's own buttons — Undock, Split, closing a view from its tab, Dock all tabs on a floating window — and for docking a window into an exact slot by dropping it on the dock's tab bar, see Windows and tabs.

docs.title: Docking to a screen edge
docs.text:
Drag a window's header to the left or right edge of the screen and a blue strip appears: let go and it docks on that side, out of the way of the viewport. Drag its header back into the middle and it floats again, where it was before.

Since 1.33 each side has one sidebar, and every window docked there is a tab of it — next to Configure Scene / Properties and the Objects list. Drop a window on a side that already has a sidebar (Add as tab lights up) and it joins as a tab; a second window on an edge no longer splits the column. A layout saved with two windows stacked on one edge comes back as two tabs. Since 1.34 every window that docks at the bottom can be a sidebar tab, with no second header, and every drop is highlighted first (Float here, Move to dock, Add as tab). Switching tabs, the tab menu, dragging a tab, the width and Full height are described in Sidebars.

Docking needs the wider layout: a computer, a tablet or an unfolded phone, where since 1.35 a finger drags a window onto the same targets. On a folded phone the panels are tabs of the bottom dock instead.

docs.title: Workspace layouts
docs.text:
Save the windows you have open — which panels, docked or floating, their sizes, the sidebars and the bottom dock, tab groups — and the toolbar under a name, and switch between arrangements in one click.

  • Where: Menu ▸ Layouts, or Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Windows & chrome ▸ Workspace layouts.
  • Save: arrange the windows, type a name, press Save. Saving under a name you already have (in any case) updates that layout.
  • Use: click a saved layout to apply it. Rename or delete it from the same list.

Menu ▸ Layouts opens the list as a regular dialog; Esc, its ✕ or a click outside closes it. On a folded phone it is the Layouts tab of the bottom dock instead (also on the dock's +) — see The dock on a phone.

Layouts are kept on this device. A reload still starts with a clean slate: a layout is applied only when you pick one.

A layout keeps the toolbar too (since 1.33): which buttons are on it and where it sits, the corner buttons, the top-right group, the touch tools, and the lift and Always on top switches. Since 1.35 it also keeps where every button cluster sits and whether it is rotated, the Connect bar's Pinned / Float choice, and the dock's splits. The desktop and the phone are kept separately in the same layout: saving on a computer (or an unfolded phone) stores the desktop toolbar, saving on a folded phone stores the phone bar, and saving the same name on the other one adds its part without touching the first. Applying a layout brings back both. The list marks each layout with a monitor and/or a phone icon for the parts it holds. Layouts saved before 1.33 restore the windows only and leave the toolbar as it is.

docs.title: The toolbar
docs.text:
Since 1.30 the toolbar is one glass bar where the accent marks the armed tool or an open window and Play is the only orange button; on a touch screen its buttons are 44 px. See The Interface.

Pressing a toolbar button never takes the keyboard: the keys stay with whatever had them — this holds for the bottom toolbar, the Connect bar, the touch tools, the draw, sculpt, spline and mesh-edit toolboxes and module toolboxes. So "press Move, then F" still frames the selection from the 3D view.

The bar at the bottom of the screen is yours to arrange. Right-click (or long-press) any of its buttons. Since 1.34 a right-click anywhere on the toolbar — between two buttons, on its edge — opens the toolbar's menu (Edit positions, Move toolbar, Always on top, Customize toolbar…), never the browser's; so do the round corner buttons. A button's own menu has:

Entry What it does Swap with ▸ exchange this button for one that is not on the bar Edit positions drag every button into place on the bar itself — see Edit positions Move left / Move right one place along the bar — past the play button when it is next Hide button take it off the bar (Customize toolbar brings it back) Move toolbar move the whole bar: with a mouse it follows the pointer — click to place it, the arrow keys nudge, Esc puts it back; on a touch screen drag the bar with your finger and lift to place it, or press Cancel above the bar. Disabled on a screen too narrow to move it Reset toolbar position back to the middle Always on top paint the bar over the dock and floating windows (by default they cover it) Lift toolbar above docked panels on by default: while the Node editor or the Explorer is docked at the bottom, the toolbar moves up above the dock Lift corner buttons above docked panels off by default: the round corner buttons (chat, microphone, AI assistant, add…) move up above the dock too; off, the dock covers them Collapse / Expand toolbar shrink the bar down to the play button, and back Customize toolbar… a checklist of every tool, the two corner stacks included: tick to show, untick to hide, ▲/▼ to reorder; Edit positions… at the top; Reset toolbar goes back to the default buttons and order

The two Lift switches are also in a corner button's right-click menu, next to Always on top, and in Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Windows & chrome.

docs.title: The "…" button
docs.text: The … at the right end of the bar opens Customize toolbar…. Since 1.34 it is a button like any other: right-click it for the toolbar menu, choose Hide button to take it off the bar, or untick … (Customize toolbar) in Customize toolbar…. In Edit positions it carries a red −, and the bar's green + offers it back. It always sits at the end of the bar. With it hidden, Customize toolbar… is still the last row of every toolbar button's right-click menu.

docs.title: When the buttons do not fit
docs.text: When there is not room for every button — you switched them all on, or a pinned sidebar takes part of the bottom edge — the buttons that do not fit move into a » button at the end of the bar. They leave from the right end first (in the order you arranged them), and Play never moves. Click » for the hidden buttons: they work exactly as on the bar, and the list ends with Customize toolbar…. Make the sidebar narrower (or unpin it) and the buttons come back by themselves — nothing is switched off, and Customize toolbar… still lists them as on the bar. Edit positions always shows every button, wrapping onto more rows when it needs to.

docs.title: The toolbar and sidebars
docs.text:
• Full-height sidebars: the toolbar never slides under one. Dragging it, or Move toolbar, stops at the sidebar's edge, and leaves room for the corner buttons beside it.
  • Edit positions lays its bar beside any open sidebar, full height or not, moving the bar only as far as it has to; while it runs, the corner buttons and the buttons beside the logo sit beside any open sidebar too. Outside it, the buttons beside the logo follow a pinned (full-height) left sidebar, like the logo.
  • The top of the screen jumps, it does not slide (since 1.36): when a sidebar is pinned, unpinned or closed, the logo, the buttons beside it, the corner buttons, the profile and the Connect bar move to their new place at once.
  • Lift corner buttons above docked panels, when on, also moves the corner buttons beside a full-height sidebar on their side, and back down to the bottom edge when the dock is hidden.

docs.title: Edit positions
docs.text: Right-click any button on the bottom toolbar — or press and hold it on a touch screen — and pick Edit positions. Every place you can arrange switches to edit mode at once.

docs.title: Moving the clusters
docs.text:
Since 1.35 the screen has six clusters you can place anywhere: the toolbar, the bottom-left and bottom-right corner buttons, the buttons beside the logo, the top-right buttons and the Connect bar. (The logo and your profile picture stay where they are.) In Edit positions every cluster has a small grip:

  • Drag the grip to move the whole cluster anywhere. It snaps to the screen's edges and centre lines, the sidebar edges and the other clusters — a dashed guide line shows what it snapped to. Clusters never overlap each other, the logo or the profile: dropped on top of something, a cluster moves to the nearest free spot.
  • Tap the grip (or right-click / long-press any button of the cluster) for its menu: Move, Rotate to vertical / Rotate to horizontal (the toolbar stands on the left edge; corner buttons lie in a row), Reset position, Reset all positions, Hide cluster / Show all (the toolbar cannot be hidden — Play lives there). The Connect bar does not rotate; its menu has Pin to top row / Float instead.
  • The Connect bar's menu works outside Edit positions too (since 1.36): right-click the Connect bar — or press and hold it on a touch screen — for Move, Pin to top row / Float, Reset position and Reset all. A moved Connect bar stays where you put it.
  • The buttons beside the logo are hidden by default on a computer. In Edit positions their menu's Show cluster turns them on (it switches on Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Touch tools), and their grip moves them like every other cluster.
  • The budget chip (Quest 3% beside the toolbar) is a cluster too since 1.39. Drag its grip — or the chip itself — anywhere; it snaps like the others and keeps its place in your layouts. Its menu (tap its grip, or right-click it) ▸ Reset position puts it back beside the toolbar (or left of it, or above it, when there is no room). Its red − hides it — a hidden chip is drawn faint in Edit positions with a green + to bring it back — and so does unticking Budget chip in Customize toolbar… (on by default).
  • ✓ applies, Esc cancels. A cluster keeps its relative place: on a smaller window, after folding or unfolding a phone, beside a pinned sidebar or above the dock. Workspace layouts carry the places and rotations.

Edit positions, in a small window: every cluster has a grip, every button a red −.

In Edit positions the budget chip has its own grip and red −.

Clusters after Rotate to vertical and Rotate to horizontal.

A cluster's grip menu, with Show cluster and Show all.

docs.title: Arranging the buttons
docs.text:
Single buttons move between the clusters as before. The places that take buttons:

  • The bottom toolbar and the two bottom corners.
  • The top-right group — Scene notes, Notifications and Connected peers, left of your profile picture. Notifications and Connected peers always stay in this group, because their panels open from that corner; Scene notes can go anywhere. Connected peers only shows while someone is connected, but in edit mode its place is always drawn so you can move it. Remove every button from this group and it disappears completely — no empty box; in Edit positions it shows again, with a + to put buttons back.
  • The row beside the logo (the touch tools: Undo, Redo and Multi-select) — since 1.34 with a mouse too, not only on a touch screen. Reorder them, drag one onto the bottom toolbar or into a corner, remove them, or put other buttons beside the logo. Once you change that row it stays shown (this switches on Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Touch tools); an empty row shows nothing. Workspace layouts keep it.
  • The Connect bar at the top carries a red − to hide it — see The Connect bar.
  • The main menu button and your profile picture stay where they are.

Then:

  • Drag any button to a new place: along the bar, into a corner, the top-right group or the row beside the logo. Play can move along the bar but always stays on it.
  • The small red − on a button removes it.
  • A stack shows one green + for its next place; it opens a list of every button from Customize toolbar… that is not placed yet (Play is never in it). Pick one to put it there.
  • Each corner — and the top-right group and the row beside the logo — holds up to four buttons; once a stack holds four, its + is gone. By default the left corner has the AI assistant and the + (add) button, the right corner Chat and the microphone.
  • With the keyboard: Tab to a button, then the arrow keys move it (← / → along the bar and into the corners, ↑ / ↓ inside a corner) and Delete removes it.
  • The round green ✓ at the top right of the toolbar applies the new layout. Esc, or a click anywhere else, cancels it.

Edit positions on a computer: the bottom toolbar.

Edit positions reaching the top right of the screen.

The Connect bar in Edit positions.

The menus name buttons by their short name — Pivot, Microphone; the toolbar's own tooltips still tell you the pivot mode and how to talk.

The layout is saved on this device, like Customize toolbar…. Reset toolbar (in Customize) or Settings ▸ Reset window positions puts everything back. A custom button order no longer shows the wrong icons after a reload. On a folded phone the app shows its own phone bar instead — arrange it by dragging items between More and the bar; there More can come off the bar and Play can move along it (see The phone bar and More).

The play button's right-click menu chooses how you play — Play (desktop), Enter VR, Enter AR passthrough (greyed out where the device cannot) — and, in a scene that is a game, Test play (start from the menu), which resets the game to its menu and starts from the Start screen. See Build a Game Loop. On a folded phone, press and hold Play for the phone's version of this menu — Play as, Test play, Move left / Move right and Arrange the bar…; see On a phone.

docs.title: The Connect bar
docs.text:
Since 1.35 the Connect bar is either pinned or floating. Open its drawer (the chevron) and use the Pinned / Float button (the lock in the drawer's header), or right-click the Connect bar (press and hold it on a touch screen) — since 1.36 in or out of Edit positions — for Move, Pin to top row / Float, Reset position and Reset all:

  • Pinned to the top row — a full-width bar along the top; the corner buttons drop below it. The default on a touch screen (an unfolded phone). With a sidebar open below it, the bar's corner on that side is square.
  • Float — the centred pill, the default with a mouse. When the top row is too full for it, it shrinks to its compact form (the status dot and the chevron); tap the dot for the full bar, and it grows back by itself when room returns.

The Connect bar's right-click menu, outside Edit positions.

Each kind of screen (touch or mouse) remembers its own choice, and layouts carry it. On a folded phone Connect is the chip in the phone's top bar, unchanged.

  • Hide or show it: in Edit positions the Connect bar at the top has a red −; press it to hide the bar. A + Connect stays in its place until you press ✓, and brings it back whenever you edit again. Or untick Connect bar in Customize toolbar… (section Top). On a folded phone the Connect chip stays.
  • Hidden stays hidden: buttons you hide (for example Notifications) stay hidden everywhere — after a reload and on the folded phone as well.

See also The Connect panel.

docs.title: The Settings window
docs.text: Settings (logo menu ▸ Settings) is a window with a grouped menu of categories on the left — on a phone, a list you tap into — a search box in the header, and one row per setting. Changes save as you make them. Since 1.26 it has its own page: see Settings.

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text:
Ctrl+K opens the command palette: one search over tools, windows, menus and every setting.

Shortcuts are inert while you type in a text field and while play mode owns the keyboard. The same list is shown in Settings ▸ Shortcuts (Ctrl+/ opens it directly), where a click on a shortcut's keys rebinds it and Reset all puts the defaults back.

The keys in the table are the 3D view's: they fire while the 3D view has focus. A panel you click in gets its own keys — see Keys follow the panel you are in.

Every keyboard layout works. A letter shortcut is matched by the letter printed on the key when there is one — AZERTY, Dvorak and QWERTZ keep their own labels — and by the key's physical position otherwise, so G, F, Ctrl+Z and WASD work on Russian, Greek, Hebrew, Arabic and CJK layouts without switching. Where the browser can tell, Settings ▸ Shortcuts shows your layout's own label beside each letter (п on your layout); where it cannot, a note says letter shortcuts follow the QWERTY position.

Finding a setting

Settings is grouped into General (Interface, Controls, Input, Touch controls, Shortcuts), Workspace (Scene, Explorer, Node types, Export) and Devices & services (VR, AI, Connection, Privacy), with About & what's new at the bottom. If you don't know which one holds what you want, type in the search box: it matches names, descriptions and the words people use — dark finds the theme, southpaw finds Swap sticks. See Finding your way.

Keys Action 1 / 2 / 3 Gizmo: move / rotate / scale (again on the active mode: hide; any mode key: bring the selection back) G Move (grab) — same as 1 W A S D Fly the camera (horizontal) Q / E Fly down / up Shift (hold) Fly 3× faster F Focus the selected object Ctrl+D Duplicate the selection (whole set) Ctrl+A Select all objects (inside Edit Mesh: every element) Delete / Backspace Delete the selection (a group asks first) Alt+click Cycle the selection through everything under the cursor (inside and behind water) Ctrl+Alt+click Ping a spot for everyone Esc Leave isolation; leave focus mode while it is on Ctrl+Space Focus mode — maximize the area under the pointer (the 3D view alone, or a docked window filling the whole window with the viewport picture-in-picture); again to restore Z Cycle the render mode: Shaded → Shaded + AO → Wireframe Tab Enter mesh edit mode — inside it Tab cycles Vertices / Edges / Faces; Esc exits I Edit / Interact mode — in Interact, clicks play with the scene instead of selecting M Toggle element snapping O Toggle the object list N Toggle the node editor T Show / hide the tool dock (with nothing docked it opens empty, ready for a drop) Ctrl+B Show / hide the left sidebar (its tabs stay open) Ctrl+Alt+B Show / hide the right sidebar Alt+E / F / A / U / S / H Explorer / Flow Code / Animation / UV editor / Shader editor / HUD editor C Toggle chat (from the 3D view only) Shift+A Add an object at the cursor (enable in Settings) P Start / stop the physics simulation Ctrl+Enter Play / enter VR (right-click the play button for modes) ` Toggle the AI quick-prompt bar Ctrl+S Save the scene Ctrl+Shift+S Save a checkpoint Ctrl+Z Undo Ctrl+Y / Ctrl+Shift+Z Redo Shift+1…5 Recall camera bookmark 1–5 V (hold) Push-to-talk while the mic toggle is off Ctrl+/ Show the shortcut list ? Keyboard cheat sheet (every panel, the focused one first)

Inside an Edit Mesh session the bare letters E I G S B F X / W J and the loop keys (L, Ctrl++/-, Ctrl+I) belong to the mesh tools — see Mesh Editing. That is why the panel shortcuts above use Alt: they keep working while a mesh session is open. Since 1.23 the mesh tools' keys can be rebound too, in their own Mesh edit group of Settings ▸ Shortcuts.

In the viewport picture-in-picture — the small 3D view shown while a docked window is maximized (see The viewport picture-in-picture) — these keys work while the pointer is over it. They have their own Viewport picture-in-picture group in Settings ▸ Shortcuts:

Keys In the viewport picture-in-picture W / E / R Move / Rotate / Scale F Frame the selection with the picture-in-picture's own camera 1 / 2 / 3, G, Delete, Ctrl+D… as in the 3D view

Over a field in Properties or Configure Scene, Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy and paste that value (or a whole section over its header) — see Copy, paste and reset values.

docs.title: Keys follow the panel you are in
docs.text:
A shortcut fires only in the panel that has focus — the one you last clicked. The table above is the 3D view's, and the node editor has its own set: see Node editor: keyboard, groups and notes. Press ? anywhere for a cheat sheet of every panel's keys, the focused panel first.

Since 1.25 this covers every panel and tool window, docked or floating: the Explorer, the Inspector, the node editor's chrome, a behaviour's graph view, the code workspace, the HUD editor, Animation, UV, Shader, Flow Code, the Profiler, previews, chat… Clicking in one gives it the keyboard, and the panel that has the keys shows an outline.

  • W A S D / Q E never fly the camera from a panel, and the 3D view's own letters (C chat, 1/2/3, P, M…) do nothing there. Click the 3D view to give it the keys back.
  • T, N and O (the tool dock, the node editor, the object list) are window management, so they also work from a panel. So do Ctrl+B / Ctrl+Alt+B — except inside the code workspace, where they toggle its own sidebars.
  • Global keys work everywhere: Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y (also with a checkbox or slider focused, and inside the Profiler timeline), Ctrl+S, Ctrl+Enter, the Alt+letter panel toggles, ? and V (push to talk).
  • The object list keeps its own keys and the scene's selection keys — see The object list from the keyboard.
  • A panel that has no keys of its own simply ignores the 3D view's letters: click the 3D view first to fly. Inside a text field or the code editor, typing is always typing.

The ? cheat sheet and Settings ▸ Shortcuts list Panels and tool windows and Object list among the places keys belong to.

docs.title: Right-click menus
docs.text:
Empty viewport — a quick right-click opens the scene menu:

  • Search objects… — find an object in the scene by name (off by default: Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Lists & menus ▸ Object search in menu).
  • Add — the full primitive catalog (meshes, building blocks, architecture — walls, doors, windows and stairs — cameras, lights, water, effects, a fluid tank) plus empty groups; objects spawn at the clicked point.
  • Undo / Redo, Ping here.
  • Selected ▸ — the selected object's own menu (shown only while something is selected).
  • Tools — Node editor, Draw mode (drag 3D strokes on surfaces, or click out an editable spline), Measure distance, Simulate physics (and Reset simulation while one runs), Recording… (a turntable or flythrough video).
  • Snapping — position / rotation / scale steps, snap to surface, element snapping, More snapping settings… (see Snapping).
  • View — Show grid, Grid & axes settings…, Show helpers in Play (debug), the Mouse wheel mode, Scene look…, Screenshot.
  • Module tools — the toolboxes of installed modules.
  • Camera bookmarks — Save current view, the saved views, Manage saved views…, Clear bookmarks.

An object (viewport or object list) — Focus camera, Duplicate, Group selection / Ungroup, Origin and Pivot point, Convert to mesh, Transform ▸ (Drop to ground, Align, Distribute), Preview camera (on a camera); Edit: Properties, Rename, Edit shader, Edit mesh, Edit spline, Sculpt mesh; Physics & effects: Physics ▸ Weld / Hinge, Effects, Enable / Disable flow effects; Share: Add note, Ping this object, Save as…; and Delete. Ctrl+Alt+click pings anywhere in the scene (since 1.25; Alt+click now cycles the selection).

Every right-click menu can be typed into. Start typing and the menu turns into a filtered list of every entry in it, submenus included; ↑/↓ walk the rows, Enter runs one, and with nothing typed → opens a submenu and ← goes back. Esc unwinds one step at a time — the text, then the search, then the submenu, then the menu. Rows show their keyboard shortcut on the right. The search list's height can be dragged, and each kind of menu remembers it. On a touch screen nothing pops a keyboard up unless you tap the search row.

With several objects selected, the menu acts on the whole set — the entries are counted ("Delete 4 objects") — and adds Group selection, Convert to mesh (merge them into one editable mesh, materials kept) and the Physics ▸ Weld / Hinge pair. With exactly two meshes selected, right-click the first one for Boolean (union, subtract, intersect — see Mesh Editing).

docs.title: VR basics
docs.text:
Enter VR from the headset button (WebXR). The essentials below get you started; the VR Guide has the full control and radial-menu map.

  • Radial menu — press B/Y on your menu hand to toggle it (or, in hold mode, hold the button and release over a sector). Its first ring is Objects, Add, Scene, Tools, Redo, Undo, Chat and Settings (every VR setting, the microphone, exit VR); the hub is Selected when something is selected.
  • Hand tracking — hands have no B/Y, so pinch and hold (about half a second) on the menu hand to toggle the radial menu; a quick pinch stays a normal click.
  • Trigger points and selects; grip grabs and moves objects; gripping with both hands grabs the world itself to reposition yourself.
  • Floating panels (menu, objects, properties, keyboard, chat…) can be grabbed and repositioned with the grip.

Note

Everything above replicates: selection locks, transforms, notes, pings and draw strokes are all visible to your peers in real time.

docs.title: Node Graph Debugger
docs.text:
New in 1.39. The debugger lets you watch your flow graphs while you play: pause the game when an event reaches a node, step through what happens event by event, read the value on every wire into and out of a node, and keep an eye on variables in a watch list.

It is yours alone. The other players in the session keep playing, and nothing you set in the debugger is saved into the scene or sent to anyone.

The Debugger paused at a Counter.

docs.title: Breakpoints
docs.text:
In the node editor, right-click a node ▸ Breakpoint (pause Play here), or select nodes and press F9. A red dot marks the node. Remove it the same way.

Breakpoints pause on events. A pure value node (Math, Number) never pauses — watch it instead; the panel says so.

docs.title: The Debugger panel
docs.text:
Open it with the bug button in the node editor's top bar. It also opens by itself when a breakpoint pauses Play. On a phone it is a bottom sheet.

  1. Set a breakpoint on the node you want to watch — an On Click, a Counter, a Set Variable.
  2. Press Play. The game runs normally until an event reaches that node. Then your view of the game pauses just before the node runs, the pointer is freed, and the panel says Paused at ‹node›.
  3. Step (F10) runs the next event: first the one that just paused you, then each event as it arrives — a click, a key, another player's action, a Delay finishing. With nothing waiting, Step runs the next event the moment it comes.
  4. Wires lists the node's inputs (←) and outputs (→) with their current values: numbers, on/off, vectors, object names. An event wire shows ● pulse when it fires, or how long ago it did. Click a neighbour to walk the graph.
  5. Watch a variable — a Set / Get Variable name, or My variable for a per-player one — or press Watch ‹node› to follow any node's output.
  6. Resume (F8) rejoins the live game. Pause (F8 while running) pauses at any moment, without a breakpoint. Leaving Play always resumes.

The debugger works in Play (and Test play). In the editor it only lists your breakpoints and watches.

Key Does F9 Breakpoint on / off for the selected nodes F10 Step: run the next event F8 Resume, or pause while running

docs.title: What "local" means
docs.text:
While you are paused, your view is frozen and events queue up for you; the session does not stop.

  • Physics, spawns and behaviour reactions keep running for the other players.
  • With other players connected, the values every player writes together (Set Game State, a shared Set Variable) stay in your paused view. Their games already made the same write, so nothing is counted twice when you resume.

Limits

Breakpoints are off in VR — on a headset the game just keeps running. Module code keeps running while you are paused.

The Debugger in the light theme.

docs.title: Several HUD Buttons, one module input
docs.text: Also in 1.39: several HUD Buttons can be wired into one module input (a Match Button's press, a Realms Button's press) — any of them presses it. A HUD Button wires straight into a module input; the Delay "bridge" older templates used is no longer needed, and the Football and Dungeon Realms templates are simpler for it.

docs.title: Edit in Blender
docs.text: Take a model to Blender (or Maya, 3ds Max, Cascadeur, any tool that reads and writes glTF) and bring it back. The object keeps its place, flows, physics and clips. There is nothing to install.

docs.title: The round trip
docs.text:
1. Right-click the object ▸ Mesh ▸ Edit in Blender…, or use Properties ▸ Model. <object name>.glb downloads, with its rig, weights and clips if it is animated, and a short card shows these steps.
  2. In Blender: File ▸ Import ▸ glTF 2.0, pick the file, and make your edits. For a model without a rig, use Object ▸ Apply ▸ All Transforms (Ctrl+A) before exporting.

  3. File ▸ Export ▸ glTF 2.0 with these settings:

    Setting Value Format glTF Binary (.glb) Include Custom Properties: this keeps the link to the object Transform +Y Up Data ▸ Mesh Apply Modifiers Animation On, for a rigged model, so its clips go along Units Metres (Scene ▸ Units ▸ Unit Scale 1.0)

  4. Drop the exported file anywhere in theprototype. It recognises the object and asks Update ""?, with no need to select anything. If you left Custom Properties off, select the object, drop the file on it and choose Replace.

docs.title: Watch the file
docs.text:
In Chrome or Edge on a computer, the card has Watch the exported file…. Pick the .glb you export from Blender, and each time you export again theprototype offers Reload, or Always reload to update on every save. Properties ▸ Model shows the watched file with Reload automatically and Stop.

Other browsers can drop the file instead. The watch is on your computer only and ends when you reload the page. The update itself reaches everyone.

docs.title: Replace a model from any file
docs.text:
Replace model… swaps an object's model for another file, whether or not it came from Edit in Blender.

  • Where: right-click an imported model ▸ Mesh ▸ Replace model…, or Properties ▸ Model ▸ Replace model… (the only place for a single primitive such as a box). Or drop a model file onto the selected object and choose Replace. Choose Add as a new object for the old behaviour, and tick Remember for this session to stop being asked until you reload.
  • Formats: .glb, .gltf, .vrm, .fbx, .stl, and .obj (pick its .mtl and textures along with it).
  • What stays: the object itself: its name, position, rotation, scale, its parent and place in the object list, its flows and every flow node pointing at it, behaviours, physics, colliders, notes, and materials you changed in theprototype, on the part with the same name. Only the model changes.
  • Undo: one Ctrl+Z puts the old model back for everyone. The new model reaches every peer and anyone who joins later.
  • Limits: a replace is refused while a simulation runs and while someone else is editing the object.

docs.title: Animations
docs.text:
A clip the old model had and the new file lacks is kept when every bone it moves exists in the new model, matched by bone name, so re-rigging or fixing weights in another tool does not lose it.

  • A clip the new file has under the same name wins.
  • A clip that names a bone the new model lacks is dropped. The message after the replace lists what was kept and dropped.
  • Clips inside the old model's file need a .glb replacement, because they are written into the new file so everyone gets them.
  • .tpanim clips follow the same rule and stay separate files; a humanoid clip stays when the new model has humanoid bones. A dropped one comes back with Ctrl+Z.

docs.title: Checks before it is placed
docs.text:
If the new model looks off, theprototype says so and offers a one-click fix, or Replace as it is:

It looks like The fix About 100× larger or smaller than the model it replaces (the centimetre / metre mix-up, common with FBX) Scale by 0.01 (or 100) Lying on its side (exported Z-up) Stand it up Transforms not applied (a scale or a quarter turn left on the file's root) Apply transforms for models without a rig; for a rig, apply them in your tool and export again

docs.title: Earlier versions
docs.text: Ctrl+Z right after an update brings back the previous one, and earlier versions come back from checkpoints.

docs.title: Let an agent do it
docs.text: Claude Code can make the whole trip for you: see the Agents + Blender recipe.

docs.title: Explorer
docs.text:
The Explorer is the session's file library — import files, organize them into folders, preview them, share them with the people you are connected to, and drag them straight into the scene.

Open it from the Explorer button in the Controls bar, or with Alt+E. It lives as a tab in the bottom dock beside the Node editor, Animation and the other editors (T shows and hides the dock), and right-clicking its button offers Open as dock tab or Open as floating window.

Local until shared

Files you import live in your browser (IndexedDB). They stay on your device until you share them — then every peer in the session has them, in the same folders. Using an asset in the scene — placing a model, assigning a sound, dropping a texture — still pushes its bytes to everyone as before.

Project scenes are the exception. The project knows every scene by name, so a scene somebody else saved appears for you as a dimmed card with a blue dot even though you hold none of its bytes — open it and it downloads from whoever has it. See Projects.

docs.title: The tree
docs.text:
The left pane, top to bottom:

  • ＋ Mount project… and any mounted projects — see Mounting a saved project.
  • Library — your own folders and files.
  • Prefabs — objects you saved with Save as… (see Prefabs). Drop a 3D object or a scene file on the row to make one; it keeps its own format.
  • Packs — built-in and imported asset packs (see Packs). Single-click opens the packs grid; double-click expands the pack list in the tree.
  • Scene — a read-only, derived view of the assets the shared scene currently uses (audio, config scripts, textures) — identical on every peer.
  • Deleted — the recycle bin, shown while it has something in it (or while you drag something over it). See Deleted.

Folder management behaves like a file manager: right-click for New folder / New subfolder (inline naming — Enter creates, Esc cancels; names can't contain * \ /), Rename inline, and Delete folder (it confirms with folder and file counts). Drag folders onto folders (or the Library root) to re-parent — moving a folder into its own subtree is refused. The tree pane has a drag-resize splitter and per-folder expand/collapse carets, all persisted.

docs.title: Importing files
docs.text:
Drag files from your computer anywhere onto the Explorer panel:

Kind Extensions Images png, jpg, webp, heic, heif (see below) Audio mp3, wav, ogg Text / config txt, json 3D objects glb, gltf, obj, stl, fbx Scenes and projects tpscene, tp

Items are capped at 25 MB each. Images and models get generated thumbnails; audio and text show icon cards.

Importing something you already have. A file is identified by its contents, so re-importing the same bytes is not a new file. The app tells you what it already has and lets you skip it, reveal it, or — for a scene — take a real copy. The rule lives in Settings ▸ Explorer ▸ "When importing files already in your library" (Ask / Skip them / Import as copies); see Projects.

Big models are optimized as they come in (1.37): over 50k triangles or with a texture over 2048 px, an import gets an LOD chain and compressed textures, and the original stays beside it — see Importing Big Models. A model's Properties (ⓘ) hold its own Import settings and Reimport.

docs.title: HEIC / HEIF photos
docs.text:
New in 1.37. Photos from an iPhone or a modern Android (.heic, .heif, Canon .hif) import like any image: drop them on the Explorer, or pick one in a texture slot (Properties ▸ Material ▸ Texture, the UV editor's material slots, a Shader Texture node, a HUD image).

The photo is decoded once, on the device it was dropped on, into a JPEG named after it (IMG_0042.HEIC → IMG_0042.jpg). From then on it is an ordinary image: it has a thumbnail, opens in the preview window, textures objects, and peers receive the JPEG — they never need the decoder. The decoder (about 1.5 MB) downloads only the first time someone imports a HEIC, and runs off the main thread.

Limits: the longest side is capped at 8192 px; only the primary image of a burst or Live Photo is kept; a damaged file is refused with Could not read : …. The original .heic is not kept in the Library.

docs.title: When a model is too heavy
docs.text:
A model is weighed before it lands. Once the file is parsed but before anything reaches the scene, its real cost — triangles, meshes and texture size — is measured against what the scene already holds on this device. Anything within budget arrives without a word. Anything heavy enough to hurt asks first, instead of arriving and wedging the tab:

This model is heavy — "city.glb" is 2.4M triangles in 180 meshes. Imported as it is, the scene would draw 9.1M triangles a frame (this model adds 4.8M with its shadow pass), above the 8M recommended for this device. It may be slow, and on a phone or headset the tab can be closed by the browser.

There are three answers:

Answer What happens Reduce to ~400k triangles, 1024px textures The mesh is simplified on a background worker. The label names the numbers it is aiming at before you commit to it, from the same planner that will do the work. Load anyway The model arrives at full detail, exactly as it is. Cancel Nothing is imported. The scene is byte-identical — no frame drew it, no peer was sent it, and there is no undo entry to clean up.

Reduce runs in the background. A card says Reducing "city.glb"… you can keep working while it runs, and the window keeps drawing throughout — that is the point of running it off the main thread. When it finishes you are told what was done and by how much:

Reduced "city.glb": 2.4M → 380k triangles (−84%), no point moved more than 0.42% of its size; textures 4096px → 1024px.

If the result is still above what the device is recommended to hold, the report says so rather than pretending otherwise. A reduction that fails imports nothing at all — it never quietly falls back to the heavy original, because avoiding that original is what you chose.

Restore original model. The original file is kept for the rest of your session, so the object's right-click menu carries Restore original model — one undoable step that puts the full-detail version back in place, with the same name, the same position and the same identity, so flows, notes and joints keep pointing at it. Ctrl+Z goes back to the reduced one.

It can be unavailable, and it says why rather than being mysteriously greyed out:

  • On anyone else's screen. Only the machine that did the import holds the original file; a peer sees the stamp and the reason, never a button that cannot work. The tooltip reads The original file is held only by whoever imported it, and only until they reload.
  • After a reload. The file is held for the session, not saved.
  • While the object is locked by another peer.

An animated model is never reduced

A rig reaches your peers as the original file's bytes, so decimating the tree would leave them reparsing something that no longer matches. The dialog says so in the same breath — It is animated, so it cannot be reduced here: its rig reaches your peers as the original file — and offers Load anyway and Cancel only.

A model the AI assistant generates goes through exactly the same gate, with the same three answers: a generated mesh is as heavy as any other.

Oversized scenes are held at the door too, with their own ask — see Performance & Budgets.

Animations and materials come along. A .glb/.gltf or .fbx keeps its animation clips — they play in the scene and are listed per object in the Animation window — and an .obj picks up its sibling .mtl so it arrives with its materials instead of plain grey. Because no exporter can carry an animation clip, an animated model is stored as its original file when you save a scene, so it comes back animated. See Saving & Sessions.

docs.title: Sharing with the session
docs.text:
Right-click a file ▸ Share with peers, or a folder ▸ Share folder, and everyone in the session gets it — in the same place in their tree. A shared folder shares whatever you drop into it later; Unshare on one file inside it takes that one back out, and the app remembers that decision over any rule. Unsharing never deletes anybody's copy.

Every card carries a small dot that says whose it is: teal for a file you shared, sky blue for a peer's, a hollow ring for one that is no longer shared but still yours. A dot in the top corner means the file is shared but its bytes are not on your device yet — open it, or right-click ▸ Download from peers.

docs.title: Ask before sharing
docs.text: Add a file while you are connected and a strip appears below the Library: Share "‹name›" with the session? with Share and Keep local. Connecting with a library full of local files asks once for all of them (Share your 12 files with the session?), and there Stash mine is the third choice. Tick Apply to all my files, now and from now on to make it a rule — everything you add from now on is shared, or nothing is and you are not asked again. File settings opens the same rule in Settings.

docs.title: Downloads happen by themselves
docs.text:
When someone shares a file or a folder your copy is fetched straight away. Switch that off for a metered connection or a very large project with Settings ▸ Explorer ▸ Download shared files automatically — shared files still appear, greyed, and download when you open them.

The pill beside the view toggle in the Explorer header is the transfer log: Downloading 3 files — 40%, Up to date, or No peers. Click it for the files in flight with their own progress, a Retry for anything that failed, and Show full log for the whole record with per-row Retry, Cancel, Show in Explorer and Remove from log.

docs.title: Deleted
docs.text:
Deleting is never destruction. Delete on a local file, or Delete for everyone on a shared one, moves it — every peer's copy of it — into Deleted, which keeps the folder structure, so a deleted folder is still a folder there. Drag files or folders onto the Deleted row to delete them too.

  • Restore on a row puts it back where it came from, on every peer; Restore folder brings a folder back whole.
  • Drag a card out of Deleted onto a Library folder to restore it there instead.
  • Delete permanently on a row frees that one file on this device.
  • Empty Deleted (N) — under Disk in the Deleted view's right-click menu — reclaims the disk on this machine and clears the record. Peers keep their own bins. It asks first, always.
  • Clear the log (N) forgets only the records whose bytes are already gone from this device; anything still restorable stays.

The view has its own View, Group (By who deleted it) and Sort options, and Show cleaned-up files lists what was already freed.

docs.title: Browsing and opening
docs.text:
The header's Thumbnails / List toggle switches views. The list has sortable columns — Name, Type, Size, Added, Owner (in Deleted: Location, Deleted by, Deleted at) — click a header to sort, drag it sideways to reorder, drag its edge to resize, and right-click the header to choose columns or Reset widths and order. Columns and sort are remembered per view.

  • Single-click selects an item and shows its details in the ⓘ Properties panel.
  • Double-click opens it in a preview window (below); text files open in the Code tab, shared live with everyone who opens them (Ctrl+S saves back to the item).
  • Right-click an item for Open, Download, Share, Rename, Delete, Properties (and Copy contents for text files, Edit image… for images — see The Image editor).
  • The search box filters the whole library by name; the breadcrumb path bar (toggleable) shows where you are.

Keyboard navigation in the grid: arrow keys move the selection, Enter opens, Backspace goes up a level, Esc clears the selection, Delete deletes the selection.

docs.title: On a phone
docs.text:
• Press and hold a file or folder to open its actions as a sheet: Rename, Duplicate, Copy, Download, Share, Properties, Delete and the rest. The sheet stays open when you lift your finger (Android's own long-press signal used to close it straight away), and the browser's own long-press menu and text callout do not appear on Explorer items.
  • Hold, then move to pick the item up and drop it into a folder.
  • While you rename an item, the selected text is readable in every theme.
  • The Explorer's toolbar scrolls sideways when it does not fit, so the project name is always reachable.

On a phone the Explorer is a tab of the bottom dock, like Properties, Objects and the other windows — see The dock on a phone. Its sidebar starts hidden so the files get the screen; open it with its edge button and it stays open next time.

docs.title: Selecting several
docs.text:
• Ctrl+click adds or removes a card; Shift+click selects the range from the last card you clicked (Ctrl+Shift+click adds the range).
  • Ctrl+A selects everything in the folder, Ctrl+I inverts the selection. With the grid focused these keys never reach the scene behind the panel.
  • Drag on empty grid space to draw a marquee (with the mouse — on a touch screen a drag scrolls the grid, and holding a card, then moving, picks it up instead). Hold Ctrl to add to what is already selected.
  • Right-click a selection for the batch actions: Download N files as .zip, Export N objects as GLTF, Share / Unshare N items, Copy, Cut, Duplicate and Delete.
  • Drag a selection onto a folder to move all of it, or into the viewport to place every object.

docs.title: The project and the scene you have open
docs.text:
The Explorer header shows where you are: ‹Project› ▸ ‹Scene› [file.tpscene], a save button and a ● while the scene has changes that are not in its latest version.

  • Click the project name to rename the project.
  • Click the scene name to find its file in the library. Double-click it — or right-click ▸ Rename scene… — to rename the scene. Every version file is renamed with it, on every peer, and Travel nodes that point at it keep working.
  • The save button does what Ctrl+S does: it saves the open scene as a new version.

Who is in each scene. A scene card shows small avatars for the people standing in that scene — you included — and a count. Its right-click menu has Join ‹name› for each of them: it travels you to that scene, where they are, even if you have not downloaded it yet (you leave the scene you are in). Unsaved changes are asked about first, as below.

docs.title: Opening a scene over unsaved work
docs.text: Opening another scene — from its menu, by double-click, or with Join — replaces what is on screen. If the scene you have open has unsaved changes, or has never been saved at all, the app asks first: Open "Arena"? with Save and open (saves a version of the current scene, then opens) or Open anyway.

docs.title: Duplicate, Copy, Cut and Paste
docs.text:
Right-click a file or a folder for Duplicate (Duplicate folder), Copy and Cut; right-click a folder or the grid background for Paste — the entry says what it holds (Paste 2 files + 1 folder). With the grid focused the keys are Ctrl+D / C / X / V, on one card or a whole selection (Duplicate 3 items).

  • A duplicate lands beside its source as Tower copy.glb, then Tower copy 2.glb; pasted into another folder it keeps its name unless that collides.
  • A cut row dims to half until you paste it, and a cut is spent by one paste; a copy can be pasted again.
  • A copy is local until you share it — unless it lands in a shared folder, which shares it like anything else you drop there.
  • Prefabs duplicate too (Prefab copy). Packs are read-only bundles: Duplicate is greyed out and says so.
  • Duplicate folder copies everything in it under a new folder beside it.

A scene is different: its name lives inside the file, so Duplicate on a scene opens the naming card prefilled with Arena copy — type a name, Enter — and makes a scene of its own, with its own version history. Copy and Paste (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V) on a scene pastes it straight away as Arena copy — a new scene with its own name and history, not a second card for the same file. A name that is already taken is refused with a toast. To duplicate a scene, select it on its own; in a bigger selection it is skipped and the toast says so.

A copy costs your peers no download

A shared file travels as a row with its own identity beside its content hash. When you duplicate a shared file — or a whole shared folder — peers who already hold the bytes make the copy from their own disk: ten copies, zero transfers. Deleting a copy removes only that copy; editing one gives it new bytes, which are sent once. A scene copy is the exception, because its new name makes it a new file: it transfers once.

docs.title: The preview window
docs.text:
Images open zoomable (− / ＋ / 1:1, drag to pan) with a pencil button that opens the Image editor, sounds open with a player, and 3D models open on a turntable with an animation transport — play, step a frame with , and ., scrub, pick a clip — and a mesh-stats line. The ← / → buttons page through the folder without closing the window, and ⌐ goes up a level.

The window's ⚙ holds two things worth knowing: Opacity fades the window so you can model against a reference picture, and Passthrough lets clicks reach the scene underneath while the header stays live to move it or switch it back. Allow multiple windows opens each file in a window of its own instead of re-pointing the one you have.

docs.title: Item properties (ⓘ)
docs.text:
The ⓘ panel shows name, kind, size, folder path, added date and the content hash (copyable), plus per-kind details — image dimensions, audio duration and channels, text line count. For 3D objects it can embed a rotatable inline 3D preview with mesh stats (triangles / vertices / meshes) — enabled by the 3D model preview toggle in the ⚙ tab. Double-clicking an object always opens the larger preview regardless of that toggle.

The ⚙ settings tab holds local preferences: single-click opens folders, show path bar, 3D model preview, stack multiple drops on one spot, confirm before updating a prefab, hide built-in packs, and the Import pack (.zip) button.

docs.title: Prefabs that are files
docs.text: Right-click an object in the viewport ▸ Save as… and choose the format. Prefab is the classic snapshot; Prefab (.glb) and Prefab (.tpscene) make a prefab that is a file — the .glb carries geometry, materials and baked animation, the .tpscene also carries animation clips, object flow graphs, shader graphs and joints — so it can be dragged into the Library, shared, and exported as the exact bytes it was saved as (Export ▸ The original file). The last two entries, glTF binary (.glb) and glTF (.gltf), are plain downloads. See Prefabs.

docs.title: A session you joined
docs.text:
When you join someone's session, a new root appears at the top of the Explorer tree, above your mounted projects and your Library: "'s session", with a banner over it: You're in 's session · saves go to .

  • On a phone the folder tree starts hidden: tap Show folder tree (the arrow at the Explorer's edge) to see it.
  • It shows the files the host chose to share (see Join a session ▸ What guests see), in the host's own folders, with their names, kinds and sizes. Thumbnails arrive a moment after the list.
  • It is read-only: you cannot rename, move, delete or drop files into it. Your own Library is never mixed with it.
  • Nothing is downloaded when you join. A file's bytes come from the host only when you open or copy it.
  • Open (double-click) — images and videos open in the preview, text files open in the text editor marked Read-only (no Save). Scenes, 3D models and sounds ask you to Copy to my library first.
  • Copy to my library (right-click a file or a folder, or drag it onto your Library) — the file becomes an ordinary file of yours, with the same name, in a folder of the same name. Several files are copied in one go.
  • Big downloads ask first. Opening or copying more than about 50 MB at once asks "Download 72 MB from ?". Cancel and nothing is transferred.
  • Save on host (the save icon on the session's row, or right-click the empty grid) saves the session's scene into the host's library, as a new version (Version history restores it). Only editors can; a view-only guest sees the button greyed with the reason — use Copy to my library instead.
  • Leaving the session removes the root. Anything you copied stays in your Library.
  • Opening one of your own scenes while you are in someone's session asks first: Leave the session and open it, or Bring a copy into this session.

docs.title: Save project with several libraries open
docs.text:
"Several libraries" means your Library plus a session you joined, or a mounted project with unsaved changes.

  • With one library open, Save (and Ctrl+S) saves it straight away, as before.
  • With several, Save asks once: every open library has a checkbox, the one you are working in (the session, while you are in one) is ticked, and each row says where it saves — This device, Save on host, Mounted project. A library you cannot save is greyed with the reason (view-only, or no unsaved changes). If the open scene has unsaved changes, the dialog says so.
  • A library is never saved into another one. You get one result line per library saved.
  • Remember my choice stores your answer in Settings ▸ Save options ▸ When several libraries are open: Ask (default) · Save the active one · Save all I can. Ctrl+S follows the same setting. The dialog links to the setting.

docs.title: Mounting a saved project
docs.text: ＋ Mount project… at the top of the tree lists the projects saved in this browser (and Import project (.tp)… for a file). A mounted project appears as its own root beside your Library: browse it, open a scene from it into the viewport, edit its files and folders, then Save changes to write them back — or Refresh to re-read it and throw your edits away. Copy to Library brings one of its files into your own project. Unmount just stops showing it; the saved project is not deleted.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: The chip in the Explorer header reads used / granted for everything this app keeps in your browser. Click it — or Storage used… under Disk in the right-click menu, or Settings ▸ Explorer ▸ Storage used — for the Storage breakdown: library files, old scene versions, deleted files, saved scenes and projects, autosave, prefabs, material presets, installed modules and the rest, each with a size — and, since 1.31, Pack downloads per pack with Clear all pack downloads. Tick what you want gone and press Reclaim; nothing is removed until you do, and it asks once more.

docs.title: Files in and out
docs.text: A session downloads as a .tpscene, a whole project as a .tp, and both import back — from the logo menu's Load, from the Sessions manager, or by dropping them on the Explorer. Right-click a scene ▸ Download (.tpscene); the Library root's menu has Export project (.tp) and a folder's has Export folder as .tp; Import project as folder (.tp)… adds a .tp file's contents to your library as one folder without opening anything. See Projects.

docs.title: Placing objects
docs.text:
New in 1.31: drag any object — a pack item, one of your Library models, a prefab — from Explorer ▸ Packs or Explorer ▸ Library onto the viewport, and a ghost shows where it will land and how big it is before you let go.

Dragging the Duck from the starter pack.

  • Drag. Press on a card and drag it over the 3D view. The ghost sits on whatever is under the pointer — the floor, a table, the side of a wall — and follows the grid when grid snapping is on; hold Shift to move it freely. "Align to surface" (snapping options) tilts it onto slopes and walls.
  • Turn it. R turns it 15° (Shift+R back); the mouse wheel turns it too while you drag.
  • Drop. Let go and it is placed exactly where the ghost stood — one undo step, and everyone in the session sees it. Hold Alt as you let go to place it at the camera's focus point instead. Drag several selected cards at once to drop them side by side in a row. A click without a drag still places the item in front of the camera, as before.
  • Cancel. Esc, dropping back on the Explorer, or letting go anywhere else places nothing and leaves nothing in the undo history.
  • Colours. The ghost turns amber when it would sit mostly inside another object (you can still place it — a cup in a cabinet is fine) and red where there is nothing to place it on (letting go there does nothing).
  • On a phone or tablet, press and hold a card and move your finger to drag it (holding still opens its actions instead); the Explorer tucks itself away so you can see where you are dropping. Items drop upright (or aligned to the surface) — the rotation keys need a keyboard.

docs.title: Ghost tiers: the real model or its box
docs.text:
Beside the pointer you see the item's width × depth × height in metres, its triangle count and its download size.

  • An item that is already loaded and under the preview budget shows as a see-through copy of the real model.
  • Anything else — not downloaded yet, or heavier than the budget — shows as its box: a wire box with its footprint on the ground, sized from the pack's own numbers. An item whose size is not known yet (an old or imported pack) shows a 1 m box labelled "size unknown" until it has been loaded once; after that its size is remembered.
  • Hovering the viewport during a drag starts the download, so the drop is quick. A placed pack item shows your Placeholder Style until its file arrives. The ghost is yours alone — nobody else sees it.

Once loaded, the ghost is a see-through copy of the real model.

docs.title: The Placement preview setting
docs.text:
Settings ▸ Scene ▸ Performance (this device only):

  • Placement preview — Full model (always the real model once loaded), Within budget (the default) or Box only.
  • Preview triangle budget — with Within budget, a loaded model above this many triangles previews as its box (50,000 on a computer, 15,000 on a phone or headset).
  • Show dimensions — the size, triangles and download size beside the pointer.

Settings ▸ Scene ▸ Performance ▸ Placement preview.

docs.title: Downloaded pack items and Delete cache
docs.text:
Explorer ▸ Packs marks the items this device has already downloaded with a ✓ (its size in the tooltip), and the filter menu inside the Packs has Downloaded to show only those. Right-click a pack item ▸ Delete cache (size) frees its download — the item stays in the pack and downloads again the next time you place it. Right-click a pack ▸ Delete downloads frees the whole pack's, and Storage lists Pack downloads per pack with Clear all pack downloads.

A pack item's menu.

docs.title: Images, audio and text
docs.text:
• Images dropped onto an object become its texture. A big photo is scaled down to 1024 px on its longest side instead of being refused — see Big photos as textures.
  • Audio and text are used where they plug in — sound nodes, scripts, and any module that claims the drop (a sample onto a pad).

Placement and texturing go through the normal replicated paths, so peers see the result immediately. In VR the radial Add menu still places in front of you; drag-to-place in VR comes later.

docs.title: Fluids: emitters, flow paths and motors
docs.text:
Since 1.25 you can pour real particle water into the open scene: it pools, splashes, lands on meshes and joins any water it is poured into. Flow paths carry it along rivers, chutes and pipes, and two new nodes turn wheels and float leaves and boats along the current. For water volumes (pools, tanks, oceans) see Water; for a glass box of particle fluid see Fluid tank.

A Fluid emitter pouring a stream into a puddle.

docs.title: Fluid emitter
docs.text:
Add ▸ Water ▸ Fluid (right-click the viewport, or the + button). It pours from its spout, 1.6 m above where you clicked; rotate it to aim, or pick Aim in its properties.

Properties ▸ Fluid emitter:

Setting What it does Emitting on / off Mode Stream (continuous) or Spill (releases Spill amount once — a bucket tipping, a leak) Rate /s · Speed · Spread ° how much, how fast and how wide it pours Aim down, up, forward or sideways Fluid drop size, viscosity, surface tension, cohesion (drops gather into puddles), friction (a puddle settles instead of skating), colour, clarity, and the look (smooth surface on a desktop, drops on a Quest) Collide with the scene the water lands on meshes instead of falling through them Pouring into water joins it water reaching a pool or tank of water is absorbed, with a ripple Restart starts the emitter again

Hard caps keep it bounded — any one of them is enough:

  • Max particles — it waits at the cap;
  • Lifetime s — older water disappears;
  • Area (width / height / depth, and how far below the spout it reaches) — water leaving the area is gone. With Area floor holds water off, it falls out of the bottom.

Each player simulates their own splash; the settings are shared and undoable. An emitter pauses while it is off-screen, and the simulation transport's Pause and Reset hold and clear it with the rest of the simulation.

docs.title: How water meets an object
docs.text:
Properties ▸ Physics ▸ Fluid is shown when the scene has particle fluid, and sets how the water meets this object:

Fluid What happens Auto the water collides; dynamic bodies are pushed None the water passes through Collide the water collides, but never pushes the object Collide + push + float light objects float on the fluid's pools

docs.title: Flow paths
docs.text:
Add ▸ Water ▸ Flow path places a path that carries water toward its end. Kind chooses what it is:

  • River / chute — steers water along it at Speed, with Pull /s for how firmly. Loop sends water that reaches the end back to the start, so a closed loop never runs dry.
  • Pipe — water at its first point comes out of its last point: a hidden pump.

A path also has a width and depth, an animated water surface (colour, opacity), its point list (Add point, ✕ to remove one) and Shape from a spline…, which lets you draw the curve with the spline tool. Physics bodies pass through a path's surface. On a Quest the surface is what you see of a river.

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
Both are in the node editor's Animation group:

  • Rotate / Motor — turns its object about one of its own axes, around its origin (a wheel on its hub), at rpm with a spin-up. Paddles and scoops it turns push and carry fluid. On a dynamic physics body during a simulation it is a motor of the given torque instead, so a load slows it. The on input switches it.
  • Float Along Flow — carries its object (a leaf, a toy boat) along the nearest flow path, or the one wired in, at the path's speed × speed, bobbing, facing the current and looping.

docs.title: Fluid budget
docs.text: Configure Scene ▸ Physics ▸ Fluid budget is one particle budget shared by every Fluid emitter in the scene; each emitter gets a share in proportion to its own Max particles. The budget is lowered automatically when frames drop, and a headset runs at most 1400 particles.

docs.title: Example: Water works
docs.text:
Menu ▸ Templates ▸ Examples ▸ Water works is a closed loop on a diorama: a scoop wheel lifts pond water into a head-race, which spills into a fountain basin; the basin overflows down a chute back into the pond, and leaves and boats ride along.

Water works: the scoop wheel.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Particle water is simulated per player: it never travels over the network, only the settings do.
  • A Fluid emitter's area is at most 16 m a side, and is shrunk to fit 600 k grid cells.
  • Up to 6000 particles per emitter on a desktop; a headset shares at most 1400 across the scene.

docs.title: VR Football
docs.text:
Two floating gates at the ends of a small pitch, one ball between them, red against blue, played with your hands. You hit the ball with the knock: it leaves at the speed you hit it, bounces off the invisible walls and slows a little. A ball through a gate is a goal for the team of whoever touched it last.

Football is a module, not a built-in: everyone playing needs it — a peer without it sees the pitch and the ball, because those are ordinary scene objects, but none of the rules. There are two ways in:

  • Templates ▸ Games ▸ Football — a ready-made pitch with the physics already set (gravity 0, ground off, Knock on). Loading it offers to install the module if you do not have it.
  • Menu ▸ Modules ▸ Browse ▸ Football, then the toolbox's Build pitch (below) — lays a pitch out in the scene you already have.

The Games tab lists Football beside the other games (see The Games tab). A game there is a scene plus a module, so its card names what it needs — Each player needs this module; loading will offer to install it, and Installed — every player needs their own copy once you have it. The row is generated from the module's own definition rather than written out separately, so the scene and the module cannot drift apart between releases.

Zero gravity, and the knock

The pitch is a zero-g scene: Configure Scene ▸ Physics with gravity 0, Ground off and Knock on, and the simulation started when play opens. The Build pitch button below sets that for you where it can; if it cannot, a toast says to set those three by hand.

docs.title: Getting a pitch
docs.text:
The quickest pitch is the Football template in Templates ▸ Games — a whole scene, with the pitch, the gates, the ball, the pads and the graph that wires them together already in it.

To build one into a scene of your own instead: with the module installed, its own window is listed under Modules in the menu and under Module tools in the viewport's right-click menu, as Football. Open it from either. The bottom half builds the ground:

Button What it does Build pitch Creates the whole pitch in the current scene: the floor, four see-through walls and a ceiling, two gates with their posts and lamps, a Football ball, two join pads, a Start match pad and a New match pad — plus the node graph that wires them together. Everything is replicated, so one person builds and everybody has it. Fit pitch Re-lays the pitch you built to the Length / Width / Gate height boxes above, in metres. Fit to room Sizes it from your headset's own room bounds, where the headset reports them; otherwise it says so and leaves you the boxes. Centre on room Moves it onto the shared room anchor — for a colocated pair standing in the same physical room.

The defaults are a living room: 5 m long, 3 m wide, gates centred at chest height.

docs.title: Playing
docs.text:
1. Touch (or click) a Join red / Join blue pad — or press the toolbox's Join red, Join blue or Spectate. You do not have to: pressing Start, or simply hitting the ball, seats an unseated player on the smaller team.
  2. Press the Start match pad, or Start in the toolbox — or just hit the ball, which kicks a match off when none is running.
  3. Hit the ball: swing a controller through it (the tip of the controller kicks; a trigger click on the ball kicks it too). On the desktop, walk into it or click it. A click, desktop or VR, only kicks within 2.5 m. Score in the other team's gate — red attacks the blue gate. The gate lamps fill up as a team scores, so the score reads from across the room without a screen.

After a goal the ball rests in the net for a moment — a GOAL! banner with the score, cheers, confetti in the scorers' colour and a buzz in their controllers — then goes back to the centre spot, a 3-2-1 countdown runs and the team that conceded kicks off with a slow nudge into its own half. The clock stops for celebrations and countdowns. A draw at the final whistle goes to a golden goal: the next goal wins. The results panel offers Rematch (same sides) or Menu.

With Serve set to button the ball waits instead of kicking off by itself; use the Serve button or a Serve node.

Desktop players join the same match: the camera you walk with is your probe, so you shoulder the ball rather than heading it, and grab-and-throw works as it does anywhere else.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
They live in the toolbox — and on the Match Rules node, which wins while it is in the graph, so a pitch you author keeps its own rules:

Row Options Default Mode duel, teams, freeforall, practice teams Win by goals, time, either goals Goals to win 1 – 20 5 Match seconds 30 – 1800 180 Serve auto, button auto Own goals count, ignore count

An own goal — your own last touch, into your own gate — lands on the right sheet rather than being handed to the other side as a goal of theirs.

Since 1.23 the game's own rules — who scored, what a goal is worth (GOAL_POINTS), when a match is over — are the Football rules script on the scene's Main graph, beside the Match Rules node. See Game rules on the Main graph.

docs.title: What is recorded
docs.text:
• Per player, for the session — goals, touches and owngoals, each written by the one peer they belong to. A new match does not clear them: a session record is a session record. A player's row goes when they disconnect.
  • The match log — at the end of a match the winner, both scores and the scorers are appended to the game's own variables (the last 50 matches). That travels inside a saved .tpscene, so reopening a scene shows the matches played in it.

docs.title: The Football nodes
docs.text:
Every rule is a node in the Football group, so a scene can be re-authored without touching the module's code. A node that is alive in the graph owns its rule on every peer; delete it and the defaults come back within a second.

Node Wire it to What it does Match Rules the pitch Owns the table above, and names the ball through its ball input (wire an Object Selector). Team Gate a gate's sensor box A ball entering this gate scores for the other team. Match Button a pad or button object action: join red / join blue / spectate / start / new match / swap sides / serve. Clicking the object — desktop or VR trigger — runs it for the clicker. Serve any static object Serves the ball when its trigger pulses. Score Lamp one lamp Lit while that team's score reaches its index — the lamps that make a gate readable. Records any static object Feeds the HUD: the per-player sheet, the score and clock line, and the saved match log.
