Football Value — A number out: red, blue, goals, myteam, lastteam, started, left, players, serves, mygoals, matches. Football Event — A pulse out: goal, redgoal, bluegoal, serve, start, over, reset, touch. Wire start and over into Set Game State so a HUD follows the match.

Never target the ball

No Football node may be wired at the ball through an Object Selector: a targeted object has its pose re-seated every frame, which fights the physics body. Match Rules targets the pitch and names the ball on its ball input instead.

docs.title: In a shared room
docs.text:
Two people in the same physical room can play it colocated — calibrate as usual, then Centre on room puts the pitch on the shared anchor so you are both standing on the same 5 × 3 metres.

Last touch is worked out on every peer from the same knock feed, so nobody has to be the referee; goals, serves and the end of a match are decided by the peer running the simulation and broadcast. A late joiner is handed the whole match state, mid-match included.

docs.title: Free Assets (CC0)
docs.text:
The Asset Browser (1.38) brings free, public-domain (CC0) assets straight into your project: models, skies (HDRIs) and texture sets from Poly Haven, and PBR materials from ambientCG. No account, no key, no attribution required — the app still keeps each asset's credit for you.

Where: main menu ▸ Free assets (CC0), or + Add ▸ Free assets (CC0)…. It is a floating window that can dock like Statistics or Chat (drag it onto the dock, or the dock's + ▸ Free assets). On a phone it opens as a bottom sheet.

The Asset Browser's Materials tab searching ambientCG for clay.

docs.title: Finding an asset
docs.text:
• Pick a tab — Models, HDRIs, Textures, Materials — then search by name or tag and narrow by category.
  • Pick a resolution: 1k (the default on a Quest or a phone), 2k (the desktop default) or 4k. Bigger files take longer to download and to reach the people in your session.

docs.title: Bringing it in
docs.text:
• Models — Add to Library downloads the model at that resolution, packs it into one .glb and adds it to the Explorer's Poly Haven folder through the same import as dropping a file there — so a big one is optimized on import like any other. Then Add to scene, or drag it from the Explorer. Everyone in the session sees it.
  • HDRIs — Use as sky downloads the .hdr into the Library and lights the scene with it (Configure Scene ▸ Environment ▸ Sky image shows it too). It reaches everyone like any sky.
  • Materials and textures — Add saves it to your material presets (the Inspector's Material swatches); Apply also puts it on the selected objects. Colour and normal maps are kept; roughness and metalness come from their maps.

A CC0 material applied to a box.

docs.title: Credits
docs.text:
Every download keeps its source — site, authors, licence (CC0) and a link. You see it in the Explorer's Properties, in the Inspector for a placed object or a CC0 material, and on the material swatch's tooltip. A model carries it inside the file, so a peer's copy — and the optimized copy the importer makes — has it too.

The Explorer's Properties naming a Poly Haven model's source.

docs.title: Offline and errors
docs.text: Lists you have opened are saved on this device (for a day), so the browser still shows them offline — a banner says when it is showing a saved list. Downloads need a connection; when a site or the ambientCG relay does not answer, the window says so in plain words and offers Try again.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A Library file is at most 25 MB (what peers can receive): a model bigger than that at the picked resolution is refused with "Pick 1k".
  • ambientCG is reached through theprototype.app's own relay (its site does not let browsers read it directly); Poly Haven is reached directly.
  • Since 1.39 a large CC0 material preset (its colour and normal maps can be several megabytes) reaches every connected person's From ‹name› swatch row too: it arrives in the background a few seconds after they connect (or after you save it), and travels only once.

The Asset Browser as a bottom sheet on a folded phone.

docs.title: Game kit
docs.text:
Almost every game needs the same handful of rules: how far a player may reach, a round with a countdown and a time limit, levels that unlock, a score, things to pick up, enemies that spawn, take damage and walk towards you. The game kit builds these once, in the app, so a game does not have to.

Each piece of the kit is available two ways, generated from the same description, so they behave identically and use the same words:

  • as Kit: node groups in the Flow editor palette — Kit: Rules, Kit: Round, Kit: Levels, Kit: Score, Kit: Pickups, Kit: Spawner, Kit: Health and Kit: Mover;
  • as api.kit.* for modules and behaviours.

Towers (Templates ▸ Games) runs on the kit — its reach rule, levels, score and round.

docs.title: One peer decides
docs.text:
In a shared session a press is seen by every peer — and a naive "add 1 to the score" then adds one per peer. The kit avoids that by having one authority peer make every change: the peer running the physics simulation, otherwise the one with the lowest peer id. Ask for a change on any peer and it becomes a request the authority applies exactly once. A kit node fired by a shared pulse is asked by every peer with the same request, so one press is one change.

  • Reads (the round phase, the score, a level's stars) are the same on every peer.
  • Events (On go, On score, On pickup) fire on every peer — the place to play a sound. A few are local on purpose: On grab refused only for the player who was refused, On new best on each device whose best was beaten.
  • A player who joins late gets the current state and does not hear old events.
  • When the authority leaves, the next peer takes over, including the enemies of a wave in progress. Someone joining does not take a running round over (since 1.48.1).
  • Clearing the scene resets the kit.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
Grab reach, jump height and play bounds.

  • Set grab reach — how far from their body (in metres) a player may take hold of something; 0 removes the limit. Every grab path obeys it: desktop Play, Interact, and the VR grip.
  • Set jump height — how high a walking player jumps (Space on the desktop, A in VR) while a Character Controller walks; 0 = no jump.
  • Set play bounds — a box a teleport must land inside.
  • Clear rules — the scene's own play settings apply again.
  • On grab refused — pulses for the player whose grab was refused (too far, or a game rule said no).

In code, a game can also veto a grab with its own rule (rules.onGrabRequest) — Towers' "climb closer to take a piece" is one.

docs.title: Round
docs.text:
A round's whole life: an intro countdown, play, a time limit, pause, won or lost, results.

  • Round setup — the intro countdown (seconds), a time limit (0 = none), what the clock running out means (lose, or win for a survive-the-timer game), and how long the won/lost moment lasts before the results.
  • Start round (two players pressing Start start one round), Restart round (works while playing), Pause round / Resume round, Win round / Lose round (with an optional reason), Add time, Back to menu.
  • Values: Round phase (menu, intro, playing, paused, won, lost, results), Round playing?, Round time, Time left, Intro countdown, Round number, Round outcome.
  • Events: On round start, On go, On round paused / resumed, On round won / lost, On results, On back to menu.

The round drives the app's shared game state, so HUD screens bound to a state and the pause menu keep working — and the pause menu's Restart restarts a kit round by itself.

docs.title: Levels
docs.text:
A level table with unlocks and stars.

  • Go to level (a locked level is refused, with the reason), Next level, Finish level (won or not, a score, a time — stars follow the game's rule and a win unlocks the next level), Set game mode (switches mode and keeps the current level).
  • Values: Current level, Level name, Level number, Level stars, Level unlocked?, Total stars, Game mode.
  • Events: On level chosen, On level finished, On level unlocked.

Progress is saved per device: every player keeps the stars they saw earned. The table feeds the pause menu's level picker automatically.

docs.title: Score
docs.text:
• Add score — points to the shared score and to the player who earned them; counted once however many peers saw the pulse. Set score, Reset score (a new round does this by itself).
  • Values: Score (shared), My score (each peer reads its own), Best score (the best this device has seen for this game and level), Leader.
  • Events: On score, On new best.

docs.title: Pickups
docs.text:
• Collect pickup — takes a pickup once for everybody (wire an On Click or On Enter into it): its points go to the shared score and to the player who took it, and it comes back after respawn seconds (0 = never). A second take before it is back is refused. Inside a pickup's own object flow, an unwired pickup means that object.
  • Reset pickups puts every pickup back (a new round does this by itself).
  • Values: Pickup available? (wire it into a Visibility node to hide a taken pickup), Pickups taken, Pickups left.
  • Events: On pickup, On pickup back, On all pickups taken (a "collect them all" win).

A pickup a module or behaviour registers can also be taken just by walking into it.

docs.title: Spawner
docs.text:
Enemies, targets and other entities: copies of a template object, each with its own health, tags and data, drawn on every peer. They are not saved and do not appear in the object list.

  • Spawn entities — make count entities of a kind, drawn as copies of the template object, at a place (unwired: where the template stands), spread out, with hit points, a speed (above 0 they get a mover) and how long a dead one stays before it is removed.
  • Remove entity, Clear entities (of a kind, or all).
  • Value: Entities alive (of a kind, or all).
  • Events: On entity spawned, On entity removed, On all entities dead — the wave is over.

A new round clears the entities.

docs.title: Health
docs.text:
Hit points on entities. Damage asked for on any peer is applied once, on the authority, and credited to the player who asked.

  • Damage entity (at 0 it dies; a dead entity takes no more), Damage in area (every living entity of a kind within a radius — a blast, a stomp), Heal entity (never above its maximum), Revive entity (back at full health).
  • Value: Entity health.
  • Events: On entity damaged, On entity healed, On entity died, On entity revived.

Code has a little more: regeneration and armour, and reads for an entity's maximum, its fraction left and whether it is alive.

docs.title: Mover
docs.text:
Steering for entities.

  • Chase — every living entity of a kind chases a target object (unwired: the nearest player), steering round walls and each other. Crowds queue at the goal instead of jostling.
  • Stop moving.
  • Knock back — throw one entity with a velocity; it comes back to rest on the ground, inside the level and out of walls.
  • On entity stuck — an entity made no headway and started a recovery: a sidestep, then a new route round the walls.

Movers treat the scene's top-level objects in their walking band as obstacles, and stay inside the game's play bounds.

docs.title: For module authors and developers
docs.text:
Every node above has a code twin under api.kit; the full table of actions, reads and events is on the Module SDK page. Logic written as a behaviour calls the same kit. Since 1.23 a module can add a piece of its own with api.kit.provide — the engine a game's rules call as kit.golf.*, kit.football.*… — see For module and game authors.

Game rules can be proved without a browser: the core repo's headless logic sim (tests/unit/sim) runs several fake peers on a fake clock through the real message validation, so "two players press Start at once" or "the host leaves mid-wave" is a unit test that runs in milliseconds. See The game kit in the core repo's MODULES.md.

docs.title: Game Rules on the Main Graph
Game rules on the Main graph
docs.text:
Every game rebuilt in 1.23 has one readable script that is its rules, sitting on the game's Main graph. Open the game, open the node editor, and the whole game is in front of you: the rules in the middle, wired to the buttons, the HUD, the sounds and the kit around it. Change a number in a panel, or change the code and press Ctrl+S, and the game plays by your rules on every player's screen.

These games ship this way: Mini Golf, Football, Dungeon Realms, The Alchemist's Escape, Sky Run, Target Toss and Marble Maze (see The Games tab).

Part of Mini Golf's Main graph at full size.

docs.title: Where it is
docs.text: Open a game from the Games tab, then open the Node editor (N). Main is the first entry under Flows. The blue note "… — read me first" says where to start.

docs.title: What is on the graph
docs.text:
• The rules node — a Behaviour node such as Mini Golf rules, Football rules or Escape rules. It holds the game's logic as plain JavaScript: holes and par, the cup, out of bounds, who scored, when a match is over, how many gems open a portal, the escape room's dial code and lever order, Sky Run's stages and fall depth, what each Target Toss target is worth and how a combo grows.
  • Its sockets connect it to the rest of the graph:
    • inputs on the left — the menu buttons (Tee off, Play again…) are wired into them;
    • outputs on the right — its state (the words the HUD shows: Hole 3 of 6 · Windmill, Strokes 2, / 8 needed…) and its moments ⚡ (a stroke, out of bounds, the ball in the cup, a goal, a portal opening), wired into banners, sounds, sparkles, controller buzzes and kit nodes (set score, win round).
  • The engine — what rules cannot be: a ball's physics body, the drag-to-putt arrow, a VR putter, a generated dungeon. It stays in the game's module, and the rules reach it as kit.golf.*, kit.football.*, kit.realms.*, kit.escape.*, kit.skyrun.*, kit.toss.* or kit.marble.*. A Code link node on Main opens the engine's source, read-only.
  • Named groups hold everything else — Hole feedback, Scorecard & HUD, Score lamps, Start menu & buttons… — with a note beside each one that explains it. Double-click a group to open it (see Groups).

docs.title: Change a number
docs.text:
You do not have to read code to tune a game. Select the rules node — or the game's settings node: Football's Match Rules, Dungeon Realms' Game Rules — open the ⓘ tab of the properties panel, and change the value:

Game For example Mini Golf Shot power (the fastest putt, m/s), Strokes before pick-up, Cup radius Football goals to win, match seconds Dungeon Realms gem share The Alchemist's Escape crank turns Sky Run jump height, fall depth, countdown Target Toss combo window, biggest combo, grab reach Marble Maze board tilt limit, turn speed

A knob on the rules node rewrites the number in the code itself, so the code and the panel always agree.

Part of Football's Main graph at full size.

docs.title: Change the rules in code
docs.text:
Double-click the rules node (or right-click ▸ Open code). The code workspace opens it; edit it and press Ctrl+S. The game reloads your rules on every player's screen, and the hole, match or floor in play carries on. Broken code never applies: the old rules keep running, and an error badge says why.

Some things to try:

Game Change Where Mini Golf make hole 1 a par 4 the HOLES table Football make a goal worth 2 GOAL_POINTS Dungeon Realms ask for one extra gem per floor EXTRA_GEMS The Alchemist's Escape change the dial code CODE Sky Run rename or re-time a stage STAGES Target Toss make a can worth more POINTS Marble Maze rename or re-time a maze MAZES

Both kinds of change are saved with the scene (they survive a reload) and reach everyone in the room.

See the logic as nodes: the rules node's Open view button shows its live node view — every event it listens to, every handler, the state it writes, the kit and engine calls it makes, and the moments it emits.

docs.title: For module and game authors
docs.text: The behaviour format grew the sockets these games use, and a module can lend its engine to rules — see For module and game authors on the Module SDK page.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Towers, Waves, Untangle, Stars Room and Jam Room are not rebuilt in 1.23: their logic stays in their module.
  • A game's menu buttons may be wired straight into its rules node's inputs (Target Toss, Marble Maze): a press runs the rules on the authority, once.
  • The rules run on one player's machine — the session's authority. A rules node edited while you are offline from the others applies when they reconnect; it is ordinary node data.
  • The live node view is read-only: change the code or the knobs.
  • A copy saved before 1.23 of Mini Golf, The Alchemist's Escape, Sky Run, Target Toss or Marble Maze has no rules node, and its game does not start in 1.23. Opening one says so and offers Open Games: open the game from the Games tab to play or remix the new version. Football and Dungeon Realms copies keep working as before.

docs.title: The Games tab
docs.text:
Templates ▸ Games lists ready-made games. Open a card, press Test play, then the game's own Start. Every game has the same pause menu (Esc, or the menu button in VR): Resume, Restart, Levels, Settings and Main menu.

The five games added in 1.20 are built into the app — they need no module download — and play on the desktop and in VR.

Since 1.23, Mini Golf, VR Football, Dungeon Realms, The Alchemist's Escape, Sky Run, Target Toss and Marble Maze keep their rules as one readable script on the game's Main graph: open the node editor to tune a number or change the code. See Game rules on the Main graph.

1.24 adds Race, built into the app.

docs.title: Tidy Main graphs
docs.text:
Since 1.25 all twelve games open on a Main graph where no card overlaps another and no wire passes through a card (a test checks every game).

  • Football, Dungeon Realms, The Alchemist's Escape, Marble Maze, Sky Run, Target Toss, Mini Golf keep the layout they had; only cards that overlapped or sat on a wire moved (Mini Golf's Hole feedback group no longer covers wires).
  • Waves is rebuilt: Main shows the run's rules (the Waves node, the crystal, won / lost) and three group cards — Enemies (one group per enemy inside), Menus & buttons and HUD readouts — each with a note.
  • Stars Room (six groups), Towers (four), Jam Room (four) and Untangle (two) put their repetitive parts in group cards with notes. Double-click a card to open it.

To lay out a graph of your own, use Tidy graph.

docs.title: The Alchemist's Escape
docs.text: An escape room in three rooms. Open the drawer, find the key, unlock the chest, set the dials, pull the levers in the right order and twist the crank to raise the gate, then place three gems to open the vault. If you are stuck for a minute in a room a hint appears (or press H). The Levels page lets you practise each of the three stages; your best time is saved on this device.

docs.title: Marble Maze
docs.text: Tilt the board and roll the marble through five mazes to the gold ring. On the desktop use WASD / the arrow keys or drag; in VR grip both handles and twist. Holes send you back to the start; three coins and a par time per maze give 1-3 stars. The last two mazes have gates that rise and sink.

docs.title: Mini Golf
docs.text: Six holes — a ramp, a windmill, a bank shot, sand and a hump. On the desktop drag back from the ball and let go to putt; in VR swing the putter. Par for every hole, a scorecard, and your best round saved. Any hole can be played on its own from the Levels page.

docs.title: Race
docs.text: Up to four players, four cars, three laps round a valley circuit: click a car, press Start, drive with WASD (R puts you back on the road). A lap counts only when you have driven all of it. Laps, speed and grip are on the Race rules node in the Main graph, and the road is a spline — move its points and the race follows. Your best race and best lap are saved on this device. See Race.

docs.title: Sky Run
docs.text: A floating obstacle course in three stages: jumps, moving platforms (they carry you), vanishing tiles and spinning arms. Flags save your spot, coins and par times earn stars, and the best time per stage is saved. In VR the comfort vignette is on by default.

docs.title: Target Toss
docs.text: A fairground booth: tin-can pyramids, swinging targets, pop-ups and a moving cart, five stages against the clock, with combos and 1-3 stars. In VR grab a ball and throw it; on the desktop hold to charge and release to throw.

docs.title: Towers
docs.text: Twelve levels of stacking: cubes, planks, wedges, barrels, arches and balls, a limited supply dealt onto racks, and a goal for each level. Your grab reach is limited (about 1.3 m from your body), so the high levels need steps — build them, then jump (desktop Space, VR A). Pieces dropped outside the build yard are lost. Later levels add wind, a narrow pedestal, a rocking plate, an outline to fill and a star to deliver. Par pieces and par time give 1-3 stars a level; the unlocks and stars are saved on this device. Built into the app.

docs.title: Stars Room
docs.text: A zero-gravity glass room full of glowing crystal stars and two planets. Knock them with your hands in VR, or walk into them on the desktop (the knock); clap to make a new star. The start screen offers Start round — light every star within two minutes, your best round saved on this device — or Free play, a sandbox with every button on the P menu. Built into the app.

docs.title: Waves
docs.text: A VR shooter: hold the crystal against five levels of waves — grunts, then runners, then tanks — pouring out of three portals. Pick a gun on the Loadout page (Blaster semi-auto, Scatter seven pellets, Beam that overheats) and an ability (Shield, Slow-mo, Pulse) that your free hand's grip fires (desktop: Q). On the desktop the gun is your view and a click fires. In a headset a Start board stands ahead of you — aim at it and pull the trigger. Options sets the music, sound effects, gun hand and vibration; choices and your best run are saved on this device. Needs the health and waves modules (the card offers to install them).

docs.title: Untangle
docs.text: A planar-graph puzzle: drag the dots until no edges cross. Press, move and release — or click a dot, then click where it goes. The Globe mode puts the same puzzle on a sphere (right-drag, two fingers or the VR stick turn it — your view only). 30 levels per mode unlock as you solve them; progress stays on this device, and every peer sees and solves the same board. In VR, drag with the trigger and hold the globe in one hand while the other moves dots. Needs the untangle module.

docs.title: Dungeon Realms
docs.text: A co-op dungeon crawl: a seeded five-floor dungeon, gems to collect, portals that unseal when enough are found, and a dragon's hoard at the top. Press Play, pick Player 1 or Player 2, walk with WASD, collect gems, stand on the portal together to climb. Two players get the identical dungeon from the same seed. Needs the Dungeon Kit and Dungeon Realms modules.

docs.title: Jam Room
docs.text: A small studio, all cabled: a piano into a speaker, a beat lab (transport, drum machine, sampler pads) and a pedal chain into a mixer. Press Start, then ▶ on the Transport, and keep the band going for eight bars; your best tempo is saved. Play with the mouse, or in VR from the cockpit. See Music Playground. Needs the music-lab and music-fx modules.

docs.title: VR Football
docs.text: Swing a controller through the floating ball and put it through the other gate. First to 5 or three minutes, golden goal on a tie. See VR Football. Needs the football module.

docs.title: Make your own
docs.text: Start with Build a Game Loop and the game kit. Games that come from a module offer to install it when you open the card.

docs.title: HUD Editor
docs.text: The HUD is the 2D layer over the game — a score, a health bar, a start menu, a pause screen. You lay it out in the HUD editor and drive it from the flow graph. For a step-by-step game built this way, see Build a Game Loop; this page is the reference.

docs.title: Opening it
docs.text:
Press Alt+H, or the ＋ in the bottom dock's tab strip ▸ HUD editor (the toolbar can carry a HUD button too — see The toolbar). Like every editor window it docks at the bottom or floats.

The HUD editor on the Stars Room's menu screen.

Part What it holds Left column, top which HUD you are editing (the document picker), then the screens of that HUD — click one to edit it; its while and input settings open under it; ★ makes it the default screen everyone starts on; ✕ deletes it; + Screen adds one Left column, below the palette: every element kind, grouped Display, Input and Layout, with a filter box — click one to add it, or drag it onto the stage Toolbar the Select and Multi-select tools, the arrange buttons, Duplicate, Delete and Snap; on the right, the stage size and element count Stage (centre) a fixed reference stage; the dashed outline is the shape of your window on it, so you can see what falls outside the frame you are actually looking at Properties (right) the selected element's own fields, its style, and its Actions

docs.title: Which HUD: the scene's, or a camera's
docs.text:
The document picker at the top of the left column chooses which HUD you edit:

  • Scene HUD — shown whatever camera you look through.
  • A camera — this HUD shows only while you look through that camera. Attach a menu to a title-shot camera and it travels with the shot (see Camera objects).

docs.title: Screens
docs.text:
A HUD holds one or more screens — named layers of elements: Menu, Playing, Paused, Results. Only one screen of a HUD shows at a time. Each screen has two settings:

Setting Options Meaning while only when asked, or a game state (menu, playing, paused, over…) show this screen automatically whenever the shared game state is that state — including for someone who joins later input game / menu game: the pointer stays locked and the screen is a readout (a score, a timer). menu: while this screen shows in play mode the pointer is freed and movement pauses, so the player can click it; hiding it locks the pointer again

Un-starring every screen means nothing shows until a node, a game state or a peer asks for one. A screen with only when asked is shown by an action (Show a HUD screen) or a HUD Screen node. A scene with at least one screen bound to a game state counts as a game: its menu waits for Start instead of painting itself over the editor, and the play button's menu offers Test play.

docs.title: Placing elements
docs.text:
• Click an element to select it, drag to move, drag the grip at its bottom-right corner to resize; Shift adds to the selection. The Multi-select tool drags a box that selects everything it touches.
  • Every element is anchored to one of nine points of the screen (the corners, the edge middles, the centre) plus a pixel offset, so it stays in its corner on any window size rather than stretching.
  • Snapping (the Snap box in the toolbar, or right-click the stage) snaps to the grid, the stage centre lines and other elements' edges. With nothing selected, the properties pane's Snapping section sets the grid step and how close an edge must come.
  • The arrange buttons need two or more selected: Align left / centres / right / top / middle / bottom, Distribute horizontally or vertically (three or more), Equalize size.
  • Ctrl+D duplicates, Del deletes, Ctrl+A selects all.
  • Right-click ▸ Apply style to… gives the selection (or the whole screen) a look in one go: Sci-fi (cyan edges, monospace), Fantasy (parchment and gold, serif), Minimal (no boxes, just text), Clean (light cards) or Follow my theme (each viewer's own theme colours).

A small mark on an element on the stage means something is wired to it — a button with no action is obvious at a glance.

docs.title: Element kinds
docs.text:
Display

Kind What it is Text a line of text. Wire a number into a HUD Text node to make it a live score Rich text text with **bold**, *italic*, {color:accent}colour{/color} and {icon:heart} glyphs Bar a filled bar, horizontal or vertical, optionally showing %: the fill is (value − min) / (max − min) — health, fuel, progress Radial progress a ring that fills — a cooldown, a charge. Takes the same value/min/max as a Bar Icon row N repeated icons off a number — hearts, ammo, keys Hotbar N slots with one selected Image an image from your Explorer (contain / cover / fill) List rows, one per line — a leaderboard, standings, an inventory Timer counts down (or up) from a HUD Timer node, off the shared clock, so everyone agrees Crosshair a centre reticle: thickness, gap, centre dot Key hint a key glyph and what it does — [E] Interact Minimap a top-down plot of the scene with you and your peers as dots Damage flash a full-screen tint that spikes when pulsed, then fades Debug level, game state, round, variables, players and fps — a pill that expands on click Custom (code) you write the render function; double-click it on the stage to edit the code. It draws text, boxes, styles, SVG and a 2D canvas in a sandbox — no event listeners or timers; use a Button for presses

Input

Kind What it is Button fires an event when pressed. Give it an action, or read it with a HUD Button node Slider drag for a number Toggle on or off (reads as 1 or 0) Dropdown one of a list (read its index or its text) Text field typed text — a player name, a room code Tabs a segmented pager; its value is the selected index Confirm a question and two buttons, which fire ‹id›-yes and ‹id›-no

Slider, Toggle, Dropdown, Text field and Tabs are read with a HUD Input node and have a shared switch: off, the value is yours alone (a volume slider); on, every player sees the same value (a host setting).

Layout: Panel (a background box to group things on — draw it first) and Scroll panel (a scrollable box of rich text: credits, a rulebook, a quest log).

Modules can add element kinds of their own; they appear in the palette like the built-ins.

docs.title: Actions: a button in two clicks
docs.text: Select a button and open Actions ▸ ＋ Add action in the properties pane. Actions are grouped — Game (start the game, pause, resume, end the game, back to the menu, reset the game, set a variable, save best score, travel to a level, reset a counter), Camera (look through a camera), HUD (show, hide or toggle a screen), Scene (count the presses, play an animation, play a sound, fire particles, apply an impulse, toggle an object's visibility) — and several can hang off one press. The pane lists them back in plain language. Behind the scenes an action is ordinary flow nodes, so you can open the node editor and extend it.

docs.title: Driving the HUD from the graph
docs.text:
Node Does HUD Screen shows, hides or toggles a screen each time it is triggered (for this player only) HUD Text puts a value into a Text element — a live score HUD Timer runs a Timer element's countdown on the shared clock — duration, display format, start automatically or on a pulse HUD Bar drives a bar's (or radial's, icon row's, hotbar's) value from a number HUD Button fires a pulse when a button is pressed HUD List / HUD Rows fill a list, or append rows to it — a log, a scoreboard feed HUD Input / HUD Set Input read what a player typed, picked or dragged — or set it

An element's own value in the properties pane is only the preview and the fallback — a node driving it always wins at runtime. See the HUD nodes.

docs.title: In VR
docs.text: A game's menu-like screens (menu, pause, results) appear on a game board in front of you; buttons there answer the laser and a poke. Since 1.24 the playing screen you lay out here also shows in the headset, arranged as you placed it, on a curved band in front of the player (or on their wrist) — see The game HUD in a headset. The band is read-only; a crosshair, a minimap and a full-screen flash have no headset form.

docs.title: Image Editor
docs.text:
New in 1.32: the Image editor crops, rotates, flips, resizes and adjusts a picture in your Explorer library. When you save, every texture made from that picture updates for everyone in the session.

The Image editor on a computer.

docs.title: Opening it
docs.text:
• Right-click an image in the Explorer ▸ Edit image…
  • The pencil button in an image's preview window.
  • Edit beside a texture in the Inspector (Material ▸ Texture).
  • The dock's + ▸ Image editor opens it as a dock tab — see In the dock.

docs.title: Looking at the picture
docs.text:
The picture fills the canvas. Scroll or pinch to zoom, drag to pan, and use Fit or 1:1 in the toolbar. The toolbar also shows the picture's size and format, and how many textures were made from it.

The sidebar on the right has two pages: Edit and Versions.

docs.title: Edit
docs.text:
• Rotate and flip: 90° left and right, mirror horizontally and vertically.
  • Crop: press Crop…, then drag on the picture to draw the box. Drag inside the box to move it, or drag a corner to resize it. The shape can be Free, 1:1 or Original, and X, Y, W and H take typed values. Enter or Apply crop applies it; Esc or Cancel cancels.
  • Resize: width and height, with Keep proportions. Quick buttons for 50%, 200% and Power of 2 (the size graphics cards handle best for textures), then Apply resize.
  • Adjust: Brightness, Contrast and Saturation sliders, applied live. Reset adjustments puts them back.

Cropping on a computer in the light theme.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
• Save (Ctrl+S) writes over the same Explorer file: same name, same folder, shared with the same people. Every material whose texture was made from this image updates, for everyone in the session, as one undo step in the scene. The toolbar says how many textures that is.
  • Save as copy writes name copy.png beside it. The original and its textures stay as they were, and the editor carries on with the copy.
  • The editor has its own Undo and Redo (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z) for edits you have not saved yet. They never touch the scene's undo. Closing with unsaved edits asks first.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
The Versions page lists every saved state of this image with a thumbnail, date and size, and Restore on each. Restore original at the top goes back to the picture as it first came in.

The Versions page.

docs.title: Textures and their images
docs.text:
A texture remembers the library image it was made from when you apply it from the Explorer. Edit in the Inspector on any other texture — one picked from disk, or one that came with an imported model — first puts it into the library as ‹object› texture.webp, then opens it, so it updates on Save the same way.

Painting over a texture in the UV editor breaks the link: a later save of the image will not paint over your strokes.

docs.title: Big photos as textures
docs.text: Pick any photo as a texture — Inspector ▸ Material ▸ Texture ▸ Set texture…, or drop an Explorer image on the object — and it is scaled down to fit 1024 px on its longest side and applied. Since 1.32 nothing is refused for being large. Only a file over 64 MB is turned away, because a phone cannot decode it.

docs.title: In the dock
docs.text:
The Image editor can live in the bottom dock like the other editors: pick Image editor from the dock's + menu while it is closed (on a phone, the Windows sheet), press its header's Dock button, or drag it onto the dock's tab bar. The dock's Undock button floats it again; floating stays the default.

  • Opened from the + with no image, it tells you to open one from the Explorer (right-click an image ▸ Edit image…). Opening an image while it is docked brings the dock tab forward.
  • Closing the tab with unsaved edits asks first, as the window does.

The Image editor as a tab in the bottom dock.

docs.title: On a phone
docs.text:
The editor is a full-width sheet between the top bar and the bottom bar, so Play stays tappable. The Edit and Versions pages sit under the picture instead of beside it, and Crop… scrolls its Apply crop button into view. Since 1.32 they start closed, so the picture gets the screen: tap ✎ (Edit) or ⟲ (Versions) under the picture to open one, and it stays open next time.

The Image editor on a phone.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Versions are kept on this device: the original plus the last 19 saves per image. Peers receive the saved image, not its history.
  • PNG, JPEG and WebP save in their own format. GIF and BMP save as PNG.
  • The largest side the editor produces is 8192 px.
  • A texture is stored at up to 1024 px, whatever the size of the image.

docs.title: Importing Big Models
docs.text: New in 1.37. A model straight out of a scanner, a marketplace or a CAD tool is often far heavier than a phone or a headset can draw. ThePrototype now optimizes such a model as it comes in, the way a game engine's importer does, and keeps your original next to it.

docs.title: What happens on import
docs.text:
When you import a model with more than 50,000 triangles or a texture larger than 2048 px:

  • Textures are resized to at most 2048 px and given a GPU-compressed copy (KTX2 / Basis). Your scene, saves and peers still get an ordinary picture; the graphics card holds the compressed copy — about a sixth to an eighth of the memory (on a Quest, 0.5–1 byte per pixel instead of 4).
  • A level-of-detail chain is added: lighter versions of the model (by default 50 %, 25 % and 10 % of the triangles) that take over as the model gets smaller on screen. Up close you always see the full model. See Levels of Detail.
  • The original file stays in the Library next to the optimized copy (Name (optimized).glb). The toast that reports the numbers offers Keep original only, which puts the original back in the scene (one undo step) and removes the optimized copy.

The work runs in the background (a few seconds for a big model); the window stays usable meanwhile.

A model under both thresholds is placed straight away (since 1.39): the optimizer is not even loaded. An asset whose Import settings say Always is still optimized whatever its size.

Measured on a test model (65,024 triangles, one 4096 px JPEG texture):

Original Optimized Texture 4096 × 4096 2048 × 2048 + KTX2 Texture memory on the GPU 85.3 MB ≈ 2.8 MB on a Quest (−97 %); 5.6 MB on a desktop GPU (−93 %) File in the Library 2.43 MB 1.63 MB (plain picture + KTX2 copy) Triangles as it gets smaller on screen 65,024 32,512 / 16,255 / 6,502 (LOD 1 / 2 / 3)

Texture resize and compression need a .glb or .gltf; OBJ, STL and FBX imports get the LOD chain only. Skinned (animated character) models keep full detail — a lighter level cannot carry its bone weights — and get the texture work.

A model that is far too heavy for this device still asks before it lands.

docs.title: Settings ▸ Import (this device)
docs.text:
The defaults for every new import, under Settings ▸ Import ▸ Import defaults:

Setting Default What it does Optimize big models automatically on off = imports arrive exactly as they are Triangle threshold 50,000 a model above this gets its LOD chain Texture threshold 2048 a texture above this (long side, px) is resized and compressed Max texture size 2048 512 / 1024 / 2048 / 4096 — the long side a resized texture gets Compress textures (KTX2) on the GPU-compressed copy LOD levels 3 Off / 2 / 3 / 4, with LOD 1 keeps, LOD 2 keeps… for each level's share of the triangles

Reset puts the shipped defaults back.

Settings ▸ Import.

docs.title: Per file: Import settings and Reimport
docs.text: Select the original file in the Explorer and open its Properties (ⓘ): Import settings has Optimize (Auto / Always / Never), LOD levels, Max texture size and Compress textures (KTX2) for that file only; Use defaults forgets them. Reimport runs the original again with these settings and updates every placed copy (one undo step each). An optimized copy's Properties show what was saved and link back to its original.

docs.title: The scene's LOD distance
docs.text: Configure Scene ▸ Level of detail ▸ LOD distance is one slider for the whole scene, shared with everyone in it: above 1 keeps full detail further away, below 1 switches to the lighter levels sooner. It applies to every model with an LOD chain.

docs.title: Exporting for Quest / web
docs.text: The other half of the pipeline is on the way out: Optimize for: For Quest / web in Save options and Settings ▸ Export writes compressed textures, compressed geometry and the LOD chain into a GLTF or a Scene file — see Publish & Export.

docs.title: Replacing a model later
docs.text: A new version of a model does not have to be a new object: Replace model… keeps the object, its flows, physics and clips.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• After an undo, or opening a .tpscene saved with Full quality, a texture is the plain (resized) picture again — the size saving stays; the GPU compression comes back on the next import or a For Quest / web save.
  • The original is kept in the Library even when it is larger than the 25 MB sharing limit; it is not shared with peers in that case.

docs.title: The Interface
docs.text: Since 1.30 every window, menu, dialog, the main HUD and the phone layout are built from one small kit of parts and one set of colours. This page is the map: where things are and what the shapes mean. Nothing you can do changed — every shortcut, setting, scrub field and panel works as before; only the look and a few placements moved.

docs.title: One accent colour
docs.text:
Blue marks what you can act on or have selected: the armed tool, a switch that is on, the chosen chip, a primary button, the focus ring. Orange is kept for things that are live — Play, recording, streaming — so it stands out where it matters. A Shared or This device badge beside a heading says who a setting affects, instead of a paragraph explaining it.

The light theme and every custom .theme.json restyle all of it; see Themes & Appearance.

docs.title: The main HUD
docs.text:
• The toolbar at the bottom is one glass bar: Move, Rotate, Scale, Interact, Play (the only orange button), then the windows you keep there (Objects, Node editor, Explorer, Animation…). The accent fill marks the armed tool or an open window. It is still yours to arrange — right-click any button (or press and hold it) ▸ Edit positions to drag the buttons into place; see The toolbar. The two corner stacks — bottom-left (the AI assistant and +) and bottom-right (Chat and the microphone) — are arranged the same way. Buttons that do not fit fold into a » button at the end of the bar — see When the buttons do not fit. Since 1.35 the whole bar, each corner stack, the buttons beside the logo, the top-right group and the Connect bar can be dragged anywhere on the screen, and the bar turned vertical — see Edit positions.
  • The logo (top-left) opens the main menu, grouped as Project · Scene · Collaborate · App — see The main menu's Project actions. A press anywhere outside the menu closes it; pressing another button (a bottom-bar tab, the bell, Play) closes it and does that button's job in the same press, and pressing the 3D view only closes it — nothing gets selected or deselected.
  • The Connect bar (top centre) shows your ID — click it to copy your invite link — and the field to join someone, with the status dot at its left end. Once you are connected it collapses to a chip: the dot, the avatars of who is here and your mic. Click the chip to open the full bar again. On a computer the dot has no words beside it — point at it to read them; see The status dot. It is either pinned along the top row or floats as a pill (its drawer chooses, or right-click it — press and hold on a touch screen — for Move, Pin to top row / Float, Reset position and Reset all); a floating bar with no room turns compact, and you can move or hide it — see The Connect bar.
  • Top right: scene notes, the notification bell (with a count) and the peers panel sit in one group beside your picture, which opens your profile menu (Customize character, Profile settings). Since 1.33 that group is arranged with Edit positions too; emptied, it leaves no box behind. Since 1.36 the profile menu opens under the profile button wherever it is, beside a pinned right sidebar too.
  • Toasts are calm cards under the Connect bar, at most three at a time; more collect behind +N more. See Toasts.
  • Someone who is speaking in voice chat gets a soft green ring on their avatar.
  • Buttons are 36–38 px with a mouse and grow to 44 px on a touch screen.

With a sidebar pinned at full height, the profile menu opens under its button, beside the sidebar.

docs.title: The command palette (Ctrl+K)
docs.text: Ctrl+K opens one search box over everything: tools (Move, Scale, Interact…), windows (Explorer, Objects, the Profiler…), menu items and every setting. Type a few letters, move with ↑ ↓, press Enter to run it; Esc or a click outside closes it. Picking a setting opens Settings already searching for that row. The palette is listed in the shortcut sheet (?) and can be rebound there like any shortcut.

docs.title: Windows and tabs
docs.text:
Every docked or floating window — Explorer, Objects, Chat, AI assistant, Notes, the Notification centre, the node editor, Flow code, Animation, UV, Shader, HUD editor, Profiler, the Code workspace — has the same header: icon, title, the window's own actions, then pin and close in the same places. Windows in one group, and the views in the bottom dock, share one tab strip: pill tabs with the view's icon and their own ✕ to close that view. More tabs than fit scroll sideways (the wheel or a swipe; the strip fades where more tabs are hidden) while + stays in place, and the strip keeps its scroll when you pick a tab. Moving, docking and tabbing are described in Floating windows.

Long names — an object or file name in a window header — stay on one line and end in "…", so they never push the window's buttons out of place. Point at the name (or press and hold it on a touch screen) to read it whole. On a narrow phone the Animation window puts the name on its own line above its controls.

docs.title: Sidebars
docs.text:
On a computer or a tablet-width window, each side of the screen holds one sidebar. Every panel docked to that side is a tab of it: Configure Scene / Properties, the Objects list and any window you dock to the edge (the Node editor, the Explorer…). Only the tab in front is shown, so opening a panel on a side that already has a sidebar brings its tab forward instead of opening a second column. The sidebar's header strip holds one tab per panel, a + after the tabs and, at its far end, the Full height button (↕) and the hide button.

  • Switch by clicking a tab (or ← / → with a tab focused).
  • Close a panel with the × on its tab. It leaves the sidebar, and its side is remembered for next time. Since 1.35 closing (or moving away) the last tab leaves the sidebar open and empty, with its + and Press + or drag a tab here — drag a tab or a floating window onto it, or hide it.
  • Add a window with the sidebar's +: it lists every window. One that is closed opens as a tab of this sidebar; one that is already open is ticked, says where it is and comes to the front there (see The "+" menus). On a touch screen windows do not join the side columns yet, so there the + opens the window as it would anywhere.
  • Show or hide a sidebar with Ctrl+B (left) and Ctrl+Alt+B (right) — ⌘ on a Mac, the same keys as VS Code — or its hide button. Hiding keeps every tab open: showing it again brings them back, and opening a panel onto a hidden sidebar shows it again. A sidebar that had nothing in it opens empty with its +. Rebind both in Settings ▸ Shortcuts (Panels); inside the code workspace the same keys toggle its own sidebars. A hidden sidebar comes back after a reload; an emptied one stays empty.
  • Right-click a tab (press and hold on a touch screen) for its menu: Close, Close others, Undock into a floating window, Move to the other side and Move to the bottom dock. Configure Scene and Properties live only in a sidebar, so their Undock and bottom dock rows are greyed out with the reason.
  • More tabs than fit scroll sideways (the mouse wheel or a swipe), like the bottom dock's tabs; the tab in front is kept in view.
  • Drag a tab anywhere — see Dragging a tab below.
  • Dock a floating window: drag it — by its header or any empty part of it — to a screen edge, or onto a sidebar (Add as tab lights up), or right-click its header ▸ Move to the left / right sidebar — it becomes a tab of that side. Hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) while you drag to place it floating over the sidebar instead — see Moving a floating window.
  • Resize by dragging the sidebar's inner edge; a double-click resets it. All tabs of a side share the width. The logo and the profile button move with the edge as you drag. On a touch screen the edge is easy to grab, the sidebar stops at its minimum width (250 px), and its content never scrolls sideways — rows that do not fit wrap onto a second line.
  • Full height: press ↕ and the sidebar runs from the top edge to the bottom edge. The buttons in that top corner (the logo and menu on the left; notes, notifications and your profile on the right) move inward at once — since 1.36 they jump to their new place instead of sliding, the Connect bar too — and the bottom dock gets narrower so it sits beside the sidebar, never under it — every docked view, Statistics, Chat, Objects, the Live profiler, the AI assistant and the Shader editor included. Press it again to fit the sidebar under the top buttons. The main menu always opens above sidebars. With one or both sides at full height the Connect bar stays a pill, centred between the logo and the corner buttons. The toolbar never slides under a full-height sidebar — see The toolbar and sidebars.
  • The header lock of Configure Scene and Properties sits beside Full height in the tab row while that panel is the tab in front — see Panel headers.
  • A pinned Properties (the pin in its header) follows your selection without pulling its tab over the Objects list when the two share a side; double-click an object (or pick Properties in its menu) to bring it forward.

Two windows as tabs in one sidebar; Full height is at the end of the tab strip.

A sidebar tab's right-click menu.

docs.title: Dragging a tab
docs.text:
Drag a sidebar tab and a highlight shows what will happen before you let go — there is never a silent drop:

Let go over Highlight What happens the other side Move to the left / right side, or Add as tab when a sidebar is already open there the panel docks on that side the bottom dock or the bottom edge Move to dock (on the dock's tab bar a marker shows the spot) the panel becomes a dock tab anywhere else in the 3D view Float here the panel becomes a floating window where you dropped it its own sidebar Stays here nothing

Dragging a floating window onto a sidebar (or a screen edge), or a bottom-dock tab onto a sidebar, shows the same highlights, painted above every panel; the window you drag turns see-through so the highlight stays readable.

Dragging a tab into the 3D view: drop it to float the window.

docs.title: Any window in a sidebar
docs.text:
Every window that can be docked at the bottom can also be a sidebar tab — the Node editor, Flow Code, Animation, UV, Shader and HUD editors, the Explorer, the Profiler, Code, the Image editor, Objects, Statistics, the Live profiler, Chat and the AI assistant:

  • Into a sidebar: drag the floating window (by its header or any empty part) to the left or right edge or onto an open sidebar, drag its bottom-dock tab onto a sidebar, right-click its dock tab or its floating header ▸ Move to the left / right sidebar, or pick it in the sidebar's + while it is closed.
  • Back to the bottom: right-click its sidebar tab ▸ Move to the bottom dock, or drag the tab onto the dock.

No second header. A window in a sidebar shows no window header of its own: the sidebar tab is its header (name, ×, menu). Windows whose header carries tools keep a slim tools row without the title, ×, Dock or +: Objects (search), the Explorer (search and filters; its search hides when the sidebar is narrower than about 520 px, as in a narrow floating window), the Shader editor, Code, the Profiler, the Image editor (the file name) and Statistics (the budget dot and re-read).

Full height: the sidebar runs from the top edge to the bottom.

Which side Configure Scene and Properties dock to, each side's width and Full height, the tab order and the tab in front are kept on this device and saved in workspace layouts. A phone keeps its bottom dock instead.

A sidebar on each side, in the Light theme. The two are shown together, cut from one screen.

docs.title: Panel headers
docs.text:
The Properties and Configure Scene headers — the panel's name and the Filter properties box — have a lock button. On a computer or an unfolded phone it sits in the sidebar's tab row, next to Full height, while that panel is the tab in front; on a phone it stays in the panel header, beside the pin.

  • Locked (the default): the header stays on top while you scroll the properties.
  • Unlocked: the header scrolls away with the properties, giving the whole panel to them — handy on a phone.

Each of the two panels remembers its own choice on this device, in a sidebar and in the phone's dock alike. Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Windows & chrome ▸ Sticky panel headers sets both at once (it shows a mixed state while they differ); searching Settings for sticky header finds it.

Every value in these two panels can be copied, pasted and reset from a right-click — see Copy, paste and reset values.

docs.title: Docked windows
docs.text:
Since 1.32 a window in the bottom dock has no ✕ or undock button of its own:

  • Close it from its tab. Every tab carries its ✕. From the keyboard, focus the tab and press Delete (since 1.46); a split pair closes together. The tab's right-click menu (Shift+F10) has Close too.
  • Undock sits at the right end of the dock's tab strip, just left of Minimize the dock. It takes the window you are looking at out of the dock as a floating window. To have it take every docked window out as one floating window with tabs instead, set Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Windows & chrome ▸ Undock button to All as one tabbed group (the default is Active window).
  • You can also drag a tab out of the strip — or right-click it ▸ Undock into a floating window — to undock that one window. A docked window moves by its tab, not by its header. The same menu has Move to the left / right sidebar (see Any window in a sidebar).
  • The dock's + lists every window that can live in the dock — the Node editor and the Image editor included, and since 1.33 also Objects, Statistics, the Live profiler, Chat and the AI assistant — the same list as the phone's Windows sheet. See The "+" menus for what a pick does.
  • An empty dock: with nothing docked, T opens the dock empty — its tab strip with only + and the line Press + or drag a tab here. Drop a floating window on its strip or its body to dock it there; T again closes it.

docs.title: The "+" menus
docs.text:
Every + — the dock's, a sidebar's, the floating Node editor's — lists every window, and since 1.35 it never makes a second copy:

  • A window that is already open — in the dock, in a sidebar or floating — is ticked and says where it is (In dock, Left sidebar, Right sidebar, Floating). Picking it brings it to the front where it is: it is not moved, docked or closed.
  • Only a closed window opens, into the + you pressed.
  • Pick several at once: hold Ctrl (⌘ on a Mac) or Shift while you click rows — each window opens and the menu stays open for the next pick. From the keyboard, type to filter and press Ctrl+Enter. A plain click opens one window and closes the menu.

To close a docked window use its tab's ×; to bring a floating window into the dock, drag it onto the dock or use its window menu (Dock to bottom).

The dock's + menu, in a small window: each row says where that window is now.

Dock any window exactly where you want it: drag a floating window by its header or any empty part of it — or tear a tab out of a tabbed window, or drag a whole tabbed window by its tab bar — onto the dock's tab bar. The window turns see-through, the tab bar is outlined and a caret shows the slot between the docked tabs where it will land; let go and it docks exactly there. This works for every editor and for Objects, Statistics, the Live profiler, Chat and the AI assistant; file and model previews, the text viewer, What's new and the tool palettes stay floating. The bottom edge of the screen still docks a window at the end of the tabs (and is the only target while the dock is minimized; an empty dock opened with T takes a drop anywhere on it). Since 1.35 this works by touch too, on an unfolded phone or a tablet. Everywhere else a floating window simply moves — over the open dock, over the sidebars, partly off screen — and stays under the cursor the whole way; a header that ends up under the Controls bar is nudged above it when you let go.

Drop on the dock's tab bar; the caret shows the slot.

Floating windows can overlap the dock: move them over it and resize them past its top edge — only the screen edge stops the resize corner. The Objects list remembers whether you last had it docked, and the toolbar button and O open it there.

docs.title: Splitting the dock
docs.text:
The bottom dock can show two windows side by side — the Node editor beside the Explorer, the Shader editor beside Statistics — with a divider between them. The pair is one tab in the dock's strip, named with a slash: Node editor / Explorer.

  • Press Split (the two-columns button left of Undock and Minimize): the tab in front is shown beside the next tab in the strip. If it is the last tab, the right pane starts empty — press its + (or drag a tab onto it) to choose its window. Press Split again (it shows pressed) to unsplit: the two windows become two tabs again.
  • Drag the divider to give one side more room (mouse, pen or touch); double-click it to centre it. With the divider focused, the arrow keys move it (Shift for bigger steps). Each pane keeps at least 15 % of the dock's width.
  • Click inside a pane to work in it — its name is bold in the pair's tab, and Undock, the tab menu and the shortcuts act on it.
  • Drag a tab onto a pane to show it there instead; the window it replaces stays a tab.
  • Drop a floating window onto a pane (since 1.39): drag it over one of the two panes — the pane lights up with Show in this pane — and release. The window docks and shows in that pane; the view it replaced stays a tab.
  • The tab menu (right-click or long-press a dock tab) has Split right and Split with ▸ (pick the partner), and on a pair Swap sides and Unsplit. Closing the pair's tab (×) closes both windows.

Splits and the divider's position are kept on this device and in workspace layouts. If the app closes one window of a pair for a while, the other fills the dock until it comes back. Splitting needs a wider screen — a computer or an unfolded phone; on a folded phone the dock is one column and a pair shows as its two ordinary tabs.

The dock split side by side, in a small window.

A floating window dragged over a pane of a split dock.

docs.title: Floating windows with tabs
docs.text:
• Statistics groups too (since 1.39): its header menu ▸ Group with…, another window's Group with… ▸ Statistics, or drag its header onto another window's header.
  • Join a window as a tab: drag a tab out of the dock and drop it onto a floating window. It joins that window as a tab instead of opening a second window.
  • Dock all tabs: a floating window with tabs has a dock button just left of Close all tabs. It puts every tab back in the dock. For a window with one tab, drag its tab to the dock, or use the window's Dock button.
  • Move it by touch: drag its tab bar — or any of its tab names — and the whole window follows your finger, on a phone or an unfolded foldable alike. A tap on a tab still switches to it.
  • Hold a tab (press and hold; right-click with a mouse) for that window's window menu: Float (undock) takes it out of the group, just beside it; Dock to bottom and Move to the left / right sidebar move only that view (greyed out for windows that always float, such as a file preview); Close closes that view and the rest of the group stays.

Layouts… (Menu ▸ Layouts) opens a regular dialog for your saved arrangements — on a folded phone, a tab of the bottom dock — see Workspace layouts.

Lists scroll with a thin scrollbar that appears only while you scroll or point at them; there are no chunky native scrollbars anywhere.

docs.title: Windows on several monitors
docs.text:
Since 1.46 any panel — or a whole dock — can live in its own browser window. Drag it to a second monitor and keep the 3D view full-size in the app. Everything stays live: it is the same app in a second window, not a copy.

A popped-out dock is its own browser window.

  • Pop out a panel: right-click a dock tab, a sidebar tab or a floating window's header ▸ Pop out into a new window. Or drag a tab out of the browser window and let go. Panels that pop out: the Explorer, Properties / Configure Scene, the Node editor, Timeline, Animation, UV, Shader and HUD editors, the Profiler, the Debugger, Chat, the AI assistant and Code.
  • Pop out a whole dock: Pop out the whole dock (dock tab menu) or Pop out this sidebar (sidebar tab menu) opens one window with every tab in it.
  • One panel, one tab: a window with a single panel shows no tab strip — its header shows the panel's name, and that name is the tab. Drag it to move the panel; right-click it for Dock back, Move to…, Always show tab strip in windows and Close. Hover shows it can be grabbed.
  • More tabs: drop a second panel on a window's header (or use the header's +) and a tab strip appears; the title becomes the first tab. Back to one panel, the strip goes again. A popped-out dock always shows its tabs, and Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Always show tab strip in windows shows them everywhere.
  • One panel, one place: a panel is only ever open in one spot. Adding it somewhere else — another window, a dock or a sidebar — moves it there. While you drag a tab, every window and dock that can take it shows a drop zone on its header. Drag a popped tab back into the app (left sidebar, right sidebar, bottom dock — or anywhere else to put it back where it was), or right-click ▸ Dock back. Closing a window docks its panels back.
  • Your windows come back: the windows you had open are remembered per monitor setup and reopen when you come back. Browsers open one pop-up per click, so if pop-ups are blocked a bar offers Open 2 windows — each click opens the next one (or allow pop-ups for the site). Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Remember windows per screen setup (Chromium asks to see every screen for this).
  • Bring all windows back (command palette, or any tab menu) puts every panel back in the app. Closing or reloading the app's tab closes its windows.
  • Keys in a popped-out window are the panel's own; undo and redo still reach the scene.
  • Not for pop-out: the Objects list, file previews, the Image editor and phone tabs. Phones, touch screens and VR keep one window — the pop-out entries are hidden there.

docs.title: Focus mode
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+Space to maximize the area under the mouse pointer:

  • over the 3D view (or a toolbar or a floating window): every panel, window and dock is hidden and the 3D view fills the screen;
  • over a docked window (the Code window, the Node editor, the Explorer…): since 1.34 that window fills the whole browser window. Its tab row runs along the top edge, so you can still switch tabs, and the window reaches every edge. The sidebars step aside while it lasts and come back exactly as they were — open, pinned, width and side — when you leave. You can still drag the window's top edge down to see the 3D view behind it.

Press Esc or Ctrl+Space again — or click Exit focus (in the tab row for a docked window, at the top for the 3D view) — and everything comes back exactly as it was; nothing is closed. Beside Exit focus on a docked window, a Viewport button shows or hides the viewport picture-in-picture without leaving focus mode. Focus mode also ends when a dialog opens or you press Play.

Focus mode, in a small window: the Viewport button shows or hides the picture-in-picture.

Without a keyboard: View ▸ Focus mode in the 3D view's right-click menu, right-click a dock tab ▸ Maximize (focus mode), or on a phone More ▸ Tools & View ▸ Focus mode (which you can also drag onto the phone bar).

Inside the UV editor and the Animation timeline Ctrl+Space keeps its own meaning (keyboard selection) while you work there; use the menu entries, or rebind focus mode in Settings ▸ Shortcuts.

docs.title: The viewport picture-in-picture
docs.text:
While a docked window fills the whole window, the 3D view shows as a small picture-in-picture (PiP) in the bottom-right corner, on top of the docked window. It is a live second view of the scene with its own camera — moving it never moves your main view.

  • Navigate: left-drag orbits, right-drag pans, the wheel zooms; on a touch screen one finger orbits and two fingers pinch and pan.
  • Edit: click (or tap) an object to select it (Shift adds). With the pointer over the PiP, W / E / R pick Move / Rotate / Scale (1 / 2 / 3 and G work too), drag the gizmo to transform, F frames the selection in the PiP, Delete deletes and Ctrl+Z undoes.
  • Move it by its title bar and resize it by the grip in its top-left corner; double-click the grip for the default size (the size is remembered); it starts in the bottom-right corner each time. ⌖ puts its camera back on your main view.
  • Show or hide it with the Viewport button beside Exit focus — filled while the picture-in-picture shows, outlined while it is hidden. Its × hides it the same way. Since 1.35 the choice is remembered for the next time you enter focus mode, and after a reload; it starts shown. The button is there only while the picture-in-picture can show — not once you have dragged the window down, and not on a folded phone.
  • It shows only while the docked window covers the whole window: drag the window down and the real 3D view is back.
  • While the 3D view is covered it is not drawn at all, so a maximized window with the PiP costs less than the normal editor.

The PiP's keys are listed in Settings ▸ Shortcuts ▸ Viewport picture-in-picture, where they can be rebound.

Focus mode on the Flow Code window, in a small window.

docs.title: Menus
docs.text:
The right-click, Add (Shift+A) and viewport menus share one style: 32 px rows, an icon per row, shortcuts right-aligned, quiet section labels.

Right-click an object and the everyday actions come first — Properties, Rename, Duplicate, Delete — then Focus, Ping and Add note, then the editing modes. Rarer work is one level down: Transform ▸ (align to ground, origin, pivot…), Mesh ▸ (convert, boolean…), Physics & effects ▸ (joints, particles, flow effects), Prefab ▸ on a placed prefab copy, and Save as… ▸. Every action and its shortcut is still there.

docs.title: The main menu's Project actions
docs.text:
The Project section at the top of the main menu has two layouts, picked in Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Lists & menus ▸ Project actions:

  • Compact (the default on a computer and an unfolded phone) is a two-column grid: New from template… across the top, then Load | Save ▾, then Import | Export…. Save saves straight away with your last-used options; its ▾ opens Save options — what to save and what the file includes. Export… opens Publish / Export.
  • List (the default on a folded phone) is one row per action — Templates, Import, Load, Save, Publish / Export — with the Project | Scene | ⚙ switch under Save; the ⚙ opens the same Save options.
  • Auto is List on a phone and Compact everywhere else. Searching the settings for burger or compact finds it.

The main menu's Project section in the Compact layout.

docs.title: Dialogs
docs.text:
Modules, Sessions, Checkpoints, Templates, Storage, Publish / Export, Import and every confirmation share one dialog style: a header with the title and close, tabs directly under it where a dialog has them, one scrolling body and the answers bottom-right. Each view has one emphasised action; a destructive answer is red. Escape, a click outside and the close button behave as before. Customize character is a drawer you can resize by its edge — see Your Character.

Since 1.32 every dialog — Modules, Sessions, Templates, confirmations — covers the whole screen, the logo and its menu button included; close it with its own ✕, Done, Esc or a click outside. Settings is a window beside your work: since 1.35 opening it no longer closes an open sidebar, the docked windows or the Node editor (on a folded phone it is a full-screen sheet, and the dock comes back when you close it). What's new opens above everything else: the logo, undo and redo, the connection pill, notifications, your profile and the bottom bar.

Questions are dialogs, outcomes are toasts. Anything that asks you to decide something destructive or blocking is a dialog: Delete flow, Restore previous session?, deleting a group or a prefab, rebuilding a mesh or terrain that discards your edits, leaving a session to join another, exporting everything when nothing is selected, a scene too large for this device. Passive results — Saved, Copied, Exported… — stay toasts and are kept in the notification centre. Requests from other people (to load a session, to take control, to see your private scene) stay cards in the corner, like connection requests: a dialog would take over your screen from afar.

A confirmation is a dialog over the dimmed screen.

docs.title: On a phone
docs.text:
Below 640 px wide — a folded phone — the app switches to a phone layout with less on screen and nothing missing. An unfolded phone and a computer share the desktop layout.

  • Top: the logo (main menu) on the left, a Connect chip in the middle and, on the right, the notification bell, the peers button (while someone is connected) and your picture. The chip shows the status dot with the state beside it — Connected, Connecting… or Offline — whenever the top bar has room; when the bar is crowded (people are connected and you are in a call, so the peers button and the microphone take the space) it shrinks to the dot and ▾. Tap it for your invite link, the join field, Info and Toasts.
  • Bottom bar: Add · Objects · Play · Explorer · More by default. Play stays the only orange control. More holds the rest: Chat, the AI assistant, Notes, Scene, the node editor and every other window, the edit tools, Statistics and Tools & View. You arrange the bar from More — see The phone bar and More.
  • A bar button toggles its view. Tapping Objects, Explorer or any view you put on the bar while its tab is on screen minimizes the dock — every tab stays open and the 3D view clears; tap it again to bring it back. With Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Windows & chrome ▸ Allow undocking on touch screens on and that window floating, the button opens and closes the floating window instead.
  • Play plays on the screen on a phone or tablet until you choose otherwise (a headset still enters VR). Press and hold Play for its menu: Play as (Play, Enter VR, Enter AR passthrough), Test play in a game scene, Move left / Move right (Play moves along the bar, and this device remembers where) and Arrange the bar…. Choosing Enter VR or Enter AR passthrough turns Play's icon into the headset (with A R for passthrough), as on a computer; Settings ▸ VR ▸ Play on the screen, even in a headset is the same choice.
  • The selection toolbar appears only while something is selected — see The selection toolbar. With nothing selected — just looking around — there is no toolbar; More ▸ Edit has Inspect, Move, Rotate, Scale, Undo, Redo, Select multiple and Interact mode, and any of them can go on the bar.
  • Panels are tabs of the bottom dock. Properties, Objects, Notes, Configure Scene, Layouts and Statistics sit in the dock beside the Explorer and the node editor — see The dock on a phone.
  • Menus are sheets that open over the dock from the bottom: the main menu, More, the profile menu, notifications, the peers panel, the Connection sheet, Add and the press-and-hold action sheets, Chat, the AI assistant, the tool palettes (mesh edit, sculpt, spline) and Customize character — see Sheets on a phone. The bar with Play stays visible and tappable. Above the dock, the Add list and the other sheets that work on the selection, the selection toolbar rides just above the top edge — never on top of it — and follows that edge in the same frame while you drag a grab bar, so you can pick an object in Objects and move or undo without closing it. While a menu is open — the main menu, the profile menu, notifications, Connection, More, an object's or the viewport's action sheet, Customize character, Settings or any dialog — the selection toolbar hides, and it comes back when the menu closes.
  • Docked windows open with their sidebars hidden: the Explorer, Node editor, UV editor, HUD editor, Profiler, Image editor and Code workspace give the screen to their work area (folded or unfolded). Open a side panel with its edge button or tab; it stays open next time, for that window.
  • The dock's + at the end of its tab strip opens a Windows sheet: every window — the six dock panels included — with a show/hide switch. With floating windows allowed on the phone (Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Windows & chrome ▸ Allow undocking on touch screens), + works as on a computer — a menu that adds a window to the dock.
  • Editors fit a phone: the Animation window shows one pane at a time, the Shader editor gives the canvas the whole screen with the palette and properties as sheets, and every toolbar that does not fit — UV editor tools, Profiler controls — scrolls sideways (with a fade where more is hidden); nothing is out of reach.
  • Settings is a list you tap into, with ‹ Back on every page; Settings and dialogs open full-screen and cover the logo while they are open.

Touch targets are at least 44 px, switches 51 × 31, and text fields use 16 px text so the browser never zooms.

docs.title: The phone bar and More
docs.text:
You choose what is on the bottom bar, and in what order, from More itself — there is no separate editor:

  • Press and hold any item in More, then drag it onto the bar; it lands where you let go.
  • Press and hold an item on the bar and drag it along the bar to move it, or up into More to take it off.
  • Play works the same way: drag it anywhere on the bar, or into More. While Play is off the bar it waits at the start of More ▸ Windows, ready to be dragged back.

The tip at the bottom of More says it: Hold and drag items to or from the bar. It goes away by itself once you have added, moved or removed an item on the bar, and stays away; Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Reset tips brings it back. A dot on an item in More means it is already on the bar, and Reset bar (at the end of More) brings back the default. With More closed nothing moves by accident: a long press on a bar item opens More and picks that item up in one gesture.

More open on a folded phone, with Move being dragged onto the bottom bar.

What can go on the bar — everything in More:

  • Windows: Add, More, Objects, Statistics, Chat, Explorer, Node editor, Animation, Scene, AI assistant, Notes, Flow Code, Shader editor, UV editor, HUD editor, Profiler, Code;
  • Edit: Inspect, Move, Rotate, Scale, Undo, Redo, Select multiple, Interact mode. Move, Rotate, Scale and Inspect work on the selection and look pressed while active;
  • Tools & View: snapping, view and camera, and Focus mode (see Focus mode).

How many: up to seven, Play included. Up to five items show their names; with six or seven on a narrow phone the bar shows icons only (each still at least 44 px wide, with its name as the tooltip and for screen readers). An eighth is refused, and the last item cannot leave — the bar is how you get back to More. If you take More itself off the bar, the app tells you once: press and hold any item on the bar to get More back.

Show switches sit at the bottom of More (and in Settings ▸ Interface). All are on by default:

Switch Off means Selection toolbar no floating Move / Rotate / Scale / Inspect strip over a selection — handy once those tools are on your bar Dock tab row the row of tabs above docked windows is hidden; the bar and More still switch views Grab handle no grab bar on docked windows and sheets (and no tap to step the size); drag the top edge to resize

The bottom of More on a phone, in the Light theme.

The bar and the switches are kept on this device; they are never shared with peers or saved in scenes, but a workspace layout saved on the phone keeps the bar. On a wider screen — an unfolded phone, a tablet, a computer — the desktop toolbar is used instead, and your phone bar is waiting for the next fold. A bar you customised in 1.32 carries over.

docs.title: The dock on a phone
docs.text:
On a folded phone the panels you work in are tabs of the bottom dock, in the same strip as the Explorer, the node editor and the other editors:

Tab What it shows Opens from Properties the selected object's properties Inspect in the selection toolbar Objects the object list the bar's Objects Notes the scene's notes; opening a note shows it as a page of the tab, closing it returns to the list More ▸ Notes Configure Scene the scene's settings More ▸ Scene, or the main menu's Configure Scene Layouts save and switch workspace layouts the main menu's Layouts, or the dock's + Statistics the scene's budgets More ▸ Statistics (since 1.34; before, a floating window)
  • All tabs share one height. Drag the dock's grab bar to resize it; swipe it down to minimize the dock.
  • A tab's ✕ closes that panel. The dock's + lists every window, these six included, with a show/hide switch.
  • More ▸ Statistics (or Statistics on your bar) toggles like any bar button: tapped while its tab is in front, it minimizes the dock. With Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Windows & chrome ▸ Allow undocking on touch screens on, Statistics floats as before.
  • Several can be open at once — the properties no longer close when you open the notes.
  • Play stays on top of whatever is open.
  • The main menu closes as Configure Scene opens, since its tab is underneath the menu. On a computer the menu stays open, above the sidebar.

The dock on a folded phone: tabs above it, the selection toolbar above them.

Folding and unfolding. Unfold the phone (or widen the window past 640 px) and each tab goes back to its place on the bigger screen: Properties and Configure Scene to their sidebar (the right side unless you moved them), Objects to its window or sidebar, Notes to the notes drawer, Layouts to the Layouts dialog. Fold it again and the same tabs come back, with the one you were looking at in front. What you open or close on the bigger screen carries over. A reload starts with a clean slate.

docs.title: Sheets on a phone
docs.text:
Since 1.32 every sheet works the same way:

  • One grab bar sits at the top of each sheet. It never scrolls away with the sheet's contents. (The Grab handle switch at the bottom of More hides it; the sheet's top edge still resizes it.)
  • Drag the bar to make the sheet taller or shorter. It stops at a minimum and a maximum height, and each sheet remembers its height on this device.
  • Swipe the bar down to the bottom to close the sheet; a tap on the bar steps its size.
