Hosted providers return the GLB as a signed CDN link. If your browser blocks that cross-origin download, the generation will finish but the import fails with a network error. If you hit this, prefer the self-hosted ComfyUI path (same-origin via your proxy).

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
• Add menu → ✨ Generate 3D model… — a small dialog: pick a provider, type a prompt, optional name, Generate. The mesh lands where you opened the menu.
  • AI assistant — just ask (“add a treasure chest by the wall”). The assistant calls generate_mesh when no primitive fits; it returns immediately and the mesh appears when ready. It won't block the conversation.
  • Console agent — pass --mesh-kind comfyui --mesh-url … --mesh-workflow path/to.json (or AGENT_MESH_* env vars) and the agent's generate_mesh tool works the same way, pushing the GLB into the session. See Console Agent.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Generated meshes replicate as full GLB data — very heavy meshes (>40 MB) are rejected, and a large one may exceed the 5 MB undo-snapshot cap (still placed, just not undoable). Keep prompts to single objects.
  • Quality is entirely your generator's — a better TRELLIS workflow or a higher hosted tier gives better meshes.
  • Generated meshes are also cached into the Explorer “Generated” folder so you can re-place them without regenerating.

docs.title: Better models with img2threejs
docs.text:
Recipe — img2threejs is a third-party agent skill (Apache-2.0, https://github.com/img2threejs/img2threejs). theprototype does not bundle or run it; your agent does, on your own machine and your own model plan.

img2threejs rebuilds an object from one picture as procedural three.js code: a THREE.Group made of primitives and generated geometry, with a hierarchy of pivots and sockets (a lid that opens, a flame that flickers, a spot to hang a pot). With the AI assistant window and the import_model tool, the result lands in your scene as an ordinary model that every peer sees, saves with the scene and undoes in one step.

docs.title: 1. Install the skill beside the agent bridge
docs.text:
On the machine where your agent (Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode) runs:

npx --yes img2threejs@latest install   # links the skill into every agent it finds
npx --yes img2threejs@latest doctor    # "managed" = Claude Code is set up
Needs Node.js ≥ 18, Git and Python ≥ 3.10. Restart the agent. Connect it to your session as in Talk to your agent (npx @theprototype/agent …) and tell it to listen.

docs.title: 2. Send a picture in the chat
docs.text:
In the AI assistant window pick your agent, then press + → From device / Camera (phones) / From Explorer, paste, or drop the picture on the window. It is shrunk on your device (long edge 1568 px, about 1 MB) and its location data is removed before it is sent. The agent sees the picture, and the bridge also saves it to a temporary file whose path comes with your message — that path is what the skill takes.

Write what you want, for example: "Rebuild this lantern with img2threejs, then import it next to the campfire."

docs.title: 3. What the agent does
docs.text:
1. Runs /img2threejs Rebuild the object in <the temp path> as a procedural Three.js model.
  2. Exports a GLB from the generated group (three.js GLTFExporter, binary, everything embedded) — keep the node names: Lid_Pivot, Flame, Socket_Handle become named objects you can select, animate and wire in Flow.
  3. Calls import_model with the file's path (the bridge reads it locally), a position and a source note (for example "img2threejs from lantern.jpg"). The app runs its own import pipeline (optimizing big textures, LOD, the device-budget check) and records where the model came from.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Materials: glTF carries standard PBR materials only. img2threejs's procedural shaders do not survive the export — ask the agent to bake them to textures, or to use standard materials (colour, roughness, metalness, emissive).
  • Self-contained GLB only, up to 25 MB: no external textures or buffers. Nothing in a GLB runs as code.
  • Draft or strict: say "low effort / draft" for a quick blockout; the skill's strict quality gate (--strict-quality) refuses shallow specs and takes longer. Start with a draft, refine the parts that matter.
  • Cost: a rebuild is several vision passes (blockout → structure → form → material → surface → lighting → interaction → optimization, each compared against your picture) on your own agent plan. A strict rebuild of a detailed object can use a lot of it.
  • Editors and admins can send pictures and import; viewers see the pictures and the models.
  • Undo removes the whole import in one step; the model's Properties show its source.

docs.title: Local & Small Models
docs.text: The assistant runs fine against a self-hosted endpoint — that's the point of the Custom provider preset. But local setups have two recurring failure modes worth knowing about: a mismatched tool-call parser on the server, and a model too small for the multi-step work you're asking of it. This page covers both, plus what the Physics tools checkbox actually gates.

docs.title: vLLM: use the right tool-call parser
docs.text:
A tool-capable model served with the wrong --tool-call-parser produces mangled tool calls. The worked example is vLLM + Qwen3.5: Qwen3.5 emits its calls as <function=X><parameter=k> XML, while the commonly-copied hermes parser expects JSON inside <tool_call> tags.

What that mismatch looks like from the app:

  • Unstreamed, the call arrives as plain text (<tool_call><function=…) with no tool_calls field — the assistant recovers these itself.
  • Streamed, the server swallows the call and emits a single delta with an invented tool name (often the object's own name — "Cube") and empty arguments. Symptom: "Applied N action(s)" with an empty viewport.

Fix it server-side for Qwen3.5:

vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B \
  --allowed-origins '["*"]' \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3

If your vLLM build rejects qwen3_xml, try qwen3_coder. Verify with a streamed curl request that includes tools: you should see incremental tool_calls deltas with real names and arguments.

Optional, to use a 24 GB card fully: --kv-cache-memory=12185112064 (vLLM logs its own suggested value at startup).

The app defends itself either way

The client detects an unusable streamed turn, retries it unstreamed, and stops streaming for the rest of the session. You can also turn Stream responses off permanently for a provider in Settings ▸ Tools & connections — recommended for any server whose tool calls only work unstreamed. Fixing the parser is still better: streaming feels much more responsive.

docs.title: How big a model do you need?
docs.text:
Tool use is the bottleneck, not prose quality. Rough guide:

Model class What works ~4B (e.g. Qwen3.5-4B) Creating and arranging primitives; single behavior nodes ("make it spin"). The floor — below this, tool calls get unreliable. 8–14B Multi-node behaviors, path patrols, basic physics tuning. 14B–32B quantized / hosted Joints, motors, multi-step assemblies ("a moving spider", "a door that swings"). Materially better at chaining tools and reading their results.

A quantized 14B–32B Qwen (AWQ or FP8) fits a single 24 GB card and is the sweet spot for physics work. Example:

vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-32B-AWQ \
  --allowed-origins '["*"]' \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
  --max-model-len 32768 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92

docs.title: The "Physics tools" checkbox
docs.text:
Behavior (flow-node) tools are always available to the assistant. Physics tools are a per-provider opt-in — the Physics tools (advanced) checkbox in the provider's form, next to Stream responses. It gates:

  • set_physics — body params (dynamic mass / static scenery / bounciness / friction / collider shape),
  • create_joints — welds and hinges (with motors),
  • control_simulation — the assistant may start the simulation on its own after a physics build, so the result comes alive without you pressing Play,
  • the physics node types (mass, bounciness, friction, angular velocity, motor) inside its flow-node vocabulary.

Why gated: a small local model fumbles multi-step physics — wrong hinge axes, jointing rotated parts, re-sending the same call — and the failure is a launched assembly rather than a misplaced box. Enable it for 14B+ or hosted models; leave it off for a 4B.

Two semantics worth knowing:

  • Undo does not stop a running simulation. A prompt is still one undo step, but starting/stopping the sim is not part of it — stop or reset the sim first, then undo reverts the objects, nodes, physics params and joints together.
  • New primitives already spawn dynamic with mass 1, so set_physics is mostly for tuning or pinning scenery (static ground and walls).

See also: AI Assistant · AI Providers (CORS and key storage notes apply to local endpoints too).

docs.title: Pixel art with Pixling and Claude Code
docs.text:
Recipe — Pixling is a third-party tool (MIT). theprototype does not bundle or run it; your agent does, on your own machine.

Pixling (MIT) makes game sprites from a JSON spec, on your machine, deterministically: the same spec renders the same bytes. With the bridge connected (Build with an AI agent), ask Claude Code for a character and it runs:

uv tool install pixling          # or: pip install pixling
pixling new hero knight          # copies an example spec to specs/knight.json — edit it
pixling build specs/knight.json --clips walk --dirs S,E,N,W
# -> out/knight/knight_walk.png: 16 frames x 4 directions of 64x48 px (rows S, E, N, W)
pixling review out/knight        # a zoomed review grid — look at it before importing

Then one tool call brings the sheet AND its spec into the session:

{ "name": "import_file", "arguments": {
    "path": "out/knight/knight_walk.png", "spec_path": "specs/knight.json",
    "frame": { "w": 64, "h": 48, "col": 0, "row": 0 }, "facing": "camera-y",
    "source": "pixling 0.3.1 build specs/knight.json --clips walk --dirs S,E,N,W", "licence": "own work" } }

Everyone sees Explorer ▸ Generated ▸ knight_walk.png + knight_walk.pixling.json and a crisp knight standing at the origin, turning to face each viewer. To change it, edit the spec, build again and import again (a new file; undo removes the old card). pixling guide and pixling pipelines explain the styles and the spec format to your agent.

How the file arrives (type checks, sizes, the card's options, undo, who may import): Talk to your agent ▸ Models and files from the agent's machine.

docs.title: AI Providers
docs.text:
The assistant needs a model to talk to. You supply one — a hosted provider like Grok or Gemini, or your own self-hosted endpoint. Configure it once in Settings ▸ Tools & connections.

Every supported provider speaks the same OpenAI chat-completions dialect, so the app uses one client for all of them.

docs.title: Adding a provider
docs.text:
1. Open Settings ▸ Tools & connections and click Add chat provider.

  2. Pick a preset — it fills in the base URL and a default model:

    Preset Base URL Notes Grok (x.ai) https://api.x.ai/v1 Needs an x.ai API key. Gemini (Google) https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/openai Google AI Studio key; OpenAI-compatibility layer. Custom (you fill it in) Any OpenAI-compatible / self-hosted server (vLLM, Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, …).

  3. Paste your API key / bearer token, adjust the model id if needed, and Save.

  4. Use Test connection to confirm the endpoint and key work before you rely on them. It answers within about 10 s and says what is wrong (see Troubleshooting below).
  5. Select the provider (the radio button) to make it active.

Signed in on theprototype.app? The cloud plugin may add a hosted provider row for you — no key, URL or model to type. It is experimental and appears only while the hosted hardware is reachable. A provider you configured yourself always stays the selected one; the hosted row sits beside it for you to switch to.

You can keep several providers side by side — for example Grok plus two self-hosted boxes — and switch the active one from the assistant window or Settings.

docs.title: Self-hosted / vLLM endpoints
docs.text:
Point the Custom preset at your server's OpenAI-compatible base (the URL that ends in /v1), set the model id to whatever your server serves, and add a bearer token if it requires one. An address typed without https://, or pasted with /chat/completions on the end, is fixed up for you — Will call … under the field shows the exact address the app will use.

Allow browser origins (CORS)

The app runs entirely in your browser and calls the endpoint directly — there is no backend proxy. A self-hosted server must therefore send permissive CORS headers, or the browser blocks the request. For vLLM, start it with:

vllm serve <model> --allowed-origins '["*"]'

Ollama: set OLLAMA_ORIGINS=https://theprototype.app. LM Studio: turn on Enable CORS in its server settings. Other servers have an equivalent allowed-origins setting. Test connection tells a server that answers without allowing this site (CORS) apart from one it cannot reach at all.

docs.title: Where keys are stored
docs.text:
Keys are stored unencrypted

API keys live in this browser's local storage, in plain text (the same place as every other setting). They never leave your device except in the requests you make to the provider you configured. Anyone with access to this browser profile can read them, and Reset settings erases them. Prefer scoped or throwaway keys, and don't enter a production key on a shared machine.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Message Meaning Invalid API key or unauthorized Wrong or expired key (HTTP 401/403). Rate limited Too many requests / quota exhausted (HTTP 429). Endpoint not found The base URL is wrong (HTTP 404) — check the /v1 path. The server answered, but does not allow this site (CORS) The server is up but blocks the browser — see the CORS note above (the message names the setting for vLLM / Ollama / LM Studio). Could not reach … Wrong address or port, the server is down, or (self-signed HTTPS) the browser does not trust its certificate yet — open <base URL>/models in a new tab, accept it, then test again. The browser blocks an http:// address on this https page Use https://, or http://127.0.0.1 for a server on this computer. No answer … within 10 s The server is slow or unreachable. Key rejected The provider refused the key (also Google's API_KEY_INVALID). Unknown model Use an id from the model list — on vLLM it is the --served-model-name value. The server is not set up for tool calls Start vLLM with --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser <parser> (Qwen3: qwen3_xml; many others: hermes). The conversation is longer than the model's context Start a new chat, or raise --max-model-len on the server. Provider server error The provider returned a 5xx — try again later.

docs.title: Talk to your agent
docs.text:
New in 1.50

Once an AI agent is in your session (Build with an AI agent), you can talk to it from the app: the AI assistant window lists the agents in the session next to your own assistant. Pick one and type — or speak — and everyone in the session sees the conversation, the replies as they stream in, and every step the agent takes in between. The agent's terminal stays a second window onto the same conversation.

docs.title: Pick the agent
docs.text:
Open the AI assistant window and choose the agent in the target list at the top, for example Claude · agent via MCP or grok-3-mini · agent REPL. Your configured assistants stay in the same list; a session can use both.

The line under the list says what the agent is doing:

  • listening — it is waiting for you; type away.
  • working — it is on a request. Its steps (A8 action lines) appear between the messages, each with Undo.
  • away — it is connected but not listening. Ask it in its terminal (below).
  • muted — the host muted it; nothing reaches it until it is unmuted.

docs.title: Make Claude Code or Claude Desktop listen
docs.text:
An MCP agent (Claude Code, Claude Desktop) only acts while its model is running, so it has to wait for your messages. In its terminal, type once:

listen to my theprototype session

It then loops by itself: wait for a message → build → reply → wait again. Whatever you type in the terminal still works, and shows in the app tagged via terminal, so the conversation is complete whichever window was used.

An agent started with npx -y @theprototype/agent repl … (your own OpenAI-compatible model) needs no terminal at all: app messages go straight in.

docs.title: Stop, mute, who may talk
docs.text:
• Stop (in the window while the agent works) ends its current request: its next scene change is refused as cancelled, and the next message starts fresh.
  • Editors and admins can ask the agent to build. Viewers can ask questions; the agent will not change the scene for them — that is enforced by the agent's page, not left to the model.
  • The host (or an admin) can right-click the agent in the Connected panel (peer menu) and choose Mute agent — nothing reaches it until unmuted — or remove it from the session.

docs.title: Pictures in the chat
docs.text:
Press + left of the microphone: From device…, Camera (phones), From Explorer, Viewport screenshot, or Selection — ask about this (a picture of the selected object on its own, with a line naming it). You can also paste a picture, drop files on the window, or drag a picture from the Explorer onto it. Up to 4 per message.

  • Every picture is shrunk on your device (long edge 1568 px, about 1 MB) and its EXIF data, including a phone's GPS location, is removed before it is sent. iPhone HEIC photos work.
  • The agent sees the picture, and its bridge also saves it to a private temporary file (removed when the bridge exits) whose path comes with your message — for a skill such as img2threejs that wants a file.
  • Keep in Explorer (the bookmark on a picture) turns it into an image in Library ▸ References, shared with the session and listed under Scene ▸ references, so it saves with the scene. Settings ▸ Tools & connections ▸ Chat pictures ▸ Keep sent pictures in Explorer keeps every picture you send (off by default).
  • Editors and admins attach pictures; viewers see them.

docs.title: Models and files from the agent's machine
docs.text:
• import_model brings a GLB the agent made or found (img2threejs, Blender, a download): a self-contained binary glTF up to 25 MB, through the app's own import (optimizing, LOD, the device-budget check). Named nodes stay a hierarchy you can select and animate, it is one undo step, everyone sees it, and the model records where it came from (tool, source, licence, who, when, file hash) in its Properties.
  • import_file brings a PNG / WebP image (up to 16 MB), a JSON file (up to 2 MB) or a .tpanim clip. The file lands in Explorer ▸ Generated for everyone, its type read from the bytes and its metadata stripped; a generator's input can ride beside it (knight_walk.png + knight_walk.pixling.json). An image is also placed as a card — crisp for pixel art, one frame of a sprite sheet, optionally turning to face each viewer. See Pixel art with Pixling.
  • Only editors' and admins' agents import; a viewer's agent is refused.

docs.title: Chats are files
docs.text:
Every conversation is a .tpchat file in Explorer ▸ Scene ▸ chats. It saves with the scene — the scene file, autosave, a cloud room's save — so a reload or someone joining later has it.

  • The history icon in the window lists the scene's chats (newest first, with search, which agent, and an unread dot); New chat (+) starts an empty one. Double-click a chat in the Explorer, or drag it onto the window, to reopen it there.
  • When you reopen an older chat, the agent receives its last 20 messages and a short summary, and can page further back itself — its own terminal does not remember the old conversation.
  • Right-click a chat in the Explorer: Open in AI assistant, Rename, Include when publishing, Download as Markdown, Download (.tpchat), Delete chat. A downloaded .tpchat dropped back in joins the scene's chats.
  • Private by default: a chat is left out of a .tpscene download, Publish, an export as a game and a .tp project export unless Include when publishing is on for it. The export says how many chats it left out.
  • Editors and admins write chats; viewers read them. A chat over about 50 MB turns its oldest pictures into thumbnails; the words are never dropped.

docs.title: In VR
docs.text: The VR AI panel talks to the same agent: type on the VR keyboard, or hold the talk button and speak (the app's voice typing). Replies come back as text.

docs.title: All Players
docs.text:
Fires a pulse once every player in Play answers yes to a condition — the group gate that makes sure nobody is left behind ("everyone is at the portal", "everyone has three laps").

Output: event — wire it into a Travel to scene node's trigger, a Set Game State, or anything else a pulse drives

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Handle Type Meaning condition boolean each player answers for themselves — a Compare, a Latch, anything true/false

Unwired, the answer is no, and the node never fires.

docs.title: Who counts
docs.text:
• Each player's copy of the graph works out the condition for that player and shares only the yes/no answer. When every player in Play says yes, every copy fires the node on its own (nothing extra is sent, so the pulse is not doubled).
  • Only players in Play count. Someone sitting in the editor is a spectator: they never hold the group up. If nobody is in Play, nobody is ready and the node does not fire.
  • It fires on the change from "not everyone" to "everyone". If one player drops back to no and then says yes again, it fires again.

The answer is only as personal as the condition you wire in. A per-player value such as Player Variable mine gives a real per-player answer; a shared value (a Get Variable, a Counter) is the same for everyone, so the gate then simply fires when that shared condition comes true while somebody is playing.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
End the race when every player has done three laps:

  1. Add a Player Variable (name laps, read mine).
  2. Add a Compare (op gte, b = 3); wire Player Variable → its a.
  3. Add an All Players; wire Compare → its condition.
  4. Add a Set Game State (state over, outcome finished); wire All Players → its trigger.

Each player's own laps comes from a Set Variable with scope player.

A Player Variable (laps.

Tip

All Players also works as a "this just came true" detector for a shared condition: a Compare cannot drive a trigger input directly, but Compare → All Players → Set Game State can (as long as someone is in Play).

docs.title: Angular Velocity
docs.text:
Gives the connected object a constant spin under physics — a rolling barrel, a spinning hazard, a rotating platform other objects can stand on.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Range Meaning axis y x / y / z the object's local axis to spin around speed 2 −10–10 radians per second (negative reverses)

Edits re-apply live mid-simulation — dial the speed while it turns.

docs.title: Physics vs animation
docs.text:
This is real rotation inside the simulation, so other objects feel it: a box resting on a spinning platform is carried around, and a rolling barrel bowls things over. The Spin animation node looks similar but only moves the object's transform — things resting on it are not pushed.

Wiring Angular Velocity alone implies a dynamic body of mass 1; add a Mass node to set a real weight.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A rolling hazard:

  1. Add a cylinder, lay it on its side, and place a few cubes in front of it.
  2. In its flow: Angular Velocity (axis z, speed 6) → Object Selector picking the cylinder.
  3. Press P — it rolls off and scatters the cubes for every peer.

docs.title: Animation Finished
docs.text:
Pulses when a once clip reaches its end — the other half of Play Animation, so a movement can hand off to whatever comes next.

Output: event — 1 for a short window when the clip finishes, 0 otherwise.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Meaning clip (the active clip) which clip to watch — leave empty for whichever is playing pulse 0.3 s how long the output stays at 1

docs.title: Which object?
docs.text:
Inside an object flow it watches that object's clips. Elsewhere, connect an Object Selector.

A looping clip never finishes, so it never fires. Use Animation Marker for a moment inside a loop.

docs.title: Everyone agrees, with no message
docs.text: Each peer's runtime reaches the end of the clip at the same moment on the shared clock, so the pulse is raised locally on every peer rather than broadcast. Nothing to lose, nothing to wait for.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A two-stage airlock:

  1. Inner door: On Click → Play Animation (play).
  2. Add an Animation Finished watching that clip.
  3. Wire it into the outer door's Play Animation (play).

The outer door starts the instant the inner one has finished, everywhere.

Tip

Wire it into a Counter to count completed cycles, or into a Sound node for a latch click at the end of a movement.

docs.title: Animation Marker
docs.text:
Pulses as the playhead crosses a named marker inside a clip — so a footstep, a puff of dust or a latch click can sit at an exact frame of a movement instead of only at its end.

Output: event — 1 for a short window as the marker passes, 0 otherwise.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Meaning name (empty) which marker to watch. Empty means any marker on the clip — one node for "every beat" pulse 0.3 s how long the output stays at 1

docs.title: Adding markers
docs.text: In the Animation window, park the playhead where you want the moment and add a marker from the marker row; double-click it to rename. Markers are part of the clip, so they save, replicate and undo with it.

docs.title: Which object?
docs.text: Inside an object flow it watches that object's clips; elsewhere, connect an Object Selector.

docs.title: Loops are handled properly
docs.text: Crossing a marker is worked out from where the playhead was last frame and where it is now — and when a loop wraps back to the start, the two real pieces of travel are tested separately. A marker just before the loop point fires once per lap, not never; one just after fires once, not twice.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Footsteps on a walk cycle:

  1. Scrub to the frame where the left foot lands and add a marker named step; do the same for the right.
  2. Add an Animation Marker with name step, and wire it into a Sound node.

Both footfalls now play at the right frame, for every peer, at any playback speed.

Tip

Leave name empty and one node fires on every marker in the clip — handy for driving a Counter or a particle burst on each beat.

docs.title: Animation State
docs.text:
Reads what a clip is doing, as a number — the readable half of Animation Finished. Use it to drive something continuously instead of only handing off at the end.

Output: number — what it means depends on read.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning clip (the active clip) which clip to read read progress see below read Output progress 0 → 1 through the clip. Measured across the A/B window when one is set, so it still reads 0 → 1 for the part you are looping playing 1 while it plays, 0 when it does not position the playhead, in seconds duration the clip's length, in seconds remaining seconds left to the end

A boolean rides a number socket perfectly well, which is why playing is here rather than on a socket of its own.

docs.title: Which object?
docs.text: Inside an object flow it reads that object's clips; elsewhere, connect an Object Selector.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A lift whose indicator light rises with it:

  1. The lift has a clip on pos.y; give the indicator its own object flow.
  2. Animation State (progress) → Map Range (0–1 → 0–4).
  3. Map Range → a Set Color or a light's intensity.

The light now tracks the lift's real position, for everyone, however the clip is retimed.

Tip

playing into a Gate is the clean way to say "only while this is moving" — a fan that spins only while its door is opening, say.

docs.title: Announce
docs.text:
A big centred banner for a moment worth celebrating — "GOAL!", "Floor 3", "Ring 2 reached". On a desktop it sits over the game; in a headset it floats in front of the player.

Output: none (a sink)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning trigger event each pulse shows the banner once value number optional — replaces {v} in the text (a level, a score, a ring number)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options text Level {v} the headline; {v} is the wired value sub — an optional smaller second line seconds 1.8 how long it stays (0.3 – 15) color #ffd76a the headline colour

The banner is local: every player's own graph fires it from the shared trigger, so everyone sees it at the same moment without anything extra crossing the network. A new banner replaces the one showing.

Tip

Don't announce the end of a round over a results screen — the screen already carries the words.

docs.title: Behaviour
docs.text:
Game logic written as a small JavaScript file (params, replicated state, event handlers, kit calls) — run once on the authority peer, with a live node view of its events, state and knobs.

This page is a quick reference for the node. The file format, who runs it and the rules the code must follow are in the full guide: Behaviours.

Output: the sockets its code declares (none by default)

docs.title: Sockets come from the code
docs.text:
A new Behaviour node has no sockets. They appear when the file declares them:

In the code On the card Type inputs: ['tap'] an input ▸ tap on the left event — a pulse runs the tap handler in on, on the authority outputs: ['taps'] where taps is a state field an output on the right, with the live value beside it typed by the field's starting value (0 → number) outputs: ['done'] where done is not a state field an output marked ⚡ event — fired by this.emit('done')

Change the declaration, save, and the sockets follow. See For module and game authors for the details.

docs.title: The card
docs.text:
• The behaviour's name and a status dot: running (with its number of handlers), loading, off or error — an error names the line, and code that could not be applied shows a warning.
  • Open view — the read-only live node view of its events, handlers, state and knobs.
  • Code (or double-click the node) — the file in the code workspace; Ctrl+S reloads it.
  • Stop / Run — switches the behaviour off and on; its state is kept.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options name Behaviour the name on the card (in the ⓘ Params tab) enabled on the Stop / Run switch; off stops its handlers and removes what it set up, the state is kept the file's params from the code each one is a row in the ⓘ Params tab; editing it rewrites the number in the code

A new node starts with a working example — a countdown that loses the round when it reaches zero — to copy from.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Three taps light a lamp:

  1. Add a Behaviour node, press Code and replace the file with:

    export default behaviour({
    name: 'Taps',
    state: { taps: 0 },
    inputs: ['tap'],
    outputs: ['taps'],
    on: {
        tap() {
            this.state.taps += 1;
        }
    }
});

    Save with Ctrl+S: the card grows a ▸ tap input and a taps output. 2. Add a Key Press (capture T) and wire it → the Behaviour's tap. 3. Add a Compare (op gte, b = 3) and wire taps → its a. 4. Wire Compare → a Visibility node's on, and Visibility → an Object Selector picking the lamp. 5. Press Play and tap T three times: the count shows on the card and the lamp appears for everyone.

A Key Press wired into a Behaviour's tap input; its taps output feeds a Compare that drives the lamp's Visibil.

Tip

Logic that is easier to wire than to write — a pulse that should hold, a delay, a one-shot — belongs in nodes such as Latch, Delay and Once. Reach for a Behaviour when the rule has loops, timers that call themselves, or several exceptions.

docs.title: Blink
docs.text:
Flashes the connected object on and off at a steady rate.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning speed number overrides the card slider when wired

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Range speed 2 0.2–10 — blink cycles per second

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A hazard beacon:

  1. Add a Blink node (speed 4) and an Object Selector targeting a small emissive-looking sphere on a pole.
  2. Wire Blink → Object Selector: the sphere strobes, perfectly in phase on every peer (the blink runs off the synced clock).
  3. Drive speed from a Proximity chain through Select to blink faster when someone gets close.

Tip

Blink toggles the object's visibility — it doesn't dim materials. For a smoother attention-getter, use Pulse (size throb) instead, or stack both into the same Object Selector.

docs.title: Body Wave
docs.text:
Bends the connected object with a wave travelling along its body — a swimming fish, a snake, a flag, a tail — stronger and faster the faster it moves, curving into turns. A shader effect: physics and picking keep the rest pose.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector, or leave it in an object's own flow)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Every range parameter has a socket (a wired value overrides its slider).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Range Meaning amplitude 0.08 0 – 0.5 sideways swing at the tail, as a share of the body length wavelength 1 0.2 – 4 body lengths per wave (1 = one S along the body) frequency 1.5 0 – 10 Hz beats per second at rest stiffness 0.3 0 – 0.95 the front share that does not bend (a fish's head) falloff 2 0.25 – 6 how sharply the swing grows toward the tail speedGain 1 0 – 10 extra Hz per m/s of speed ampGain 0.5 0 – 5 extra amplitude per m/s turnBend 0.5 0 – 2 how far the body bows into a turn forward +z axis the nose axis (the wave runs from it to the tail) side horizontal horizontal / vertical the bend direction: horizontal = a fish or snake, vertical = a whale or dolphin reverse off the wave runs tail → head (a flag rippling toward its pole)

The bend is computed in the vertex shader over every mesh in the object (and over a fallback LOD group's real model), measured along the forward axis from the nose. Each waving mesh gets its own copy of its material while the wave runs (so two fish sharing a material can swim differently); the original comes back, with any edit you made meanwhile, when the wave stops. Saves are untouched.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A flag on a pole: a plane flag whose pole edge points -x — set forward -x, side horizontal, reverse on, stiffness 0, amplitude 0.15, frequency 2.

Note

The shadow keeps the rest shape, and normals are not bent — keep the amplitude modest for close-ups.

docs.title: Bounce
docs.text:
Bounces the connected object up and down off its resting height, like a dribbled ball.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning amplitude number overrides the card slider when wired speed number overrides the card slider when wired

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Range amplitude 0.5 0–3 (bounce height) speed 2 0–10 (bounces per interval)

The motion is a rectified sine — the object rises from its base position and lands back on it, never dipping below.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A pickup that begs for attention:

  1. Add a Bounce node (amplitude 0.3, speed 3) and an Object Selector targeting a coin object.
  2. Wire Bounce → Object Selector — the coin hops in place on every screen.
  3. Stack a Spin node into the same Object Selector for the full collectible look: effects combine, each adding its own offset.

Tip

Several effects can feed one Object Selector — they all apply from the object's base transform each frame.

docs.title: Bounciness
docs.text:
Sets how much the connected object rebounds in the physics simulation (restitution).

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning value number overrides the card slider when wired

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Range value 0.3 0–1 — 0 lands dead, 1 rebounds with almost all its energy

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A super-ball versus a beanbag:

  1. Place two spheres side by side, a few units above the ground.
  2. Give each a Mass node (kg 1) wired to its own Object Selector.
  3. Add a Bounciness node per sphere: 0.9 into the first selector's chain, 0.05 into the second.
  4. Right-click ▸ Tools ▸ ▶ Simulate physics: the super-ball keeps bouncing while the beanbag thuds flat.

Tip

Bounciness only matters once the object has a Mass (or collides with something that does) — physics parameters are read when the simulation starts, not per frame.

docs.title: Camera Follow
docs.text:
Makes your view follow an object from behind and above, as a third-person or chase view. Something else moves the object, and the camera just keeps up.

Output: effect (optionally wire into an Object Selector to pick the object)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Handle Type Meaning trigger event start following the target stop event let go target object the object to follow, from an Object Selector

The object is found in this order: the target input, then an Object Selector the node's output is wired into, then the owner of the object flow the node sits in.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: None. The framing is fixed: the view sits about 4.5 m behind the object and 2.2 m above it, turns with the object's facing, eases after it and keeps looking at it. This is the same chase view Possess Object uses.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
• It moves your view only. The trigger is shared, so every player's copy reacts to it and each player's view follows on their own screen. Nothing else is sent.
  • It doesn't take the controls and doesn't move the object. Use it when something else moves the object: physics, an animation, a path, another player.
  • While it follows, dragging to orbit the view is switched off. On stop, orbiting comes back, centred on where the object ended up.
  • A new trigger for another object switches to that one. Following stops if the object is deleted or when you enter VR.
  • A pulse that happened before the node was added doesn't start it.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Follow a wandering box with C and stop with X:

  1. Create a box and name it Rover.
  2. Add a Wander and an Object Selector that picks Rover. Wire Wander → Object Selector so the box drifts around.
  3. Add a Camera Follow and wire the same Object Selector into its target.
  4. Add a Key Press on C into trigger and a Key Press on X into stop.
  5. Press C: the view swings in behind the rover and follows it. Press X to let go.

A Wander moving the Rover through an Object Selector.

Tip

Camera Follow moves the player's own view. To move a camera object (a chase camera you can cut to, with an offset and damping you choose), use Camera Rig.

docs.title: Camera Rig
docs.text:
Moves a scene camera object so it follows a target, looks at it, or both — a chase camera behind a car, a camera that keeps a player in frame. New in 1.27; find it in the palette under Game.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector that picks a camera)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning target object what to follow and look at — an Object Selector offset vector3 the offset from the target; wire a Vector3 here instead of using ox / oy / oz

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Meaning mode both both, follow (position only) or lookat (turn only) space world world, or target: the offset turns with the target — use it for a chase camera that stays behind a car ox / oy / oz 0 / 2 / 5 the offset from the target, in metres damping 0.25 seconds of lag; 0 follows rigidly aim 0 a height above the target to look at

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A chase camera for a car:

  1. Add a camera: right-click ▸ Add ▸ Camera ▸ Perspective.
  2. Add a Camera Rig and wire it into an Object Selector that picks the camera. (Or put the Camera Rig in the camera's own graph, where it moves that camera with no Object Selector.)
  3. Wire a second Object Selector, picking the car, into target.
  4. Set space to target. The offset is now measured along the car's own axes: the defaults (oy 2, oz 5) put the camera 2 m up and 5 m along the car's Z axis — if it ends up in front of the car, make oz −5. The camera now stays behind the car and turns with it.
  5. To see through the camera, use Set Active Camera or the camera's Preview.

A camera object.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• It moves camera objects only. Wired to anything else it does nothing, and a toast says so.
  • It never moves the editor view or another player's view. Every player's copy of the camera follows on their own screen.
  • While a rig is attached, the rig decides where the camera is. Remove the rig and the camera goes back to where you placed it.

Tip

The older Camera Follow node (under Character) moves the player's view behind an object. Camera Rig moves a camera object instead, so a game can cut between several rigged cameras with Set Active Camera.

docs.title: Character Controller
docs.text:
Sets how the player moves in Play: walking with gravity and a jump, or flying, at the speed you choose. There's nothing to trigger. The node works by being in the scene.

Output: effect (nothing to wire, because the card is a declaration and not an action)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning speed number overrides the speed slider when wired jumpHeight number overrides the jumpHeight slider when wired eyeHeight number overrides the eyeHeight slider when wired

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options mode fly fly, walk speed 0.1 0.01 – 1: distance per frame (0.1 is about 6 m/s at 60 fps), the same number the scroll wheel changes jumpHeight 1.2 0 – 5 m: how high a jump goes (walk mode) eyeHeight 1.7 0.2 – 3 m: the eye's height above the ground (1.7 is a standing person) gravity on off: no falling and no jump. The eye stays at eyeHeight above the floor

docs.title: With a controller, and without one
docs.text:
A scene that has no Character Controller node uses the built-in Play movement, unchanged. WASD move and the scroll wheel changes speed. The camera stays at eye height, and you fly with Q / E only when the scene allows flying. There's no jump and no falling.

Adding the node changes that for every player in the scene:

No controller walk fly Moving WASD, at the built-in speed WASD on the ground, at speed WASD, at speed Jump none Space (one jump per press) none Gravity none (pinned at eye height) the scene's gravity, so you fall off edges and land none Flying (Q / E) only if the scene allows it no yes, unless Configure Scene ▸ Play ▸ Flying is Removed

A controller on fly at speed 0.1 moves you exactly as far as the built-in movement does, so you can rebuild the default with nodes and then change one thing. Delete the node and Play is back to the built-in movement.

docs.title: What a walker stands on
docs.text:
How a walker meets the world depends on what is running:

  • A physics simulation is running: the player is a capsule that collides with the scene. Walls stop you, you climb slopes and steps, and you can stand on a box.
  • No simulation, but a dungeon module is in the scene: you walk the dungeon's corridors and stop at its walls.
  • Neither: you walk on the scene's ground plane (height 0 when the ground is off). You still fall and land, but you can't bump into objects.

A held Space gives one jump, and landing with it still held doesn't jump again. A game kit's jump height rule overrides jumpHeight while it is set. A gamepad drives the walker too (left stick moves, right stick looks; see Settings ▸ Input), and on a phone the touch controls add a Jump button.

docs.title: More than one controller
docs.text: Only one Character Controller is used: the newest one in the scene wins, and a message says how many there are. Every player picks the same one, so everybody moves the same way.

docs.title: Multiplayer
docs.text: Nothing is sent over the network. Every player's copy of the scene has the same graph, so every player gets the same controller, and it moves that player's own view.

docs.title: The Player's code
docs.text: Double-click the card (or right-click ▸ Open code) to steer speed, jump height, eye height, gravity or the mode every frame from the player's keys, for example to sprint while Shift is held. See The Player's code.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A walker whose jump you can tune while you play:

  1. Add Character ▸ Character Controller and set mode to walk.
  2. Add a Slider and set Min 0 / Max 5 in its ⓘ tab, then set it to 2.
  3. Wire the Slider into the controller's jumpHeight input.
  4. Press Play. WASD walks and Space jumps. Drag the slider to jump higher or lower.

A Slider wired into the jumpHeight input of a Character Controller set to walk.

Tip

To change speed from the graph (a sprint key, a mud patch), use a Move Speed node. To read the player's WASD as numbers, use Move Input.

docs.title: Code link
docs.text:
Points at the module or kit file whose code runs part of this game — double-click (or Open code) to read it. It does nothing at runtime; it is how the Main graph shows where every rule lives.

Output: none — it has no sockets, no value and no effect

docs.title: Where you meet it
docs.text:
On a game's Main graph. Some of a game's logic lives in code rather than in nodes — a module's engine, a game-kit piece — and a Code link is the signpost to it, so nothing that runs the game is hidden from the graph.

  • Older scenes: when you open a scene saved before the Main graph existed, the app adds one Code link per module the scene needs, in a column on the left of Main, titled ‹module› — rules in module code. Nothing about how the scene runs changes. See The Main graph.
  • The shipped games use one to open their engine — see Game rules on the Main graph.
  • Your own: add one from the palette's Logic group to say where a rule lives.

docs.title: The card
docs.text: The card shows the title, then module/file in small type, and an Open code button. Open code, a double-click, or right-click ▸ Open code opens the file in the code workspace, read-only — a module's code runs the same for everyone, so it cannot be edited where it is (see Module code).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Edited in the node editor's ⓘ Params tab.

Parameter Default Options title (empty) what this code does, up to 80 characters module (empty) the module's id, e.g. minigolf (or kit for a game-kit file) file (empty) the file inside it, e.g. module.js (for the kit, a piece such as round.js); empty opens the module's main file

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A link to Mini Golf's engine:

  1. On the Main graph, add a Code link from the Logic group.
  2. In ⓘ Params, set title Mini Golf engine, module minigolf, file module.js.
  3. Double-click the card: module.js opens read-only in the code workspace.

A Code link card titled Mini Golf engine pointing at minigolf/module.js.

docs.title: Collider
docs.text:
Overrides the collision shape (see Colliders) the physics simulation uses for the connected object — the flow equivalent of the Inspector's Physics ▸ Collider pick, and it wins over it.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Why override the shape
docs.text: Physics doesn't collide your triangles; it collides a simple stand-in. A box is fast and forgiving, but a ball resting in a box-shaped bowl never rolls. Pick the shape that matches what the object should feel like.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning shape box box, sphere, capsule, cylinder, cone, hull, trimesh, custom, object scale 1 multiplies the whole shape (0.25–4) — a slightly smaller collider stops objects looking "held apart" sensor off makes the shape a trigger volume: nothing bounces off it, but overlaps fire On Enter / On Exit group inherit the collision group: default, a – d, water; inherit keeps the Properties choice

Shapes in short: hull shrink-wraps the mesh in a convex skin (exact for ramps and gems, seals concave openings); trimesh uses the object's own triangles (exact mesh — static and kinematic bodies only); custom uses the compound collider you authored in Edit collider…; object hulls the geometry of a different object — wire that object's Object Selector into the node's source input, e.g. give a detailed statue the collider of a simple crate.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning source object only for shape: object — the object whose geometry becomes this collider

docs.title: Live edits
docs.text: Changing a parameter rebuilds the collider mid-simulation — no restart, and joints and velocity survive. Tweak a bumper's shape while the ball is still rolling.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A marble run where the ball actually rolls:

  1. Build a ramp (Add ▸ Wedge) and drop a sphere above it.
  2. In the sphere's flow: Collider (shape sphere) → Object Selector picking the sphere.
  3. Press P to simulate — the ball rolls instead of sliding like a crate.
  4. Turn on Show collider (Inspector ▸ Physics) to see the green wireframe that physics is really using.

Tip

Physics nodes are read when the simulation starts and re-applied live on edits — they don't tick per frame like animation nodes. Pair Collider with Mass, Bounciness and Friction.

docs.title: Color Picker
docs.text:
Outputs a color chosen with a swatch — the color source for anything that paints.

Output: color

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Where color #ff4000 color swatch on the card

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
1. Add a Color Picker, a Set Color node and an Object Selector targeting your cube.
  2. Wire Color Picker → Set Color's color input, and Set Color → Object Selector.
  3. Pick a color: the cube repaints instantly for everyone in the session.

Tip

The color socket (amber) only fits color inputs — in practice that means Set Color. In older scenes you may find a Color Picker wired straight into an Object Selector; that legacy connection still paints the object, but new graphs go through Set Color.

docs.title: Compare
docs.text:
Compares two numbers and outputs true or false.

Output: boolean

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Handle Type Meaning a number left side b number right side

Unwired inputs use the card values.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options op gt gt (>), lt (<), eq (=), gte (≥), lte (≤), neq (≠) a, b 0, 0 fallback fields on the card

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Reveal a prize after five clicks:

  1. Wire an On Click node into a Counter (see those pages for the click setup).
  2. Add a Compare (op gte, b = 5); wire Counter → a.
  3. Add a Visibility node and an Object Selector targeting the prize object.
  4. Wire Compare → Visibility's on input, and Visibility → Object Selector: the prize pops in on the fifth click — for everyone.

Tip

A boolean feeds numeric inputs as 0/1, so a Compare can also gate a speed: wire it into a Select node's index to jump between two values.

docs.title: Counter
docs.text:
Counts trigger pulses and outputs the running total.

Output: number (the count, shown live on the card)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning pulse event each pulse applies the operation once — wire an On Click here reset event a pulse here sets the count back to 0, whatever op is — a new round, a restart button

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options op count up count up, count down, reset to 0 — applied per pulse step 1 how much each pulse adds/subtracts

The count rides the shared trigger log, so all peers hold the same number — including peers who join later.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A three-hit piñata:

  1. Wire an On Click to an Object Selector picking the piñata, and On Click → Counter's pulse.
  2. Add a Compare (op gte, b = 3); wire Counter → a.
  3. Wire Compare → a Visibility node's on, and Visibility → an Object Selector targeting the hidden candy object.
  4. Three clicks from anyone in the session and the candy appears.

Tip

The operation applies to every pulse the Counter receives — use count down with a starting logic chain for countdowns, and step to move in bigger increments.

docs.title: Custom Node
docs.text:
Your own reusable node, designed in the app: named controls plus a per-frame script — shared with everyone in the session.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: One number input socket per range control in the definition — so other nodes can drive your parameters.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Defined by you in the Node Designer (right-click the canvas ▸ Custom ▸ New custom node…):

Field Meaning Name how the node appears in the palette's Custom group Controls range (min/max/step slider) or select (comma-separated options) — each becomes a card control and arrives in code as data.<key> Code runs every frame: object, base ({pos, rot, scale, visible}), data, time

Save for everyone replicates the definition to all peers; existing instances re-render and re-run live. Edit later via Edit definition on any instance.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Build a "Wobble" node once, use it everywhere:

  1. Right-click ▸ Custom ▸ New custom node…; name it Wobble, keep the speed range control.
  2. Code: object.rotation.z = base.rot[2] + Math.sin(time * data.speed) * 0.3; — Save for everyone.
  3. Add a Wobble from the palette, wire it into an Object Selector targeting a signpost: it sways; the speed slider tunes it live.

Warning

Custom-node code must stay deterministic (no Math.random(), no accumulation) — every peer runs it independently and must land on the same result.

docs.title: Delay
docs.text:
Passes a pulse on after a set number of seconds — the timing of a fuse, a door that closes later, a cooldown.

Output: event (a pulse, seconds after the trigger)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning trigger event starts the wait cancel event drops a pulse that is still waiting seconds number overrides the card slider when wired

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options seconds 1 0 to 60 on the slider; how long to wait pulse 0.3 how long the output pulse lasts, in seconds (in the ⓘ Params tab, not on the card)

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
• Only the newest trigger counts. A trigger that arrives while the Delay is still waiting starts the wait again from the new trigger; the earlier pulse never comes out. A stream of triggers faster than seconds therefore produces nothing until it stops — then one pulse, seconds after the last one.
  • Cancel drops the waiting pulse if it arrives at the same moment as the trigger or after it. A cancel before the trigger is history and does not stop it — cancel, then trigger, still fires.
  • The fire time is worked out, not scheduled. Each player computes "trigger time + seconds" on the shared clock from the one trigger every player received, so the pulse comes out at the same moment everywhere and nothing extra is sent. Changing seconds (or what is wired into it) while a pulse is waiting moves that pulse.
  • Late joiners: a pulse that was still waiting when someone joined comes out for them too; pulses that already happened before they joined do not fire again.

Delays can be chained (Delay → Delay) to add their times up; a loop of Delays does not repeat. The output counts as a pulse for every event input, including a Counter's pulse and a Latch's set.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A door that lets you through for three seconds:

  1. Add a Key Press (capture E), a Delay (seconds 3) and a Latch with initial on.
  2. Wire Key Press → Latch's reset and Key Press → Delay's trigger; wire Delay → Latch's set.
  3. Add a Visibility node and an Object Selector picking the door; wire Latch → Visibility's on, and Visibility → Object Selector.
  4. Press Play, tap E: the door vanishes, and three seconds later it is back.

A Key Press resetting a Latch and triggering a three-second Delay that sets the Latch again.

Tip

For a cooldown, wire the action's pulse into a Delay's trigger and the Delay into a Latch's set, with the same pulse into the Latch's reset: the Latch reads false while the action is cooling down. Pressing again during the cooldown restarts it.

docs.title: Device Level
docs.text:
The live output level of the connected audio device (or a wired one) as a number - a meter you can drive anything with.

Output: number

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Input Type Meaning target object the device to meter (the object graph's owner when unwired)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Device Level of a speaker into Map Range into a Pulse node on a lamp: the lamp throbs with the music. Or into a HUD Bar for a level meter.

Note

Every peer evaluates its own copy of the graph from the same shared transport and the same replicated pulses, so nothing about the music is sent per frame. See Music Playground.

docs.title: Device Param
docs.text:
Writes a number into one parameter of the connected audio device every frame - an LFO on a cutoff, a fader on a level.

Output: effect (reaches the device through an Object Selector, or the object graph's owner)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Input Type Meaning value number the value to write every frame

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Where key level which parameter of the device to write (the keys its Inspector section shows)

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A Time node (mode sin, rate 5) into Map Range (-1..1 -> 200..2000) into Device Param with key cutoff on a filter pedal: an LFO sweeps the filter, identically on every peer, and nothing crosses the wire - the value already travels as the graph. Values are clamped to the parameter's declared range.

Note

Every peer evaluates its own copy of the graph from the same shared transport and the same replicated pulses, so nothing about the music is sent per frame. See Music Playground.

docs.title: Distance
docs.text:
Measures the live distance between two things in the scene.

Output: number (world units; live readout on the card)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Handle Type Meaning a object first point — wire an Object Selector, or a Vector3 for a fixed world point b object second point — same options

With either input missing, the output is 0.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: None on the card beyond the readout.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A proximity fuse with a readable dial:

  1. Add two Object Selectors, picking a "player" cube and a "mine" sphere; wire their outputs into Distance's a and b.
  2. Add a Compare (op lt, b = 2); wire Distance → a.
  3. Wire Compare → a Visibility node's on, then Visibility → an Object Selector targeting an explosion decal: it appears whenever the two objects come within 2 units.
  4. Drag the cube around and watch the Distance card tick live.

Tip

If you only need "near / not near", Proximity does the compare for you in one node.

docs.title: Effect Burst
docs.text:
A short burst of particles — sparkles, confetti, smoke or sparks — at a wired object, or in front of the player when nothing is wired. Made for the moment a coin is collected, a ring is reached or a goal is scored.

Output: none (a sink)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning trigger event each pulse fires one burst at object optional — where the burst happens

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options kind sparkle sparkle confetti smoke sparks count 48 particles in the burst (4 – 96) lift 0 metres above the object (−2 – 4) color the kind's own any colour (#4f86e6)

Bursts are local and pooled: every player's graph fires its own from the shared trigger, and nothing is saved into the scene.

Tip

An additive sparkle can vanish against a bright sky — pair it with a confetti burst there.

docs.title: Float Along Flow
docs.text:
Carries the connected object along a Flow path — a leaf, a toy boat — at the path's speed, bobbing and turning with the current, looping at the end. Uses the nearest Flow path unless one is wired.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Handle Type Meaning path object the Flow path to ride — wire an Object Selector picking it speed, bob number override the card sliders when wired

With path unwired it rides the Flow path nearest to where the object was placed, if one is within about 4 m; with none in reach the object stays where it is.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options speed 1 0 to 5 — a multiplier on the path's own Speed; 0 holds it in place on the path bob 0.03 0 to 0.3 m — how far it rises and falls on the water align on turn the object to face along the current; off keeps its placed facing

docs.title: How it moves
docs.text:
• Where you place it sets its lane. The object keeps its height above the path's line and its own turn relative to the current; moving it in the editor re-anchors it there. The placed pose is what the scene saves.
  • It always loops. At the end of the path it starts again at the beginning, whether or not the path itself loops.
  • The same everywhere. Its spot on the path is worked out from the shared clock, so every player — and anyone who joins later — sees it at the same place with nothing sent. Floaters placed at different spots bob out of step with each other.
  • It follows the path's line only, so it needs no particle water to move.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A toy boat on a river:

  1. Add ▸ Water ▸ Flow path, and place a small object (the boat) on it.
  2. Add an Object Selector picking the Flow path and a Float Along Flow; wire Object Selector → Float Along Flow's path.
  3. Add a second Object Selector picking the boat; wire Float Along Flow → it. The boat sails down the river and comes back round at the end.
  4. Raise speed to 2 for a faster current, or bob for choppier water.

An Object Selector picking a Flow path feeds Float Along Flow's path input; Float Along Flow drives the boat's.

Tip

The nearest-path rule means a leaf dropped on a river needs no path wire at all — wire one when two paths run close together and you want to choose. For a path drawn as a spline, or ping-pong and run-once travel, see Follow Path.

docs.title: Flow Input
docs.text:
Declares a public input socket for an object flow — the way the Scene flow feeds a value into an object's own graph.

Output: the declared type (number / boolean / vector3 / color)

Only meaningful inside an object flow. In the Scene flow it has nothing to feed it and simply outputs its fallback.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning name value the socket label shown on the embedded Object Flow node vtype number value type — number, boolean, vector3 or color fallback 0 what the node outputs while nothing is wired into it from the Scene

Changing the type resets the fallback to a sensible default for that type.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Think of the object flow as a function and Flow Input as one of its parameters. Whatever the Scene wires into the matching socket of the embedded Object Flow node arrives here on the same tick. Unconnected, you get the fallback — so the object still behaves sensibly on its own.

Renaming or deleting the node updates the embedded card's sockets everywhere and disconnects any stale wire cleanly.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A lamp whose brightness the Scene controls:

  1. Select a lamp object and create its flow.
  2. Add Flow Input (name brightness, type number, fallback 1) and wire it into whatever drives the light.
  3. In the Scene flow, right-click the lamp ▸ Add flow to Scene graph, then wire a Slider into the card's new brightness socket.
  4. Drag the slider — the lamp reacts, and so does every peer's.

docs.title: Flow Output
docs.text:
Declares a public output socket for an object flow — the way an object publishes a value back to the Scene flow.

Input: any value type (the socket is gray = accepts anything)

Only meaningful inside an object flow.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Meaning name out the socket label shown on the embedded Object Flow node fallback 0 published while nothing is wired in

docs.title: Values, not effects
docs.text: Animation and effect nodes (Spin, Pulse, Sound… — the orange sockets) cannot wire into a Flow Output: they do something, they don't carry a value. Publish the value that drives them instead — the Time, Math, Slider or Loop node feeding the effect.

docs.title: One frame of latency
docs.text: Outputs are collected at the end of a tick and delivered to the Scene on the next one. That single frame is invisible in practice and is what makes flows safe to compose without infinite loops.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A pressure plate that reports its state:

  1. In the plate's flow, wire an On Enter → Counter chain into a Flow Output named presses.
  2. Embed the plate in the Scene flow (right-click ▸ Add flow to Scene graph).
  3. In the Scene, wire the card's presses socket into a Compare node (>= 3) and on into a door's Object Flow input — three presses, the door opens.

docs.title: Follow Path
docs.text:
Moves the connected object along a smooth path — a drawn Spline, a Flow path or its own waypoints — at a speed, looping, ping-ponging or once, facing along it and leaning into the turns. An offset spreads several riders out along one path.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector, or leave it in an object's own flow — it then moves that object)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning path object the path to ride: a Spline (Draw ▸ Spline) or a Flow path. Unwired, the node rides its own points speed, offset, bank, maxBank number override the card sliders when wired

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Range / options speed 0.5 -5 – 5 m/s (negative rides it backwards) offset 0 0 – 1: where along the path it starts (0.5 = halfway round) mode loop loop (wraps, a closed path circles) · pingpong (there and back) · once (stops at the end) align on face along the path pitch on tilt up and down with the path (off keeps the nose level — a car, a walker) bank 0.5 0 – 1: how much it leans into turns maxBank 30 0 – 80°: the steepest lean forward +z the axis the model's nose points along: +z, -z, +x, -x points — world-space waypoints, used when nothing is wired to path (templates and the AI assistant write them)

The path is a centripetal Catmull-Rom curve through the points (the spline tool's own curve), walked at constant speed by arc length. The pose is a pure function of the path and the shared clock, so every peer sees the object at the same point — nothing is sent while it moves. Banking comes from the path's curvature times the speed: a tight bend at speed leans further than a gentle one.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Two fish circling a tank, half a lap apart:

  1. Draw a closed Spline around the inside of the tank and hide it (eye icon in the object list).
  2. Give each fish a Follow Path node (in its own flow), wire the spline's Object Selector into path.
  3. Speed 0.4, bank 0.7; the second fish gets offset 0.5. Add a Body Wave so they swim, not slide.

Tip

A model whose nose is not along +Z (most rigs face +Z, many imported cars face +X) — set forward instead of rotating the model.

docs.title: Friction
docs.text:
Sets how much the connected object grips surfaces in the physics simulation.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning value number overrides the card slider when wired

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Range value 0.5 0–1 — 0 slides like ice, 1 grips hard

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
An ice patch:

  1. Build a ramp from a rotated cube and place a box at its top.
  2. Wire a Mass node (kg 2) and a Friction node into an Object Selector picking the box.
  3. Set Friction to 0.05 and right-click ▸ Tools ▸ ▶ Simulate physics: the box glides down and far past the ramp. Re-run with friction 0.9 and it barely creeps.

Tip

Like all physics nodes, Friction is read once at simulation start — tweak, re-simulate, compare. The run replicates: one peer simulates, everyone sees the same motion.

docs.title: Game Music
docs.text:
Declares the scene's background music: one of seven built-in looping tracks, quiet under the game sounds, playing only while someone plays.

Output: none

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning on number / event optional — music plays while this is on (unwired = always)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options preset arcade arcade ambient dungeon stadium space puzzle studio volume 0.7 0 – 1 (under the player's own Music volume) while always always (the whole of Interact/Play) or round (only while a round runs)

It is a declaration, not a trigger: the music is there while the node says so and stops when the player goes back to editing. Each player hears it on their own device, in time with the others.

docs.title: Gamepad Axis
docs.text:
A gamepad stick axis as a number between -1 and 1, with a dead zone of its own.

Output: number (the stick's position, from -1 to 1, multiplied by scale)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options axis lx lx, ly, rx, ry (see below) deadzone 0 0 – 0.9: readings this close to the centre count as 0 scale 1 -4 – 4: multiplies the reading invert off flips the sign Axis Stick -1 is +1 is lx left, sideways left right ly left, forward/back pushed forward pulled back rx right, sideways left right ry right, forward/back pushed forward pulled back

Only the two sticks are axes. The triggers (L2, R2) are read as buttons with Gamepad Button.

The card shows the live value, so you can trim the dead zone against a real reading, and no gamepad detected while no pad is connected.

docs.title: Dead zones
docs.text:
There are two dead zones, applied in order:

  1. The player's stick deadzone (Settings ▸ Input, 0.05 – 0.4, default 0.15). It hides stick drift at rest, and the rest of the travel is stretched back to the full range. A stick just past the deadzone reads close to 0, not a sudden 0.15.
  2. This node's deadzone, your game's own threshold. It's a hard cut: anything at or below it reads 0, and anything above it passes through unchanged. With deadzone 0.5 the output stays 0 until the stick is past halfway, then reads 0.5 or more.

The node's deadzone defaults to 0, so only the player's deadzone applies unless you ask for a second one. scale and invert are applied after the dead zones.

docs.title: Local to each player
docs.text:
A stick is the player's own hardware, so every player's copy of the graph reads their own pad. The output is a different number on each player's machine, and that's by design: it is never sent to the others. The card says so: local to this player, peers do not see this value. To move an object every player sees, let the player drive it with Possess Object, which sends the object's movement to the others.

The output is 0 when the pad is switched off under Settings ▸ Input, unplugged, or while an app dialog is open. The node reads the sticks as they are, so the player's swap sticks and invert Y settings don't apply to it. Reading a stick doesn't take it away from the built-in movement (left stick moves, right stick looks).

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Show a sign while the left stick is pushed hard to the right:

  1. Create a box and name it Sign.
  2. Add a Gamepad Axis (axis lx, deadzone 0.5) and a Compare (op gt, b 0). Wire the axis into Compare's a.
  3. Wire Compare into a Visibility node's on input, and Visibility → an Object Selector that picks Sign.
  4. Push the stick right past halfway: the sign appears on your screen. Other players see it only when they push their own sticks.

A Gamepad Axis on lx with deadzone 0.5 wired into a Compare.

Tip

Pushing a stick forward reads negative on ly and ry. Turn on invert if you want forward to read +1.

docs.title: Gamepad Button
docs.text:
Fires a pulse, or holds a level, while a gamepad button is pressed. It's the gamepad's counterpart of Key Press.

Output: event (1 while the button is held, a short pulse per press; 0 otherwise)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options button A the button to watch (see below). Pick it from the list, or press capture on the card and then the button edge down down: pulses on press, and stays at 1 while held. up: pulses on release. held: the same as down, read as a level pulse 0.3 s how long a single press keeps the output at 1 action (for players) empty a name such as Jump. The button appears under it in the player's Controls list

The buttons follow the standard gamepad layout:

Button Where it is A, B, X, Y the four face buttons: bottom, right, left, top (Cross, Circle, Square, Triangle on a PlayStation pad) L1, R1 the shoulder buttons L2, R2 the triggers. They count as pressed past halfway Select, Start the two small centre buttons L3, R3 pressing a stick in Up, Down, Left, Right the d-pad

The card shows no gamepad detected while no pad is connected. You can still pick a button from the list without a pad.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
It works the way Key Press does. Each press travels as one small shared message, so every player's graph sees the same pulse, and anyone's button press fires the node. Holding the button re-pulses it, so the output stays at 1 for as long as it is down (except with edge up, which waits for the release).

A gamepad and the keyboard never fire each other's nodes: a Key Press can't be fired by a pad, and a Gamepad Button can't be fired by a key. To accept both, wire a Key Press and a Gamepad Button into the same input. Two event wires into one input fire on either.

The pad goes quiet when it is switched off under Settings ▸ Input, when it is unplugged, and while an app dialog is open.

A gamepad already works in a scene with no gamepad nodes: the left stick moves, the right stick looks, and the d-pad and A move through and press HUD buttons. Gamepad Button is for a game that wants buttons of its own. Stick deadzone, look sensitivity, invert-Y and swapping the sticks are the player's own settings under Settings ▸ Input (see A character that walks).

docs.title: Players can move it
docs.text: Fill in action (for players) and the button appears under that name in the game menu's Accessibility ▸ Controls list. A player can move it to any other button there, and the node follows their choice. See Making your game accessible.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A lamp that shows while A is held:

  1. Create a sphere and name it Lamp.
  2. Add a Gamepad Button (button A, action Light).
  3. Wire it into a Visibility node's on input, and wire Visibility → an Object Selector that picks Lamp.
  4. Hold A on the pad: the lamp appears on every player's screen, and it hides again when you let go.

A Gamepad Button on A wired into the on input of a Visibility node.

Tip

For a stick, use Gamepad Axis. It gives a number instead of a pulse.

docs.title: Game Setting
docs.text:
Adds one row to the game's Settings — the page in the game's pause menu, on the desktop and in VR — and outputs this player's value. Each player's choice is saved on their own device, for this game, and never sent to anyone.

Output: the value — true/false for a toggle, a number for a range, the picked option for a choice

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning id my-setting a name unique to this game; the saved value is kept under it, so changing it starts the setting afresh label My setting the row's label in Settings kind toggle toggle, range or choice default (toggle) on the starting value of a toggle min / max (range) 0 / 1 the slider's ends (step 0.1) options (choice) — comma-separated: easy, normal, hard

The row appears while the node is in the graph and goes when it is deleted. Until a player changes it, the node outputs the default.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Let each player choose whether claps make stars:

  1. Add Game Setting — id clap-stars, label Make stars with a clap, kind toggle, default on.
  2. Wire it into an On Clap node's enabled.
  3. Test play, open the pause menu ▸ Settings: the row is there, and switching it off stops your claps only.

See Build a Game Loop for the pause menu and per-game settings.

docs.title: Game Sound
docs.text:
Plays one of the built-in game sounds when a pulse arrives — no audio files needed. Placed at a wired object (it pans and fades with distance), or everywhere when nothing is wired.

Output: none (a sink)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning trigger event each pulse plays the sound once at object optional — where the sound comes from

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options sound coin click pop whoosh success fail hit kick shoot laser explosion coin levelup goal whistle cheer step ring sparkle hurt portal

Sounds play only while someone is playing (Interact or Play), on each player's own device, at the Game sounds volume in Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Sound.

docs.title: Caption
docs.text: Leave caption blank and players with captions on see the sound's name ([coin], [explosion]); type your own words to say more (The gate creaks open), or - to never caption it. Very frequent sounds (step, click, pop) have no default caption. See Making your game accessible.

docs.title: Game Start
docs.text:
Fires once when the game starts (Play, or a round reset) - the place to spawn, reset counters and arm timers.

Output: event

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Input Type Meaning camera object a camera to activate as the game starts (optional)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Where state playing the game state that counts as "started"

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Wire Game Start into a Spawn node's trigger and into a Set Variable that zeroes the score: every round begins from the same clean slate on every peer.

docs.title: Game Time
docs.text:
The round clock: seconds since the round started, the same on every player's screen. It stops while the game is paused. It can also read the time left, the round number, or whether the game is playing.

Output: number (shown live on the card)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options read elapsed elapsed (seconds into the round), remaining (length − elapsed, never below 0), round (how many rounds have started), playing (1 while the state is playing, else 0) length 60 1–3600 s — the round length remaining counts down from

Set length with the slider on the card; remaining is the only reading that uses it.

docs.title: How the clock works
docs.text:
