Game Time has no clock of its own. It is worked out from the moment the round started, which is part of the shared game state, so two players mid-round read the same time, and a player who joins later reads the right time as soon as they arrive.

  • A new round (playing entered from menu or over, see Set Game State) starts it from 0 and adds 1 to round.
  • paused freezes it, and resuming carries on with no jump: paused time never counts.
  • over and menu do not stop it — elapsed keeps rising until the next round starts. A full reset on Set Game State zeroes it; the round count is kept.
  • Before any round has started it reads 0.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A bridge that appears 30 seconds into the round:

  1. Add a Game Time (read elapsed).
  2. Add a Compare (op gte, b = 30); wire Game Time → its a.
  3. Add a Visibility node; wire Compare → its on.
  4. Add an Object Selector picking the Bridge; wire Visibility → Object Selector. Start the game: the bridge shows up for everyone at the same moment, and is hidden again when the next round starts.

Game Time (elapsed) into a Compare (at least 30).

Tip

Actions ▸ Show the round time in the HUD editor wires a Game Time (remaining, 60 s) into a HUD Text for you. For a time limit that actually ends the round, use Kit: Round from the game kit.

docs.title: Gate
docs.text:
Boolean logic — AND, OR, NOT, XOR — on two inputs, or up to eight.

Output: boolean

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Handle Type Meaning a boolean first condition b boolean second condition (ignored by not) c … h boolean extra conditions, added with + input (since 1.27)

Unwired a and b use the card values.

docs.title: More than two inputs
docs.text:
Since 1.27 Gate takes up to eight inputs, named a to h. Press + input on the card to add a socket, and − on a row to remove that socket.

op With more than two inputs and true when all wired inputs are true or true when any wired input is true xor true when an odd number of wired inputs are true

The extra inputs c to h have no value of their own: an input with no wire is skipped. Removing a socket moves the wires after it down one name (removing b turns c into b), one Ctrl+Z puts it all back, and groups around the node update their sockets too. Compare stays two-input.

A Gate with four inputs inside a group.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options op and and, or, not, xor

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A door that opens only when both pressure plates are occupied:

  1. Set up two Proximity nodes, one per plate (each fed by two Object Selectors).
  2. Add a Gate (op and); wire the Proximities into a and b.
  3. Wire Gate → a Visibility node's on input, then Visibility → an Object Selector targeting the door barrier — the barrier shows only while both plates are active. Flip the Gate to or for either-plate behavior.

Tip

not is a simple inverter: it looks only at a and ignores b entirely — handy right before a Visibility to turn "near" into "hide".

docs.title: Get Variable
docs.text:
Reads a named shared variable as a number — the read side of Set Variable, live on every player's screen.

Output: number (shown live on the card)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options name score the variable to read — the same name the Set Variable writes

A name nothing has written yet reads as 0.

docs.title: What it reads
docs.text:
Get Variable reads the shared variables: the ones a Set Variable with scope shared writes, and the shared count of the Collectibles module. They travel with the game state, so every player — including one who joins later — reads the same number, and the read itself sends nothing.

It does not read per-player numbers (Set Variable scope player); use Player Variable for those. It does not read what Store Value saved on the device either; that is Stored Value.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A door that disappears once the team has 10 points:

  1. Add a Get Variable (name score).
  2. Add a Compare (op lt, b = 10); wire Get Variable → its a.
  3. Add a Visibility node; wire Compare → its on.
  4. Add an Object Selector picking the Door; wire Visibility → Object Selector. The door stays while the score is under 10 and vanishes for everyone when it reaches 10.

Get Variable score into a Compare (less than 10).

Tip

To show a variable on screen, select a HUD Text element and pick Actions ▸ Show a variable in the HUD editor: it wires a Get Variable into a HUD Text for you.

docs.title: Controller Buzz
docs.text:
Vibrates the VR controllers with a named pattern when a pulse arrives.

Output: none (a sink)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning trigger event each pulse plays the pattern once

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options pattern success tap bump hit success fail rumble heartbeat hand both both, left, right

Vibration only happens in Interact and Play — never while editing — and only on the device of the player whose graph fired it. The app already buzzes for you when a laser touches something clickable, a press lands, a grab starts or a hand knocks a body.

docs.title: HUD Bar
docs.text:
Drives a HUD bar element's fill from a number — health, fuel, progress.

Output: none (it writes into its element)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning value number how full the bar is, between min and max min number the empty end — wired, it replaces the card's min max number the full end — wired, it replaces the card's max

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options element (none) the bar to drive — see below min 0 −1000 to 1000 max 100 −1000 to 1000 format (empty) an optional label drawn on the bar; {v} is replaced by the value, so {v} HP reads 75 HP

The fill is (value − min) / (max − min), kept between empty and full. The node's min and max replace the ones set on the element in the HUD editor, which are only the preview. A bar with show % turned on in the HUD editor shows the percentage instead of the label.

docs.title: Picking the element
docs.text:
The bar itself is made, placed and styled in the HUD editor. On the card, element opens the scene HUD's elements grouped by screen; the pipette button lets you click the element on the HUD editor's stage instead, and Enter id manually... takes a typed id. A name that matches no element shows amber.

It drives more than the plain Bar:

Element What the value does Bar the fill, horizontal or vertical Radial progress how far the ring is filled — the same min / max maths Icon row how many icons are filled (the element's own max sets how many there are) Hotbar which slot is selected, counting from 0

Selecting one of these in the HUD editor and choosing an Actions ▸ Show ... entry builds a HUD Bar already pointing at it. Like the other HUD nodes it updates the screen about ten times a second, and every player sees the same fill when the value comes from shared state.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A bar you can drag:

  1. In the HUD editor, add a Bar element.
  2. Add a Slider node (value 20, Min 0, Max 40) and a HUD Bar picking the bar.
  3. Wire Slider → HUD Bar's value, and set the HUD Bar's min to 0 and max to 40.
  4. Drag the slider: the bar fills and empties with it.

A Slider wired into a HUD Bar's value.

Tip

For a health bar, keep the health in a variable and wire a Get Variable into value, with max set to the starting health — the bar then empties as the variable goes down.

docs.title: HUD Button
docs.text:
Fires a pulse when a HUD button is pressed - the on-screen counterpart of On Click.

Output: event

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Where element (none) the HUD button element, picked on the card

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: HUD Button into a Counter into HUD Text: an on-screen button that counts its own presses for everyone.

docs.title: HUD Input
docs.text:
Reads a HUD input element — what the player typed, picked, dragged or switched — as a value for the graph.

Output: number (or text, when read is text)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None — it reads its element.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options element (none) the Slider, Toggle, Dropdown, Text field or Tabs to read — see below read value what to read from it — see the table below fallback 0 −1000 to 1000 — what it reads while the control has no value yet read Gives value the control's number: a slider's position, a toggle as 1 or 0, the selected tab index a dropdown's position in its option list, counting from 0 (a Tabs element gives its selected tab); a choice that is not in the list reads fallback text the value as text: what was typed into a text field, a dropdown's chosen option on 1 when on (a toggle that is on, or any number above 0), else 0

index is what a Switcher wants; on can feed a Gate or a Visibility node.

docs.title: The fallback
docs.text: The node reads fallback until the control actually holds a value — until the player first moves it, or a HUD Set Input writes it. The start value set on the element in the HUD editor is what the player sees, but it is not what this node reads before then. Set fallback to the same number as the control's start value. Loading a scene clears every control's value, so the fallback applies again.

docs.title: Mine or everyone's
docs.text:
Each input element has a shared switch in the HUD editor:

  • off (the default) — the value is each player's own. Every player's HUD Input reads their own control, so anything it drives can differ per player: a volume slider changes only your volume.
  • on — one value for everyone; a change by any player reaches all of them, including players who join later. Use it for a host setting such as the difficulty.

docs.title: Picking the element
docs.text:
The control is made, placed and styled in the HUD editor. On the card, element opens the scene HUD's elements grouped by screen; the pipette button lets you click the element on the HUD editor's stage instead, and Enter id manually... takes a typed id. A name that matches no element shows amber.

Quicker: select the control in the HUD editor and choose Actions ▸ Read its value, Read which option or Read its text — each adds this node, already pointing at it, with read set to match.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A speed slider with a readout:

  1. In the HUD editor, add a Slider (min 0, max 100, start value 50) and a Text element.
  2. Add a HUD Input picking the slider, read value, fallback 50.
  3. Add a HUD Text picking the text, format Speed: {v}; wire HUD Input → HUD Text's value.
  4. Press Play and drag the slider: the text follows — on your screen only, because the slider is not shared.

A HUD Input reading a slider.

Tip

To let a press read the control at that moment, wire the HUD Input into the value of the node the press drives — a Store Value behind a Save button keeps the player's setting on their device.

docs.title: HUD List
docs.text:
Names a HUD List element and sets its title and how many rows it shows — an inventory, objectives, the players. The rows themselves are written into the list by a HUD Rows node, a Leaderboard, a module, or typed on the element in the HUD editor.

Output: none (it writes into its element)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning trigger event on the card, but the node does not use it — the title and row count apply all the time

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options element (none) the List element — see below title (empty) a line shown above the rows; empty shows no title rows 5 1–20 — how many rows the list shows

docs.title: Where the rows come from
docs.text:
A list is written into, it is not a value that flows along a wire — there is no list socket. The rows on screen are, in order of preference:

  1. rows pushed in by a HUD Rows node, a Leaderboard or a module;
  2. otherwise the rows typed on the element in the HUD editor (one per line).

The list shows the first rows it holds, up to rows. Without a HUD List node naming the element, the element's own max rows setting is the limit instead.

docs.title: Picking the element
docs.text: The List element is made, placed and styled in the HUD editor. On the card, element opens the scene HUD's elements grouped by screen; the pipette button lets you click the element on the HUD editor's stage instead, and Enter id manually... takes a typed id. A name that matches no element shows amber.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A titled top-three:

  1. In the HUD editor, add a List element.
  2. Add a Leaderboard picking the list (variable score) — it fills the rows, one per player.
  3. Add a HUD List picking the same list, title Top players, rows 3.
  4. Press Play: the list shows Top players and the three highest scores. Nothing needs wiring between the two nodes; they meet at the element.

A Leaderboard and a HUD List side by side.

docs.title: HUD Rows
docs.text:
Appends, replaces or clears rows in a HUD List element on a pulse — a log, a chat, a scoreboard feed.

Output: none (it writes into its element)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning trigger event each pulse applies op once text number the row to write — a number, or text from a source that gives text (a player's name). Unwired, the card's text is used

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options element (none) the List element to write into — see below op append append (add the row at the end), set (replace every row with this one), clear (empty the list) text (empty) the row when nothing is wired into text — a fixed line such as GAME OVER

Known problem in 1.42

The card does not draw its trigger and text sockets yet, so this node cannot be wired in the node editor. For a list that fills itself from per-player numbers, use a Leaderboard; for fixed rows, type them on the List element in the HUD editor.

docs.title: How the rows behave
docs.text:
• Once per pulse. The node acts when a new pulse arrives, never every frame, so append adds one row per press.
  • Everyone holds the same rows with nothing extra sent: every player's machine runs the same pulses in the same order.
  • Late joiners do not see rows appended before they arrived — they start from the rows typed on the element. A list that must be right for a joiner should be rebuilt with set, or be a Leaderboard.
  • The list shows its first rows. It holds up to 64, but shows only as many as its row limit (the HUD List node's rows, else the element's max rows). Once the list is full, newer appends are kept but not shown — clear or set to start over.
  • clear empties the pushed rows, so an element with rows typed on it in the HUD editor shows those again.

docs.title: Picking the element
docs.text: The List element is made, placed and styled in the HUD editor. On the card, element opens the scene HUD's elements grouped by screen; the pipette button lets you click the element on the HUD editor's stage instead, and Enter id manually... takes a typed id. A name that matches no element shows amber.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A press log:

  1. In the HUD editor, add a Button and a List element.
  2. Add a HUD Button picking the button, and a HUD Rows picking the list, op append, text Bell rung.
  3. Wire HUD Button → HUD Rows' trigger.
  4. Each press adds a Bell rung row to the list, on every player's screen.

The example's nodes.

docs.title: HUD Screen
docs.text:
Shows, hides or toggles a whole HUD screen (a named layer of elements) each time a pulse arrives — open a pause menu, a map, a results screen.

Output: none (it changes which screen the HUD shows)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning trigger event each pulse applies the action once — wire a Key Press, a HUD Button, an On Game State

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options screen (none) the screen to show or toggle, picked on the card — not needed for hide action show show, hide, toggle

docs.title: Picking the screen
docs.text: The screens themselves are made in the HUD editor. On the card, screen opens a list of the scene HUD's screens; New screen... adds an empty one and picks it, Open HUD editor takes you there to fill it, and Enter id manually... takes a typed id or screen name.

docs.title: What each action does
docs.text:
action Effect show that screen replaces whatever screen of the HUD is showing (a HUD shows one screen at a time) hide drops the choice a HUD Screen node made, so the HUD goes back to what it would show on its own: the screen whose while matches the game state, else the default (★) screen, else nothing. It needs no screen picked toggle shows the screen, or does a hide if that screen is already the one showing

A screen picked by this node wins over the screens' while settings until something hides it. The choice is forgotten on Restart and Test play, and, in a game, when you leave play mode — so the next Play does not open on a stale pause screen.

docs.title: Who sees it
docs.text:
The chosen screen is kept on each player's own machine and is never sent. But the node runs on every player's machine when its pulse arrives, and the usual triggers — Key Press, HUD Button, On Click — are shared pulses. So one player pressing P opens the pause screen for everyone in the session, and one player's Resume closes it for everyone.

A player who joins later is not moved by a press that happened before they arrived. To make sure a joiner lands on the right screen, bind the screen to a game state with its while setting in the HUD editor instead.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A pause screen:

  1. In the HUD editor, add a screen named Pause with a Button labelled Resume on it.
  2. Add a Key Press (capture P) and a HUD Screen (screen Pause, action show); wire Key Press → HUD Screen's trigger.
  3. Select the Resume button in the HUD editor and choose Actions ▸ Hide a HUD screen: that adds a HUD Button wired into a second HUD Screen set to hide.
  4. Press Play and tap P: the pause screen opens; Resume puts the game's own screen back.

A Key Press wired into a HUD Screen set to show.

Tip

Set the Pause screen's input to menu in the HUD editor, so the pointer is freed and the player can click Resume. To actually stop the round clock as well, wire the same Key Press into a Set Game State (paused).

docs.title: HUD Set Input
docs.text:
Writes a value into a HUD input element when a pulse arrives — to prefill, clear or correct it: a Reset button that puts the volume back, a difficulty the host sets.

Output: none (it writes into its element)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning trigger event each pulse writes the value once value number the value to write — wired, it replaces the card's value; text works too, for a text field options number a comma-separated list (Easy, Normal, Hard) that replaces a dropdown's own options while it is wired

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options element (none) the Slider, Toggle, Dropdown, Text field or Tabs to write into — see below value 0 −1000 to 1000

Known problem in 1.42

The card does not draw its trigger, value and options sockets yet, so this node cannot be wired in the node editor.

docs.title: How the write behaves
docs.text:
• Once per pulse, never every frame — so it never fights the player's own hand on the control.
  • As if the player had set it. A HUD Input reading the control sees the new value, and the element's shared switch decides whether it travels: shared, everyone gets the value; not shared, it stays on each machine.
  • The pulse decides who. The node runs on every player's machine when its pulse arrives, and a HUD Button press or a Key Press is a shared pulse — so a Reset button resets the control on every player's screen, even a control that is not shared.
  • Late joiners are not re-sent a press from before they arrived; a shared control's current value reaches them on its own.
  • The pulse also pokes the element: aimed at a Damage flash, it makes the screen flash.

docs.title: Live dropdown options
docs.text: With something wired into options, the dropdown offers that list instead of the options typed in the HUD editor, and it follows the list as it changes — no pulse needed. A HUD Input reading index counts in the live list. Delete the node and the typed options come back.

docs.title: Picking the element
docs.text: The control is made, placed and styled in the HUD editor. On the card, element opens the scene HUD's elements grouped by screen; the pipette button lets you click the element on the HUD editor's stage instead, and Enter id manually... takes a typed id. A name that matches no element shows amber.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A Reset button for a volume slider:

  1. In the HUD editor, add a Slider (start value 50) and a Button labelled Reset.
  2. Add a HUD Button picking the button, and a HUD Set Input picking the slider, value 50.
  3. Wire HUD Button → HUD Set Input's trigger.
  4. Drag the slider, then press Reset: it jumps back to 50.

The example's nodes.

docs.title: HUD Text
docs.text:
Writes a number into a HUD text element through a format such as Gems: {v} — a score, a count, a readout.

Output: none (it writes into its element)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning value number the number to show — wire a Counter, a Get Variable, a Math node format any wire text here to replace the whole format — a Behaviour's status line, a Stored Value read as text

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options element (none) the HUD element to write into — see below format {v} the text to show; {v} is replaced by the number, so Gems: {v} reads Gems: 3. Text without {v} is shown as typed; an empty format shows just the number decimals 0 0–4 digits after the point

The score display needs nothing else: Counter → HUD Text is a live score, because the Counter already counts the shared pulses.

docs.title: Picking the element
docs.text:
The node does not draw anything itself. The element — a Text, or anything else that shows a line of text (Rich text, Key hint, Scroll panel, a Timer) — is made, placed and styled in the HUD editor. On the card, element opens the scene HUD's elements grouped by screen; the pipette button lets you click the element on the HUD editor's stage instead, and Enter id manually... takes a typed id. A name that matches no element shows amber.

The quicker route is the other way round: select a Text element in the HUD editor and use Actions — Show a variable, Show a counter or Just show text each build this node already pointing at it.

The text the node writes replaces the element's own label while the game runs; the label typed in the HUD editor is the preview. The card shows what the element is showing right now. Updates reach the screen about ten times a second.

docs.title: Who sees what
docs.text: Every player's machine works the text out from the same graph, so a shared source (a Counter, a Get Variable) shows the same text to everyone, including players who join later. A per-player source — a HUD Input on a local control, a Player Variable reading mine — shows each player their own number.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A button that counts its own presses:

  1. In the HUD editor, add a Button and a Text element.
  2. Add a HUD Button picking the button, a Counter and a HUD Text picking the text.
  3. Wire HUD Button → Counter's pulse, and Counter → HUD Text's value.
  4. Set the format to Presses: {v}. Press Play and click the button: the text counts up, for every player.

A HUD Button wired into a Counter.

Tip

One HUD Text per element. Two nodes writing the same element fight over it, and the last one in the graph wins.

docs.title: HUD Timer
docs.text:
Runs a countdown in a HUD Timer element from its duration, formatted like {v}s — it starts by itself or on a pulse.

Output: number (the seconds left)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning start event a pulse starts (or restarts) the countdown from the full duration duration number the length in seconds — wired, it replaces the card's duration

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options element (none) the Timer element to write into — see below duration 60 1–600 seconds format {v} {v} is replaced by the seconds left, so {v}s reads 42s decimals 0 0–2 digits after the point autostart on count down with no pulse; off, the timer holds at the full duration until a pulse arrives on start

The countdown is worked out from the shared time stamp of the pulse that started it, so every player reads the same time left with nothing extra sent, and it stops at 0. The output is the same number, so a Compare on it can end the round when it reaches 0.

docs.title: Picking the element
docs.text:
The Timer element is made, placed and styled in the HUD editor; the duration on the element is only a preview, this node owns the real one. On the card, element opens the scene HUD's elements grouped by screen; the pipette button lets you click the element on the HUD editor's stage instead, and Enter id manually... takes a typed id. A name that matches no element shows amber.

Known problem in 1.42

A pulse wired into start is not picked up yet. A timer with autostart off therefore stays at its full duration, and one with autostart on reads 0. Until that is fixed, show a round clock with a Game Time node (read remaining, length 60) wired into the value of a HUD Text that points at the same Timer element — HUD Text takes the same {v}s format.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A one-minute round clock, as the node is meant to be used:

  1. In the HUD editor, add a Timer element to the playing screen.
  2. Add a Game Start and a HUD Timer picking the Timer element; wire Game Start → HUD Timer's start.
  3. Set duration 60, format {v}s, and turn autostart off.
  4. Every round, the clock counts down from 60s on every player's screen.

A Game Start wired into a HUD Timer's start.

docs.title: Impulse
docs.text:
Pushes or spins a physics body when an event fires — a jump, a kick, a cannon, a nudge.

Inputs: trigger (event) · force (vector3) · target (object) Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
On the rising edge of whatever is wired into trigger — On Click, Key Press, On Impact, On Rest, a Toggle — the object gets one shove. Holding a trigger high does not keep pushing: it is one impulse per event.

The push is applied by the peer running the simulation and everybody sees the same result, because the trigger itself is replicated. There is no extra network traffic for this node.

It needs a running simulation

Every physics write is gated on physics actually running. Press P (or the ▶ button) first — with the simulation stopped the node tells you so instead of doing nothing quietly.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning mode impulse impulse shoves the body; torque spins it space world world = the force is in world axes; local rotates it by the object's own rotation, so "forward" stays forward as the object turns

The strength comes from the force input — wire a Vector3. With nothing wired it uses (0, 5, 0), a modest hop.

docs.title: Choosing the object
docs.text:
Three ways, all equivalent:

  • Impulse → Object Selector — the classic wiring: "this force is applied to that object".
  • Object Selector → target — the selector as a value: "this force acts on that object". One selector can feed several nodes this way.
  • Nothing at all, if the node lives in an object's own flow (double-click an object in the node editor's Graphs tree) — it targets that object.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A jump key.

  1. Give a box a Dynamic body: select it, Inspector ▸ Physics ▸ Mode = Dynamic.
  2. In the node editor: Key Press (code = Space) → Impulse trigger.
  3. Vector3 (0, 7, 0) → Impulse force.
  4. Impulse → Object Selector, and pick the box.
  5. Press P to start physics, then Space. Every peer sees the same hop.

A spinning turntable. Same graph with mode = torque and a Vector3 of (0, 4, 0) — each press adds spin about Y.

A cannon that fires where it points. Set space = local and a Vector3 of (0, 0, -12); rotate the barrel and the shot follows it.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Set Velocity — replace a body's speed outright instead of adding to it
  • On Rest — fire when the thing you pushed has settled again
  • Physics — bodies, ground, gravity and the simulation controls

docs.title: Jiggle
docs.text:
Makes the connected object jiggle — it lags behind when moved, wobbles like jelly on impact and sways in the wind; skinned models swing their bone chains (tails, hair, antennae).

Output: effect (put it in the object's own graph, or wire it into an Object Selector)

Find it in the palette under Effects ▸ Jiggle.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Range Meaning stiffness 120 5 – 600 how hard it springs back to its real pose damping 0.15 0 – 1 how quickly the wobble dies down gravity 0.3 0 – 2 how much it sags max offset 0.35 0 – 1 the furthest it may stray from its real pose wind 0 0 – 20 how much it sways in the wind wobble 0.08 0 – 0.4 the size of the squash and stretch when it lands or is hit wobble Hz 3 0.5 – 10 how fast it wobbles falloff 1.5 0.25 – 4 how much more the far end moves than the held end pivot bottom bottom / center / top where it is "held" bones (globs) empty text for a rigged model: name patterns such as hair*, tail*; empty = the ends of every chain

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text: Jiggle is a look: it never changes the object's real position, so physics, saving and the other players are unaffected. The settings are shared; each player sees their own wobble from the motion they see. An object with several materials on one mesh jiggles only through its bones.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A jelly that wobbles when it lands:

  1. Add a cube and give it a Dynamic body (Properties ▸ Physics).
  2. In its own flow, add Jiggle: pivot bottom, wobble 0.2.
  3. Press P and drop it — it squashes on the floor and wobbles back. Drag it with the gizmo and it lags behind.

Tip

For an antenna or a tail on a static object, raise gravity and wind and lower stiffness: it droops and sways on its own. See Fluid Tank & Jiggle.

docs.title: Joint
docs.text:
Attaches two objects to each other when an event fires — a hinge, or a rigid weld.

Inputs: trigger (event) · a (object, the anchor) · b (object, the attached) Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
On the rising edge of trigger the two objects are joined, exactly as if you had used Physics ▸ Weld or Physics ▸ Hinge from the object menu: the joint becomes part of the scene, replicates to every peer, appears in saves, and can be undone with Ctrl+Z.

That is the difference between this and the rest of the physics nodes — Impulse and Set Velocity act on a running simulation and leave nothing behind, while Joint authors scene data.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Meaning kind revolute revolute = a hinge that turns about one axis; weld = rigidly fixed together axis y which axis the hinge turns about vel 0 motor speed (rad/s) — leave at 0 for a free-swinging hinge maxForce 100 how hard the motor may push to reach that speed

docs.title: Choosing the objects
docs.text:
a is the anchor and b is the thing attached to it. Wire an Object Selector into each. If you leave a unwired it falls back to the node's own target (the Object Selector it feeds, or its owner object), so the minimum wiring is one selector into b.

Start the objects world-aligned

A hinge axis is interpreted in both bodies' frames, so objects that begin with a rotation can make the solver fight itself and throw the assembly apart. Build the joint on unrotated objects and rotate the finished assembly, or use weld.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A door that installs itself.

  1. A thin box for the door with a Dynamic body, a wall with a Static one.
  2. Put the door's origin on its hinge edge — a revolute joint anchors on the origin, which is what makes it swing on the hinge rather than the middle.
  3. On Click (the wall) → Joint trigger, kind = revolute, axis = y.
  4. Object Selector (wall) → a; Object Selector (door) → b.
  5. Press P and click the wall. The door is hinged for everyone, and it stays hinged in the saved scene.

A motorised wheel. kind = revolute, vel = 6, maxForce = 200, with the chassis in a and the wheel in b. See also the Motor node, which drives joints that already exist — and can drive one side of a vehicle at a time.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Motor — change the speed of existing hinges, per side
  • Physics — joints, bodies and the simulation controls

docs.title: Key Press
docs.text:
Fires a pulse while a keyboard key is pressed — the bridge from your keyboard into the graph.

Output: event — 1 while the key is held (a short pulse per press), 0 otherwise

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning key KeyR the key to watch — click the button on the card and press a key to capture it pulse 0.3 s how long a single press keeps the output at 1

The key is stored as a physical key code (KeyR, Digit1, Space…), so it works the same across keyboard layouts and with Shift held. Presses are ignored while you are typing in a text field.

Each press travels as one tiny replicated message with a shared timestamp — every peer's graph computes the same pulse, and anyone's key press fires the node. Holding the key re-pulses it, so the output stays at 1 for as long as the key is down.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Press R to spin an object:

  1. Add a Key Press (capture KeyR), a Spin and an Object Selector picking the target.
  2. Wire Key Press → Spin's speed input, and Spin → Object Selector.
  3. Hold R: the object spins while the key is down and stops when released.

Tip

Inside an object flow you can skip the Object Selector — a Key Press wired into a Spin's speed drives the flow's owner directly.

docs.title: Action (for players)
docs.text: Fill in action (for players) (Jump, Open the door) and the key appears under that name in the game menu's Accessibility ▸ Controls list, where a player can move it to any key that suits them. Every Key Press follows the player's layout. See Making your game accessible.

docs.title: Latch
docs.text:
Holds a boolean until told otherwise — set, reset and toggle pulses make it a memory bit. Every trigger in the graph is a short pulse; a Latch is how a pulse becomes something that stays: a door that stays open, a gem that stays collected, a light that stays on.

Output: boolean (true after a set, false after a reset)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning set event a pulse turns it on (true) reset event a pulse turns it off (false) toggle event a pulse flips it

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options initial off what it reads before anything has set or reset it (toggles flip from this value) reset each round off forget every set, reset and toggle from earlier rounds — see below

docs.title: How it decides
docs.text:
• Set and reset: the most recent one wins. The Latch compares when its last set and its last reset arrived. If both arrive at the same instant it reads as set.
  • Toggle flips whatever set/reset says. A set or reset starts the flipping over, so set after any number of toggles always reads true.

The pulses come from the shared trigger log every player already has, so all players read the same value with nothing extra sent. A player who joins later is caught up on that log: set and reset are exact for them. Toggle is the one part that can be off — the number of flips is copied from another player rather than worked out — until the next set or reset puts everyone back in step. Prefer set / reset in a multiplayer game when it matters.

docs.title: Reset each round
docs.text:
With reset each round on, a set, reset or toggle from an earlier round counts as never having happened, so the Latch falls back to initial when a new round starts — and also while the game is on its menu or the round is over. That is how a collected gem comes back next round with no reset wire to draw and nothing to send.

It only takes effect once the scene's game has been started at least once (see Build a game); in a scene without a game the Latch behaves as if the option were off. Off is the default, so a Latch in a graph without a game never changes because somebody pressed Start.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A lamp you switch with a key:

  1. Add a Key Press (capture E) and a Latch; wire Key Press → Latch's toggle.
  2. Add a Visibility node; wire Latch → its on.
  3. Add an Object Selector picking the lamp; wire Visibility → Object Selector.
  4. Press Play and tap E: the lamp appears, tap again and it is gone — for every player.

A Key Press wired into a Latch's toggle.

Tip

For "hide it once it is picked up", wire the pickup's pulse into reset with initial on, and turn on reset each round so the pickup returns every round. A Store Value keeps a result after the round ends — a round-scoped Latch reads initial again the moment the round is over.

docs.title: Leaderboard
docs.text:
Ranks the players by their own per-player variable (laps, score) into a HUD List element, highest or lowest first, top N rows.

Output: none (it writes rows into its element)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None — it reads the players and their numbers by itself.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options element (none) the List element to fill — see below variable laps the name of the per-player variable to rank by order desc desc (highest first — a score), asc (lowest first — a best time) format {name} — {v} how each row reads: {name} is the player's name, {v} their number, {rank} their place ({rank}. {name} {v}) decimals 0 0–3 digits after the point for {v} limit 10 1–20 — the most rows it writes

docs.title: Where the numbers come from
docs.text:
Each player has their own copy of a per-player variable — written by a Set Variable with scope player, or by a collectible whose scope is player (see Build a Game Loop). Read one player's number with a Player Variable.

The pulse decides who scores. A Set Variable runs on every player's machine when its pulse arrives, so a shared pulse — a HUD Button press, a Key Press — adds to every player's own number at once. A pulse only one machine sees counts for that player alone: an On Hit with who set to me, or a player-scoped collectible.

  • One row per player in the room, named by their player name. A player who has not scored yet is listed with 0 rather than left out; a player who disconnects drops off.
  • Same order on every screen. Players on the same number are always listed in the same order.
  • Nothing is sent. Every player's machine builds the same list from numbers it already has, and keeps it up to date all the time — so it is right for a player who joins mid-game, unlike rows appended with HUD Rows.
  • Nothing resets by itself. Per-player numbers carry over between rounds. To start each round from 0, wire an On Game State (playing) into a Set Variable (scope player, op set, value 0).

docs.title: Picking the element
docs.text:
The List element is made, placed and styled in the HUD editor. On the card, element opens the scene HUD's elements grouped by screen; the pipette button lets you click the element on the HUD editor's stage instead, and Enter id manually... takes a typed id. A name that matches no element shows amber.

Quicker: select the List element in the HUD editor and choose Actions ▸ Show a leaderboard — it adds this node already pointing at the list, ranking laps.

How many rows show is also up to the list: the element's max rows (5 unless you change it), or the rows of a HUD List node naming the same element. Raise it if limit is higher.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A race to collect gems:

  1. Make a few objects collectible with scope player, counting into gems — see Build a Game Loop (it uses the Collectibles module). Each pickup now counts for whoever made it.
  2. In the HUD editor, add a List element, select it and choose Actions ▸ Show a leaderboard. On the Leaderboard card, set variable to gems.
  3. For each player's own count, add a Player Variable (gems, read mine) wired into a HUD Text's value, format My gems: {v}.
  4. Press Play with friends: the list ranks everyone by their gems, and each player sees their own count.

A Leaderboard ranking the gems variable.

Tip

For a race, rank lap times with order asc and decimals 2, so the fastest time sits on top.

docs.title: Look At
docs.text:
Keeps the connected object facing a target — another object or a fixed point — every frame.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning target object what to face — an Object Selector (follows the object live) or a Vector3 point

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: None on the card — everything comes from the wired target.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A turret that tracks a moving target:

  1. Add an Object Selector picking the "target" sphere; wire its output into Look At's target.
  2. Add a second Object Selector picking the turret object.
  3. Wire Look At → that Object Selector.
  4. Drag the sphere around the scene: the turret rotates to face it continuously, on every peer's screen.

Tip

The orientation is managed from the object's base transform — disconnect the Look At and the object returns to its original rotation.

docs.title: Loop
docs.text:
Sweeps a number from one value to another over time, repeating — a ready-made animation ramp.

Output: number

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning from / to 0 / 1 the swept range rate 1 sweeps per second mode wrap wrap (snap back and restart), pingpong (bounce back and forth), once (run to the end and stay)

Driven by the synced clock, so the sweep is at the same point for every peer.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A searchlight that pans back and forth:

  1. Add a Loop: from 0, to 3, rate 0.3, mode pingpong.
  2. Add an Orbit node and an Object Selector targeting the light's visible housing.
  3. Wire Loop → Orbit's radius input, and Orbit → Object Selector.
  4. The object now swings out to radius 3 and back in a smooth cycle.

Tip

Loop is like Time with the range built in — reach for it when you'd otherwise chain Time → Map Range.

docs.title: Map Range
docs.text:
Remaps a number from one range to another — the glue between free-range sources and bounded parameters.

Output: number

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning a number the value to remap

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning inMin / inMax 0 / 1 the expected input range outMin / outMax 0 / 1 the produced output range clamp on keep the result inside the output range

a at inMin produces outMin; a at inMax produces outMax; everything between interpolates linearly. With clamp off, values outside the input range extrapolate.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
1. Add a Time node (mode sin) — it outputs −1…1.
  2. Add a Map Range: in −1…1 → out 0.2…2, clamp on.
  3. Wire Time → Map Range's a, Map Range → a Spin node's speed input, and Spin → an Object Selector targeting your cube.
  4. The cube's spin speed now breathes smoothly between 0.2 and 2.

Tip

Reverse outMin/outMax (e.g. 1 → 0) to invert a signal without extra nodes.

docs.title: Mass
docs.text:
Gives the connected object weight for the physics simulation — objects with a Mass fall and collide.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning kg number overrides the card slider when wired

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Range kg 1 0.1–100

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Knock down a tower:

  1. Stack a few cubes into a tower and place a sphere above them.
  2. Add a Mass node (kg 5) and an Object Selector picking the sphere; wire Mass → Object Selector.
  3. Right-click the viewport ▸ Tools ▸ ▶ Simulate physics: the sphere drops into the tower. Objects without a Mass act as static obstacles.
  4. Stop the simulation — the result stays, as a single undoable step.

Tip

Physics nodes don't run per-frame like animations — they are read once when the simulation starts. One peer runs the simulation at a time and everyone watches the same outcome. Pair Mass with Bounciness and Friction to tune how it lands.

docs.title: Math
docs.text:
Combines numbers with an arithmetic operation — two, or up to eight — or shapes one (sine, rounding, clamping…).

Output: number (live result on the card)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Handle Type Meaning a number first operand b number second operand c … h number extra operands, added with + input (since 1.27)

Unwired a and b use the values typed on the card.

docs.title: More than two inputs
docs.text:
Since 1.27 Math takes up to eight inputs, named a to h. Press + input on the card to add a socket, and − on a row to remove that socket.

  • With add, sub, mul, div, min or max, Math combines every wired input left to right: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, and 10 − 1 − 2 = 7. The other operations use only a and b, and the card greys the extra inputs out.
  • The extra inputs c to h have no typed-in value. An input with no wire is skipped, so an empty socket never multiplies your result by zero.
  • Removing a socket moves the wires after it down one name: removing b turns c into b, so each wire stays on the same value. One Ctrl+Z puts it all back, and groups around the node update their sockets too.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options op add add, sub, mul, div, min, max, mod, pow, sin, cos, abs, round, floor, clamp, neg a, b 0, 0 fallback fields on the card

Division and modulo by zero return 0 instead of exploding; mod always returns a positive result.

docs.title: Shaping one value (1.23)
docs.text:
These operations work on a; b is a setting, or is not used:

op Result pow a to the power b (aᵇ) sin / cos sin(a) or cos(a), times b — b = 0 counts as 1, so a fresh node gives plain sin(a) abs |a| round / floor a rounded to the nearest whole number / down clamp a kept between 0 and b (b of 0 or less = between 0 and 1) neg −a

A HUD Button, On Game State or HUD Timer can be wired into a or b since 1.23 — see Value wires.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Scale a slider into degrees of travel:

  1. Add a Slider (Min 0 / Max 10) and a Number set to 0.5.
  2. Add a Math node (op mul); wire Slider → a, Number → b.
  3. Wire Math → an Orbit node's radius input, and Orbit → an Object Selector targeting a moon object: the slider now sweeps the orbit radius from 0 to 5.

Tip

min/max double as one-sided clamps: wire a value into a and type the limit into b. For a swing back and forth, wire a Time node into a of a sin node and set b to the size of the swing.

docs.title: Measure
docs.text:
Reads a number off an object: how tall it is, where its top is, how fast it is going.

Input: target (object) Output: number

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Measure reports one number at a time, picked by the read parameter. Sizes come from the object's collider shape — the same measurement the physics engine builds its body from — so what you read is what the simulation uses, and it costs nothing per frame.

Like Velocity, it is a local readout: every peer computes it from data everyone already has, so it puts nothing on the wire.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Meaning read top top — the world Y of the object's highest pointbottom — the world Y of its lowestheight — how tall it isy — the object's own position Yspeed — how fast it is moving (m/s)

docs.title: Choosing the object
docs.text: Wire an Object Selector into target, or drop the node unwired inside an object's own flow to read that object.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
"Is the stack tall enough?"

  1. Object Selector (the top crate) → Measure target, read = top.
  2. Measure → Compare a, with b = 3 and op = greater than.
  3. The Compare output is a boolean you can wire into a Gate, a Visibility node for a "win" sign, or a HUD readout.

A speedometer. read = speed → Map Range (0…20 → 0…1) → a Set Color that reddens as the object goes faster.

Where does it rest? read = bottom tells you whether a crate is actually sitting on a pad or hovering above it.

Note

speed is exact on the peer running the simulation and a close approximation elsewhere, because other peers derive it from the ~10 Hz position stream. Anything that must agree exactly between peers should be decided on the simulating peer.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Velocity — speed only, same local-readout rule
  • Distance — how far apart two objects are

docs.title: Motor
docs.text:
Drives every hinge joint attached to the connected object — the flow way to make wheels turn, turntables spin and doors swing under power.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Select the body, not the wheel: the node powers every revolute (hinge) joint touching the connected object, so one Motor on a car chassis drives all four wheels. It overrides a motor configured on the joint itself.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Range Meaning vel 3 −20–20 target rotation speed (negative reverses) maxForce 100 0–500 how hard the motor may push to reach that speed — low force means a heavy load slows it down side all all, +x, −x, +z, −z which hinges to drive, by where they sit on the object

Both re-apply live mid-simulation, so you can tune speed while the car is driving.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A powered turntable:

  1. Add a cylinder for the base and a plate above it; connect them with a hinge (select both ▸ right-click ▸ Physics ▸ Hinge).
  2. In the plate's flow: Motor (vel 2) → Object Selector picking the plate.
  3. Press P. Raise vel while it spins to speed it up.

docs.title: Driving one side: steering
docs.text:
side narrows the motor to the hinges on one side of the object, judged by where each joint is anchored. Two Motor nodes on the same chassis — one +x, one −x — are a differential drive: give them the same speed and the vehicle goes straight, different speeds and it turns, opposite speeds and it spins on the spot.

  1. On the chassis flow, add two Motor nodes, side = +x and −x.
  2. Wire each into an Object Selector picking the chassis.
  3. Drive them from two Key Press → Select chains, or from a Slider each while you tune it.

With side = all (the default) one node drives every hinge on the object identically, which is what it always did.

Tip

No hinge, no motion — Motor needs a revolute joint to act on. Create one from the object menu (Physics ▸ Hinge) or from the Joint node. For a free spin with no joint at all, use Angular Velocity instead.

docs.title: Move Input
docs.text:
The player's own movement keys as numbers — the W/A/S/D axes — for driving things by hand.

Outputs:

Handle Type Reads x number D = 1, A = −1, neither or both = 0 y number W = 1, S = −1, neither or both = 0

Each player reads their own keys: a player pressing nothing reads 0, whatever anyone else is pressing, and nothing is sent over the network. That is what you want for "my turret turns with my keys", and the wrong tool for a value every player must agree on.

Move Input reads the keyboard only. For a gamepad stick use a Gamepad Axis.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Wire Move Input's x into a Spin node's speed through an Object Selector: A and D spin the object by hand — a turntable, a crane, a valve.

docs.title: Move Speed
docs.text:
Reads the player's movement speed, and sets a new one when a pulse arrives. Use it for sprint, mud or slow motion.

Output: number (the movement speed in force right now)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning set event on each pulse, write value as the new movement speed value number the speed to write; overrides the card slider when wired

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options value 0.1 0.01 – 1: distance per frame (0.1 is about 6 m/s at 60 fps)

docs.title: Which speed is in force
docs.text:
One speed moves the player, and every Move Speed node reads that same number:

  1. the last speed written, by a Move Speed's set pulse or by the scroll wheel in Play;
  2. otherwise the Character Controller's speed;
  3. otherwise this card's value.

A written speed stays until something writes again. Nothing on the card has to stay wired. Changing the Character Controller's speed, or deleting the controller, clears the written speed. Written speeds are kept between 0.001 and 100.

The units are the Character Controller's: distance per frame, the number the scroll wheel has always changed. Each scroll notch multiplies the speed by a fixed step, so the readout follows the wheel.

docs.title: Multiplayer
docs.text: The set pulse is shared, so a set changes the speed for every player, each on their own machine. The scroll wheel is local: it changes only your own speed, and only your own Move Speed readouts show it.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Hold Shift to sprint:

  1. Add a Character Controller and set mode to walk.
  2. Add a Key Press (capture Shift, edge down) and a Move Speed with value 0.25. Wire the Key Press into Move Speed's set.
  3. Add a second Key Press (capture Shift, edge up) and a second Move Speed with value 0.1. Wire them the same way.
  4. Press Play: holding Shift walks fast, and letting go walks at the normal speed.

Two Key Press nodes on Shift.

Tip

A Key Press fires for anyone's key, so in a multiplayer game this sprint is shared: one player's Shift speeds everybody up. For a per-player sprint, use the controller's Player code, which reads each player's own keys.

docs.title: Note Trigger
docs.text:
Plays a note on the connected audio device when a pulse arrives - a drum pad, a sampler pad, a synth key.

Output: effect

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Input Type Meaning trigger event the pulse that plays the note note number the note number (60 = middle C; a drum machine's pad n is 36 + n) velocity number 0..1

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Where note 60 default note velocity 0.9 default velocity

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
An On Impact sensor on a crate into Note Trigger (note 36) on a drum machine: every time the crate lands, the kick fires - on every peer, from the same replicated pulse, once per pulse.

Note

Every peer evaluates its own copy of the graph from the same shared transport and the same replicated pulses, so nothing about the music is sent per frame. See Music Playground.

docs.title: Number
docs.text:
A constant numeric value — the simplest source node.

Output: number

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Where value 1 number field on the card Step 1 ⓘ Params tab — the increment the field's arrows use

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
1. Add two Number nodes (say 3 and 4) and a Math node set to mul.
  2. Wire them into Math's a and b inputs — the card shows the live result (12).
  3. Wire Math → a Bounce node's speed input, and Bounce → an Object Selector targeting your cube: the cube bounces at the computed rate.

Tip

Set Step to 0.1 (or smaller) when you're feeding parameters that live in a 0–1 range — the field's up/down arrows then move in useful increments.

docs.title: Object Flow
docs.text:
Embeds an object's own graph into the Scene flow as a single card — the way to compose object flows into a bigger machine without opening each one.

Sockets: whatever the embedded flow declares with Flow Input / Flow Output

docs.title: Adding one
docs.text:
• right-click the object in the viewport ▸ Add flow to Scene graph (an object with no flow gets one, with a Flow Input and a Flow Output to start from — one Undo; greyed out while someone else holds the object), or
  • add an Object Flow node from the palette (Object Flow group) and pick the object.

Only objects that already have a flow are listed, and a flow can't embed itself.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning flowUuid — which object's flow this card represents (pick from the card)

Double-click the card to open that object's flow in the editor.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Values you wire into the card reach the flow's Flow Inputs on the same tick. Values the flow publishes through its Flow Outputs come out of the card on the next tick (one frame of latency — see Flow Output).

The card's sockets track the flow's interface: rename, retype or delete a Flow Input/Output and every embedded card updates, dropping wires that no longer have a home. Delete the object's flow and its cards disappear with it.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
One lamp design, three lamps:

  1. Build the behaviour once in a lamp's flow, with a Flow Input brightness and a Flow Output isOn.
  2. In the Scene flow, embed all three lamps as Object Flow cards.
  3. Wire one Slider into all three brightness sockets — one control, three lamps, in sync for every peer.

Tip

Prefer small object flows with a clear interface over one huge Scene graph: they travel with the object into prefabs and saved scenes, and the Scene flow stays readable.

docs.title: Object Selector
docs.text:
Binds the graph to a scene object — the sink every effect must reach, and an object reference for sensor nodes.

Output: object (a reference to the picked object — feeds Distance, Proximity, Look At)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning (left) effect any effect chain: animations, actions, Script, Sound, physics, module and custom nodes

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Where object -None- dropdown of scene objects on the card

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
1. Add a Spin node and an Object Selector.
  2. Pick your cube in the Object Selector's dropdown.
  3. Wire Spin → Object Selector: the cube starts spinning, in sync on every peer.
  4. Add a second Object Selector picking the same cube and wire its output into a Distance node to measure from it — one node type, two roles.

Tip

Effects only touch the scene through an Object Selector — a Spin node dangling on the canvas does nothing. If an object refuses to animate, check its right-click menu: Disable flow effects mutes a single object.

docs.title: Once
docs.text:
Lets exactly one pulse through until it is re-armed — a checkpoint, a pickup, a first-time event.

Output: event (one pulse, at the moment of the first trigger)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning trigger event the first pulse here passes; every later one is ignored rearm event lets the next trigger through again

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options reset each round off re-arm by itself at the start of every round — see below pulse 0.3 how long the output pulse lasts, in seconds (in the ⓘ Params tab, not on the card)

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
• The first trigger is remembered and comes out as one pulse. Every trigger after that — from anyone — is ignored while the Once is spent.
  • Rearm forgets that first trigger: the Once is ready again and the next trigger passes.
  • All players work this out from the same shared trigger, so they agree on which press was first with nothing extra sent. A player who joins later is told the Once is already spent, so a door opened before they arrived stays open for them and does not fire again.

docs.title: Reset each round
docs.text:
With reset each round on, a Once spent in an earlier round counts as armed again when a new round starts — a collectible counts once per round. Between rounds (game menu, round over) a round-scoped Once lets nothing through, and a press there does not re-arm it.

It only takes effect once the scene's game has been started at least once (see Build a game); in a scene without a game it behaves as if the option were off.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A treasure chest that pays out only once:

  1. Add an On Click and an Object Selector picking the chest; wire On Click → Object Selector.
  2. Add a Once; wire On Click → Once's trigger.
  3. Add a Counter; wire Once → Counter's pulse.
  4. Add a Key Press (capture R); wire it → Once's rearm.
  5. Press Play and click the chest a few times: the Counter reads 1. Press R and the next click counts again.

On Click on the chest feeding a Once.

Tip

Once is the opposite of a Latch: a Latch holds a value, a Once passes a single pulse. For a pickup that should both count once and disappear, wire the same pulse into a Once (for the score) and a Latch (for the visibility).

docs.title: On Clap
docs.text:
Fires a pulse when a VR player brings both hands together and holds them there for a moment — a clap. It carries where the hands met, so a Spawn or an Effect Burst can make something right there.

Outputs: event, plus point (vector3 — where the hands met) and by me (boolean)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The clap is detected from your own hands, in VR, while you are in Interact or Play (never in the editor). With who set to anyone the pulse is shared: every player's node fires, all with the same point, so a Spawn wired to it makes one object there for everyone. With me it stays on your device — a buzz in your own hands, a private effect.

Nothing is watched for unless some graph has an On Clap node that is switched on.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning enabled boolean unwired = on. Wire a Game Setting toggle here to let players switch it off

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Meaning who anyone anyone — the pulse is shared with every player; me — it fires on your device only hands closer than (m) 0.1 how close the hands must come (0.03–0.3) held for (s) 0.25 how long they must stay together (0–1) at most one per (s) 1 a cooldown, so one clap is one pulse (0.2–5)

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Make a star with a clap (this is how the Stars Room does it):

  1. On Clap → a Spawn node's trigger, and On Clap's point → the Spawn's place.
  2. Wire the star you want copied into the Spawn's source.
  3. A Game Setting toggle Make stars with a clap → On Clap's enabled, so a player who claps by accident can turn it off.

docs.title: On Click
docs.text:
Fires a short pulse when its object is clicked — the bridge from user input into the graph.

Output: event — outputs 1 for a short window after the click, 0 otherwise (the card's dot lights up while pulsing)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning pulse 0.3 s how long the output stays at 1 after a click

On Click watches the object picked by the Object Selector it is connected to — that connection is what tells it which object to listen on. A desktop click or a VR trigger press on that object fires the pulse. The click travels as one tiny replicated message with a shared timestamp, so every peer's downstream logic agrees.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A click counter button:

  1. Add an On Click, an Object Selector picking your button cube, and a Counter.
  2. Connect On Click to the Object Selector (identifies the watched object) and On Click → Counter's pulse input.
  3. Click the cube in the viewport: the Counter ticks up — by exactly one, on every peer.

Tip

Event pulses convert to numbers/booleans, so On Click can also feed a Visibility on input directly — the target flashes visible for the pulse window on each click.

docs.title: On Enter
docs.text:
Fires a pulse when something enters a trigger volume — the checkpoint, doorway and pressure-plate node.

Output: event (wire into a Particles trigger, a Counter, a Set Color, or an Object Selector)

docs.title: Setting up a trigger volume
docs.text:
A trigger volume is an object whose collider is a sensor: things pass straight through it, but overlaps are reported. Two ways to make one:

  • Inspector ▸ Physics ▸ Sensor on the object, or
  • a Collider node with sensor on, wired to the object.

Scale a box over your doorway, make it a sensor, and hide it (Inspector ▸ visibility) if you don't want it seen.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: While a simulation runs, the peer stepping the physics detects the overlap starting and pulses the node for everyone (the same replicated trigger stamp On Click uses). Each pair fires once per entry — re-entering fires again.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Meaning pulse 0.3 how long the pulse stays high (seconds)

docs.title: Targeting
docs.text: Like On Click, the node acts on the object it reaches in the graph: wire it into an Object Selector, or drop it unwired inside an object's own flow to target that object.

docs.title: Only with, and other
docs.text: Wire an Object Selector into only with and the node fires only when the other body is that object (or a spawned copy of it). The other output carries the body it touched — wire it into Look At, Distance and the like. The other body travels with the trigger, so every peer reads the same object. A contact with the ground plane reports an empty other. Since 1.22 the node sits in the palette's Physics group. See Contact filters.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A checkpoint that celebrates:

  1. Add a box over your track, scale it into a gate, tick Physics ▸ Sensor.
  2. In its flow: On Enter → Particles (trigger input, emission burst, preset Confetti) and On Enter → Counter to count laps.
  3. Press P and drive or throw something through the gate.

Tip

Pair with On Exit to know when the object leaves again — e.g. a door that opens on enter and closes on exit.

docs.title: On Exit
docs.text:
Fires a pulse when something leaves a trigger volume — the other half of On Enter.

Output: event (wire into a Particles trigger, a Counter, or an Object Selector)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Needs a sensor collider, exactly like On Enter (Inspector ▸ Physics ▸ Sensor, or a Collider node with sensor on). While a simulation runs, the peer stepping the physics notices the overlap ending and pulses the node for everyone through the same replicated trigger stamp.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Meaning pulse 0.3 how long the pulse stays high (seconds)

docs.title: Targeting
docs.text: Wire it into an Object Selector, or leave it unwired inside an object's own flow to target that object.

docs.title: Only with, and other
docs.text: Wire an Object Selector into only with and the node fires only when the other body is that object (or a spawned copy of it). The other output carries the body it touched — wire it into Look At, Distance and the like. The other body travels with the trigger, so every peer reads the same object. A contact with the ground plane reports an empty other. Since 1.22 the node sits in the palette's Physics group. See Contact filters.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A door that closes behind you:

  1. Make a sensor box in the doorway (Inspector ▸ Physics ▸ Sensor).
  2. In its flow: On Enter → Set Color (green) and On Exit → Set Color (red) on the door frame's Object Selector.
  3. Press P and roll a ball through — the frame flips colour as the ball passes and again as it leaves.

docs.title: On Game State
docs.text:
Fires a pulse when the shared game state becomes the one you pick — the hook for "when the round starts" or "when the game is over". With edge exit it fires when the game leaves that state instead.

Output: event — 1 for a short moment (0.3 s) after the change, otherwise 0

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options state playing menu, playing, paused, over edge enter enter (the game switched to this state), exit (it switched away from it)

docs.title: How it fires
docs.text:
The game state itself is shared (see Set Game State). Each player's copy of the graph watches it and pulses this node on its own when the state changes. The pulse itself is never sent over the network, so each player gets exactly one pulse per change.

  • Resuming counts as entering playing. paused → playing fires playing / enter just like a fresh start does. If something must happen only at the start of a new round, drive it from the Start button's own pulse instead.
  • It is not a replay. A player who joins mid-round receives the current state, not the pulses they missed. Anything that has to be right for a late arrival — which screen shows, which camera you look through — is better bound to the state itself: a HUD screen's while setting (HUD Editor), a Game Start node, or Game Time playing.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Keep each player's best score when a game ends:

  1. Add an On Game State with state over, edge enter.
  2. Add a Store Value (key mygame-best, mode max); wire On Game State → its trigger.
  3. Add a Get Variable (name score); wire it → Store Value's value.
  4. Every time the game reaches over, each player's device keeps the higher of its saved best and the final score.

On Game State (over) pulses a Store Value whose value comes from Get Variable score.

Tip

Wired into a number input, On Game State reads 1 for the moment after the change and 0 otherwise, just like On Click.

docs.title: On Grab
docs.text:
Fires a pulse when a player picks up the connected object — a desktop carry in Play or Interact, or a VR grip in Interact.

Output: event

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options pulse 0.3 seconds the output stays high

Wire an Object Selector into it, or put it in the object's own flow. Pair it with a Game Sound (pop) for a crate that sounds like it was lifted, and with On Impact (hit) for when it lands.

docs.title: On Hit
docs.text:
Fires a pulse when a hand or a player knocks the connected object — the trigger half of the knock.

Outputs: event (wire into a Particles trigger, a Counter, or an Object Selector), plus two named value outputs — speed (number) and by me (boolean).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
While a simulation runs and the scene's Knock block is on, an open VR hand or the desktop camera hitting a dynamic body sends one hit message. Every peer pulses this node from that message's own timestamp, so the pulse happens at the same moment on every screen.

The card shows hit! while it is pulsing and idle the rest of the time, with the last accepted hit's speed and by me beside it. Those two hold their value until the next hit — a burst scaled by speed reads the speed of the hit that fired it.

The scene needs the knock switched on: Configure Scene ▸ Physics ▸ Knock. Without it nothing knocks anything and this node never fires. See the knock.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning min m/s (minSpeed) 0 ignore hits slower than this, so a brush past an object does not count who anyone anyone fires for every hit, me only for hits your own hand made, others only for everybody else's

who is read separately on each peer, against whoever sent the hit. So me pulses on one screen only — the hitter's — which is what makes a per-player count work: wire it into a Set Variable with scope player, and each person counts their own touches with no second writer.

docs.title: Targeting
docs.text: Like On Click, the node acts on the object it reaches in the graph: wire it into an Object Selector, or drop it unwired inside an object's own flow to target that object.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Sparks in proportion to the hit:

  1. Give the object a Dynamic body (Inspector ▸ Physics) and switch Configure Scene ▸ Physics ▸ Knock on.
  2. In its flow: On Hit → Particles (trigger input, emission burst), and On Hit's speed output → a Map Range → the emitter's count, so a hard hit throws more sparks than a nudge.
  3. Press P, enter play mode, and walk into it — or put a hand through it in VR.

Score only your own touches: On Hit with who set to me → Counter.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• On Impact — the object hitting something else, rather than being hit by a person
  • Physics & Simulation — the scene block that arms all of this
  • Module SDK — api.onHit and api.hitLog, the same feed for a module

docs.title: On Impact
docs.text:
Fires a pulse when, in a physics simulation, the connected object hits something — from any side, or only when it lands (the From option).

Output: event (wire into a Particles trigger, a Counter, or an Object Selector)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: While a simulation runs, the peer stepping the physics detects each real contact — a falling crate hitting the floor, a thrown ball hitting a wall — and pulses this node for everyone (the trigger rides the same replicated stamp as On Click). Gentle settling and rolling are filtered out: the two objects must close fast enough along the contact (or, with From: landing only, the object must actually be falling), and each object has a short cooldown so bounces don't spam.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning minStrength 1 minimum impact speed (m/s, along the contact; downward with landing only) — raise it so only hard hits count direction (From) any side any side: a hit from any direction — a ball thrown at a wall or a target; landing only: landings only (before 1.45 every On Impact worked this way)

New in 1.45. From: any side is the default for a new node. On Impact nodes in scenes saved before 1.45 keep landing only, so they fire exactly as they did.

docs.title: Targeting
docs.text: Like On Click, the node fires for the object it reaches in the graph: wire it into an Object Selector (directly or through other nodes), or drop it unwired inside an object's own flow to target that object.

docs.title: Only with, and other
docs.text: Wire an Object Selector into only with and the node fires only when the other body is that object (or a spawned copy of it). The other output carries the body it touched — wire it into Look At, Distance and the like. The other body travels with the trigger, so every peer reads the same object. A contact with the ground plane reports an empty other. Since 1.22 the node sits in the palette's Physics group. See Contact filters.

docs.title: On the object that was hit
docs.text:
New in 1.40. On Impact also fires on a static or kinematic (flow-animated) object when a falling body lands on it — a pressure plate, a target, a moving platform — with other = the body that landed. Put On Impact in the plate's own flow and it fires when a crate drops onto it. Two dynamic bodies still fire only for the one that was falling, so nothing fires twice.

The threshold is a closing speed over 1.2 m/s (raise minStrength for harder ones), each body at most every 0.3 s. With From: landing only it counts only downward speed, so a ball thrown sideways into a wall fires nothing.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Sparks + a thud when a crate lands:

  1. Give the crate a Dynamic body (Inspector ▸ Physics).
  2. In its flow: On Impact → Particles (trigger input, emission burst, preset Sparks), and On Impact → Counter if you want to count landings.
  3. Press P, lift the crate with the gizmo, drop it. Sparks on landing, for every peer.

Note

Simplest version, no flow editor at all: set a particle emitter's Emission to On impact in the Inspector — see Particle Effects.

docs.title: On Rest
docs.text:
Fires a pulse when a physics body has finished moving — the counterpart to On Impact, which fires when it starts.

Output: event (wire into a Counter, Play Animation, Impulse, or an Object Selector)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
While a simulation runs, the peer stepping the physics watches each dynamic body. When one has been still — under 0.05 m/s and 0.1 rad/s — for seconds, this node pulses once for everybody, on the same replicated stamp On Click uses. It re-arms as soon as the body moves again, so a crate that is knocked over fires again when it settles.

It deliberately does not use the physics engine's own "sleeping" flag: bodies never sleep in this app (a moving platform must be able to wake whatever is resting on it), so sleep would never fire.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Meaning seconds 0.5 how long the body must stay still before it counts as settled pulse 0.3 how long the output stays high

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Score a landing. Count how many crates have come to rest on a pad:

  1. On Rest (unwired, inside the crate's own flow) → Counter.
  2. The counter's value is a number you can wire into a HUD readout, a Compare for a win condition, or a Play Animation.

A domino chain. On Rest → Impulse on the next object: each piece settles, then nudges its neighbour.

Cleanup. On Rest → Set Velocity with everything zeroed, to make sure a settled stack is really asleep before you score it.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• On Impact — the moment of contact, not the moment of stillness
  • Velocity — the live speed, if you want a threshold of your own

docs.title: On Sequence Event
docs.text:
Fires a pulse when a running Timeline sequence passes a named event item, or reaches its end (end). New in 1.39; find it in the palette under Animation.

Output: event — 1 for a short window as the event passes, 0 otherwise.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Meaning sequence (empty) which sequence to listen to. Empty means any sequence event (empty) which event item to watch. Empty means any event; end pulses when a sequence that does not loop finishes pulse 0.3 s how long the output stays at 1

docs.title: Every player, by themselves
docs.text: Each player runs the same sequence from the same moment and passes the event item themselves, so the node fires on every device without a message. A preview in the Timeline editor fires no graph events — only a sequence playing in the game does.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
An intro, then the game:

  1. In the Timeline, build an intro sequence and turn its Autoplay on.
  2. Add On Sequence Event with event end → Set Game State playing.
  3. Enter Play: the intro runs, and the game starts the moment it ends.

Tip

Put an Event item named doors halfway through a cutscene and wire On Sequence Event doors → Play Animation: the doors open exactly on that beat.

docs.title: Orbit
docs.text:
Circles the connected object around its resting position on the horizontal plane.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning radius number overrides the card slider when wired speed number overrides the card slider when wired

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Range radius 1 0–5 speed 1 −5 to 5 (negative reverses direction)

The object's base position is the orbit's center — move the object and the whole orbit moves with it.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A planet and its moon:

  1. Place a sphere ("planet") and a smaller sphere ("moon") at the same spot.
  2. Add an Orbit node (radius 2, speed 1) and an Object Selector targeting the moon.
  3. Wire Orbit → Object Selector: the moon circles the planet.
  4. Add a second Orbit (radius 0.5, speed 4) on a third, tiny sphere placed at the moon's spot for a satellite.

Tip

Drive radius from a Loop in pingpong mode for a spiral-in / spiral-out effect.

docs.title: Orient to Velocity
docs.text:
