Turns the connected object to face the way it is moving, smoothly, leaning into turns — put it after Wander, Orbit or any mover so it looks where it goes.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector, or leave it in an object's own flow)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning turnSpeed, bank, maxBank, minSpeed number override the card sliders when wired

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Range / options turnSpeed 4 0.1 – 30 per second: how quickly it swings round to the new heading bank 0.5 0 – 1: how much it leans into turns maxBank 30 0 – 80° minSpeed 0.02 m/s below which it keeps its last heading (a hovering object does not spin) pitch on tilt up and down with the motion forward +z the model's nose axis

It reads the object's motion after every other effect on it has run (the runtime orders movers first, whatever order the graph lists them in), so it works with any mover — Wander, Orbit, Bounce, a script. Each peer smooths its own copy; they converge on the same heading.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: A drone that faces where it drifts: Wander (area = the room) + Orient to Velocity (turnSpeed 3, bank 0.8) on the drone's flow.

docs.title: Particles
docs.text:
Emits a particle effect from the connected object — the flow-graph version of the Particle Effects feature, so you can drive emission, colour and bursts from other nodes.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector, or drop it in an object's own graph to target that object)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning count number overrides the particle count speed number launch speed gravity number + rises, − falls size number particle size offset vector3 spawn point, relative to the object center (local axes) color color tints the whole system (overrides the gradient) trigger event fires a burst-mode emitter on each pulse

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Pick a preset on the card to seed everything, then adjust:

Parameter Default Notes preset Sparkles re-seeds every value emission continuous continuous or burst (triggered) count 80 particles speed preset launch speed gravity preset + rises, − falls size preset particle size sprite preset dot · streak · puff · star · confetti space local local rides the object, world trails behind

Full property reference (lifetime, turbulence, opacity, blending, colour gradient) is on the Particle Effects page.

docs.title: Practical examples
docs.text:
Confetti when a button is clicked

  1. Add a Particles node, set emission = burst, preset = Confetti.
  2. Add an On Click node and an Object Selector targeting the emitter's object.
  3. Wire On Click → the Particles node's trigger input, and the Particles node → the Object Selector.
  4. Click the object in the viewport — confetti bursts for everyone.

A dial that controls emission

Wire a Slider into count to let anyone in the session turn the effect up or down — the value is shared live.

Emit from a specific point

Wire a Vector3 into offset to move the spawn point — e.g. (0, 1, 0) puts it at the top of a unit object instead of the center. On Click through the node also works: wire On Click → Particles → Object Selector and clicking that object fires the burst.

Note

Particles are deterministic (each peer computes the same motion from the synced clock). A burst fired from a trigger rides the same replicated pulse as On Click / Key Press, so every peer sees it. This node is independent of an emitter set on the object from the Inspector — you can even run both.

docs.title: Path patrol
docs.text:
Walks the connected object along a series of waypoints you click into the scene, facing along the path.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Where waypoints none (needs 2+) Capture clicks button on the card, then click points in the viewport; Clear resets speed 1 slider on the card (0.1–5) mode loop loop (closes the circuit) or ping-pong (walks back and forth)

The object moves at constant speed along the whole polyline and turns to face its direction of travel. Waypoints are absolute world positions, so the patrol route stays put even if you drag the object.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A guard on rounds:

  1. Add a Path patrol node and an Object Selector targeting the guard object; wire them.
  2. Press Capture clicks on the card, then click 4–5 spots on the ground around your building. A Placing waypoints box counts your points and has Undo last point; press Done (or Esc) when you have them all.
  3. Set mode loop: the guard now walks the circuit endlessly — on every peer, at the same point of the route.

While you place points the object holds still on your screen, so you can still click it. Placing also ends when you deselect the object, click the object itself (that selects it), click the node editor, press Play or mute the node.

Tip

While a patrol is active the waypoints own the object's position — pause it by disconnecting the edge (right-click ▸ Disconnect), and the object returns to its resting spot.

docs.title: Player Variable
docs.text:
Reads a number kept per player — laps, touches, a personal score. Each player reads their own, or you can read one named player's, the team total, or the highest.

Output: number (shown live on the card)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options name laps the per-player variable to read, up to 40 characters read mine mine (this player's own number), sum (everyone's added up), max (the highest anyone holds), peer (one player's, named below) peer (empty) a player's peer id — used only when read is peer

A player who has not written the name yet counts as 0, and max reads 0 when nobody has it.

docs.title: Where the numbers come from
docs.text:
Each player's numbers are written by a Set Variable with scope player, and only that player can change them. Every player holds a copy of everybody's numbers, so sum, max and peer read the same everywhere, while mine is different on every screen. That is the point of it: it is the number a player's own HUD shows.

  • A player who joins later receives everyone's numbers as they connect.
  • A player's numbers survive leaving Play and travelling to another scene. When a player disconnects, the others drop their numbers, so the totals no longer include them.
  • Nothing resets them for a new round, and they are not saved with the scene.

This is a different store from Get Variable, which reads the one shared number of that name. A Leaderboard lists every player's number in a HUD list.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Count each player's own bell rings on their own HUD:

  1. Add an On Hit (who me) and an Object Selector picking the Bell; wire On Hit → Object Selector. The bell needs a dynamic body and the scene's Knock on — see On Hit.
  2. Add a Set Variable (name rings, op add, scope player); wire On Hit → its trigger, and a Number (value 1) → its value.
  3. Add a Player Variable (name rings, read mine) and wire it into a HUD Text's value.
  4. Each player's HUD counts only the rings they made. Switch the Player Variable to sum to show the team's total instead.

Known problem in 1.42

Step 2 cannot be wired by hand yet: the Set Variable card does not draw its trigger and value sockets (see Set Variable). The Player Variable half of the example works as shown.

The example's nodes.

docs.title: Play Animation
docs.text:
Plays a keyframed clip on an object — the bridge from an event into an authored animation. Wire an On Click to it and a door opens for everybody who sees it clicked.

Output: none (it acts on the object).

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning trigger event each pulse performs the action — wire On Click, Key Press, Timer or Animation Finished here

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options clip (first clip) which clip to drive — leave empty for the object's active one action toggle toggle, play, stop, restart speed 1 playback rate (0.1–4×); it changes the clip's data not at all

toggle is the one you want for a door: the first pulse plays it forward, the next plays it backwards to shut it again.

docs.title: Which object?
docs.text:
Inside an object flow the node targets that flow's own object, so a door's graph needs no wiring at all. In the scene graph, or to drive something else, connect an Object Selector.

It also drives clips a model was imported with, not only ones you keyed yourself.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A door anyone can open:

  1. Give the door a clip (a rot.y channel from 0 to 90°, with its origin on the hinge).
  2. In the door's object flow, add On Click → Play Animation, action toggle.
  3. Click the door. It swings open on every peer at the same moment; click again and it shuts.

Tip

Chain Animation Finished out of the same clip to fire a latch sound, start the next door, or count how many times it has been opened.

docs.title: Play Sequence
docs.text:
Plays, stops, toggles or restarts a Timeline sequence (camera shots, clips, audio, events) for every player when a pulse arrives. New in 1.39; find it in the palette under Animation.

Output: none (it acts on the sequence).

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning trigger event each pulse performs the action — wire On Click, On Enter, Key Press or On Sequence Event here

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options sequence (none) which sequence to play; Open in Timeline jumps to it action play play, stop, toggle, restart

docs.title: Every player, one moment
docs.text:
The pulse is shared, so every player starts the sequence from the same moment and runs it on their own device: the clips start together, each device plays the audio, and each player's own view cuts to the camera shots. Nothing else is sent.

A sequence with Autoplay on needs no node at all — it starts when a player enters Play, and when an exported game opens.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A cutscene when someone presses a button:

  1. In the Timeline, build a sequence named door with a camera shot on the door and the door's opening clip.
  2. Add On Click (on the button) → Play Sequence, sequence door, action play.
  3. Click the button in Play. Every player's view cuts to the door as it swings open, then comes back.

Tip

Chain an On Sequence Event with event end to do something once the cutscene is over.

docs.title: Point Grab
docs.text:
Decides whether players may pick objects up by pointing at them — the VR grip ray from a distance, or the desktop crosshair carry. While its enabled input reads off, only a hand that actually touches an object moves it.

Output: none — it is a declaration the scene makes while it is in the graph

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning enabled boolean unwired = on (pointing picks things up). False turns pointing off

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: The node is read every frame; if any Point Grab node reads off, pointing is off. With no Point Grab node in the scene pointing works as it always has. It is each player's own switch — wire it to a per-player Game Setting and each person chooses for themselves — and the editor is never affected.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: A zero-gravity room where things should only move when you touch them: a Game Setting toggle Point to move stars (default off) → Point Grab's enabled. Players who prefer the grip ray can switch it back on in the game's Settings.

docs.title: Possess Object
docs.text:
Puts the player in control of an object when a pulse arrives: a vehicle, a turret, a ball. A second input hands it back.

Output: effect (optionally wire into an Object Selector to pick the object)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Handle Type Meaning trigger event take control of the target release event hand it back target object the object to drive, from an Object Selector speed, turnSpeed, eyeHeight number override the card sliders when wired

The object is found in this order: the target input, then an Object Selector the node's output is wired into, then the owner of the object flow the node sits in.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options camera chase chase, orbit, first, none speed 4 0.1 – 30 m/s driving forward or back turnSpeed 2.5 0.1 – 10: how fast it turns, in radians per second eyeHeight 1.7 0.2 – 3 m above the object: the eye for the first camera mouseLook off first camera only: the mouse turns the object and tilts the view camera What the view does chase sits behind and above the object, eases after it and looks at it orbit keeps orbiting around the object as it moves; drag and zoom as usual first looks out from the object, eyeHeight above it, facing where it faces none stays where it is

docs.title: Driving
docs.text:
While you hold an object, the keys drive it instead of you. The controls are tank-style: W / S (or ↑ / ↓) drive forward and back along the way it faces, and A / D (or ← / →) turn it. In VR the left stick does the same. Your own movement pauses until you let go.

You let go when the release input pulses, or when you press Esc. With mouseLook on, leaving the pointer lock also lets go. Entering VR lets go too. If trigger and release pulse in the same moment, the release wins. A new trigger while you already hold something lets go of it first.

Things worth knowing:

  • Holding an object selects it, so other players see the usual lock highlight and can't grab it. If another player already has it, a message says who.
  • If the object can't be found, a message says there is nothing to possess.
  • The object's movement is sent to the other players about ten times a second. A physics object follows your driving during a running simulation and becomes physical again when you let go.
  • An animation on the object pauses during the ride and carries on from where you left it.
  • Letting go records the whole ride as one undo step.
  • mouseLook needs a click in the page first. Without one, a message says so and you steer with A / D instead.

The trigger is shared like every pulse, so in a multiplayer session each player's copy of the graph reacts to it, and the player who locks the object first ends up holding it. Possess Object is simplest in single-player games, or with a trigger only one player can reach.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Drive a box with F and let go with G:

  1. Create a box and name it Cart.
  2. Add an Object Selector that picks Cart, and a Possess Object. Wire the selector into Possess Object's target.
  3. Add a Key Press on F and wire it into trigger. Add a Key Press on G and wire it into release.
  4. Press F: the view moves behind the cart and WASD drive it. Press G to hand it back.

Two Key Press nodes wired into the trigger and release inputs of a Possess Object.

Tip

To have the camera follow something that moves by itself, such as a physics car, an animation or another player, use Camera Follow instead. It moves the view without taking the controls.

docs.title: Proximity
docs.text:
True while two things are within a radius of each other — a distance sensor with the threshold built in.

Output: boolean (card shows near / far live)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning a object first point — an Object Selector or a Vector3 world point b object second point — same options

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Where radius 3 number field on the card

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
An automatic porch light:

  1. Add two Object Selectors — one picking your "visitor" cube, one picking the doormat object — and wire them into Proximity's a and b.
  2. Set radius to 2.
  3. Wire Proximity → a Visibility node's on input, and Visibility → an Object Selector targeting the glowing lamp object.
  4. Drag the cube toward the doormat: the lamp appears at 2 units and vanishes when the cube leaves.

Tip

Combine two Proximity nodes with a Gate for and/or conditions, or invert one with Gate not.

docs.title: Pulse
docs.text:
Throbs the connected object's scale in and out around its resting size.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning amount number overrides the card slider when wired speed number overrides the card slider when wired

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Range amount 0.2 0–1 — how far the scale swings (±20% at 0.2) speed 2 0–10

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A heartbeat that responds to distance:

  1. Add a Distance node between two Object Selectors (your avatar-marker and a heart object).
  2. Add a Map Range: in 0…10 → out 3…0.5, clamp on (closer = faster).
  3. Wire Distance → Map Range → a Pulse node's speed input.
  4. Wire Pulse → an Object Selector targeting the heart: it beats faster as the marker approaches.

Tip

Pulse multiplies the object's base scale, so resizing the object with the gizmo keeps the throb proportional.

docs.title: Random
docs.text:
A random number in a range — deterministic, so every peer sees the same "random" value.

Output: number

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: seed (number) · reroll (event)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Where min / max 0 / 1 fields on the card interval 0 field on the card — seconds between re-rolls; 0 = one fixed value integer off round down to a whole number, so the output can be used as an index

Each Random node is seeded by its own identity and the shared clock: with interval set, it re-rolls every interval on all peers simultaneously; with interval 0 it holds one stable value.

docs.title: Seeding it yourself
docs.text:
Wire a number into seed and the value becomes a pure function of that number — same seed, same result, on every peer and every reload. That is what makes procedural generation authorable in a graph: one Slider or Number node is the seed for a whole layout, and typing 7 instead of 6 gives everybody the same different world.

Pulse reroll (from a Key Press or On Click) to advance to the next value in the sequence without waiting for an interval.

docs.title: Seeded example
docs.text:
A "new layout" button that everyone agrees on:

  1. Number (value 1) → Random seed, with min 0, max 4 and integer on.
  2. Key Press (KeyN) → Random reroll.
  3. Wire Random into a Select that picks one of several positions, then into an Object Selector.
  4. Press N: every peer jumps to the same next arrangement.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Give a hovering drone an erratic wobble:

  1. Add a Random with min 0.5, max 3, interval 2.
  2. Add a Shake node and an Object Selector targeting the drone.
  3. Wire Random → Shake's speed input, and Shake → Object Selector.
  4. Every 2 seconds the shake speed jumps to a new value — identical on every screen.

Tip

Add several Random nodes for several independent streams — each node rolls its own sequence.

docs.title: Rotate / Motor
docs.text:
Turns the connected object about its own local axis — and about its origin, so a wheel turns on its hub — at a set rpm. Paddles and scoops it turns carry water from Fluid emitters. On a dynamic physics body during a simulation it becomes a real motor: torque-limited, so a load slows it.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Handle Type Meaning on boolean true turns it, false stops it — off rests the object at its placed pose rpm, torque, spinUp number override the card sliders when wired

Unwired, on is true; you can also switch it in the ⓘ Params tab.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options axis x x, y, z — the object's own axis, so a tilted wheel still turns about its axle rpm 10 −120 to 120 turns per minute; negative turns the other way torque 50 0 to 2000 N·m — how strong the motor is (motor mode only) spinUp 1 0 to 10 seconds of ramp from standstill to full speed (see below)

docs.title: Two ways of turning
docs.text:
Turning (the usual case). When the object is not a dynamic body in a running simulation, its angle comes straight from the shared clock and the rpm. Every player sees the same angle without anything being sent, and a late joiner sees it at the right angle at once. During a simulation the turning object still pushes the dynamic bodies it touches, and its paddles carry particle water.

Motor. When the object is a dynamic body and a simulation is running (P, see Physics), physics owns its pose, so the node pushes instead: every frame it applies a twist about the axle toward the target rpm, never more than torque allows. A heavy wheel, or water piling into its scoops, slows it down; raise torque to make it stronger. The push is applied by the player running the simulation. With on false the motor stops pushing and the wheel turns freely.

Unlike Spin, Rotate / Motor keeps turning about the object's own axle when the object is tilted, and has the motor mode. To power the hinge joints on a body, use Motor.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A turntable you can switch off:

  1. Add a cylinder for the turntable.
  2. Add a Rotate / Motor (axis y, rpm 30) and an Object Selector picking the cylinder; wire Rotate / Motor → Object Selector. It starts turning.
  3. Add a Toggle (on) and wire it → Rotate / Motor's on. Untick the Toggle: the turntable goes back to its placed pose; tick it and it turns again, for every player.

A Toggle wired into a Rotate / Motor's on input.

Spin-up

The spin-up ramp is measured on the shared clock, which every player shares from its daily start, not from the moment the node is switched on. In practice the object is already at full speed when you look, and switching on back to true jumps to the clock's angle instead of ramping up.

docs.title: Script
docs.text:
Write a small piece of code — the escape hatch when no built-in node fits. A Script node works two ways:

  • As an effect (the default): code that runs every frame on the connected object.
  • With typed sockets (since 1.20): a small function with named, typed inputs and outputs — a value other nodes can read, like a Math or Compare node you wrote yourself.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector), or the outputs you declare.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Handle Type Meaning a, b, c number optional wired values, readable in code as data.a, data.b, data.c

A node with typed sockets has the inputs you declare instead.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Where code Edit code on the card (or a double-click) opens it in the code workspace inputs / outputs Typed sockets… above the code in the workspace input values the ⓘ Params tab of the node editor's side panel: the value each typed input uses while nothing is wired into it

Your code receives:

  • object — the connected THREE object,
  • base — its logical resting transform {pos, rot, scale, visible} (restored before every frame — apply offsets from it),
  • data — this node's data, including wired a/b/c,
  • time — synced seconds.

Errors show on the card.

docs.title: Edit code opens the code workspace
docs.text:
Since 1.23 Edit code — or a double-click on the node — opens the script as a tab in the code workspace, the same place behaviours, script files and module code open. Type, then press Ctrl+S (or Save): code that does not parse is not applied, the banner names the line, and the node keeps running its last good version. Tick Live on the tab to apply your edits as you type instead, the way the old Script panel did.

From the same tab, Save as file keeps the code as a .js file in your Explorer that several nodes can run, and Use file… runs one you already have. A Script node that a module ships bound to its own file opens read-only, with Make editable copy — see Main graph & node properties.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
1. Add a Script node and an Object Selector targeting your cube; wire Script → Object Selector.
  2. Click Edit code and enter: 
    object.position.y = base.pos[1] + Math.sin(time * 2) * 0.5;
  3. The cube bobs — identically on every peer, because the code is a pure function of base and time.

Warning

Keep scripts deterministic: no Math.random(), no accumulating (rotation.y += …). Compute everything from base, data and time, or peers will drift apart.

docs.title: Runaway and slow scripts
docs.text:
A script cannot freeze the app:

  • A loop that never ends is stopped after a million iterations in one run, and the card shows a Script loop limit error.
  • A script that is slow every frame — more than about 8 ms, for half a second in a row — is paused, with a paused: too slow badge on the card, so the rest of the scene keeps its frame rate. Editing its code starts it again.

If a scene's scripts hang so badly that the editor never gets a frame, open it in safe mode.

docs.title: Where your code runs
docs.text:
Since 1.43.1. Scripts run in a sandbox — a separate JavaScript engine, not the app page — so a scene you open from someone else cannot read your keys or your sign-in, or send anything off your device (Security). What that means for your code:

  • object is a view of the object: uuid, name, position, rotation, scale, quaternion, visible, userData and the material's values (color, opacity, emissive …), with the usual helpers (set, copy, add, multiplyScalar, setHSL, lerp …). What you change on it is applied to the real object after the call. It has no parent, children or geometry — reach other objects through inputs or api.object().
  • There is no document, window, network, storage or timers, and one call may run for at most a quarter of a second.
  • Changing transforms is cheap; touching material every frame costs more, so set colours when they change.
  • A scene with scripts loads the engine while it opens, so scripts start as the scene appears.

docs.title: Typed sockets
docs.text:
Press Typed sockets… above the code in the code workspace to declare your own sockets. + input and + output add one; give each a name and a type.

Types Inputs number, boolean, vector3, color, object, event Outputs number, boolean, vector3, color, object, any
  • Read an input as inputs.<name>. Every input arrives in one shape for its type: a number, true/false, [x, y, z], a colour string; an object input is {uuid, name, position}. An unwired input reads as its type's zero (null for an object).
  • Fill the outputs by returning them: return { allow: …, gap: … }. A node with outputs is a value node — other nodes read its sockets, and the card shows each output's live value. It is a pure function of its inputs and time, so it gets no object to move.
  • A node with inputs but no outputs is still an effect: it drives its object as before, with inputs beside data.
  • An any output passes what you return through unchanged — text for a HUD Text's format socket, for example.
  • The helpers dist(a, b), lerp and clamp are there for you, and so is the api object.
  • An unwired input uses the value set for it in the ⓘ Params tab.
  • Renaming or removing a socket removes the wires that went into it. Back to a, b, c returns the node to the plain effect.
// inputs: hand (vector3), piece (object), reach (number) — outputs: allow (boolean), gap (number)
if (!inputs.piece) return { allow: false, gap: 0 };
const gap = dist(inputs.hand, inputs.piece.position);
return { allow: gap <= inputs.reach, gap };

Outputs carry values only — a script cannot fire an event.

docs.title: Sockets follow the code
docs.text: Start reading inputs.speed, or return { hit: … }, and when you save the code the node grows that socket (as a number; change its type in the socket list). Sockets are never removed for you, because a wire may hang on one — remove them yourself in the socket list. This works for scripts with typed sockets; a plain a/b/c script keeps its three inputs.

docs.title: The api object
docs.text:
A script with typed sockets also gets api:

Call Returns Where api.object(uuidOrName) {uuid, name, position} or null any script api.raycast(from, dir, max?) the first object hit, {uuid, name, point, distance}, or null (max defaults to 100 m) any script api.keys() the keys held on this device, e.g. ['KeyW', 'Space'] scripts without outputs (effects) api.spawn('/create sphere') true when the object is created scripts without outputs (effects)
  • api.keys() is local input: each player holds different keys, so it is only for things that one player drives (a paddle whose position then reaches everyone). A value script that calls it is refused.
  • api.spawn() takes a /create … command. Every player runs every effect script, so only the room's host creates the object, once, for everyone. It is limited to 4 a second and 50 per script (editing the code resets the count).
// inputs: from (vector3) — outputs: hit (boolean), gap (number)
const ray = api.raycast(inputs.from, [0, -1, 0], 20);
return { hit: !!ray, gap: ray ? ray.distance : 20 };

docs.title: The lint
docs.text:
A script with typed sockets runs on every peer and must give every peer the same answer, so code that cannot is refused with its line, before it runs:

Not allowed Instead Math.random, crypto randomness wire a Random node into an input Date.now, new Date(), performance.now read time (the synced clock) the page: document, window, navigator, globalThis, fetch, eval, new Function, import()… reach the scene through your inputs storage: localStorage, sessionStorage, indexedDB — this device's state is not the game's timers: setTimeout, setInterval, requestAnimationFrame, queueMicrotask compute from time a loop with no way out (while (true) with no break, return or throw) give it an exit

A plain a/b/c script is not held to the lint — it keeps running as it always did — but the code workspace shows the same findings as advice.

docs.title: Select
docs.text:
Picks one of up to four values by an index: a, b, c or d.

Output: the picked value (a number, or whatever is wired into the picked socket)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Handle Type Meaning index number rounded to the nearest whole number: 0 picks a, 1 b, 2 c, 3 d. Booleans work too: false = a, true = b a number first value b number second value c number third value (optional) d number fourth value (optional)

Unwired inputs use the card values.

The index is capped at the highest slot the node uses: with only a and b in use, anything above 1 still picks b, exactly as a two-way Select always did; wire or set c or d and they become reachable. Below 0 picks a.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default index, a, b 0, 0, 0 (fallback fields on the card)

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Sneak mode for a patrolling guard:

  1. Add a Toggle ("sneak") and wire it into a Select node's index.
  2. Wire two Number nodes into a (2 — normal) and b (0.5 — sneaky).
  3. Wire Select → a Path patrol node's speed input, and Path patrol → an Object Selector targeting the guard.
  4. Flip the toggle: the guard's walking speed switches instantly.

One of four speeds at random: a Random node (min 0, max 3, integer on) into index, and four Number nodes into a–d.

Tip

Pairs perfectly with Switcher (its index output drives Select) and Compare. Need more than four options? Chain Selects, or reach for a Script.

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
Fires its four outputs one after another from a single trigger — a step-by-step timeline: "light 1, then light 2 half a second later, then the door".

Outputs:

Handle Type Fires step1 event wait 1 seconds after the trigger step2 event wait 1 + wait 2 seconds after the trigger step3 event wait 1 + wait 2 + wait 3 seconds after the trigger step4 event wait 1 + wait 2 + wait 3 + wait 4 seconds after the trigger

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning trigger event starts the sequence

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options wait (step 1) 0 seconds before step 1 — 0 fires it at once wait (step 2) 0.5 seconds between step 1 and step 2 wait (step 3) 0.5 seconds between step 2 and step 3 wait (step 4) 0.5 seconds between step 3 and step 4 pulse 0.3 how long each step's pulse lasts, in seconds (in the ⓘ Params tab, not on the card)

Each row on the card reads wait N … stepK: drag the number to change it. A step's name lights up (●) while it pulses.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
• The waits add up. Each one is the gap since the step before it, not a time from the start — so with the defaults the steps fire at 0, 0.5, 1 and 1.5 seconds.
  • One trigger runs all four steps. It does not advance one step per pulse; leave a step unwired if you need fewer.
  • A new trigger starts over. Steps that had not fired yet from the previous trigger are dropped, and the sequence runs again from step 1.
  • Same moment for everyone. Every step's moment is worked out from the one shared trigger time on the shared clock, the way a Delay is, so every player sees each step at the same moment and nothing extra is sent. A player who joins mid-sequence sees the remaining steps fire; steps that already happened before they joined do not fire again.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Count one, two, three — and back to zero:

  1. Add a Key Press (capture G) and a Sequence; wire Key Press → Sequence's trigger.
  2. On the Sequence, set the waits to 0, 1, 1, 1.
  3. Add a Counter. Wire step1, step2 and step3 into the Counter's pulse, and step4 into its reset.
  4. Press Play and tap G: the Counter reads 1, 2, 3 a second apart, then 0.

A Key Press triggering a Sequence whose first three steps count up a Counter and whose fourth step resets it.

Tip

Steps are ordinary pulses, so each one can drive anything an event drives — a Latch set, a Spawn, a sound, another Sequence for more than four steps.

docs.title: Set Active Camera
docs.text:
Makes a camera object the active view for every player when a pulse arrives.

Output: effect (through an Object Selector, or its own camera input)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Input Type Meaning trigger event the pulse that switches the view camera object the camera object to make active (or the node's camera parameter)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Where camera (none) a camera object's uuid, picked on the card

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Wire an On Enter trigger volume at a doorway into Set Active Camera with the room's camera: walking through the door cuts to that room's view for every player.

docs.title: Set Color
docs.text:
Paints the connected object's material with a color, re-applied every frame.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning color color the color to apply — usually a Color Picker

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Where color #ff4000 swatch on the card (used when nothing is wired)

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A shared team-color control:

  1. Add a Color Picker, a Set Color and an Object Selector targeting your flag object.
  2. Wire Color Picker → Set Color's color, and Set Color → Object Selector.
  3. Anyone in the session can now open the picker and restyle the flag — everyone sees the change instantly.

Tip

You can skip the picker and use the swatch on the Set Color card itself; wiring a Color Picker just makes the color reusable across several Set Color chains.

docs.title: Set Game State
docs.text:
Switches the shared game state — menu, playing, paused or over — when a pulse arrives. Every player follows the same state: it is the one switch a Start, Pause or Game Over button writes to.

Output: none (an action)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Handle Type Meaning trigger event each pulse makes the switch once — a HUD Button, an On Click, a Delay, All Players

The trigger needs a pulse. A true/false value (a Compare) wired straight in does nothing; put an event node such as All Players between them.

Known problem in 1.42

The card does not draw its trigger socket yet, so this node cannot be wired by hand in the node editor. Until that is fixed, let the HUD editor build it: select a button and pick one of the game actions (see the tip at the end of this page) — the action adds a Set Game State already wired to the button.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options state playing menu, playing, paused, over outcome (empty) a short word stored with the state, up to 40 characters — won, lost — meant for over full reset off on: back to menu and the round clock to zero, whatever state says

docs.title: What each state does
docs.text:
• playing from menu or over starts a new round: the round number goes up by one and the round clock (Game Time) starts again from 0. From paused it resumes the same round, and the clock carries on where it stopped.
  • paused stops physics, animations and the round clock for everybody. Flow logic and the HUD keep running, so a pause menu still works.
  • over ends the round with the outcome text. The clock is not zeroed.
  • menu goes back to the menu. Only full reset also zeroes the round clock, so a Game Time readout on the menu shows 0 instead of the last round's time. A reset keeps the round count and the variables.

HUD screens set to show while a state (see HUD Editor) and Game Start nodes react to the state by themselves; On Game State pulses when it changes.

docs.title: In multiplayer
docs.text:
The pulse is shared, so every player's copy of the graph makes the same switch at the same moment, and the newest write wins. It does not matter who pressed the button. A player who joins later receives the current state, round, clock and outcome on arrival. A Set Game State node you add only acts on pulses that come after it was placed: an old click never starts a game.

The state is saved with the scene. Leaving Play on your own puts the game back on its menu; with other people in the session, the game resets once the last player has been out of Play for ten seconds.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A start button and a pause key:

  1. Add an On Click and an Object Selector picking a Start box; wire On Click → Object Selector.
  2. Add a Set Game State (state playing); wire On Click → its trigger.
  3. Add a Key Press (capture P) and a second Set Game State (state paused); wire Key Press → its trigger.
  4. Press Play and click the box: the round starts for everyone. P pauses it, and a click on the box resumes it.

The example's nodes.

Tip

The HUD editor builds these for you: select a button and pick Actions ▸ Start the game, Pause, Resume, End the game, Back to the menu or Reset the game.

docs.title: Set Look
docs.text:
Switches a camera's look — its post-processing — on or off when a pulse arrives, and by default also looks through that camera.

Output: effect

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Input Type Meaning trigger event when to apply it camera object the camera whose look to switch. Unwired = the scene's own look on boolean true turns the look on, false turns it off

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning on true the value used when on is not wired activate true look through it too — also make that camera the active view, because a camera's look only shows while you look through it

Each player applies it on their own screen when the (shared) trigger arrives, so every view ends up the same without a message of its own. It changes what you see, never the scene's saved look.

If you switch activate off and nobody is looking through that camera, nothing changes on screen — the app says so once, and suggests a Set Active Camera node.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: A dream sequence: a Game Start pulse into Set Look with the Dream cam wired into camera — every player cuts to that camera with its soft-focus look. A second Set Look with on false on the round's end turns it off again. See Switching looks from a node graph.

docs.title: Set Shader Uniform
docs.text:
Writes one number inside an object's shader graph, so a trigger, a timer or a counter can drive how the material looks — a panel that heats up when you stand near it, a glow that pulses when something is picked up, dissolve that runs on a countdown.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Meaning uniform (empty) the name of the value to write, as shown in the Shader editor value 0 the number to write (usually wired, not typed)

docs.title: Finding the uniform name
docs.text:
A shader graph's numbers, colours and vectors each compile to a named value. To find the name:

  1. open the Shader editor on the object,
  2. click the node whose parameter you want to drive (a Float node, say),
  3. read the uniforms list in the ⓘ info pane on the right — it shows names like u_rgh_value,
  4. paste that into this node's uniform field.

Only numbers can be driven this way. Colours and vectors are not yet supported, so to animate a colour, drive a number and turn it into a colour inside the graph — a Gradient or a Mix between two colours does this well, and is usually nicer to author anyway.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Writing a uniform does not recompile the shader, so this is cheap enough to run every frame.

Each peer writes the value locally, and no message is sent. It does not need one: the value arrives through the flow graph, which is already deterministic and replicated, so every peer computes the same number and writes the same result. This is the same approach Set Color takes.

If the object has no shader graph, or the name does not match anything in it, the node does nothing — it will not error or break the material.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A crystal that glows brighter as you approach:

  1. Give the crystal a shader graph: Float (0) → Surface emissive, and a Colour → Surface albedo.
  2. Select the Float node and copy its uniform name from the ⓘ pane.
  3. In the crystal's flow: Proximity (radius 4) → Map Range (0–1 in, 3–0 out) → Set Shader Uniform (paste the name) → Object Selector picking the crystal.
  4. Walk towards it. The glow rises as you close in, on every peer's screen at once.

Swap Proximity for a Timer or a Counter and the same wiring gives you a timed dissolve or a charge-up that steps each time something happens.

docs.title: Set Variable
docs.text:
Writes a named number when a pulse arrives — a score, lives, a difficulty. With scope shared it is one number the whole game shares, with no object needed to hold it; with scope player it is your own number, one per player.

Output: none (an action)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Handle Type Meaning trigger event each pulse writes once — an On Click, a HUD Button, an On Hit, On Game State value number the amount to set, add or subtract — wire a Number, a Counter, a Math result (unwired: 0)

The card has no field for the value: wire one in. The HUD editor's Actions ▸ Set a variable builds a Set Variable that adds 1 to score.

Known problem in 1.42

The card does not draw its trigger and value sockets yet, so this node cannot be wired by hand in the node editor. Until that is fixed, let the HUD editor build it: select a button and pick Actions ▸ Set a variable, which adds a Set Variable already wired to the button (it adds 1 to score).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options name score the variable's name, up to 40 characters op set set (replace), add, subtract scope shared shared (one number for the game), player (this player's own row)

docs.title: Shared or per player
docs.text:
shared player Read it with Get Variable Player Variable, Leaderboard Who writes it every player's copy of the graph, newest write wins only the player it belongs to A player who joins later gets it with the game state gets every player's row when they connect Kept with the scene when it is saved, and across Travel to scene while the player is connected, across Travel too; leaving Play keeps it, and when they disconnect the others drop it. Not saved with the scene

Neither kind is reset by a new round. A game that wants a fresh start writes it: a Set Variable with op set and nothing wired into value (0), driven by the Start button's pulse.

The trigger decides who acts, the scope decides whose number. A shared pulse (an ordinary On Click) runs the node on every player's copy of the graph. Into a player-scope Set Variable, that adds to everybody's own number ("everyone scores when the boss falls"). A pulse only one player sees — an On Hit with who me — adds to that player's number alone.

One event, one change (since 1.48.1)

A shared pulse runs the node on every player's copy, but a shared variable changes once for the whole session: one click adds 1 once, and a toggle (set to NOT the value) flips once. Before 1.48.1 every player applied the change itself, so add could count two or three times. A player-scope variable has only one writer, so it never doubled up.

A player can hold up to 64 per-player names. Variables are separate from Store Value, which keeps a number on one device across reloads and never shares it.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Add a point to the shared score with each click on a coin:

  1. Add an On Click and an Object Selector picking the Coin; wire On Click → Object Selector.
  2. Add a Set Variable (name score, op add, scope shared); wire On Click → its trigger.
  3. Add a Number (value 1); wire it → Set Variable's value.
  4. Read the score with a Get Variable named score, or show it on screen with the HUD editor's Actions ▸ Show a variable.

The example's nodes.

docs.title: Set Velocity
docs.text:
Sets a physics body's speed outright — to launch it at an exact velocity, to hold it at a constant one, or to stop it dead.

Inputs: trigger (event) · linear (vector3) · angular (vector3) · target (object) Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Impulse or Set Velocity?
docs.text:
Impulse adds — a shove on top of whatever the body was already doing, so a heavy crate moves less than a light one. Set Velocity replaces — the body is travelling at exactly what you asked for, whatever its mass and whatever it was doing before.

Use Impulse for anything that should feel physical (a kick, a jump, an explosion). Use Set Velocity when you want a number to be true: a conveyor at 2 m/s, a reset that stops everything, a projectile that always leaves at the same speed.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning mode once once sets the velocity on the rising edge of the trigger; continuous keeps re-applying it every frame the trigger stays high

Speeds come from the inputs — wire a Vector3 into linear (m/s) and/or angular (rad/s). With nothing wired it uses (0, 0, 0), which is a full stop.

continuous is a hold, not a force

While the trigger is high the velocity is re-applied each frame, so friction and collisions still act between frames but never win. The body will not accelerate past the number you set, and it stops decaying the moment you let go. It needs a running simulation like everything else here.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Stop everything (a reset key).

  1. Key Press (code = KeyX) → Set Velocity trigger, mode = once, nothing wired into linear.
  2. Set Velocity → Object Selector ▸ your crate.
  3. Press P, throw the crate around, then X — it drops where it is.

A conveyor.

  1. Toggle (on) → Set Velocity trigger, mode = continuous.
  2. Vector3 (2, 0, 0) → linear.
  3. Point it at a box resting on a belt. While the toggle is on the box travels at a steady 2 m/s; flip it off and friction takes over.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Impulse — add force instead of replacing velocity
  • Velocity — read a body's current speed
  • Measure — read its height, top or bottom

docs.title: Shake
docs.text:
Jitters the connected object around its resting position — rumble, nervousness, impact feedback.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning intensity number overrides the card slider when wired speed number overrides the card slider when wired

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Range intensity 0.2 0–1 speed 10 1–30

The jitter is layered sine waves, not randomness — deterministic, so every peer sees the exact same wobble.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
An engine that rumbles harder as it spools up:

  1. Add a Slider (Min 0 / Max 1) as the throttle.
  2. Add a Shake node and an Object Selector targeting the engine block.
  3. Wire Slider → Shake's intensity input, and Shake → Object Selector.
  4. Push the slider: the block trembles more violently — smoothly, and in sync for everyone.

Tip

Shake offsets from the base position each frame, so dragging the object moves its shake center along with it.

docs.title: Slider
docs.text:
An interactive slider that outputs a number — the quickest way to hand-tune any numeric input live.

Output: number

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Where value 20 slider on the card Min 0 ⓘ Params tab Max 40 ⓘ Params tab

The output is always clamped to the Min–Max range, so retune the range freely — stale values can't escape it.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
1. Add a Slider and set Min 0 / Max 5 in the ⓘ tab.
  2. Add a Spin node and an Object Selector targeting your cube.
  3. Wire Slider → Spin's speed input, and Spin → Object Selector.
  4. Drag the slider: the cube's spin speed follows in real time — on every peer's screen.

Tip

In older scenes a Slider wired directly into an Object Selector scales the target object (20 = neutral 1×). That legacy behavior still runs for saved graphs, but new graphs should drive a node parameter instead — it's clearer and works with any effect.

docs.title: Sound
docs.text:
Plays an audio file from the connected object — positional 3D sound that everyone hears.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning volume number overrides the card slider when wired

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Where file — dropdown of the audio files in your Explorer library volume 0.8 slider, 0–1 radius 5 m slider, 1–30 — how far the sound carries loop on checkbox ▶ Play / ■ Stop stopped button on the card

Picking a file pushes its bytes to your peers automatically (by content hash), so everyone builds the same audio chain — late joiners fetch it too.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A campfire with crackle:

  1. Drag an mp3/ogg/wav into the Explorer.
  2. Add a Sound node and an Object Selector targeting the campfire object; wire them.
  3. Pick the file on the card, set radius 8, loop on, press ▶ Play.
  4. Everyone hears the fire — from the fire's position, fading with distance as they move around.

Tip

Looping sounds run off the synced clock, so all peers hear the same phase. Wire volume from a Slider for a shared mixing knob.

docs.title: Caption
docs.text: The caption field (1.41) is the line players with captions on read while the sound plays — [rain on the roof], [engine starts]. It shows each time the sound starts. See Making your game accessible.

docs.title: Spawn
docs.text:
Makes copies of an object while the simulation runs — crates off a conveyor, targets, debris, ammo, waves of anything.

Inputs: trigger (event) · at (vector3 — an offset from the template) · place (vector3 — copies land exactly here; wins over at) · source (object — the template) Output: effect (or wire the template into source)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
On the rising edge of whatever is wired into trigger — Key Press, On Click, Timer, On Enter — the node copies its template object and drops the copy into the scene with a live physics body. The copy inherits the template's physics, material and geometry, so a dynamic template gives you something that falls.

Copies are transient. They live for the run and nothing else: they are never written into a saved scene, they leave nothing on the undo stack however many times you fire, and they all disappear when the simulation stops. That is the whole design — a run's debris is not scene content.

A copy answers to its template's events. Event nodes that target the template — an On Hit, an On Click, an On Enter through an Object Selector — fire for its copies too, so a star you spawn behaves like the stars you placed.

place takes a point in the world: wire an On Clap point into it and the copy appears where the hands met.

The peer running the simulation makes the copy and everybody else receives it through the ordinary object sync, so two peers never disagree about what exists. Nothing extra goes on the wire for this node.

It needs a running simulation

A copy made with physics stopped would be inert, which is exactly the problem this node exists to remove — so with nothing simulating it refuses and says so instead of quietly doing nothing. Press P (or the ▶ button) in the editor first. You cannot start a simulation from inside Play mode; if you want both, turn on simulate on play in the scene's physics settings.

Give the template a body

If the template has no physics, the copies just hang in the air where they appear. Select it, then Inspector ▸ Physics ▸ Mode = Dynamic. The node warns you once when it notices.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning copies per fire 1 how many appear per event (hard limit 20) max alive 32 how many this spawner keeps alive; when it is full, the oldest copy disappears as each new one arrives min seconds between 0 a floor between fires. A trigger edge is not a rate limit on its own — a held key re-fires several times a second spread 0.5 metres of random scatter, so a batch does not stack in one column

There is also a ceiling of 200 live copies across every spawner in the scene, whatever the individual numbers say. An unbounded spawner in a shared session is both a memory problem and a griefing vector, so the limits are enforced when the copies are made and not merely suggested on the card.

docs.title: Where the copies appear
docs.text: The at input (and the x/y/z on the card) is an offset from the template, not a world position — so a node with nothing wired drops copies just above an object you can already see. Wire a Vector3 into at to aim it, or a Math chain if you want the point to move.

docs.title: Choosing the template
docs.text:
The same three ways as every other action node:

  • Object Selector → source — "copy that object". The usual choice.
  • Nothing at all, if the Spawn node lives in an object's own flow (double-click the object in the node editor's Graphs tree) — it copies that object.
  • Keep the template somewhere visible in the scene. It stays editable, and a scene file that ships a spawner is self-documenting because you can see what it makes.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A crate dispenser on a key.

  1. /create box, then Inspector ▸ Physics ▸ Mode = Dynamic. This is the template — move it somewhere visible and off the floor.
  2. In the node editor add Scene ▸ Spawn.
  3. Add Triggers ▸ Key Press (code = KeyG) → Spawn trigger.
  4. Add an Object Selector naming the box → Spawn source.
  5. Press P to start physics, then G: a copy appears 3 m above the template and falls.

A burst. Set copies per fire to 5 — five at once, scattered by spread.

A capped fountain. Set max alive to 8 and hold G: the count climbs to 8 and stays there, the oldest copy vanishing as each new one lands. That is the recycling, and it is what makes a spawner safe to leave running.

A conveyor. Drive trigger from a Timer and set min seconds between to 2 for one crate every couple of seconds.

docs.title: Things worth knowing
docs.text:
• Nothing spawns until the next real press after you wire up a fresh Spawn node to a trigger that has already fired. That is deliberate: without it, a node arriving on a peer would adopt the last stamp it sees and spawn on connect.
  • Stopping the simulation removes every copy at once, and Ctrl+Z will not bring them back — there is nothing to undo, by design.
  • Saving mid-run saves the template only. Reload a scene you saved with forty crates in the air and you get the one box back.
  • A copy does not carry the template's animation clips, object flow or shader graph. Each of those replicates a whole document per object, and volume is a spawner's whole point.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Impulse — shove a copy the moment it appears
  • On Rest — fire when a spawned body has settled
  • Counter — count what you have made
  • Physics — bodies, ground, gravity and the simulation controls

docs.title: Spin
docs.text:
Rotates the connected object continuously around one axis.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning speed number overrides the card slider when wired

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Range axis y x / y / z (dropdown) speed 1 −5 to 5 (negative spins the other way)

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
The classic first graph:

  1. Add a Spin node and an Object Selector; pick your cube in the selector.
  2. Wire Spin → Object Selector — the cube starts turning, at the same phase on every peer.
  3. For a live speed control, add a Slider (Min −5 / Max 5 in the ⓘ tab) and wire it into Spin's speed input.

Tip

The rotation is computed from the synced clock, not accumulated — pausing to drag the object and letting go resumes cleanly, and late joiners see the identical angle.

docs.title: Stored Value
docs.text:
Reads what a Store Value node saved on this device — the read side of a best score. Each player sees their own number.

Output: number or text (shown live on the card)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Options key best the same key the Store Value writes output number number, or text for a saved string

Nothing saved yet reads as the fallback (0).

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Show "Best: 12 m" on a menu screen: Stored Value (key towers-best) → a HUD Text with the format Best: {v} m. The number updates the moment a Store Value writes it.

Modules can read and write the same kind of storage through api.storage — see Module SDK.

docs.title: Store Value
docs.text:
Saves a value on this device when a pulse arrives — a best score, the tallest tower, the level a player reached — so it survives a reload. It is never sent to other players and never written into the scene file.

Output: none (a sink)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning trigger event each pulse writes once — wire On Game State (over), a HUD Button or a Counter value number what to save — wire a Counter, a Get Variable, a Measure

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Options key best the name it is saved under — give each game its own (towers-best, not best) mode max set (overwrite), max (keep the highest), min (keep the lowest — a best time), add (a running total)

docs.title: How it is stored
docs.text:
Values live in the browser's local storage under tp:scene:<scene name>:<key>. A game loaded from the Games tab has no scene name yet, so it uses untitled — which is why every game should use a game-specific key, or two games' bests would share one slot.

Each player keeps their own copy. A trigger that fires for everyone (a shared Game State) saves on every device; a per-player trigger saves only for the player who earned it.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
"Best height" in Towers:

  1. On Game State (over) → Store Value's trigger.
  2. The round's tallest height (a Math max over the ring latches) → value.
  3. key towers-best, mode max.
  4. A Stored Value with the same key feeds the Round-over screen's HUD Text.

Tip

A round-scoped latch reads "not set" the instant the round ends, so a Round-over screen should read the STORED value, not the latch. Write a set 0 at round start and a max on every hit.

The HUD editor's Actions → Save best score builds this chain for a button in one step.

docs.title: Switcher
docs.text:
A radio-button list that outputs the index of the selected item — a hand-operated multi-way switch. Since 1.27 it is also a multi-way switch for values: each item has its own input, and the value output passes on whatever is wired into the selected item.

Outputs:

Output Type Meaning (plain) number the selected item's index: 0, 1, 2… value the Inputs carry type whatever is wired into the selected item's input

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Input Type Meaning index number chooses the item from the graph; a wired index overrides the radio buttons one per item the Inputs carry type the value passed on while that item is selected

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Where items cube, pyramid ⓘ Params tab — edit, add (＋ Add item) or remove entries Inputs carry number ⓘ Params tab — number, boolean, vector3, color or object selection first item radio buttons on the card

docs.title: Switching values
docs.text:
Pick an item with its radio button, or wire a number into index to choose from the graph. The value output then passes on the selected item's input — a speed, a colour, a target object.

  • The plain output is still the selected index, so graphs made before 1.27 keep working unchanged.
  • Removing an item in the ⓘ tab keeps the other wires on their items.
  • Changing Inputs carry removes the wires the new type cannot accept, and a toast says how many. Ctrl+Z brings them back.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Build a two-speed fan switch. Since 1.27 the shortest way is the value output: rename the items to slow and fast, wire a Number of 0.5 into the slow input and one of 4 into fast, and wire value → a Spin node's speed (Spin → an Object Selector targeting the fan, as below). The classic way, with the index and a Select node, still works:

  1. Add a Switcher and rename its items to slow, fast (ⓘ tab).
  2. Add a Select node; wire Switcher → Select's index input.
  3. Add two Number nodes (0.5 and 4) wired into Select's a and b.
  4. Wire Select → a Spin node's speed input, and Spin → an Object Selector targeting your fan object.
  5. Click the radio buttons: the fan flips between slow and fast for everyone.

Tip

The index output pairs naturally with Select (pick between two wired values) and Compare. Legacy note: in older scenes a Switcher with cube/pyramid items wired straight into an Object Selector swaps the target's geometry — kept working for saved graphs.

docs.title: Time
docs.text:
The synced clock as a value — the heartbeat behind almost every animation recipe.

Output: number (live readout on the card)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Where mode sin dropdown on the card: t (seconds), sin, saw, pingpong rate 1 slider on the card (0.1–5) — time multiplier

Modes: t = raw seconds (ever-growing), sin = smooth wave −1…1, saw = ramp 0…1 that snaps back, pingpong = 0…1…0 triangle. All peers read the same shared clock, so the phase matches everywhere.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Make a cube's spin "breathe":

  1. Add a Time node (mode sin).
  2. Add a Map Range node: in −1…1 → out 0.2…2.
  3. Wire Time → Map Range's a, Map Range → a Spin node's speed input, and Spin → an Object Selector targeting your cube.
  4. The spin speed now swells and eases in a smooth loop.

Tip

sin is centered on zero — pass it through Map Range whenever a parameter wants a positive range.

docs.title: Timer
docs.text:
A delay line: outputs its input as it was a set number of seconds ago.

Output: number

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Handle Type Meaning a number the signal to delay

Unwired, it simply outputs its own a value.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Meaning delay 1 seconds of delay

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A gate that reacts two seconds after you approach:

  1. Set up a Proximity node between your avatar-marker object and a doorway (two Object Selectors → Proximity).
  2. Add a Timer (delay 2); wire Proximity → Timer's a (booleans pass through as 0/1).
  3. Wire Timer → a Visibility node's on input, and Visibility → an Object Selector targeting a welcome sign.
  4. The sign appears two seconds after the objects come close — and disappears two seconds after they part.

Tip

Feed the same source into an effect directly and through a Timer into a second object's effect to build echo/wave choreography between objects.

docs.title: Toggle
docs.text:
A checkbox that outputs true or false — a hand-operated on/off switch.

Output: boolean

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Where on off (false) checkbox on the card

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A light switch for a lamp object:

  1. Add a Toggle, a Visibility node and an Object Selector targeting the lamp.
  2. Wire Toggle → Visibility's on input, and Visibility → Object Selector.
  3. Tick the checkbox: the lamp appears and disappears — for every peer at once.

Tip

Booleans convert to numbers automatically (false = 0, true = 1), so a Toggle can also feed numeric inputs — e.g. into a Select node's index to switch between two wired values.

docs.title: Transport
docs.text:
The shared music transport as a number - beat, bar, phase, bpm or playing - identical on every peer.

Output: number

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Where read beat what to read: beat, bar, phase (0..1 through the loop), bpm, playing (0/1) or loopBeats

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Transport (read phase) into a Spin node: an object turns exactly once per loop, in phase with the drum machine on every peer - the same shared transport the devices are scheduled on.

Note

Every peer evaluates its own copy of the graph from the same shared transport and the same replicated pulses, so nothing about the music is sent per frame. See Music Playground.

docs.title: Travel to scene
docs.text:
Loads another saved scene by name when a pulse arrives - a door to the next level, replicated to everyone.

Output: effect

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Input Type Meaning trigger event the pulse that loads the scene

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Where level (none) the saved scene, picked on the card by name

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: An On Enter volume at the exit door into Travel to scene with the next level: everyone in the room travels together, and a late joiner lands in the new scene.

docs.title: Vector3
docs.text:
An x/y/z triple — used as a direction, an offset, or most often a fixed point in the world.

Output: vector3

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Where x, y, z 0, 0, 0 number fields on the card

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Make a signpost that always faces a spot:

  1. Add a Vector3 and set it to 0, 1, 5.
  2. Add a Look At node and an Object Selector targeting your sign.
  3. Wire Vector3 → Look At's target input, and Look At → Object Selector.
  4. Drag the sign around: it keeps turning to face the point at (0, 1, 5).

Tip

A vector3 can stand in wherever an object is expected: wire one into Distance or Proximity to measure against a fixed world point instead of a second object.

docs.title: Velocity
docs.text:
Outputs how fast the connected object is moving right now, in metres per second.

Output: number

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Handle Type Meaning target object the object to measure — wire an Object Selector, or leave it unwired inside an object's flow to measure that object

Reads 0 when the object is at rest, and falls back to 0 if it stops receiving movement for about half a second.

docs.title: Local, not replicated
docs.text: Each peer works out its own number. On the peer running the simulation it is exact; on the others it is an approximation from the ~10 movement updates a second that arrive over the network. Close enough to drive a speedometer or a colour ramp, but don't use it for anything that must match exactly on every screen — for that, drive the value from something deterministic (a Time or Counter node) instead.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A speedometer that glows:

  1. Get something moving — throw a ball with the gizmo mid-simulation, or drive the car from the modules library.
  2. In its flow: Velocity → Map Range (in 0–12, out 0–1) → Set Color, so it shifts from blue to red as it speeds up.
  3. Press P: the faster it moves, the hotter it looks.

Tip

Feed Velocity into a Compare node (> 8) plus a Gate to trigger something only above a speed threshold — a sparks burst when you're actually going fast.

docs.title: Visibility
docs.text:
Shows or hides the connected object based on a boolean.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning on boolean true = visible, false = hidden (numbers and event pulses convert automatically)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Where on visible checkbox on the card (used when nothing is wired)

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
1. Add a Toggle, a Visibility node and an Object Selector targeting a wall.
  2. Wire Toggle → Visibility's on, and Visibility → Object Selector.
  3. Untick the toggle: the wall vanishes for every peer; tick it back and it returns.

Swap the Toggle for a Proximity, Compare or On Click source and the same chain becomes a sensor-driven door, an unlockable, or a click-flash.

Tip

Visibility is base-managed: disconnect the node (or delete the chain) and the object returns to the visibility it had before.

docs.title: Wander
docs.text:
Drifts the connected object around a smooth, never-repeating target inside an area object (a water volume, a room) or a box around where it was placed — fish, birds, fireflies, idle drones.

Output: effect (wire into an Object Selector, or leave it in an object's own flow)

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Handle Type Meaning area object stay inside this object's bounds (shrunk by margin). Unwired: a box of rx × ry × rz half-extents around the object's resting position speed, seed, margin, rx, ry, rz number override the card sliders when wired

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Range speed 0.3 0 – 3: how fast the target moves (1 ≈ one wide swing every 6 s) seed 0 0 – 999: 0 = take it from the object, so copies never move in step margin 0.2 0 – 2 m kept clear of the area's sides rx, ry, rz 1, 0.3, 1 half-extents of the box when no area is wired

The target is three octaves of smooth noise per axis at incommensurate rates — it never repeats, never jumps, and always stays inside the box. It is a pure function of the shared clock, so every peer sees the same wanderer in the same place.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Clownfish that potter about the tank:

  1. Give the fish a Wander node and wire an Object Selector of the water volume into area; margin 0.4, speed 0.2.
  2. Add Orient to Velocity so it faces where it is going, and Body Wave so it swims.
  3. Duplicate the fish: with seed 0 each copy wanders its own way.
